nodes.description: The learning process of reinforcement learning requires a substantial amount of data resources.
Collecting a large amount of training data in the real world is costly and often poses risks.
Therefore, data-efficient reinforcement learning is crucial.
Utilizing pixel data to learn effective state representations has proven to be a potent strategy for achieving data-efficient reinforcement learning.
Inspired by the success of mask-based pretraining in the fields of natural language processing and computer vision, the authors explore mask-based modeling in RL.
Building upon this analysis and directly inspired by prior joint-embedding work, the authors introduce the Mask-based Predictive Representation (MPR) learning method.
In reinforcement learning, agents continuously update their own experiences through interaction with the environment, but pre-trained models cannot be updated along with the agent as it evolves.
Most pre-training methods learn compressed representations by reconstructing the pixel space.
MPR reconstructs the masked image sequence within the latent space using contextual cues from continuous frames, rather than the input space.
This strategic choice of reconstructing in latent rather than pixel space effectively reduces the computational complexity usually associated with pixel-level reconstruction.
The replay buffer disrupts the correlation between sequences to train a more robust policy.
MPR leverages the correlation between consecutive frames to enhance the informativeness, predictiveness, and consistency of the learned representations in both spatial and temporal dimensions.

This continuous frame prediction enhances the agent's awareness of the global context information in the entire input observations and encourages the state representations to be more predictive in spatial and temporal dimensions.
The encoding of global predictive information is encouraged into each frame-level state representation, achieving better representation learning and further promoting policy learning.
Instead of predicting the features of a state in pixel space, MPR learns to predict them in the embedding space, drawing inspiration from joint-embedding predictive architectures.
This approach of predicting in embedding space helps to reduce the interference of redundant information in high-dimensional state-action spaces.
The original observation sequence is divided into equal blocks, and the same mask is applied to each image in the same block to form the masked observation sequence.
Whether to generate another mask for the sequence can be determined by setting R, which provides different perspectives of information; when R=2, the length of the masked sequence doubles.
In DMControl experiments, R=1, while in Atari benchmarks, R=2.
Context sequence images have a 40x40 mask randomly added to the center of each 100x100 image, since crucial task information is often located at the image center in many RL benchmarks.
The aim is to encourage the context encoder f to predict the missing features to provide a better representation for the policy network effectively.
The high-level features of images obtained through the target encoder contain contextual information, serving as the learning targets.
These contextual-information targets can guide the model to acquire more effective representations and enhance the agent's understanding of the specific task.
The parameters of the target encoder are updated by an exponential moving average of the context encoder weights with momentum coefficient τ.

Considering the correlation between sequences in reinforcement learning, MPR uses not only single images but also rich contextual information within sequences to assist in predicting missing information in images.
A network consisting of two layers of attention mechanisms, referred to as the predictive decoder, is employed to generate prediction information.

Following mask-based modeling in computer vision, the decoder primarily predicts mask features to fill in missing information, rather than reconstructing images in pixel space, since pixel-space reconstruction is computationally expensive.
MPR directly predicts the target feature in the latent space to avoid redundant learning, similar to prior joint-embedding approaches.
Considering the MPR model has fewer network parameters and higher performance, it can be argued that the proposed masking strategy effectively improves upon the MLR model.
The masking strategy improving upon MLR results in MPR achieving higher sample efficiency.
In the DMControl-100k experiment, MPR achieved performance improvement in 5/6 tasks, with an average task score of 830.0, a 7.5% increase compared to MLR's 772.8, and a 4.1% median score improvement.
In the DMControl-500k experiment, MPR outperforms MLR in 5 of 6 tasks, with average task performance improved by 1.5%.
MPR and MLR perform similarly on DMControl-500k, but MPR requires less computational resources and achieves higher average scores.
In discrete control tasks (Atari), there is significant discontinuity between adjacent states.
The incorporation of multi-view information (via R) benefits MPR by facilitating smoother learning in the presence of state discontinuity, thereby enhancing its policy.
MPR outperforms other models in 11 out of 26 games in the Atari benchmark, with competitive scores in the remaining games.
MPR achieves scores exceeding human performance in 5 games: Boxing, Freeway, Jamesbond, Krull, and Road Runner.
Previous works on masked image modeling reveal that the mask ratio has a significant impact on model performance, consistent with which MPR investigates varying mask proportions from 10% to 90%.
The performance of MPR initially improves and then declines with the increasing mask ratio.
The performance of MPR is optimal when the mask ratio is 40%.
Mask strategy has a significant impact on representation learning, and in MPR the mask strategy is related to the block size.

A block size of 8 corresponds to the same mask being used at every time step (MPR_time), while a block size of 1 corresponds to a different mask at every time step (MPR_spatial); sizes 2 and 4 correspond to spatial-temporal masking.

Different tasks require different mask strategies: Finger-spin, Walker-walk, and Ball-in-cup-catch favor the time strategy (block size 8); Cheetah-run favors the spatial strategy (block size 1); Cartpole-swingup and Reacher-easy favor spatial-temporal strategies (block sizes 4 and 2 respectively).
Generally, a deeper predictive decoder depth implies lower sample efficiency and more wall clock time.
MPR achieves optimal performance when the predictive decoder depth is 2; increasing the depth beyond this reduces the effectiveness of the model's policy learning.
A smaller sequence length means that the model cannot use contextual information, resulting in a lower average score of 737.
As the sequence length increases, the model's performance improves, reaching an average score of 830 at length 8.

Further increasing the sequence length leads to a significant decline in model performance because longer sequences provide more contextual information, and MPR tends to over-rely on the predictive decoder to predict latent embeddings by learning from other states.

All models with mean squared error as the loss function have average task scores lower than 767 (the lowest score among cosine-similarity models), indicating precise latent reconstruction is unnecessary.
This indicates that in MPR or reinforcement learning with similar auxiliary prediction targets, it is unnecessary to precisely reconstruct embeddings in the latent space.
Several MPR variants with cosine similarity as the loss function are close to (MPR-a: 769) or surpass (MPR-r: 786) the average task score of MLR (772.8), demonstrating the effectiveness of MPR.
Adding action token to MPR or setting R=2 both lead to a decrease in MPR performance.
This may be because excessively long context sequences fail to provide effective information for the agent and instead reduce the efficiency of representation learning.
MPR's masking method is independent of patch size, allowing the predictor to decouple from patch size and masking method, unlike MLR.
Since the mask is independent of patch size, a variety of masks (e.g., SAM segmentation instance masks or BLIP language-image masks) can be adopted to enhance self-supervised learning effectiveness.
Adopting varied mask types could thereby improve the sample efficiency of RL agents.
MPR does not incorporate action sequence information in its implementation, as a difference from MLR.
This design choice is because action sequence information has been demonstrated not to enhance MPR performance in continuous control.
MPR employs only one projection predictor with no online projection head following the predictive decoder, as a difference from MLR.
In comparison to MLR, this reduction in the model's parameter count promotes policy learning, rendering MPR an enhanced version of MLR.

3D sensor data (RGB-D, point clouds, voxels) is noisy, sparse, and high-dimensional; voxels scale cubically with resolution, point clouds struggle with variable density and occlusion, and dense 3D features often exceed memory budgets for real-time control.
Self-supervised 2D object-centric methods excel at complex multi-object manipulation but cannot recover occluded regions or model precise 3D geometry essential for contact-rich tasks.

Prior 3D object-centric approaches (patch-based point-cloud methods, neural-rendering variants) typically operate on colorless or synthetic data, rely on rendering-side inverse problems, or fail to yield practical low-dimensional representations for policy learning.

The paper introduces 3D-DLP, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning model that decomposes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles, extending the Deep Latent Particles framework.
3D-DLP is presented as the first self-supervised object-centric scene representation operating on colored 3D voxels, with a unified framework covering RGB-D, occupancy-voxel, and RGB-voxel inputs.
Deep Latent Particles (DLP) is a particle-based self-supervised object-centric VAE model whose latent space is a set of particles representing scene entities.
Each DLP foreground particle factorizes into disentangled stochastic attributes: 2D keypoint position, scale, composition order, transparency, and appearance features.
DLP and related patch-, slot-, and particle-based self-supervised object-centric methods are restricted to 2D RGB inputs and do not account for 3D observations such as RGB-D or voxels.
3D-DLP extends the particle-based DLP framework to directly process RGB-D and voxel inputs with a compact, flexible representation.

RGB point clouds have variable cardinality and lack a canonical grid, making it difficult to batch examples, exploit translation-equivariant convolutions, and instantiate DLP's keypoint-proposal and cropping pipeline.
To address point cloud irregularity, the point cloud is voxelized into a regular grid storing aggregated color per voxel, providing a dense 3D tensor analogous to a 2D image.

Voxels provide a natural substrate for extending 2D DLP to 3D by replacing 2D with 3D convolutions, extracting particle-centered crops via a 3D spatial transformer, and decoding canonical cubic particle patches placed into the global grid.
2D DLP's spatial-softmax (SSM) based keypoint prior fails on sparse, discontinuous voxel grids, as verified in the ablation analysis.
The paper introduces an appearance-aware K-means prior that forms joint appearance-geometry features (CIELAB color plus normalized 3D position) per occupied voxel to propose keypoint locations.
Clustering in the joint appearance-geometry space uses weighted K-means with lightness weights, biasing toward visually informative surface regions.
The appearance-aware, lightness-weighted K-means clustering produces particle centers that align with object surfaces and color boundaries far more effectively than geometry-only clustering.
The improved alignment of K-means-derived particle centers with object surfaces and boundaries enables robust object discovery in colored 3D voxel scenes.
Using MSE reconstruction loss alone can match brightness with gray colors (zero chrominance), causing a gray-collapse failure mode illustrated in Figure 5.
Chroma loss separates color into luminance (channel mean) and chrominance (color residual), penalizing only chrominance error on occupied voxels.
Because chroma loss forces true hue/saturation fidelity by penalizing chrominance error, it prevents the gray-collapse failure mode that MSE alone exhibits.
Ablation results confirm chroma loss significantly improves color fidelity compared to using only MSE reconstruction loss.
3D-DLP-VC substantially outperforms non-object-centric AE and VAE baselines in Masked PSNR across GenericShapes, RGB-D-SD-v2, and MimicGen datasets, while remaining competitive on IoU.

The modest IoU gap relative to the deterministic AE is attributed to 3D-DLP's VAE-based sampling of noisy latents via the reparameterization trick, trading minor reconstruction crispness for a disentangled, semantically structured latent space.

As data diversity increases (more object types, locations, colors) across synthetic datasets, the particle-based inductive bias yields noticeably sharper, more faithful reconstructions compared to non-object-centric methods.
Perturbing particle 3D keypoints moves corresponding objects, while scaling attributes resize them, demonstrating the latent particles encode semantic, editable 3D object properties.
The demonstrated controllability of latent particle attributes validates 3D-DLP representations for downstream multi-object reasoning tasks.
3D-DLP-VC extracts particle tokens from voxelized point clouds that are fed into a diffusion-based policy (3D EC-Diffuser) for downstream robotic manipulation.
3D-DLP-VC + EC-Diffuser achieves the highest mean success rate (48.1%) on 12 MimicGen tasks, outperforming 2D-DLP single/multi-view and voxel-only EquiDiff baselines, winning 6 of 12 tasks.
Among matched-compute methods, 3D-DLP wins 9 of 10 RLBench tasks with large margins, and surpasses the non-matched-compute PerACT voxel policy on 7 of 10 tasks.

The consistent gains of 3D-DLP over matched 2D-particle and voxel-only baselines on both MimicGen and RLBench demonstrate that 3D object-centric representations improve downstream robotic manipulation performance.
On the Coffee Preparation task, the coffee cup is not cleanly isolated in the learned decomposition, capping downstream control performance and revealing a representation limitation.
Algorithmic tasks are a critical frontier for testing neural network performance, with algorithmic computation benchmarks increasingly used as models become more capable.
This benchmarking trend has contributed to a renewed interest in understanding how neural networks can learn and reliably compute algorithms.
While the computational capabilities of neural networks have been theoretically established, less is known about when training can reliably recover desired representations.

Many results provide only probabilistic learning guarantees, which are typically approximate and inadequate for computational tasks requiring iterative execution, where approximation errors can compound and invalidate computations.

This concern is echoed by György et al., who argue that reliable deductive reasoning in learning-based systems requires moving beyond high performance on sampled reasoning tasks and toward exact learning.

Back de Luca et al. move toward non-approximate learning guarantees for binary algorithms by encoding algorithmic instructions directly in the training set rather than using standard input-output examples.
Those results apply only to feedforward networks, which are poorly suited to variable-size inputs, limiting the scope of the guarantees.
This work extends these results to graph neural networks, using Neural Tangent Kernel theory in the infinite-width regime to derive exact learnability results for graph algorithms.
Unlike the feedforward results of Back de Luca et al., this work's architecture is better suited to graphs because every node shares the same local model.
Consequently, the number of instructions remains constant or grows only logarithmically with the maximum graph size imposed by finite-memory constraints.

In contrast, executing the same algorithms with a feedforward model would require encoding the entire graph in the input vector, leading to instruction counts that scale linearly or quadratically with the maximum node count.
The approach applies to graphs of arbitrary size, but any fixed feature dimension limits the largest graph that can be processed correctly.
In general, implementations impose a bound on the maximum node degree, and some algorithms additionally require a bound on the node count.

Under these conditions, exact learnability is established for Message Flooding, Breadth-First Search, Depth-First Search, Bellman-Ford, and more generally, any algorithm within the LOCAL model of distributed computation.
The closest work to this paper is Back de Luca et al., which establishes exact learning guarantees via Neural Tangent Kernel theory.
Both this work and Back de Luca et al. build on the NTK framework introduced by Jacot et al. and Lee et al.

This work adopts a similar proof strategy but extends the analysis to graph neural networks, whose architecture is more naturally aligned with graph algorithms than the feedforward networks of Back de Luca et al.
This alignment yields a more efficient training dataset and embedding dimension, as extensively discussed in the Results section.
The framework is initialized by training a set of shared local MLPs on the same data to exactly execute local instructions for every node.
The trained MLPs are then used within a message passing architecture, enabling processing of entire graphs using the same local rules.
This local training and global inference perspective is conceptually related to classical label propagation and its connections to graph neural networks, more commonly studied in node classification.

Beyond exact learnability, prior work provides probabilistic guarantees for approximating Turing-computable functions, but these are non-exact and rely on distributional assumptions over training and test data.
Such distributional assumptions are natural when learning from input-output samples, but because this work trains directly on instructions, it avoids input distributions altogether.

For graph algorithms, other works study specific GNN variants trained on handcrafted datasets, showing that achieving sufficiently low error on a sparsity-regularized objective forces the learned GNN to implement the target algorithm and extrapolate to arbitrarily large graphs under structural constraints.
However, these results do not guarantee that standard gradient-based training reaches this near-optimal regime.
Broader theoretical work studies neural-network computation by relating architectural expressive power to formal models of computation.
Closest to this work is Loukas, which establishes an expressive-power equivalence between GNNs and the LOCAL model of distributed computing.

That prior work only focuses on comparing expressive capabilities; in contrast, this work provides exact learnability results by showing that the proposed GNN architecture can learn any algorithmic execution in LOCAL, with explicit upper bounds on both message size and local memory.
The approach constructs a GNN from an ensemble of MLPs, each trained on the same non-graph binary data to perform local operations and differing only by random initialization.
The central idea is to use the ensemble's mean local prediction within a GNN structure to execute steps of graph algorithms exactly.

The GNN is formally defined as combining a node-local function's output through complementary projection matrices with an aggregation over the adjacency matrix, so local and neighborhood-aggregated components are combined.
The node-local function represents node-local behavior, computed by applying an input encoding, then the MLP ensemble, then the entry-wise Heaviside step function to binarize outputs.

The encoding function structures inputs into functional blocks and orthogonalizes values within each block before processing, which removes unwanted correlations and is crucial for correct algorithmic execution, applied efficiently blockwise.

The Heaviside step function is applied to the ensemble outputs before message passing to binarize them, preventing conflicting signs from being mixed during aggregation that could otherwise produce incorrect outputs.

Instead of relying on a single trained local model, the method averages across multiple independently trained MLPs, which from the NTK theory perspective better approximates the NTK predictor capturing the desired algorithmic behavior.

The complementary masks separate which parts of the representation are propagated versus kept local, reducing unwanted correlations during message passing while preserving locality; the shared parameter kM is application-dependent since required shared information differs across algorithms.

MLPs are trained on non-graph data for local operations and then integrated into a GNN architecture, so that this separation between local training and global inference via aggregation ensures the target graph-level algorithm can be realized by learning only simple local computations.

Rather than training on an algorithm's initial input and final output, the method trains at the level of individual instructions embedded in each sample, then applies this learned step iteratively over multiple rounds during inference to execute the full algorithm.

The main learnability result shows that the GNN architecture can learn to execute exactly any algorithm expressible in the LOCAL model, up to an arbitrarily chosen memory, on graphs with maximum degree D.

Theorem 5.1 states that for a LOCAL-model algorithm running for L rounds with finite bounds on state, message, and memory size, there exists a training dataset scaling linearly with state/message size and quadratically with maximum degree, such that the GNN learns to perfectly execute the algorithm in O(L) iterations, with arbitrarily high probability given sufficient ensemble size.

The proof utilizes a proxy computational model, the graph template matching framework, which executes algorithms on graph-structured data using a local function on binary vectors together with an aggregation mechanism for message passing.

The theorem is proved in two steps: showing any LOCAL-model algorithm with bounded memory on a bounded-degree graph can be expressed in the template matching framework, and showing the GNN can learn to execute that framework.

In the graph template matching framework, each node has a binary vector with two sections: a computation section storing local state and algorithm variables, and a message section used solely for communication.

A local function operates on the node vector and is defined by a set of templates, each corresponding to a distinct, non-overlapping block of input bits; the output is the bitwise OR of the labels of all matching templates.

Each node is assigned a local ID unique within its 2-hop neighborhood, dividing its message section into communication slots so a node writes its outgoing message only to its designated slot, preventing distortion during binary aggregation.

At each round, after applying the local function, the message sections of neighboring nodes are aggregated for message passing, similar to the aggregation-and-update mechanism of Message Passing Neural Networks.

Unlike the LOCAL model's computation step, which is assumed to compute any Turing-computable function in a single iteration, a single application of the local template-matching function cannot; nevertheless, iterative applications of it can compute any Turing-computable function.

To show the framework can simulate any LOCAL-model algorithm, a Turing machine (called a LOCAL Turing machine) is characterized that, given a node's previous state and received messages, computes the next state and outgoing message in finitely many steps.
A set of templates implementing this Turing machine is constructed whose number scales linearly with the sizes of the LOCAL state and messages, and quadratically with the maximum degree D.

By initializing the computation and message sections identically to the LOCAL model and applying induction, the template matching framework is shown to simulate the LOCAL model with a number of iterations proportional to the number of LOCAL rounds.

A training dataset containing each template-label pair of the local function as a sample, encoded via the input encoding, suffices to train an NTK predictor that, followed by a Heaviside function, exactly recovers the ground truth for any input at inference.

Assuming the MLP ensemble is trained on the same dataset, NTK theory together with a concentration bound for Gaussian random variables shows the ensemble mean, followed by Heaviside, matches the NTK predictor output with arbitrarily high probability determined by the ensemble size.

The message-preserving projection matrix implements the aggregation step of the template matching framework, while the computation-preserving matrix preserves the local component, so together the GNN yields the same node-wise output as one iteration of the template matching framework.
The conclusion of Theorem 5.1 shows the architecture can learn any LOCAL-model graph algorithm, but it does not give a direct way to construct training data for a given algorithm.

To address this, concrete learnability results are derived for Message Flooding, BFS, DFS, and Bellman-Ford, bypassing the need for their LOCAL model implementations and instead encoding local operations directly in the template-matching framework.
These algorithms are canonical primitives spanning traversal (BFS/DFS), local message propagation (Message Flooding), and shortest paths (Bellman-Ford).
Assuming bounded maximum degree, test-graph size is unrestricted unless the algorithm necessitates unique global node IDs.

Message Flooding does not use global IDs, so it applies to arbitrarily large graphs, whereas BFS, DFS, and Bellman-Ford use global IDs, limiting the test-graph size according to the bit precision used to store variables.
The number of GNN iterations needed to simulate these algorithms can exceed the step complexity of their classical centralized counterparts.

This gap arises because information propagates locally rather than via global access (requiring time proportional to graph diameter), and because the GNN executes bitwise micro-instructions rather than high-level primitives, so one algorithmic step may require multiple GNN iterations.

This granularity also makes it inappropriate to directly compare the number of GNN iterations with the number of LOCAL rounds, since LOCAL round complexity abstracts away all local computation performed between communication steps.

The main difference from Back de Luca et al. lies in the architectures: their model is a feedforward network operating on a single input vector, whereas this work's is a GNN with message-passing capabilities.
This architectural distinction has important implications for the graph size, instruction count, and ensemble complexity that the two frameworks can handle.

Whereas the feedforward model must encode the entire graph in the input vector (bounding graph size by vector length), this work's model captures structure via message passing, so the node-feature length scales only with bit precision and does not grow with node count when global IDs are unnecessary.

In the feedforward setting, instruction count scales at least linearly with maximum node count; in this work's setting, all nodes share the same local processor, so instruction count grows polynomially with maximum degree and only logarithmically with maximum node count when IDs are required.

Since ensemble complexity scales quadratically with embedding dimension in both frameworks, and this work's embedding dimension grows polynomially in maximum degree and only logarithmically in node count (versus at least linearly for the feedforward encoding), this framework yields asymptotically smaller ensembles for large, bounded-degree graphs.
The experiments empirically validate the results of Section 6 and include an ablation on the architecture.

Since the theory concerns infinite-width MLPs and may require prohibitively large ensembles, all experiments use Message Flooding, the only algorithm feasible with the available computational resources.
Nevertheless, the correctness of the instructions used in Theorems 6.1-6.4 is empirically verified, as discussed in a supplementary section.
Numerical and theoretical lower bounds on the ensemble size required to learn Message Flooding are computed to illustrate the ensemble-complexity scaling outlined in Section 6's theorems.

The numerical bound is obtained by computing an NTK predictor from the Theorem 6.1 proof dataset, extracting the output's Gaussian mean and covariance, then applying a Gaussian concentration bound with a union bound over all iterations.

The theoretical bound is obtained by analyzing the NTK output mathematically as the input dimension scales with bit precision and squared maximum degree, leveraging Back de Luca et al.'s theoretical NTK analysis.

Both the theoretical and numerical bounds grow as a quadratic function of bit precision and a quartic function of maximum degree, indicating that correct execution can require ensembles already in the thousands even for small parameter values.
The MLP ensemble is empirically trained to validate the NTK predictor approximation for algorithmic execution, showing that accuracy rises with ensemble size until full accuracy is reached.
Because of its simplicity and the fact that trees typically require smaller ensembles, Message Flooding on trees is used as a suitable testbed, feasible for larger bit precision and degree values.
Perfect accuracy convergence with ensemble growth is observed, with slower convergence for larger message bits or maximum degree, matching the expected increase in required ensemble size.

The empirical results are substantially more optimistic than the theoretical bounds, attributed mainly to the conservativeness of the union bound, which sums per-iteration failure probabilities and ignores dependencies across iterations.

An ablation study on Message Flooding tests whether the binary encoding and the Heaviside function are necessary for the theoretical framework's results, comparing applying Heaviside before versus after aggregation, using the NTK predictor to eliminate approximation noise.
The masking scheme is not ablated because removing it breaks the separation between local computation and communication, directly invalidating any execution.

Accuracy decreases with node count for all variants except the main model; because Message Flooding training samples are independent of tree size, the baseline GNN generalizes to arbitrary node counts.

Without the encoding, correlations with non-matching training samples can shift predictions from ground truth; if Heaviside is applied after aggregation, negative neighbor contributions can flip positive bits and corrupt messages, and without Heaviside these distortions accumulate across iterations and degrade performance further.

The results rely on assumptions of bounded-degree graphs, finite-precision identifiers, and infinite-width NTK-based analyses, which naturally lead to large ensemble requirements and restrict the class of graphs and algorithms that can be handled efficiently.

A promising direction for future work is to relax these assumptions by analyzing finite-width training dynamics, improving scalability, and extending the framework and learnability guarantees to other architectures such as transformers and attention-based graph models.
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, yet their large scale often renders them impractical for resource-constrained environments.
Architectural changes and the verbose 'think' responses preceding answers can significantly increase inference latency and computational memory requirements.
These challenges render many powerful VLMs impractical for resource-limited settings like smartphones and augmented reality (AR) devices.

There is a growing imperative within the research community to develop VLM designs that achieve a compelling balance between strong vision-language capabilities, low inference latency, and a lightweight model footprint.
RIL is introduced as an approach for developing high-performing, efficient VLMs that avoids architectural modifications and the need for lengthy 'think' responses.
RIL is an efficient training algorithm integrating principles from both GRPO and the GAIL framework.
The central objective of RIL is to enable smaller VLMs (e.g., 7B models) to effectively mimic the text generation style of significantly larger VLMs (e.g., 72B models).

Prior works have argued that natural language response-based distillation is more effective than high-dimensional feature distillation, emphasizing the importance of utilizing the language head—referred to as the verbalization effect.
Motivated by the verbalization effect, RIL began by leveraging the similarity in natural language responses between teacher and student models.
RIL employs an LLM-based discriminator trained to distinguish between the text responses generated by the student (small VLMs) and the teacher (large VLMs).
The discriminator's output provides a similarity reward signal, guiding the student VLMs, which act as a generator, to produce responses increasingly akin to those of the teacher.
To maintain training stability and prevent the generator or discriminator from overpowering the other (the balance problem), the discriminator's architecture initially mirrors that of the generator.
Relying on continuous discriminator scores (ranging from zero to one) to assess similarity to large VLM outputs can introduce ambiguity into the learning signal.
To ensure a clearer and more decisive reward, the discriminator's similarity score is converted into a binary value.
The discriminator, by design, focuses on stylistic similarity and does not inherently verify factual correctness against ground truth answers, which could otherwise lead to performance degradation.
RIL mitigates the discriminator's lack of factual verification by incorporating an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide a separate binary reward signal based on the accuracy of the generated response.

A challenge arises during the GRPO phase: if the student VLMs, due to their more limited knowledge, fail to generate any correct responses for a given task, they struggle to identify effective learning pathways.
To provide clearer guidance, RIL incorporates text responses from both student and teacher VLMs during the GRPO training step.

This strategy of incorporating both student and teacher responses during GRPO not only stabilizes RIL training but also creates opportunities for the student VLM to potentially surpass the performance of larger teachers.

Sourcing text responses from multiple large teacher VLMs significantly boosts student performance beyond what a single teacher can achieve, owing to the richer diversity of responses and the consequently more robust discriminator.

This enriched learning environment is further enhanced during the GRPO step: by incorporating text responses from both student and teacher VLMs, the student is provided with clearer exemplars for reaching correct answers.

RIL demonstrates particular synergy with distillation-based VLMs; these models show marked performance improvements because their inherent feature alignment through distillation complements RIL's objectives.

A crucial practical advantage of RIL is its inference efficiency: trained models do not require an explicit 'think' phase before generating answers, thereby maintaining the same inference speed as the original student VLM.

Table 2 shows that for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, using both Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL3-78B as teachers yields a MathVista score of 79.7, versus 74.5 with Qwen2.5-VL-72B alone and 74.6 with InternVL3-78B alone.
RIL's reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge for accuracy evaluation offers substantial advantages in applicability.

Unlike methods such as DeepSeek-R1 and its variants, which often use conventional answer parsing for reward computation, RIL is not limited to domains with predefined metrics (e.g., math or image grounding).
Conventional parsing struggles with open-ended general visual questions, such as 'How to cook this dish?' based on a food image, or 'Summarize this movie' from its poster.
Parsing poses a challenge to flexibly compare different types of answers, e.g., if a response is 'The answer is twenty percent' but its ground truth is '20'.

The versatile evaluation power of LLM-as-a-Judge enables RIL's successful application to a broad spectrum of visual question answering tasks, fostering strong performance in recognition, OCR, common-sense reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and chart/document understanding.

Generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL) is a foundational framework in imitation learning, employing a generator (e.g., small student VLMs) that attempts to replicate expert behavior (e.g., large teacher VLMs) by producing indistinguishable outputs, while a discriminator distinguishes generator from expert.

By framing imitation learning as a minimax game, GAIL leverages adversarial training to align the behavior of the generator with that of the expert without explicitly defining a reward function, relying only on discriminator scores.

Based on GAIL's effectiveness, RIL integrates reinforcement and imitation learning for VLMs with four key modifications: (1) combining GRPO and GAIL with explicit reward design, (2) binarizing the discriminator's output scores to stabilize training, (3) incorporating LLM-as-a-Judge to evaluate answer rewards, and (4) utilizing teacher-generated text responses during GRPO updates as direct guidance.
These four modifications not only stabilize RIL training but also provide a mechanism for student VLMs to potentially exceed the performance of teacher VLMs.

RIL does not require an explicit think-answer process, thereby maintaining the same inference speed, and it is independent of any particular image embedding methods or language tokenizers used in the student or teacher VLMs.

With the student (small) VLMs serving as the generator, the effective pre-training of the discriminator is crucial; without adequate pre-training, it would yield unreliable scores, undermining its utility and potentially degrading overall model performance.
To prepare for pre-training, N text responses are generated for each given question from both the student VLMs and the teacher VLMs, forming a dataset used to train the discriminator.
The discriminator Dφ is trained to maximize an objective that pushes it to output a score approaching one for student responses and zero for teacher responses.

To elicit the scalar discrimination score, the standard language head of the VLM is replaced with a linear discriminator head, computing the score via sigmoid on the final sequence token's representation.
The RIL process commences after an initial supervised finetuning (SFT) phase for the student VLMs, acting as a crucial warm-up that acclimates the student to the target data distribution.
For each question in a training batch, G responses are generated from the current student VLMs and G responses are retrieved from teacher VLMs, yielding a combined set of 2G responses.
Within each RIL iteration, the discriminator is first updated on the 2G responses, ensuring it maintains its ability to distinguish student from teacher outputs as the student VLMs evolve.
The student VLMs are then updated using an objective derived from Dr.GRPO, an advanced variant of GRPO that provides unbiased advantage estimates.

The total reward for each response is a composite signal comprising two binary components: a similarity reward (based on the discriminator score being below 0.5) and an answer reward (factual correctness via LLM-as-a-Judge).

The inclusion of the answer reward is essential, as the discriminator alone primarily captures stylistic similarity and does not guarantee factual accuracy, the absence of which could lead to significant performance issues.
RL agents trained solely with GRPO or its advanced variant Dr.GRPO, without the discriminator or associated similarity rewards, are evaluated as baselines to isolate RIL's component contributions.

As shown in Table 1, RIL, which integrates reinforcement and imitation learning elements based on Dr.GRPO and GAIL, demonstrably outperforms RL-only approaches, confirming the efficacy of the unified training algorithm.
Table 1 shows RIL (Dr.GRPO + GAIL) raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B's MathVista score from 67.8 (base) to 74.5, compared to 69.5 with RL (Dr.GRPO) alone.

RIL-trained student VLMs exhibit highly competitive performance against a range of recent open-source and closed-source models, substantially narrowing the performance gap to state-of-the-art VLMs and, in several instances, surpassing them.

Table 5(a) shows that a single update iteration (µ=1) for both discriminator and student VLMs is sufficient for strong performance, and balanced accuracy decreases monotonically as µ increases from 1 to 12.
More update iterations, especially for student VLM updates, can risk overfitting.
The impact of the KL-divergence penalty coefficient β on RIL performance is examined in Table 5(b).
Results confirm that while constraining policy updates is crucial for stability, an overly restrictive penalty (large β) can hinder performance.
Table 5(c) details the importance of updating different parameter groups within the student VLMs during RIL.
Training the self-attention layers, word embeddings, and the language head yields more significant gains than updating feed-forward networks (FFN) or layer normalization parameters.
Table 5(d) investigates the necessity of continuously updating the discriminator during RIL training.
A fixed (not updated) pre-trained discriminator can outperform RL-only baselines, but overall RIL efficacy still critically depends on leveraging a continuously trained discriminator during RIL.
For Qwen2.5-VL-7B on MathVista, no discriminator scores 69.5, a fixed pre-trained discriminator scores 75.3, and a continuously updated discriminator scores 79.7.

Table 5(e) shows that replacing LLM-as-a-Judge for answer rewards with conventional answer parsing significantly degrades performance, particularly on general visual questions where fixed parsing rules are inadequate.
This highlights the need for flexible, LLM-based evaluation of answer correctness.
Table 5(e) also affirms that while initial SFT is beneficial for capturing the training data distribution, RIL subsequently delivers substantially larger improvements.
RIL's effectiveness is examined on student VLMs already trained on distillation methods like MiniLLM, DistilLLM, LLaVA-KD, and VLsI.

RIL proves particularly potent for distillation-trained models compared to non-distillation counterparts, likely because prior feature alignment through distillation primes them for RIL's alignment mechanisms.
The binary similarity reward introduced in Sec. 3.3 enables more efficient and stable training of RIL.
As shown in Fig. 6, the binary reward consistently outperforms continuous and multi-level discretizations, suggesting that binary feedback provides clearer and more reliable learning signals.
This improvement arises because models often struggle to interpret subtle differences in continuous rewards (e.g., why a score of 0.21 should be preferred over 0.20).
RIL leverages the diversity of responses generated by large VLMs, which tend to produce more varied and higher-quality answers beyond the ground truth answers used in SFT training datasets.

As illustrated in Fig. 7, increasing the number of teacher-generated responses consistently improves the student model's performance, demonstrating that richer supervision from diverse teacher outputs enhances the student VLM's overall generalization ability.
RIL exploits diverse, high-quality teacher responses to guide smaller VLMs toward learning more flexible responses beyond fixed ground truth answers.

Unlike conventional distillation, which typically requires student VLMs to replicate the high-dimensional logit features of teacher models, RIL operates exclusively on generated text responses in natural language.

This fundamental difference liberates RIL from restrictive feature-level constraints, such as the need for identical image embedding strategies or perfectly aligned language tokenizers between student and teacher VLMs.

Common distillation methods often rely on KL divergence—a static, non-trainable metric devoid of contextual understanding—but RIL employs a trainable discriminator which assesses natural language responses directly, learning to discern nuanced similarities and stylistic differences.
The adaptability of the trainable discriminator in capturing contextual relationships makes RIL a particularly flexible and powerful approach for lightweight VLM enhancement.
While RIL demonstrates significant strengths, its current implementation has been focused primarily on the post-instruction tuning alignment phase.

A promising avenue for future research involves extending the utility of the discriminator to the initial visual instruction tuning stage itself, hypothesizing it could offer benefits for more efficient instruction following from the outset.

LoRA fine-tunes a pretrained LLM cost-effectively, but the fine-tuned model is often limited to the domain it is trained on, with performance not improving or sometimes worsening on other domains due to catastrophic forgetting.
In-context learning adapts models to new tasks by conditioning on examples from the task in the prompt, rather than updating model weights.
Prompt-based ICL approaches have limited expressivity, and their gains may diminish as the complexity of in-context information rises.
In-weights meta-learning trains models on a variety of tasks in a way that supports generalization across tasks, with MAML being a popular instantiation of this idea.

MAML-en-LLM adapts the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning framework to LLMs, but requires a large amount of computation and memory, using second-order gradient updates and saving a model for each task, making it hard to apply at scale.
Reptile is a meta-learning algorithm with constant scaling with respect to the number of tasks, but it does not retain the full expressivity of MAML.

The generalization limits of LoRA fine-tuning, the expressivity limits of ICL, and the computational cost of MAML-style meta-learning together motivate developing a meta-learning approach for LLMs that is practical at scale and can be combined with ICL.

Amortized Bayesian Meta-Learning improves on MAML-based frameworks by representing uncertainty with a Bayesian approach, treating global parameters as random variables and minimizing a negative evidence lower bound via variational inference.
ABML amortizes inference over the parameters so that memory no longer increases linearly with the number of tasks, unlike MAML which must cache task-specific parameter copies.

Extending ABML to LLMs introduces the challenge of specifying a generative model over LLM weight space, since LLM weights are far higher-dimensional than in the small-model settings ABML was originally designed for.

To define the generative model and efficiently characterize uncertainty at LLM scale, ABMLL uses LoRA adapters to express both local/global model weights and their variance, with mean and variance parameters computed as LoRA outputs.
ABMLL introduces four pairs of LoRA adapters (Bµθ Aµθ, Bσθ Aσθ, Bµϕ Aµϕ, Bσϕ Aσϕ) to compute the mean and variance of both global and task-specific (local) weight distributions.
ABMLL introduces a new prior over global variables, p(θ) = N(µθ;0,I)·Gamma(1/σθ²; a0,b0), that accounts for the spread of pretrained parameters.

Combining LoRA-parameterized mean/variance adapters with the new prior yields the ABMLL generative process θ~p(θ), ϕi~p(ϕi|θ), Di~LLM(ϕi), giving a concrete, scalable instantiation of amortized Bayesian meta-learning for LLM weights.
LLMs are often overparameterized, meaning the dimensionality of the weight-space probabilistic quantities is very large relative to the data space.
Because of this overparameterization, the KL terms KL(qθ(ϕi|Di)‖p(ϕi|θ)) and KL(q(θ)‖p(θ)) can overwhelm the reconstruction quantity log p(Di|ϕi) in the training objective.
Prior work such as β-VAE and Bayesian neural network approaches introduce hyperparameters to temper the likelihood versus regularization terms in similar objectives.

Inspired by this idea, ABMLL introduces hyperparameter β multiplying both KL terms, giving a modified objective that controls how close task-specific parameters are to global ones and how close global parameters are to the prior.

The value of β must be tuned per the ablation study: β=1 (no tempering) drops performance significantly, and extremely small β (log10β=-16) also degrades performance by making the objective degenerate.
ABMLL is evaluated by fine-tuning LLaMA3-8B and Qwen2-7B on the CrossFit and UnifiedQA datasets.

Experiments use three settings: cls-45 (train and evaluate on distinct classification tasks), cls-23 (train on a mix of task types, evaluate on the same classification tasks), and narrower transfer to NLI, paraphrasing, and MCQA.
Five baselines are compared: the off-the-shelf pretrained model, regular LoRA trained on shuffled data, structured LoRA trained task-by-task without a global variable, and Reptile.

Because Structured LoRA matches ABMLL's task-by-task training structure but drops the global variable, comparing it against ABMLL isolates the effect of the proposed generative model itself, separate from just the training data ordering.
ABMLL and Reptile achieve evidently higher accuracy than the pretrained, regular LoRA, and structured LoRA baselines on cls-45 accuracy and ECE curves.
Among the meta-learning methods, ABMLL performs best on both accuracy and ECE on cls-45 and cls-23, with performance slightly but consistently better than Reptile.
On tasks with more distinct train-evaluation differences (NLI, Para, MCQA), ABMLL's performance is tied with Reptile, possibly because the tested ability is harder to acquire through training tasks.
Despite introducing four pairs of LoRA adapters, ABMLL increases peak memory by only 7.6% over regular LoRA on cls-45, since pretrained weights must be computed in both cases regardless.

Together, ABMLL's consistent accuracy/ECE advantage over non-meta-learning baselines and its small memory overhead over regular LoRA demonstrate that meta-learning can work effectively and scalably at the scale of LLaMA3-8B and Qwen2-7B.

Meta-learning is a complementary approach to ICL, and scaling meta-learning to LLMs makes it possible to combine the two techniques, motivating a comparison of MetaICL, Reptile-MetaICL, and ABMLL-MetaICL.
ABMLL-MetaICL outperforms regular LoRA by over 10% in accuracy on several datasets and significantly outperforms regular MetaICL, showing the strongest synergy with ICL among the compared methods.
The two meta-learning methods (Reptile-MetaICL, ABMLL-MetaICL) also generalize better than MetaICL to LegalBench and ChemBench, domains distant from the CrossFit/UnifiedQA training data.

The combined evidence that ABMLL-MetaICL beats both non-meta-learned LoRA and plain MetaICL, including on out-of-domain legal/chemistry tasks, supports that in-weights meta-learning provides gains complementary to, not merely redundant with, in-context learning.
Model pruning removes redundant parameters (a percentage of neurons per layer embedding, sorted by magnitude) to test efficiency and probe robustness to loss of spurious correlations.
Bayesian neural networks are known to be resource-efficient, motivating the hypothesis that ABMLL's Bayesian formulation should confer added robustness under pruning.

Across NLI and Para pruning experiments, ABMLL is significantly more robust against pruning than pretrained, regular LoRA, structured LoRA, and Reptile, maintaining much higher accuracy at 20-30% pruning.

Because ABMLL's performance is much more robust to pruning than the alternatives, this suggests ABMLL learns generalizable features that are not as tightly tied to specific parameters, consistent with a Bayesian approach to scalable, robust adaptation.

Convergence properties of non-smooth first-order methods are typically analyzed assuming global Lipschitz continuity (uniformly bounded gradients), which is mathematically convenient but imposes significant limitations.
Global Lipschitz continuity may fail even for the training loss of simple two-layer ReLU networks.

Theory based on bounded gradients provides limited insight into the empirical success of Adam-type methods, since under bounded gradients SGD already attains optimal convergence rates, leaving no theoretical gap for Adam to fill.
Despite extensive efforts to develop better optimizers, Adam and AdamW remain widely used and highly competitive, often outperforming AdaGrad, SGD, and Signum.

The combination of bounded-gradient theory offering no advantage to Adam-type methods and their proven empirical superiority motivates searching for a relaxation of the bounded-gradient assumption together with a suitable convergence theory.

The paper introduces the class of (M0,M1)-Lipschitz, or generalized Lipschitz, functions, where gradient norms are bounded by an affine function of the optimality gap, as the relaxation motivated above.
The (L0,L1)-smoothness / generalized smoothness condition, bounding the Hessian norm by an affine function of the gradient norm, was introduced to relax standard global Lipschitz-gradient smoothness.

Reducing the order of derivatives by one in the generalized smoothness condition (Hessian bounded by affine function of gradient), and recalling the zeroth derivative is the function itself, leads precisely to the generalized Lipschitz condition (gradient bounded by affine function of optimality gap).
A known lemma shows that generalized (L0,L1)-smoothness implies the gradient norm is bounded by an order term combining L0 times the optimality gap and L1 times the optimality gap.

Since standard L0-smoothness and M0-Lipschitzness imply analogous bounds on the gradient norm, replacing the L0-part of the smoothness-implied bound with its M0-analogue leads to the proposed generalized Lipschitz condition.
This same parallel between generalized smoothness and generalized Lipschitzness motivates the generalized Hölder smoothness condition studied later, which interpolates between the two.

Lemma 1 shows Assumption 1 (generalized Lipschitzness) holds iff an equivalent inequality bounding function value differences by an exponential factor in the distance between points, scaled by the optimality gap, holds for all pairs of points.
In the special case M1=0, Lemma 1's inequality matches the standard definition of Lipschitz functions, bounding function value differences by a multiple of the distance.
In the general case M1>0, Lemma 1's bound includes an additional exponential factor that cannot be removed in general, as illustrated by basic examples.

Lemma 1 implies that restricting the generalized Lipschitz function to the ball QR of radius R yields a globally M-Lipschitz function on QR, with M and F (the max optimality gap) as defined via M0, M1, and R.
The constants M and F resulting from the ball restriction may scale exponentially in R*M1, per Lemma 1 and the preceding discussion.
Because M and F can scale exponentially, convergence rates obtained by naively reducing to standard Lipschitz continuity on QR can be overly pessimistic, especially when R*M1 is large.
In contrast to the naive ball-restriction approach, the paper shows that Assumption 1 can be utilized more directly to obtain fast convergence rates without exponential factors.

Constant-stepsize projected GD under Assumption 1 achieves iteration complexity containing an exponential factor exp(O[RM1]), an improvement over the naive ball-restriction reduction but still exponential.

The GD complexity bound has an informal two-phase interpretation: an initial sublinear-rate regime that can be exponentially long, followed by a slower rate matching standard GD for M0-Lipschitz functions.

Normalized GD and GD with Polyak stepsizes (Theorem 2) require only a fixed number of initial iterations of order [RM1]^2 before reaching the optimal rate, so their overall complexity contains no exponential factors, significantly improving on plain GD.

Under the stochastic generalized Lipschitz Assumption 2, both SGD (Theorem 3) and AdaGrad-Norm (Theorem 4) achieve the same iteration complexity, which contains exponential factors, analogous to the deterministic GD case.

Gradient normalization and Polyak stepsizes, which removed the exponential factor in the deterministic setting, generally break the unbiasedness property crucial to stochastic convergence analysis, so this fix does not directly extend to the stochastic setting.
Normalized SGD can diverge even on simple one-dimensional convex problems, as shown by a known counterexample, confirming the fix's inapplicability.

Because normalization/Polyak-stepsize fixes do not transfer to the stochastic setting, the paper is motivated to find an alternative construction (leading to clipped AdamW) that still significantly improves upon SGD and AdaGrad-Norm rates.

The algorithm construction reduces to an online linear optimization problem with a regret bound, where the iterates z_k are generated by an online learning algorithm and combined via a weighted update rule parameterized by alpha_k and pi_k.

Lemma 2 shows that the expected suboptimality of the resulting iterate x_K is controlled by the initial gap plus the expected regret of the online optimization subroutine, for general choices of the alpha_k/pi_k parameters.

Choosing the default schedule 1/alpha_k = pi_k = k, combined with SOLO-FTRL as the online learner, yields Algorithm 1, closely resembling AdamW with scalar stepsizes and clipped updates but using simple (non-decayed) averaging.
Theorem 5 and Corollary 2 show the complexity bound for Algorithm 1 (default averaging) does not improve upon the corresponding bounds for SGD and AdaGrad-Norm, still exhibiting exponential factors.

The main limiting factor behind Algorithm 1's lack of improvement is the default choice of parameters, which corresponds to simple averaging of gradients and squared gradient norms rather than exponential decay.

Replacing the default schedule with a constant parameter alpha_k=alpha in eq. (18) yields Algorithm 2, which coincides with scalar-stepsize AdamW with clipped updates, and induces exponential decay in the moment-accumulation lines.

With a sufficiently small constant alpha_k, the iterates in the update scheme remain stable (x_k approximately equal to x_{k-1}), which intuitively implies stability of the gradients across iterations.
The stability of function values under small constant alpha is formally exploited to establish an improved regret upper bound in Lemma 4, going beyond the simple-averaging bound in Lemma 3.

Combining Lemmas 2 and 4 yields Theorem 6 and Corollary 3, showing Algorithm 2 achieves a fast linear convergence phase up to precision epsilon-hat=O[G0/G1], significant when R*G1 is large, and eliminating exponential factors from the complexity.
A constant choice of alpha_k is no longer optimal once the target precision falls below the threshold epsilon-hat, motivating a two-stage schedule.

A two-stage schedule for alpha_k (large constant value initially, then a second-phase value depending on target accuracy) extends the improved regret bound and yields a combined guarantee achieving fast linear convergence in phase one and optimal sublinear convergence in phase two, with overall complexity order [RG1]^4 + [RG0/epsilon]^2.

Several advanced averaging schemes (primal averaging, online-to-batch conversion, others) are aesthetically appealing and can improve practical performance, but there was previously no theoretical evidence they improve convergence rates over classical Polyak-Ruppert averaging.
Theorem 7 is identified as the first result showing that the eq.(18) averaging scheme yields significantly improved convergence guarantees, specifically under the unbounded-gradient Assumption 2.

The alternative RMSProp-vs-AdaGrad interpretation of exponential decay yields meaningful convergence guarantees for RMSProp, but these do not improve upon AdaGrad's guarantees and therefore fail to explain the benefit of exponential decay.

Because this paper's analysis shows AdamW obtains improved guarantees by exploiting iterate stability (absent in AdaGrad/RMSProp), it demonstrates the RMSProp-AdaGrad analogy for explaining Adam's exponential decay may be inaccurate.
Recurrent models factor computation along input/output symbol positions, generating hidden states as a function of the previous hidden state, which precludes parallelization within training examples.
The inherently sequential nature of recurrent computation becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, since memory constraints limit batching across examples.
The paper proposes the Transformer, a model architecture that eschews recurrence and relies entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.
Because it removes sequential recurrence, the Transformer allows significantly more parallelization than recurrent models.
The Transformer can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after training for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight for each value comes from a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.
Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V, dividing dot products by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax.
For large values of d_k, dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients.
The dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) specifically to counteract the vanishing-gradient effect that would otherwise occur at large d_k.

Dot-product attention can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code, making it much faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention despite similar theoretical complexity.
With a single attention head, averaging inhibits the ability to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

Multi-Head Attention linearly projects queries, keys, and values h times with different learned projections, performs attention in parallel on each projection, then concatenates and projects the results.
Because each head uses a reduced dimension (d_k = d_v = d_model/h), the total computational cost of multi-head attention is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.

The decoder's self-attention sub-layer is modified with masking (setting illegal values to -infinity before softmax) to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions, preserving the autoregressive property.
The length of the paths forward and backward signals must traverse between any two positions is a key factor affecting the ability to learn long-range dependencies; shorter paths make it easier.
A self-attention layer connects all positions with O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length between any two positions.
A recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations and has O(n) maximum path length between positions.

Self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimensionality d, which is most often the case for sentence representations in state-of-the-art translation models.
To improve computational performance for very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to a neighborhood of size r, which would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r).

As a side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models, since inspected attention distributions show individual heads learning distinct, often syntactically/semantically meaningful behaviors.
Because the Transformer contains no recurrence and no convolution, information about the relative or absolute position of tokens must be injected for the model to make use of sequence order.
Sine and cosine functions of different frequencies are added to the input embeddings as positional encodings, with each dimension corresponding to a sinusoid of a different wavelength.

The sinusoidal function was chosen partly because, for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be represented as a linear function of PE(pos), hypothesized to help the model learn to attend by relative position.
The sinusoidal positional encoding was chosen over learned positional embeddings partly because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training.
Experiments substituting learned positional embeddings for the sinusoidal version produced nearly identical results (Table 3, row E).
The big Transformer model achieves 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, outperforming the best previously reported models, including ensembles, by more than 2.0 BLEU.
The big Transformer achieves 41.8 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-French, a new single-model state of the art, at less than 1/4 the training cost of the previous state-of-the-art single model.
Even the base Transformer model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles on English-to-German, at a fraction of the training cost of any competitive model.

The Transformer's parallelizable, non-recurrent architecture is what allows it to achieve these translation quality results with substantially less training time/compute (FLOPs) than prior RNN- and CNN-based approaches.
Varying the number of attention heads while holding computation constant shows single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops off with too many heads.
Reducing the attention key size d_k hurts model quality, suggesting that determining compatibility is not easy and a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may help.
Rows (C) and (D) of the ablation table show that, as expected, bigger models achieve better performance.
The ablation results show dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting.
Constituency parsing presents specific challenges because the output is subject to strong structural constraints and is significantly longer than the input.
Prior work found that RNN sequence-to-sequence models have not been able to attain state-of-the-art results on constituency parsing in small-data regimes.
A 4-layer Transformer with d_model=1024 was trained on the WSJ portion of the Penn Treebank, both in a WSJ-only setting and a larger semi-supervised setting.

Despite only minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning, the Transformer performs surprisingly well on constituency parsing, outperforming all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar.
In contrast to RNN sequence-to-sequence models, the Transformer outperforms the BerkeleyParser even when trained only on the 40K-sentence WSJ training set.

Recent theoretical work argues that human concepts are most plausibly represented as high-dimensional vectors, explaining typicality, similarity, relations, and compositionality through geometric structure.
The vector-space framework resonates with the success of modern foundation models, which learn rich embedding spaces where meaning is encoded in geometric relations among vectors.

If the brain organizes concepts in vector spaces, comparison and learning are likely driven by similarity, suggesting contrastive learning as a biologically plausible approximation of the brain's own optimization principle.
This reasoning motivates investigating contrastive objectives as biologically plausible candidates to reverse the brain's loss function for brain decoding.

Spatial averaging over millions of neurons, temporal filtering of fast dynamics, observation noise, and limited sample size relative to dimensionality act together to smooth and linearize the measured fMRI signal.

Because macroscale factors linearize the measured signal, what fMRI captures is effectively a first-order approximation of underlying neural computations, despite neurons being individually non-linear.

A recent large-scale fMRI study showed that linear models not only match but often outperform a wide range of non-linear approaches across predictive accuracy, residual structure, and computational efficiency.

The linearization of the observable signal due to macroscale measurement factors provides a principled explanation for why linear models can be highly effective in fMRI decoding despite the non-linear nature of underlying neural processes.

Prior work employing contrastive learning within deep architectures for brain encoding/decoding leaves it unclear whether performance gains stem from the contrastive objective itself or from architectural complexity.
To the authors' knowledge, no prior work has conducted systematic benchmarking isolating the contribution of the training objective from that of architectural depth, across multiple modalities.

This paper addresses the gap directly by providing a systematic and controlled comparison across decoder types (ridge, linear contrastive, non-linear/MLP contrastive) under matched conditions across three input modalities.

The decoder architecture applies a subject-specific alignment layer A_k that maps each subject's neural input to a shared dimensionality before further linear projections to the output embedding space.

The model is trained with a contrastive loss inspired by NT-Xent, computing cosine similarity between predicted and target embeddings and encouraging each prediction to be most similar to its paired target relative to other batch members.

The same linear contrastive model architecture and training objective is applied independently across image, language, and music modalities, each with its own dataset, ROI definition, and target embedding space.

Across image (NSD), language (HUTH), and music (GTZAN) modalities, the linear contrastive model consistently achieved the highest Top-1 and Top-3 retrieval accuracies, outperforming both ridge regression and the non-linear contrastive variant.
The retrieval advantage of the linear contrastive model is qualitatively evident in sharper diagonal activations in the sample-wise cosine similarity matrices compared to ridge regression.

Despite introducing additional parameters and activation functions between the subject aligner and mapping layer, non-linear models consistently underperformed compared to the linear contrastive approach across all three modalities.

Feature-wise evaluation confirmed that linear mappings lead to stronger correlations between predicted and ground-truth embeddings, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large, suggesting the contrastive objective itself (not model complexity) is the critical factor.
Removing the subject-specific alignment layer A_k corresponds to training a separate anatomical-only model per subject, defining the Anatomical-CL ablation baseline.
Removing the subject-alignment layer (Anatomical-CL) reduces Top-1 and Top-3 retrieval performance across all three datasets (NSD, HUTH, GTZAN) compared to the full Linear-CL model.
The consistent performance reduction from removing subject alignment confirms the benefit of learning a shared functional space across subjects via the joint contrastive objective.

Contrastive objectives directly operationalize the vector-geometry view of concepts by maximizing angular similarity between matched pairs and enforcing separation from distractors, aligning the training loss with the retrieval evaluation metric.

In practice, the negative set in the contrastive objective acts as a data-driven regularizer, suppressing nuisance-variance directions in fMRI while amplifying directions aligned with semantic information.

Whereas ridge regression minimizes pointwise L2 error, implicitly prioritizing magnitude alignment, contrastive learning preserves and sharpens the relational structure of the embedding manifold, explaining its systematic outperformance of ridge.

The same contrastive advantage holds even when mapping into embedding spaces (like LLaMA3 language embeddings) that were not trained contrastively, indicating a general advantage of geometry-aware objectives rather than mere contrastive-to-contrastive alignment.

Because fMRI signals reflect averages over millions of individually non-linear neurons, filtered in time and smoothed by observation noise, the effective signal approximates a first-order (Taylor-linear) expansion of underlying neural processes.
Given that fMRI approximates a first-order expansion, linear mappings are not just a simplifying choice but may be the most explainable and faithful representation of the observable data.

Non-linear layers, while increasing expressivity, relax the inductive bias that preserves embedding geometry; in the small-to-moderate fMRI data regime, this flexibility can rotate/distort informative directions and amplify noise-driven variance.

The rotation/distortion of informative directions and amplified noise-driven variance from non-linear flexibility ultimately degrades retrieval accuracy, explaining the observed non-linear underperformance.

When decoding with rich pretrained representations, most of the relevant non-linear structure is already embedded upstream in the foundation models, so the decoder's role is not to discover new features.
Because non-linear structure is already captured upstream, the decoder's role is to align noisy brain measurements with an existing embedding geometry rather than to discover new features.
Linear contrastive mappings are well suited to the geometric-alignment role: they provide stable optimization, suppress nuisance variance, and maximize discriminative alignment.
fMRI responses exhibit strong inter-subject variability in both anatomical organization and functional topography.
Prior cross-subject decoding frameworks show anatomical alignment alone is insufficient for high-level semantic decoding; subject-specific functional alignment is typically required.

The subject-alignment layer A_k is jointly optimized inside the contrastive objective (rather than as a separate preprocessing step), learning linear subject-specific transformations that project each subject's activity into a common functional space.

High-quality neural activity datasets at scale have provided enough data to solve the brain-activity-to-visual-semantic-representation mapping sub-problem on an individual basis, driving a surge in high-fidelity within-subject reconstructions.
Despite within-subject progress, current brain decoding models cannot generalize across subjects, necessitating per-subject models or subject-specific fine-tuning.

The cross-subject generalization failure is rooted in profound inter-subject variability in neural signals arising from differences in anatomical structure and functional organization shaped by development, individual experience, and neuroplasticity.

As a result of this variability, the mapping function learned for one individual is ineffective for another, necessitating retraining or fine-tuning via gradient descent, a data-intensive and computationally demanding process.

Developing a data-efficient generalizable cross-subject visual decoding model is essential for building population-wide theories and enabling brain-computer interface, cognitive assessment, and personalized diagnostic applications.

A principled approach recognizes neural decoding as fundamentally an inverse problem, which should be constrained by an accurate forward model (encoding model) characterizing how a subject's brain represents information.

Given a sufficient number of voxels (far exceeding the embedding dimension) and error-free encoder functions, the stimulus can in principle be uniquely solved for by inverting the encoding model via least-squares minimization over voxel prediction errors.

In practice, encoder forward models can be biased and inaccurate, the choice of metric/distance may affect the solution, and the system may be under-determined (fewer voxels than stimulus representation dimensionality).

Because real-world inversion is imperfect and under-determined, rather than learning decoders that map neural representations directly to stimuli, the approach takes a meta-learning view and learns a model to perform in-context functional inversion across a variable number of voxels.

Following the meta-learning reformulation, the decoding process first estimates per-voxel encoder weights in-context, then builds a decoder that performs contextual integration across multiple voxels/brain regions for subject-specific functional inversion.
The two-stage in-context learning process enables generalization to novel subjects without any fine-tuning and with relatively small amounts of new subject data.

In Stage 1, a pretrained BrainCoRL-based transformer infers per-voxel response function weights from a context of stimulus-activation pairs for a single voxel, repeated independently across all voxels of interest, without any fine-tuning.
In Stage 2, each voxel is represented by a context token formed by concatenating its Stage-1 predicted response parameters with the measured activation for the novel stimulus.

A learned transformer takes the voxel context (tokens across a variable number of voxels, up to the subject's total voxel count) as input and approximates the aggregated inverse mapping to estimate the image embedding.

Because the approach constructs context per-subject over voxels rather than aligning voxels anatomically across subjects, it requires neither anatomical alignment nor stimulus overlap across subjects, and flexibly adapts to novel subjects with different voxel counts.

Because the number and identity of available voxels varies across subjects, the model must be invariant to both the number and order of voxel tokens, unlike typical sequential language-model transformers.

To accommodate variable-length contexts and remain length/order invariant, the model adopts logit scaling (scaling attention logits by log of context length) and omits positional embeddings, using a [CLS] token for output.
A hybrid loss combining a cosine embedding loss with an InfoNCE contrastive loss is used to jointly achieve fine-grained embedding alignment and instance-level discriminability.
The training strategy is inspired by LLM pipelines and consists of three stages: pretraining, contextual extension, and supervised fine-tuning.

The pretraining stage adopts an analysis-by-synthesis scheme using no real fMRI data, simulating a large population of voxels via sampled synthetic weights and Gaussian-noise beta responses, with a fixed voxel-context size of 200.
