The second stage introduces variable-length contexts by randomly drawing the number of voxels from Uniform(200, 4000), enabling the model to become robust to changes in context length.

In the final stage, the model is optimized on real fMRI measurements using subject-specific beta values and voxel response parameters from the pretrained BrainCoRL across different image-context sizes, leading to fast convergence and effective adaptation to biologically realistic neural signals.

Across all four leave-one-subject-out conditions on NSD, BrainCoDec (using only 200 of 9,000 support images) delivers consistently stronger Top-1/Top-5 retrieval performance than both MindEye2 (with anatomical alignment) and TGBD, without any subject-specific fine-tuning or retraining.
Increasing either the image context size (Stage 1) or the voxel context size (Stage 2) consistently improves decoding performance across all subjects and visual backbones (CLIP, DINO, SigLIP).

With only 200 images and 4,000 voxels, BrainCoDec achieves similar accuracy to inference using the full context (all ~9,000 images and all higher-visual-cortex voxels), showing the framework needs only a fraction of subject-specific data for comparable performance.

Ablation comparing four configurations shows both fine-tuned variants (with and without subject holdout) significantly outperform pretrained-only (synthetic data) and gradient-based direct-inversion baselines in cosine similarity.

The performance gap between training with subject holdout (novel-subject generalization scenario) versus training on seen subjects is marginal, underscoring that contextual fine-tuning -- not subject-specific training -- is what drives accurate cross-subject decoding.

For each semantic category (faces, places, food, words), test images eliciting the strongest activation in the corresponding functional voxels are identified, and the corresponding category-selective regions are masked out to evaluate resulting decoding performance.
The model exhibits remarkable robustness to targeted regional dropout, with masking category-related ROIs leading to minimal performance degradation for most categories.

Because masking a specific category's selective region has minimal impact, this indicates BrainCoDec does not rely on any single functional region to perform aggregated decoding, consistent with distributed representation learning.
Attention weights from the last layer are extracted while decoding test images from distinct semantic categories, using the same activation-based selection criterion as the ROI-dropout analysis.

Face-related stimuli elicit elevated attention in face- (FFA) and body-selective (EBA) voxels, while place-related stimuli elicit elevated attention in place-related regions (PPA, OPA, RSC), matching independent functional-localizer t-value maps.
The correspondence between learned attention patterns and known functional-localizer maps confirms that BrainCoDec learns to allocate selective focus consistent with established cortical semantics.

Projecting voxelwise attention weights across the full test set via UMAP produces clear semantic clustering (body/face-selective regions vs. scene-selective regions), mirroring known representational gradients in visual areas.

The emergent semantic clustering in the UMAP embedding demonstrates that the model internalizes not merely how to perform functional inversion, but where to find semantically relevant neural representations.

BOLD5000 was acquired on a 3T scanner (vs. NSD's 7T) with different stimulus timing, a substantially different image set, different voxel size, and a different subject pool, providing a stringent test of new-scanner adaptation.
A model trained on the four NSD subjects (no subject held out) is evaluated directly on BOLD5000 subjects using 5-fold cross-validation, without any additional training on BOLD5000 data.

Despite the substantial scanner, timing, image-set, voxel-size, and subject-pool shifts, BrainCoDec achieves strong retrieval performance on BOLD5000, consistent across held-out subjects and image-encoder backbones.
BrainCoDec exhibits a similar contextual scaling trend on BOLD5000 as on NSD, with retrieval performance improving as the number of in-context image-brain pairs increases.

Because the model transfers pretrained knowledge to new scanners without retraining, this is valuable in practical applications where retraining new models for new subjects or scanners is resource-intensive and time-consuming.
A stationary point can be a global minimizer, a poor local minimizer, or a saddle point; first-order information alone does not distinguish among these possibilities.
In highly non-convex landscapes, large regions of near-zero gradient may exist far from any global solution.

Algorithms following gradient-based dynamics can stagnate in near-zero-gradient regions, producing iterates certified as theoretically successful while being arbitrarily suboptimal in objective value.
Because stationary points can be far from global solutions and gradient-based methods can get stuck there, stationarity-based guarantees are a weak proxy for actual optimization success.
In long training runs of modern ML models, the gradient norm has been observed not to decrease, and in some cases to increase, toward the end of training.

This state of affairs motivates the central question of the paper: how to obtain global convergence guarantees for non-convex problems without relying on gradient-based dynamics and gradient-norm metrics.

Escaping stationary points via explicit perturbed-gradient methods or implicit mini-batch noise typically yields guarantees that remain fundamentally local, at best ensuring convergence to approximate second-order stationary points.

The Ball Proximal Point Method (BPM) is a trust-region-type method where each iterate is obtained by minimizing the objective over a ball of radius t centered at the current point, via the set-valued broximal operator.
BPM was found to converge linearly without the strong convexity assumptions required by methods like the classical Proximal Point Method (PPM).
Unlike PPM with finite steps, which can only produce approximate solutions, BPM can attain the exact global minimum in a finite number of iterations using finite radii.
Despite BPM's strong convergence guarantees and evidence that it can handle non-convexity, existing analyses focus almost exclusively on convex objectives, with only limited non-convex treatment.

Motivated by the gap between BPM's demonstrated non-convex potential and its convex-focused existing analysis, this paper revisits BPM to identify structural conditions enabling global convergence in the non-convex setting.

The broximal oracle is very powerful and generally intractable: if the radius is sufficiently large, a global solution can be found in one step, meaning solving the subproblem can be as hard as solving the original problem.

Because the broximal oracle is generally intractable, the paper treats BPM as a conceptual tool for isolating a novel class of non-convex functions for which global convergence can be established, rather than as a practical algorithm.

The original convex analysis of BPM relies on the Second Brox Theorem, which shows that for convex f there exists a coefficient such that a specific inner-product inequality holds between the current point, the broximal update, and any reference point.

Specializing the Second Brox Theorem's inequality to the reference point being a global minimizer yields a nonnegative inner-product relation between the step direction and the direction to that minimizer.

This observation motivates dropping convexity altogether and instead directly postulating the geometric alignment inequality as an assumption (Assumption 3.1), independent of any convexity assumption.

Assumption 3.1 posits that outside a t-neighborhood of the global minimizer set, the inner product between the step direction (x minus broximal update u) and the direction toward a fixed global minimizer is non-positive, i.e., the broximal step is aligned toward the global minimizer.
The relaxation restricting Assumption 3.1 to points outside the t-neighborhood of the minimizer set is essential; imposing the condition for all x would force uniqueness of the global minimizer.
Under Assumption 3.1 alone, having broxtf(x) equal to the singleton {x} does not necessarily imply that x is a global minimizer, leaving a gap that must be addressed by an additional assumption.

Assumption 3.2 states that if the broximal operator at x is the singleton {x} (x is a strict minimizer within its own ball), then x must already be a global minimizer, ruling out 'bad' local minima detectable at scale t.
A proper, closed function belongs to the class of Broximal Aligned Functions if it satisfies both Assumption 3.1 and Assumption 3.2 for a given radius t and geometry X.
Under Assumption 3.1, as long as the algorithm makes progress (x_k not equal x_{k+1}), a non-decreasing function-value step must be followed by a strict decrease at the next step.
The non-decrease-then-strict-decrease pattern implies that the distance between iterates two steps apart exceeds the radius t, formalized in Lemma A.4.

Building on Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, the main convergence theorem (4.1) relies on the fact that every second BPM iterate is separated by a distance of at least t, unless a global minimizer has already been reached.

Theorem 4.1 shows the distances from the iterates to the global minimizer are non-increasing, with a quantified decrease of at least t^2/3 every third iterate when the current ball does not yet contain a global minimizer.
Theorem 4.1 concludes that after a sufficient finite number of iterations K (of order the squared initial distance over t^2), the BPM iterate is exactly a global minimizer.
The one-dimensional function f(x) = |x| + 10*sin(x) has infinitely many local minima spaced every 2*pi, yet satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 for any radius t >= 2*pi.

Example 1 demonstrates that the Broximal Aligned function class does not preclude the existence of multiple local minima, in contrast to classical conditions where all stationary points are globally optimal.
A function with minimizer set Xf = {0, a} for a nonzero vector a is shown to belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any t > 0, despite having a disconnected minimizer set.
Both Example 1 and Example 2 belong to the Broximal Aligned class for suitable t, yet fail to satisfy any of the classical generalized-convexity conditions listed in the paper's comparison table.
Strictly quasiconvex functions belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.
Pseudoconvex functions belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.
Functions that are zeta-quasar convex with respect to a global minimizer belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.
Functions satisfying the aiming condition with a unique global minimizer belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

Because quasiconvexity, pseudoconvexity, quasar convexity, and aiming (with unique minimizer) all imply Broximal Alignment, while Examples 1 and 2 show functions in the Broximal Aligned class satisfying none of these conditions, the Broximal Aligned framework strictly generalizes these classical non-convex function classes.
For many objectives of practical interest, particularly in modern ML, exactly minimizing f over balls B_X(x,t) is computationally intractable.
One practical approximation strategy is to approximately solve the broximal subproblem itself, e.g., via sampling-based approaches or an iterative method run up to prescribed accuracy.

A second practical approximation strategy replaces the original objective with a simpler local model, such as a linearized or quadratic trust-region subproblem, which is often tractable and sometimes has closed-form solutions.

The Muon optimizer can be interpreted as performing approximate broximal steps by minimizing linearized local models over non-Euclidean balls induced by the spectral norm, illustrating that local-model approximations extend beyond the Euclidean setting.
Fairness of machine learning predictions is widely required by legal frameworks, notably in credit lending and law enforcement.

Causal fairness leverages causal theory to ensure a sensitive attribute does not affect prediction outcomes, directly relating to legal terminology requiring outcome independence from sensitive attributes.
Existing works on causally fair predictions commonly focus on settings with no unobserved confounding, assuming the causal structure is fully known.
The assumption of no unobserved confounding is fairly strong and unrealistic in practice.
Due to unobserved confounding, causal fairness may be violated, and predictions can cause harm as they may actually be unfair.

In predicting prison sentences, unobserved confounders such as housing situation, family background, and birthplace can bias predictions if not accounted for, even when race is excluded and offense/crime history are controlled.
Sensitivity models are common tools for partial identification under unobserved confounding, but they perform partial identification on interventional effects (level 2 of Pearl's ladder).
Causal fairness involves nested counterfactual effects (level 3 of Pearl's ladder), which differ from the interventional effects that sensitivity models directly handle.
Because of the level mismatch between interventional effects and nested counterfactuals, it is not possible to directly apply existing sensitivity models to the causal fairness setting.

The only prior work analyzing sensitivity of fairness to unobserved confounding (Kilbertus et al. 2019) focuses on counterfactual fairness, allows confounding only between covariates, and relies on restrictive non-linear additive noise model assumptions.
To the authors' knowledge, no work has analyzed the sensitivity of causal fairness specifically (as opposed to counterfactual fairness) to unobserved confounding.
The combination of the level mismatch, the narrow scope of prior sensitivity-fairness work, and the absence of causal-fairness-specific sensitivity analysis establishes the paper's research gap.
The paper adopts the Standard Fairness Model with data V = {A, Z, M, Y}: sensitive attribute A, observed confounders Z, mediators M, and outcome Y.
The setup uniquely allows three types of unobserved confounding: direct (U_DE, between A and Y), indirect (U_IE, between A and M), and spurious (U_SE, between A and Z).
Path-specific causal fairness is defined via three effects: counterfactual direct effect (Ctf-DE) for A→Y, indirect effect (Ctf-IE) for A→M→Y, and spurious effect (Ctf-SE) for Z→A.
Ctf-DE measures direct discrimination based on the sensitive attribute.
Ctf-IE and Ctf-SE together measure indirect discrimination through factors related to the sensitive attribute, potentially acting as proxies.
Causal fairness is achieved when DE, IE, and SE are zero or close to zero, operationalized via user-defined thresholds.
Under unobserved confounding, the path-specific causal fairness effects (DE, IE, SE) are not identifiable from observational data, so naive estimates are biased.
As a remedy, the paper moves from point identification to partial identification, deriving upper and lower bounds for DE, IE, SE under a sensitivity model.

Each CF is decomposed into identifiable parts and unnested (single-intervention) interventional effects, since sensitivity analysis operates on interventional (level-2) effects while CF involves nested (level-3) counterfactuals.
The unnested interventional effects are then bounded using the GMSM sensitivity model, yielding upper and lower bounds for each CF.

The generalized marginal sensitivity model (GMSM) is adopted because it handles discrete mediators and both discrete/continuous outcomes, and subsumes many existing sensitivity models (e.g., MSM) as special cases.
Lemma 1 shows each CF can be written as a monotonically increasing function of a sum of unidentifiable single-intervention effects plus an identifiable term q.
The unidentifiable single-intervention effects in Lemma 1's decomposition are exactly the type of effect that causal sensitivity analysis can bound.
The identifiable term q in the decomposition can be directly estimated from observational data.
Using the unnested expressions, Theorem 1 derives explicit closed-form upper and lower bounds on DE, IE, and SE under the GMSM for binary sensitive attribute A and discrete Z.
Theorem 1's bounds are independent of the distribution and dimensionality of unobserved confounders and specific SCM formulations, applying to discrete, categorical, and continuous outcomes.
The derived bounds are sharp/optimal, meaning the supremum/infimum equality in the bound definition holds exactly.
The wider the interval between CF+ and CF-, the more sensitive the path-specific effect is to unobserved confounding, giving less confidence in unconfounded estimates.

Since path-specific causal fairness is unidentifiable under confounding, the derived bounds CF+ and CF- are used to limit the worst-case (maximum deviation from zero) unfairness of the prediction model.
To train the model, P±(y|z,m,a) in the bounds is replaced by the non-random predicted outcome f_θ(a,z,m), requiring only estimation of P±(m|z,a) via pre-trained density estimators.
The training objective is formulated as minimizing prediction loss subject to worst-case fairness bound constraints |CF+_E|,|CF-_E| ≤ γ_CF for each CF in {DE, IE, SE}.
To solve the constrained optimization with gradient-based solvers, augmented Lagrangian optimization is used to convert it into a single loss function with an estimated Lagrange multiplier.

Algorithm 1 iteratively computes upper/lower CF bounds via Theorem 1, updates the Lagrangian loss, and updates the predictor parameters, checking convergence on both prediction loss and fairness constraints.
Baselines for causal fairness under unobserved confounding are absent in prior literature.

Because no baselines exist, the paper compares three models with identical network architecture: Standard (no fairness constraint), Fair naive (fairness assuming no unobserved confounding), and Fair robust (the proposed framework).
Fair naive considers causal fairness only under the assumption of no unobserved confounding, so it is expected to underestimate true unfairness when confounding is present.
Because the three models share identical network architecture, any fairness improvement can be attributed specifically to the tailored learning objective rather than model capacity.
Bounds are derived for causal fairness metrics under different sources of unobserved confounding, serving as a refutation strategy for practitioners.
A novel neural framework is developed for learning fair predictions with worst-case guarantees on the extent of causal fairness violation due to unobserved confounding.
The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated in experiments on synthetic and real-world data, including a real-world case study predicting prison sentences.
Existing works in fair ML cover bias detection, fair prediction, and fair decision-making, but largely focus on static settings.
Fairness in temporal contexts, particularly survival/time-to-event (TTE) analysis, remains relatively underexplored.
Current approaches to fair survival analysis adopt statistical fairness definitions rather than causal ones.
Statistical fairness definitions, even with unlimited data, cannot disentangle the causal mechanisms that generate disparities.
Causal fairness literature introduces important causal fairness notions but is concerned with the static setting only, with few dynamic-setting exceptions.
There remains a need for a deeper understanding of how causal reasoning can be applied to fairness in temporal/TTE data, which this paper aims to fill.
The Standard Fairness Model (SFM) cluster causal diagram is adapted to survival analysis, with protected attribute X, confounders Z, mediators W, survival time T, and censoring time C.
T and C are assumed unobserved; instead the pair (M, δ) is observed, where M = min(T,C) and δ indicates whether the observed event is death.
Absence of a bidirected arrow between T and C in the SFM implies T ⊥ C | X, Z, W, i.e., the censoring mechanism is conditionally independent of the survival mechanism.
The T ⊥ C | X,Z,W assumption allows application of standard survival-analysis tools such as conditional Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen estimators.
The SFM further encodes lack-of-confounding assumptions: no bidirected edges between {T,C,M,δ} and {X,Z,W}, and none between X,W or Z,W.
These lack-of-confounding assumptions are important for identifying the different causal effects of X on the survival curve.
The total variation measure TV_{x0,x1}(t) = P(T>t|X=x1) - P(T>t|X=x0) is used to quantify survival differences across demographic groups at time t.
The goal is to decompose the TV disparity into contributions from the direct (X→T), indirect (X→W→T), and spurious (X⇢Z→T) pathways.

The decomposition proceeds in two steps closely related to the two types of assumptions encoded in the SFM: Step 1 (inference of P(T|X,Z,W)) and Step 2 (inference of causal effects of X on functionals of P(T|X,Z,W)).
Under T⊥C|X,Z,W, the likelihood for T depends only on (M,δ), so conditional Kaplan-Meier/Nelson-Aalen estimators validly recover P(T|X,Z,W).
Given P(T|X,Z,W), a mapping Φ = ϕ(P(T|X,Z,W)) is defined so the TV measure can be rewritten as E[Φ|X=x1] - E[Φ|X=x0].
Theorem 1 (Causal Reduction) shows that Φ's structural mechanism f_Φ(x,z,w)=ϕ(P(T|X=x,Z=z,W=w)) makes Φ a deterministic function of X,Z,W, not depending on noise variables.
Because Φ is a deterministic function of X,Z,W, it can be added as a new node to the causal diagram, yielding a reduced causal model.
Using the reduced model, x-specific direct (x-DE), indirect (x-IE), and spurious (x-SE) effects of X on Φ are defined analogously to standard causal fairness effects.
The TV_{x0,x1}(Φ) disparity measure decomposes as TV = x-DE - x-IE - x-SE, following prior causal-fairness decomposition results.
Because Theorem 1 applies to Φ(t) for any t, the pathway decomposition of disparity can be performed at each individual time point, yielding a time-resolved explanation of disparity evolution.
Proposition 1 shows that, under the SFM, the potential outcome E[Φ_{xy,W_xw}(t)|X=xz] is identifiable as a weighted sum over Z,W of conditional expectations of Φ, using estimable propensities.
Random survival forests (RSF) are used to non-parametrically estimate P(T|X,Z,W) via the conditional cumulative hazard function, from which the survival function is obtained.
Proposition 2 gives a plug-in model-based estimator for the potential outcome E[Φ_{xy,W_xw}(t)|X=xz] using the fitted f(x,z,w) and estimated propensities.
Because X,Z,W are time-invariant in this setting, the estimated propensities do not depend on time, making the temporal causal decomposition computationally inexpensive.
Theorem 2 derives a novel influence function for the potential outcome ψ under censored data, enabling doubly-robust debiasing of the model-based estimator.

The influence function is used with cross-fitting: nuisance functions are fit on one fold via xgboost while the influence function is evaluated on the remaining fold, with folds swapped to obtain a one-step debiased estimate.
Individuals may be simultaneously at risk of multiple distinct event types, motivating the competing risks (CR) extension beyond the basic non-informative-censoring case.
In the CR setting only M = min(T1,...,TK,C) and the event-type indicator δ are observed, not the individual event times.
Competing events may have unobserved common causes, represented as bidirected edges among T1,...,TK.

Because only the minimum event time is observed and competing events may share unobserved causes, identifying the full joint distribution P(T1,...,TK|X,Z,W) is generally infeasible without strong assumptions like independence of failure times, which rarely hold.
As a result, most competing-risks approaches, including this work, focus on cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) rather than the full joint distribution.
CIFs explicitly account for competition: increasing one event type's rate necessarily reduces the CIFs of the remaining events, and CIFs sum with all-cause survival to 1.

By the Causal Reduction Theorem, each Φ_k(t) := CIF_k(t) is a deterministic functional of P(T1,...,TK|X,Z,W) and hence a deterministic function of (X,Z,W), enabling the same direct/indirect/spurious decomposition for each cause k.
In the informative censoring (IC) setting, T ⊥ C | X,Z,W no longer holds (a bidirected T⇢C arrow exists), so standard survival-analysis tools are not directly applicable.
Because T⊥C|X,Z,W fails, inference of S(t|X,Z,W) is not possible without additional assumptions, motivating a sensitivity analysis approach.
The joint survival function H(t,c)=P(T>t,C>c) is assumed to follow an Archimedean copula parameterized by Kendall's τ, the sensitivity parameter.
The classical copula-graphic estimator (CGE) assumes that at each grid point only one of S(t) or G(t) jumps, recursively identifying S(t) and G(t) from CIFs.
In this setting, estimation proceeds on a fixed grid of estimated CIFs where both Ŝ and Ĝ may jump at the same grid point, violating the classical CGE's disjoint-increment assumption.
Because the disjoint-jump assumption is violated, the classical CGE must be adapted: τ no longer uniquely identifies S(t_{i+1}), G(t_{i+1}).
Theorem 3 derives sharp, closed-form bounds on S(t_{i+1}) and G(t_{i+1}) given prior values and CIF increments, which collapse to point estimates as the grid is refined.
Point estimates of S(t) and G(t) are obtained via midpoint interpolation of the derived bounds, yielding a point-identified estimator as the grid becomes refined.

After recovering Ŝ(t), the Causal Reduction Theorem is invoked again to compute direct/indirect/spurious effects of X on S(t), quantifying causal fairness under informative censoring via sensitivity analysis on τ.
The case study uses the ANZICS Adult Patient Database, covering 181 hospitals across Australia (Jan 2023-Jul 2024), yielding 249,958 patients, 10,436 (~4.2%) Indigenous.
Indigenous status and sociodemographic variables may share common causes but neither causes the other, motivating the X⇢Z spurious relationship as in prior literature.
Clinical variables are temporally downstream of X and Z (e.g., indigenous status may influence illness severity via healthcare-access disparities), justifying their role as mediators W.
The censoring mechanism is related to the data extraction process (an administrative reason), justifying the non-informative censoring assumption for the death-outcome analysis.
Death censoring has unobserved common causes with readmission (latent illness severity, unmeasured frailty, care quality), so the readmission analysis falls under informative censoring.
The causal structure has two acknowledged limitations: genetic variation may confound X→W, and geographic remoteness may confound X, W, and T jointly.
The raw TV disparity measure for death rises then falls, with confidence intervals including 0 after T=80 days, appearing to suggest little disparity.
The direct effect decreases up to T=50 days then stabilizes, with its sign implying minority patients experience improved survival along the direct path.

The indirect effect decreases over time, implying reduced minority survival along this pathway (due to higher chronic/acute illness burden), reaching ~3% difference by T=50 days and continuing to amplify to T=180 days.
The spurious effect increases up to T=180 days, implying improved minority survival along the spurious pathway, related to lower average age at admission.
Together, the near-zero TV measure masks substantial, opposing pathway-specific effects — a pattern that would be missed by standard statistical fairness analysis.
The readmission TV measure increases over time, indicating higher readmission burden for minority patients.
Sensitivity analysis is performed via Route II (population-level copula) with τ ∈ {0.1,0.5,0.8}, assuming T1,T2 are positively correlated due to shared causes.
Along both the direct and indirect pathways, minority patients show increased readmission burden, with the indirect effect attributed to more complicated admission diagnoses and worse chronic health.
Along the spurious pathway, minority patients again show lower readmission burden, likely due to lower average age at ICU admission.
Despite the directional findings, the confidence bounds for the direct effect do not allow definitive conclusions about effect sizes.
Causal fairness is formalized for survival analysis, proving the Causal Reduction Theorem that enables identification and decomposition of group disparities in TTE settings.
The framework is instantiated in three regimes (non-informative censoring, competing risks, informative censoring), with identification results derived for each (Prop. 1).
Two new technical results are proven: a doubly robust estimator for censored data, and sharp bounds for copula-graphic estimation under non-disjoint increments.
Race differentials in post-ICU mortality are analyzed, demonstrating that causal fairness for TTE yields scientific insights missed by standard statistical fairness analyses.
Randomized controlled trials remain the gold standard for establishing causal relationships, but are not always feasible due to ethical or logistical constraints.
Researchers may consider causal inference on large-scale observational, retrospective data as a bridge between gold-standard RCTs and ubiquitous real-world data.
When observational data are curated to follow a set of assumptions, causal inference can be applied to emulate an RCT, yielding valid treatment effect estimates.

Causal ML shows promise because ML excels at extracting signals from multi-modal data (images, notes, time-series), allowing adjustment on complex confounders that traditional statistical methods struggle to incorporate.
Drawing valid causal inferences requires justifying assumptions in the data and modeling choices; the flexibility of ML increases the risk of erroneous findings.
Inappropriately drawing causal conclusions from ML carries risks to medical science and potentially patient safety.
Despite advances in causal ML, its limitations remain largely under-appreciated across disciplines, and this gap in shared knowledge may impact the validity of findings.
When estimating causal effects from observational data, treatments are often non-randomly assigned, confounding direct comparisons of outcomes.
The causal relationships between treatment, outcome, and other relevant variables can be modeled using a causal directed acyclic graph (DAG).

The structure of a causal DAG implies a set of independence conditions between variables that generate identifiability assumptions, determining when a causal interpretation of treatment effects is tenable.
Constructing an accurate DAG with input from domain experts is a crucial first step in ensuring meaningful causal conclusions.
By default, most ML approaches are optimized for predictive performance.
Because ML is optimized for predictive performance, ML models may leverage spurious associations to make predictions even when an underlying causal relationship exists.
This tendency to exploit spurious associations means ML introduces new challenges in verifying (and can obscure violations of) the causal identifiability assumptions.
The overlap assumption requires every patient to have a non-zero probability of receiving the treatment.
Overlap can be partly assessed by fitting a propensity score model to predict treatment assignment from variables that could influence it, per the causal DAG.
If the propensity model is well-specified, high discriminative performance implies low overlap, while poor discriminative performance indicates more randomness in treatment assignment.
If the model is poorly specified, near-random discriminative performance could simply indicate underfitting rather than true overlap.
Issues with model specification can be mitigated in part using standard supervised ML techniques such as cross-validation for model selection.
To more thoroughly evaluate overlap, one should consult domain experts, ideally those responsible for assigning the treatments, who can help identify settings where overlap is impossible.
The assumption of no unobserved confounding is unverifiable in observational data.
Identifying confounders generally requires domain expertise.

If potential confounders (e.g., social determinants of health, patient preferences) are unavailable in the data, a causal interpretation may be untenable if their influence could flip the conclusions.
Even if unmeasured confounders are believed small in magnitude, they should be acknowledged as a limitation when communicating findings.
As further assurance, one can employ sensitivity analyses that quantify the magnitude of an unobserved confounder necessary to change the conclusions.
SUTVA requires that all patients receive the same version of treatment (consistency) and that no patient's outcome is affected by others' treatment assignments (non-interference).
Consistency violations may arise from hidden variation in the treatment variable, e.g., dose strength.
When sources of treatment variation are inadvertently treated as confounders (e.g., dose strength), subsequent adjustment can wash out the treatment effect.
Interference may occur when treating one patient affects outcomes for others, as in nosocomial infection management, where an ML model might use room ID (predictive of transmission) as a feature.

ML practitioners with limited clinical expertise may overlook the causal significance of variables like dose strength or room ID and include them in model development purely because they boost predictive performance.

The predictive utility of dose strength suggests it should be incorporated into the treatment definition, whereas the utility of room ID reflects interference rather than treatment, requiring different handling.
Without domain expertise, researchers risk mistaking predictive associations for sources of treatment effect heterogeneity or genuine causal factors.
It is essential to first define a causal DAG, then examine the data for potential assumption violations using domain expertise and empirical checks.
The flexibility of ML models increases the risk of overfitting to spurious signals that may obscure violations of overlap, exchangeability, and SUTVA.
Careful selection of confounders, treatment/outcome definitions, and associated models in collaboration with domain experts can mitigate assumption-violation risks or quantify their potential impact.
For ML practitioners it is tempting to incorporate all observed covariates as predictors to adjust for confounding.
Irrelevant variables may be spuriously correlated with the outcome.
Some variables may be causal mediators — intermediate variables caused by the treatment that influence the outcome, occurring along the DAG path from treatment to outcome.
Adjusting for mediators dilutes estimates of treatment effects, since the treatment may not get credit for changes in outcomes it caused via the mediator.
One can avoid including mediators by consulting the DAG and ensuring all predictors are measured before treatment and follow-up.
Metalearners allow users to plug in base models of arbitrary complexity and estimate treatment effects from combinations of the base models' outputs.
Indirect estimators (S-learner, T-learner) estimate the outcome under each treatment assignment separately given covariates, then take the difference.
Because the treatment effect is the difference between two separate predictions, errors in either prediction can be magnified and distort the final estimate.

In high-dimensional data, model-simplifying techniques like regularization can shrink away treatment heterogeneity, flattening outcome estimates and potentially causing a premature conclusion of no treatment effect.

Direct estimators (X-learner, DR-learner, R-learner, double ML, orthogonal statistical learning) use base-model outputs to model the treatment effect directly in a second step, via pseudo-outcomes or residual-based isolation, since the true effect is never directly observed per individual.
Although base-model errors can still bias direct methods' estimates, direct methods are often more robust to these errors than indirect methods.
Consulting the causal DAG when choosing covariates reduces the risk of including irrelevant variables and mediators.
The method of combining base model outputs (indirect vs. direct) impacts the quality of treatment effect estimates.
Indirect methods are attractive for their simplicity, but if the accuracy of base models is a central concern, direct methods may be preferable.
In causal inference only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed, so there is no 'true' treatment effect available for held-out validation as in standard supervised ML.
Because there is no ground-truth treatment effect, the standard ML paradigm of comparing predicted to observed outcomes on a held-out test set does not apply to causal effect evaluation.

One strategy is a global null analysis using a synthetic treatment with no true effect, allowing estimated effects to be directly evaluated similarly to supervised ML since the expected effect is zero.
To complement a global null analysis, one can perform a negative control analysis (a treatment with no effect per expert knowledge) or plasmode simulation when feasible.
Another strategy is comparing estimates across different modeling approaches and assessing whether sign and magnitude are stable, since each approach encodes different assumptions.
Stability across modeling approaches builds confidence in results but these analyses do not supersede evaluation through RCTs or grounding in real-world causal mechanisms.
Gold-standard validation is generally infeasible in observational causal inference.
Causal ML results from observational data should be treated as causal hypotheses rather than definitive findings.
These hypotheses can then be prioritized for testing in RCTs or evaluated against plausible physiological or biological mechanisms.
Without well-justified causal assumptions and ML modeling choices, analyses may yield conclusions that are misleading.
A roadmap is proposed that organizes recommendations for using causal ML in observational data into questions addressing causal assumptions, modeling, and evaluation.
Although not exhaustive, the roadmap offers a foundation for interdisciplinary teams to ground their causal ML analyses.
Compared to animals, ML is limited at transfer to new problems and forms of generalization beyond sampling from the same distribution (horizontal/strong/OOD generalization).
This shortcoming is unsurprising given that ML often disregards information animals use heavily: interventions, domain shifts, temporal structure, treating these as nuisance to be engineered away.
The majority of current ML successes boil down to large-scale pattern recognition on suitably collected i.i.d. data.

A substantial literature on robustness (Issue 1) documents that deep networks are sensitive to distribution shifts like blur, noise, rotation, viewpoint, with no definitive consensus on solving this via augmentation/pretraining alone.

It has been argued that fixes like augmentation may not be sufficient, and generalizing well outside the i.i.d. setting requires learning not mere statistical associations but an underlying causal model, which models distribution shifts via interventions.

Modular representations where modules correspond to physical causal mechanisms allow an agent facing a new environment to adapt only a few modules, requiring fewer examples since most knowledge/modules can be re-used without further training.

A set of coupled differential equations describing physical mechanisms allows predicting future behavior, reasoning about interventions, and reading off causal structure — the gold standard, most detailed model.
A statistical model tells us how some variables predict others as long as experimental conditions don't change; it does not refer to dynamic processes and cannot predict intervention effects.

Causal modeling lies between differential equations and statistical models: like physics, it predicts intervention effects, but causal discovery arrives at such models in a data-driven way with weak generic assumptions rather than requiring expert-derived differential equations.

A taxonomy ranks models by capability: mechanistic/structural-causal/causal-graphical models can predict under distribution shift and (for the first two) answer counterfactuals, while statistical models can only predict in the i.i.d. setting.
Questions like P(Y|X) can, subject to suitable assumptions, be provably answered by observing sufficient i.i.d. data from P(X,Y).
The stork/birth-rate example shows a statistical model may predict well even with no causal link, so accurate predictions may not suffice to inform decisions like interventions.
Interventional questions involve actions taking us out of the usual i.i.d. setting; interventions change the joint distribution, so classical statistical learning guarantees no longer apply.
On the other hand, learning about interventions may allow training predictive models robust against the naturally occurring distribution changes in the real world.
Counterfactual problems (reasoning about why things happened, imagining consequences of different actions in hindsight) can be more difficult to answer than interventional questions.

This may be a key challenge for AI since an intelligent agent may benefit from imagining action consequences and understanding retrospectively what led to outcomes; counterfactuals are especially critical in reinforcement learning.
In the SCM viewpoint, each observable Xi is the result of a deterministic assignment Xi := fi(PAi, Ui) depending on its graph parents and an independent noise term Ui.

The noises U1,...,Un are assumed jointly independent; if they were not, by the Common Cause Principle there should be another variable causing their dependence, meaning the model would not be causally sufficient.

The graph structure plus joint noise independence implies a canonical causal factorization P(X1,...,Xn) = Π P(Xi|PAi), distinct from other valid but entangled factorizations like the reverse-chain one.

While many entangled factorizations are mathematically valid, only the causal factorization (4) is the one that decomposes the joint distribution into conditionals corresponding to the actual structural assignments — the causal mechanisms responsible for the statistical dependencies.
Both causal graphical models and SCMs allow computing interventional distributions, but only SCMs (via fixing noise-variable values) allow computing counterfactuals.
Reichenbach's Common Cause Principle: if X and Y are statistically dependent, there exists a variable Z that causally influences both and renders them independent when conditioned on Z.

Without additional assumptions, the three causal explanations (X→Y, X←Y, or a common confounder) cannot be distinguished using only observational data over X,Y, since they realize the same class of observational distributions.

With more than two observables, nontrivial conditional independence properties implied by causal structure become available, generalizing the Reichenbach Principle and making causal discovery surprisingly easier than the two-variable case.

The causal generative process is composed of autonomous modules that do not inform or influence each other; the conditional distribution of each variable given its causes does not inform or influence the other mechanisms.
Applied to the causal factorization, ICM implies changing/intervening on one mechanism P(Xi|PAi) does not change any other mechanism P(Xj|PAj) for i≠j.
ICM also implies knowing some other mechanisms P(Xi|PAi) (i≠j) does not give information about mechanism P(Xj|PAj).

In contrast, under a non-causal (entangled) factorization, changing a physical mechanism will typically affect many or all terms simultaneously, since the entangled factorization does not isolate mechanisms.

Any real-world distribution is viewed as a product of causal mechanisms; a change in the distribution when moving to a related domain will always be due to changes in at least one of those mechanisms.
Sparse Mechanism Shift: small distribution changes tend to manifest in a sparse or local way in the causal/disentangled factorization, usually not affecting all factors simultaneously.

Under a non-causal (entangled) factorization, many or all terms will be affected simultaneously as a physical mechanism changes, unlike the sparse effect seen in the causal factorization — motivating the 'disentangled' terminology.

Although conditional independencies implied by the Markov condition hold irrespective of function complexity in principle, conditional independence testing is a notoriously difficult problem for finite datasets, especially with continuous multi-dimensional conditioning sets.

In the two-variable case, the ternary concept of conditional independence collapses, so the Markov condition has no nontrivial implications, echoing the earlier two-variable underdetermination result.

Both the finite-sample CI-testing problem and the two-variable underdetermination problem can be addressed by making assumptions on function classes, analogous to how finite-sample generalization in ML requires assumptions on function classes.

Restricting to an additive noise model Y=f(X)+V (rather than allowing f to depend arbitrarily on noise) both reduces the effective function class size and, under genericity assumptions, breaks the symmetry between cause and effect: one cannot generally fit an additive noise model in the reversed direction.

By the SMS hypothesis, much causal structure is assumed to remain invariant across changing environments, so distribution shifts (from interventions, non-stationary time series, or multiple views) can significantly help identify causal structure.
Contexts/environments can likewise be interpreted as different tasks, providing a connection to meta-learning.

Prior work ties generalization in meta-learning to invariance properties of causal models, using the idea that a causal model should adapt faster to interventions than purely predictive models, later extended to multiple variables and unknown interventions via continuous-optimization causal discovery.
Traditional causal discovery and reasoning assume the units are random variables already connected by a causal graph.
Real-world observations (e.g., objects in images) are usually not structured into those causal units to begin with.

This gap motivates causal representation learning: learning the causal variables S1,...,Sn connecting to observations X=G(S1,...,Sn) from data, rather than assuming them given, paralleling how ML moved beyond requiring symbols be given a priori.

It is challenging to state general conditions under which coarse-grained variables admit causal models with well-defined interventions; defining suitable units amounts to coarse-graining more detailed models (SCMs, differential equations, time series).

To combine SCM and representation learning, one should embed an SCM into larger ML models whose inputs/outputs may be high-dimensional and unstructured but whose inner workings are partly governed by an SCM, parameterized with a neural network.

The result may be a modular architecture where different modules can be individually fine-tuned and re-purposed for new tasks, with the SMS hypothesis used to enforce the appropriate sparse-change structure.

An encoder q maps observations to a noise-variable bottleneck U; a mapping f(U) determined by structural assignments produces causal variables; a decoder p reconstructs the observation, trained via reconstruction error to satisfy p∘f∘q≈id.

If the causal graph is known, the network topology implementing f can be fixed accordingly; if not, the decoder learns the composition p∘f as a single unspecified part, i.e., one only learns an autoencoder p̃∘q.

Much existing work on disentanglement focuses on independent factors of variation, which is the special case where the causal graph is trivial (all parent sets empty), a special case of the more general ICM Principle.

Object-centric representation learning can also be viewed as a special case of disentangled factorization: objects should be building blocks of an overall causal factorization, complemented by mechanisms like orientation and lighting.

The problem of recovering exogenous noise variables is ill-defined in the i.i.d. case since there are infinitely many equivalent solutions yielding the same observational distribution; additional assumptions or biases are needed to favor certain solutions.

To make the representation causal, one can apply the ICM Principle (statistically independent Ui, independent mechanisms via invariance across problems, sparse changes to actions, or independent intervenability); SMS is theoretically sufficient given suitable training data and can be used as a supervision signal even with nontrivial parent sets.

Which factors of variation can be disentangled depends on which interventions can be observed, and different supervision signals can be used to identify different subsets of factors and their granularity.

Agents face limited training data and computational resources, motivating modular structures that mirror modularity in the world so components/mechanisms can be re-used across environments, tasks, and settings.
A sensible inductive bias for learning such transferable modular models is to look for independent causal mechanisms, which may help transfer modules across substantially different domains.
Deep learning excels at learning representations preserving statistical properties, but does so without regard to interventional properties of the variables it analyzes.

Causal representation learning should move beyond statistical dependence structures towards models supporting intervention, planning, and reasoning, realizing 'thinking as acting in an imagined space.'

If the causal graph is X→Y, ICM implies P(X) contains no information about the mechanism P(Y|X), implying SSL using unlabeled data to improve estimation of P(Y|X) should be futile in the causal direction.

In the anticausal direction (prediction target opposite the causal generative process), a measure of dependence between P(X) and P(Y|X) is strictly positive, implying the input distribution can be informative about the conditional, so SSL may be possible.

This prediction was empirically corroborated, establishing a bridge between the structure of learning problems and the causal direction of real-world data-generating processes, inspiring follow-up work in ML and statistics.
Adversarial attacks constitute minute, human-imperceptible changes to inputs that alter a classifier's output; test examples in this setting are not drawn from the training distribution.
In the causal setting, if a predictor approximates the causal mechanism (which is by definition valid under every allowed intervention), one may expect adversarial examples to be harder to find.

Recent work supports this view: a defense against adversarial attacks solves the anticausal classification problem by modeling the causal generative direction (analysis by synthesis), or reconstructs the input via an autoencoder before classification.
Structures composed of autonomous modules, as given by a causal factorization, should be relatively robust to swapping out or modifying individual components.

A scoring system using only causal features (e.g., debt paid off, which causally affects repayment) rather than non-causal correlates (e.g., address) can be more robust to strategic behavior by agents gaming the score.

Restricting the test distribution P† to lie in a set PG of interventional distributions over a causal graph, worst-case OOD risk is the max expected loss over P†∈PG, and a robust predictor solves the corresponding minimax problem using a subset of environment distributions E⊂PG.
If the observed environment set E does not coincide with the full possible set PG, there is an additional estimation error that may be arbitrarily large in the worst case.

Enriching the training distribution (e.g., pre-training on huge diverse corpora) is one way to approximate the minimax OOD objective, but only helps if the new distribution is diverse enough to contain information about other distributions in PG.

Data augmentation increases data diversity via artificially generated interventions (rotation, translation, flipping); one can view this as specifying a set of interventions E the model should be robust to.

Self-supervision learns useful representations of P(X) via pretext tasks with artificially generated labels, converting an unsupervised problem into a supervised one, aiming to extract features informative about the data-generating distribution.
RL is closer to causality than mainstream ML in that on-policy learning effectively directly estimates do-probabilities for interventions specified by the policy.
As soon as off-policy learning is considered, especially in the batch/observational setting, issues of causality become subtle.

Many current model-based RL approaches only build partial models of the environment; since they don't observe every time step, the environment may become an unobserved confounder affecting both actions and reward, addressable via a backdoor-criterion conditioning on the policy.

Learning invariances in a causal graph structure is proposed as a path to RL generalization; causal models may allow modeling the environment as independent mechanisms so not all mechanisms need re-learning under distribution shift.

Offline RL learns a policy from a fixed trajectory dataset without environment interaction; succeeding requires inferring consequences of actions not seen during training, essentially a counterfactual inference problem, made harder by distribution mismatch between current and data-collection policies.
Significant OOD generalization of learned physical simulators may not be necessary if experimental conditions are carefully controlled, though the simulator must be retrained if conditions change.

In healthcare, if a clinical system is trained on doctors' actions in controlled settings, it will likely provide little additional insight compared to doctors' own knowledge and may fail unexpectedly when deployed.
An understanding of causality may be necessary to recommend treatment options that are personalized and reliable, beyond merely automating existing decisions.
Causal mediation analysis helped disentangle effects contributing to Covid-19 case fatality rates when a textbook Simpson's paradox was observed.

In astronomy, causal models identifying and removing shared instrument-noise patterns across confounded stars led to the discovery of 36 planet candidates (21 later validated), including one later found to show water vapor in its atmosphere.

A critical question is why not just train a huge model that learns environment dynamics including all possible interventions, expecting a big network to generalize across them given enough diverse data.
If data is not sufficiently diverse (an a priori untestable assumption), the worst-case error to unseen shifts may still be arbitrarily high, per the earlier OOD risk analysis.

The causal approach makes a model's generalization-relevant assumptions more explicit and aligned with our understanding of physics and human cognition (e.g., via the ICM Principle); when these assumptions are valid, a learner using them should fare better than one that does not.

If a model succeeds across an environment's interventions, one may want to transfer it to different but related environments; the ICM principle points to decomposing knowledge into independent, recomposable pieces, motivating modular ML architectures.

Future work should understand under which conditions non-linear causal relations can be learned at scale, which training frameworks best exploit ML scalability for this, and provide evidence of advantages over non-causal representations on real-world tasks.

Future work should address that current disentangled representations are still distributed in a fixed-format vector, unable to dynamically change representation size (e.g., number of objects), and should investigate task-dependent extraction of high-level variables.

Future work should disentangle the benefits of individual robustness-improving components (scaling, augmentation, self-supervision) and build a taxonomy of inductive biases, understanding how pre-training design choices causally impact transfer and robustness.

Future work should address deriving abstract causal variables from high-dimensional pixel representations and recovering causal graphs in RL settings, essential for robust and versatile model-based RL.
Standard fairness approaches often treat data as static points in high-dimensional space, ignoring the underlying generative structure.
Sensitive attributes do not merely shift data distributions but causally warp the geometry of the data manifold itself.
Distributional alignment (matching P(Z|do(A=a)) across a) is often insufficient for complex data manifolds where A also affects correlation structure and variance.
In the Warped Swiss Roll problem, one group resides on a tightly coiled manifold and another on a loose one, illustrating structural warping beyond mean shift.

A model that aligns points in latent space can map distinct geometries to the same region without correcting the underlying structural warping, yielding representations that are statistically indistinguishable but geometrically unfaithful.
A representation is truly fair only if the geometry of the mapping from latent space to data space is invariant to the sensitive attribute.
CMF enforces geometric invariance by penalizing differences in the Pullback Metric Tensor (first-order geometry) of the decoder between factual and counterfactual pairs.
CMF enforces geometric invariance by penalizing differences in the Hessian (second-order geometry) of the decoder between factual and counterfactual pairs.
By enforcing constraints on the Jacobian and Hessian of the decoder, CMF ensures that distances and shapes in the latent space are preserved across demographic groups.
Counterfactual fairness and related SCM-based extensions encode fairness constraints at the level of predictions or representations, assuming a fixed geometry of the latent space.
These approaches ensure fairness primarily by controlling statistical dependencies rather than geometric or structural ones.
Fair representation learning methods typically treat embeddings as flat Euclidean spaces and evaluate fairness via prediction invariance or statistical independence, not geometric structure.

Work on Riemannian VAEs and geometry-aware generative models studies latent geometry as an inherent property of generative models, not as an object regularized for fairness under sensitive-attribute interventions.
To the authors' knowledge, no prior work examines how interventions on sensitive variables should preserve local geometric properties such as curvature, metric tensors, or geodesic flows.

CMF introduces a fairness criterion assessed at the level of geometric invariance rather than statistical independence or causal effects alone, unifying SCMs, differential geometry, and fair representation learning.
An SCM is assumed where observed features X are generated by an invertible mechanism from exogenous noise U and sensitive attribute A: X = f(U, A).
U represents intrinsic individual properties (e.g., talent, health), while A acts as a parameter that warps the manifestation of U into X.
The representation-learning goal is to recover a representation z approximately equal to U that is invariant to A.
An encoder-decoder (autoencoder) framework is used where the decoder D: Z -> X defines a smooth manifold M embedded in X.
The geometry of the latent space is characterized by the Pullback Metric Tensor G(z) = J_D(z)^T J_D(z), measuring how infinitesimal distances scale under the decoder map.
If the representation is fair, local manifold scaling should not depend on A, i.e., G(z_factual) ≈ G(z_counterfactual).
The metric tensor only captures first-order local linearities (stretching), motivating a second-order extension to capture bending and twisting.
Since the decoder is vector-valued, the curvature constraint is defined dimension-wise via the Hessian H_k(z) = ∇²D_k(z) for each output dimension k.
The model is trained to minimize L = L_task + L_align + λ_geo · L_geo, combining reconstruction/prediction loss, counterfactual alignment, and geometric regularization.
L_align = ||E(x) - E(xcf)||^2 enforces standard counterfactual alignment of encoder outputs.

L_geo is the novel contribution, combining the Frobenius-norm difference of metric tensors and a weighted sum of Frobenius-norm differences of per-dimension Hessians between factual and counterfactual latents.
Minimizing L_geo forces the model to learn a representation where the causal intervention do(A) acts as an isometry (preserving distances and shapes), not merely a translation.
A synthetic SCM is constructed with A in {0,1} and U ~ Uniform(0,4π), where observed features X in R^3 are generated via a frequency/radius parameter w = 1.0 + 0.5A.
The construction creates a manifold that is tighter and more twisted when A = 1, directly instantiating causal geometric warping by the sensitive attribute.
The synthetic dataset is used because the ground-truth geometry is known, enabling direct evaluation of geometric invariance.
ELU activations are used instead of ReLU because they are twice-differentiable (C² continuous), which is required for stable Hessian computation.
The Baseline autoencoder exhibits extremely high geometric errors (Metric Error 16.39, Curvature Error 4.32).
The high baseline geometric error confirms that the standard autoencoder learns to rely on the sensitive attribute A to reconstruct the warped manifold.
CMF reduces the Metric Error to 0.018, an approximately 1000x reduction relative to baseline.
CMF reduces the Curvature Error to 0.046, an approximately 100x reduction relative to baseline.
The large reductions in metric and curvature error demonstrate that CMF successfully creates a representation geometrically invariant to A.
Despite heavy geometric regularization, classification accuracy drops only negligibly from 1.000 (Baseline) to 0.995 (CMF).
The negligible accuracy drop proves that the intrinsic variable U, which predicts Y, was preserved by CMF's representation.
Reconstruction MSE increases from 0.070 (Baseline) to 0.754 (CMF), reflecting the cost of not using A as a reconstruction shortcut.

The MSE increase is expected: the Baseline 'cheats' by using A to perfectly reconstruct the warped data, while CMF must find a compromise manifold fitting both demographic groups without encoding the warping factor.
Together, the near-perfect fairness metrics with only a negligible accuracy drop and a moderate MSE increase quantify CMF's fairness-utility trade-off.
The Baseline latent space visualization is sharply divided by the sensitive attribute A (shown as Red/Blue clusters).
The CMF latent space visualization shows distributions overlapping across A while preserving intrinsic structure U.
The high accuracy score alongside distributional overlap confirms that CMF's alignment did not destroy the causal information required for prediction.
Fairness is formalized as a geometric invariance problem requiring stability of the Riemannian metric and curvature under causal intervention.
A differentiable loss function is proposed that aligns the Jacobian and Hessian of the generator across counterfactual worlds.
CMF is experimentally validated on a non-linear SCM, introducing Geometric Invariance Error (GIE) metrics to quantify disentanglement of structural bias.

If a scene can be decomposed into object-level representations, a model no longer needs to have seen a whole concept to recognize it, and such compositional structure should in principle generalize robustly to novel concepts and resist catastrophic forgetting.
Existing continual learners represent scenes as rigid global embeddings, discarding object structure entirely, which fails precisely on novel concepts.
Recent attempts to introduce slot attention into continual learning similarly fail to generalize to truly novel concepts.
Despite the theoretical promise of compositional structure, both global-embedding continual learners and existing slot-based continual learners fail to realize it in practice on novel concepts.
The authors trace the unrealized potential to two intertwining problems: how object representations are extracted (architecture), and how they are optimized (training objective).
For slot routing to isolate objects without supervision, the feature space must possess patch-level semantic geometry, such that patches of the same object naturally cluster together.

Through local self-distillation objectives, self-supervised models such as the DINO series and iBOT learn patch-level geometry in which patches from the same object naturally cluster together in feature space.

Vision-language models such as CLIP and OpenCLIP also develop spatially structured patch representations, as contrastive alignment with language implicitly encourages the encoder to ground visual features in semantically coherent regions.

Supervised Vision Transformers are trained with global cross-entropy for inter-class discrimination and never develop local geometric structure, leaving their patch tokens too noisy for reliable object decomposition.

Because slot routing requires patch-level clustering, and only self-supervised or vision-language backbones reliably provide it while supervised ViTs do not, self-supervised patch geometry becomes a strict structural prerequisite on which the proposed approach is built.
Even given correct self-supervised patch geometry, the slot representation architecture itself may re-introduce noise, so correct backbone geometry is necessary but not sufficient.
Standard slot attention takes the GRU hidden state sk as the slot representation, updated via a patch-wise weighted mean of value-projected tokens.
The recurrent GRU bottleneck encodes routing dynamics (how to suppress competing slots), intertwining spatial logic with visual content and corrupting the backbone's semantic structure.

To preserve the backbone's semantic geometry, COMPOSE discards the GRU state entirely and instead computes an L2-normalized attention-weighted aggregate directly from the frozen backbone features (Eq. 2).
Unlike the latent GRU state, the attention-weighted aggregate is a direct readout of patch features, bypassing the recurrent bottleneck and residing strictly within the backbone's semantic space.
Bypassing the recurrent bottleneck yields a substantial gain in slot purity on COCO validation, as reported in the appendix.
The foundational intuition in compositional learning is to match query and support scenes part-by-part, typically realized via a set-to-set nearest-neighbor Chamfer distance objective.

Under any part-level nearest-neighbor objective, the gradient direction applied to each slot is governed by slot-specific factors (its own projection and its matched target), so different slots receive structurally divergent gradients (Takeaway 1).

This slot-specific gradient pressure forces each slot to optimize its own local similarity independently, causing slots to over-specialize to recurring local patterns such as a specific texture or edge over many training episodes.

When confronted with a novel concept, over-specialized slots fail to find meaningful matches because their learned features are too narrowly tied to the training distribution, constituting the 'compositional trap'.

A holistic objective applied to the router-weighted averaged slot embedding propagates a shared gradient direction across all slots, since the router weights act as constants with respect to the projection head, so gradients differ only by a non-negative scalar per slot.

Because the holistic gradient direction is shared across slots (differing only by scalar weight), training holistically aligns the entire slot set toward a shared class identity rather than forcing local, part-level specialization.

To escape the compositional trap, COMPOSE strictly separates phases: holistic class-identity training (no part-level Chamfer gradients) and compositional, part-level matching only at gradient-free inference.
Training purely with a holistic objective introduces the complementary failure mode of slot collapse, where slots converge to redundant directions, requiring a redundancy-reduction mechanism.
VICReg enforces a per-dimension variance-hinge, which conflicts with the prototype CE objective because neural collapse drives within-class variability to zero, triggering the hinge.

A cross-correlation penalty on the off-diagonal entries of the standardized correlation matrix of slot projections (inspired by Barlow Twins) harmonizes with prototype learning by encouraging distributed feature utilization without rigid per-dimension variance constraints (Eq. 3).

Because CE is invariant under orthogonal rebasings of the projection head, every CE-optimum admits a free orthogonal rebasing that is simultaneously cross-correlation-optimal, so decorrelation along this direction incurs no CE pushback (Appendix G.2.1).

Spectral whitening has a strictly positive lower bound on L2-normalized embeddings, and variance-hinge, though nominally feasible via uniform scaling, is dynamically antagonistic to CE in the tight-cluster regime, unlike the cross-correlation penalty.

Given that the cross-correlation penalty is theoretically compatible with prototype CE while variance-hinge and whitening alternatives are antagonistic, COMPOSE adopts the cross-correlation penalty λd‖C−I‖²F as its redundancy-reduction term in the training loss.

Phase I updates only a trainable router and projection head on top of a frozen ViT backbone and frozen slot attention, framed as attention-based multiple instance learning pooling over the K slots (Eq. 4).

The projection head W2 is applied per-slot to produce unit-norm slot embeddings and applied to the router-weighted aggregate to produce a holistic embedding, with linearity ensuring the holistic embedding equivalently aggregates the per-slot projections (Eqs. 5-6).

The router and projection head are jointly optimized using a holistic prototype cross-entropy loss on cosine similarity to class prototypes, plus the cross-correlation redundancy-reduction penalty, with no part-level Chamfer matching applied (Eq. 7).
In Phase II, all network weights are frozen and no gradient reaches any component; inference instead exploits the preserved slot geometry learned in Phase I.

Before matching, slot features are centered by subtracting the per-image slot mean, removing shared background/illumination biases while preserving inter-slot differences that carry compositional structure (Eq. 8).
The final score blends a holistic cosine-similarity score from Phase I embeddings with a bidirectional Chamfer compositional-matching score over top-κ centered slots, weighted by γ (Eqs. 9-11).

By freezing the backbone and slot attention across both phases, COMPOSE prevents representation drift and strictly bounds catastrophic forgetting, in addition to enabling novel-concept generalization.
On CGQA, other meta-trained methods degrade on the non-compositional (noc) split, with TransSlot reaching 69.68% and MetaProtoNet 79.32%.
Even CoFiMA, which fully fine-tunes DINOv2 in about 4 hours per dataset, trails COMPOSE by 2.17 percentage points on noc, despite its much larger training cost.

Because full fine-tuning still underperforms COMPOSE's frozen-backbone approach on noc, this confirms that fine-tuning does not by itself recover the structural invariances needed for novel-concept generalization, supporting the paper's architectural diagnosis.
COMPOSE achieves 94.14 ± 0.64% accuracy on the unseen-concept split of CGQA with Ha = 92.92, exceeding all compared zero-shot, offline-meta, and PTM-based CIL baselines (Table 1).
Swapping the frozen backbone while holding all other COMPOSE components fixed shows noc rising monotonically with pretraining quality: 88.69% (DINOv1) → 90.09% (iBOT) → 94.14% (DINOv2) (Table 2).

The monotonic relationship between backbone pretraining quality and noc accuracy empirically confirms that noc is sensitive to how densely the backbone encodes spatial object identity, validating the paper's central claim that self-supervised patch geometry is a structural prerequisite.
On FSCIL, COMPOSE reduces catastrophic forgetting dramatically relative to Comp-FSCIL on CIFAR-100, with forgetting falling from 27.91% to 3.54%.

COMPOSE achieves the best AA on CIFAR-100 FSCIL (84.02%) and competitive AA on CUB-200/miniImageNet, and the highest AA on CIFAR-100 CIL (91.36%) and ImageNet-A (79.55%), with competitive results on ImageNet-R.
Because the backbone remains frozen throughout continual training, representation drift is eliminated as the primary source of catastrophic forgetting across all standard CL benchmarks.

The Chamfer-trained variant COMPOSE-CT shows higher forgetting than COMPOSE, confirming that training with part-level Chamfer matching trades compositional retention for per-class router stability, reinforcing the case for the phase-separated design.
Replacing holistic training with Chamfer-based training (COMPOSE-CT) drops noc by 2.51 pp on CGQA, confirming that Chamfer matching should be restricted to inference.

Removing the redundancy-reduction (cross-correlation) term causes a larger noc drop than removing Chamfer-avoidance alone (−5.56 pp on CGQA), establishing decorrelation as the primary driver of noc performance.
On CGQA, removing holistic scoring collapses Ha by 5.91 pp and removing Chamfer scoring drops it by 1.78 pp, showing both blended-score components are necessary.
On COBJ, removing inference-time Chamfer scoring marginally improves noc (+0.20 pp), confirming holistic scoring alone suffices under noisier slot decomposition on natural images.

Replacing the SCA-refined attention-weighted slot aggregates with raw GRU states drops noc by 3.64 pp (CGQA) and 7.73 pp (COBJ), with Ha dropping correspondingly, confirming the representation-pollution diagnosis.

The larger COBJ degradation from using raw GRU states than from removing decorrelation shows that on natural images, slot representation quality is the dominant bottleneck, exceeding even the contribution of redundancy reduction seen on CGQA.

HyperTransformer (HT) is a Transformer-based hypernetwork that meta-learns from few-shot episodes and generates the weights of a smaller, specialized CNN directly from the support set, decoupling the domain-knowledge model (Transformer) from the learner (CNN).
When there is only a single task, the continual few-shot learning problem reduces to a standard few-shot learning problem, which HT is already effective at solving.
To extend HT to a continual sequence of tasks, the paper proposes recursively re-using the CNN weights generated for previous tasks as input to the HT when generating weights for the next task.

Because the previous task's generated weights are fed back in as input, the generated CNN weights themselves act as a representation of previously learned tasks, with the HT trained to update these weights so the new task is learned without forgetting past tasks.

This weight-reuse approach is different from most continual learning algorithms, which typically rely on replay buffers, weight regularization, or task-dependent architectural changes, requiring the least additional conceptual overhead since it imposes no explicit anti-forgetting constraint.
The recursive weight-reuse mechanism, applied to the HT architecture, constitutes the proposed Continual HyperTransformer (CHT).

For each task t, the CHT generates weights theta_t as a function a_psi of the current support set S(t) and the previous task's weights theta_(t-1), such that theta_t is suited for all tasks 0 through t.
When learning from task t, the learner does not have access to the support set of past tasks and must rely solely on the input weights theta_(t-1) as its source of information about previous tasks.

At each step t, the loss J_t(psi) sums the individual losses of the generated weights theta_t evaluated on the query sets of every task 0 through t, and the overall training objective sums J_t over all steps up to T.

The CHT generates a sequence of weights {theta_tau} such that each is suited for all tasks up to that point (theta_0 works only on task 0, theta_1 on tasks 0-1, etc.), enabling a 'preemptive' approach where the model can be run for any number of tasks up to T without needing the exact final task count specified in advance.

Because the HT's parameters do not depend on task information and only take the weights theta and support set as input, the CHT can operate as a recurrent system, extending to generate weights for additional tasks beyond those it was originally trained on.

The original HT used cross-entropy loss, which is unsuited for continual learning because the number of classes it predicts is tied to the number of parameters in the head layer of the generated weights.

Because more tasks mean more total classes, using cross-entropy would require the CNN architecture to be adjusted as the number of tasks increases, violating the design principle of a fixed, recurrent CHT architecture.

An alternative of fixing the head layer to K-way classification and only predicting within-task class information (domain-incremental learning) causes classes with the same label but different tasks to collide in the embedding space, especially since labels are randomly assigned per episode.
The Appendix shows that this fixed-head, within-task approach's accuracy decreases dramatically as the number of tasks increases, becoming impractical even for just two tasks.
Coming up with a fixed arrangement of T*K points is also suboptimal since it is not possible to place that many points equidistant from each other in a fixed-dimensional space for large T.

A more elegant solution is to learn the location of class prototypes directly from the support set using a prototypical loss, computing each class/task prototype as the average embedding of its support samples.

Prototypes support two prediction modes: task-incremental (softmax over ell-2 distances to prototypes within the known task) and class-incremental (softmax over distances to prototypes across all classes for all seen tasks).

Empirically, CHT models trained with the class-incremental objective perform well in both class-incremental and task-incremental settings, while models trained with the task-incremental objective perform well only in the task-incremental setting and rarely outperform class-incremental-trained models.

Because true continual learning should not reuse support samples after a task is processed, prototypes are frozen after being computed rather than recomputed at every subsequent step, with only marginal performance difference compared to recomputing.
