MAML identifies initial weights phi_0 such that any task tau, adapted via a few gradient descent steps from phi_0, reaches a task-specific local optimum of the task loss.

If any label assignment in training tasks is equally likely, it is natural for the initial model to not prefer any particular label, motivating choosing label-independent initial logit weights W_0, b_0.

Expanding the model around phi_0, the lowest-order label-dependent correction is given purely by adjustments to the final logits layer (delta W, delta b), i.e., in lowest order the model only adjusts the final layer to adapt the pretrained embedding to a new task.

Deriving a single gradient-descent step on cross-entropy loss for the logit weight and bias shows that the resulting label assignment effectively relies on computing a dot-product of the embedding with per-class 'prototypes' -- the same averaged-embedding quantity used in the prototypical loss.

Because the first-order MAML update on cross-entropy loss naturally produces prototype-like class representations, the prototypical loss approach can be viewed as a special case of a simple one-step MAML-like learning algorithm.

Comparing weights generated from all four batches at once, from two recursive halves, and from four fully sequential recursive steps, all three configurations achieve statistically indistinguishable test accuracy (67.9%, 68.0%, 68.3%, within +/-0.4% error).

HT trained with just the first batch or first two batches (i.e., without the recursive mechanism providing later batches) performs significantly worse (56.2% and 62.9% respectively) than the full sequential recursive processing.

Because sequential recursive updating matches performance achievable only by processing all samples in a single pass with the original HT, this validates that the proposed weight-update mechanism can incrementally absorb information from multiple batches as effectively as seeing them all at once.
For task-incremental learning on Omniglot, no signs of catastrophic forgetting were observed for CHT.

CHT exhibits positive backward knowledge transfer on Omniglot: performance on earlier tasks (e.g., theta_1) is often higher than on theta_0, and theta_2 higher still, with overall performance increasing as the number of trained tasks T increases.

On tieredImageNet, results were better than the ConstPN baseline and performance for every training task remained roughly stable across generated weights (no catastrophic forgetting), but the positive backward-transfer effect was less pronounced than on Omniglot.
CHT consistently outperformed the ConstPN (task-agnostic, no-memory) baseline, particularly when applied to the same or fewer tasks than it was trained on.

Although CHT accuracy decreased slightly when applied to more tasks than it was trained on, the decrease was not significant; even a model trained on only T=3 tasks still outperformed ConstPN when extended to one or two additional tasks.

In the class-incremental setting, accuracy decreases as more tasks are included in the prediction, which is expected since the generated CNN size stays fixed while the number of classes to predict grows.

For Omniglot in the class-incremental setting, positive backward transfer again occurs (CHT models trained on more tasks perform better overall), and for a fixed trained T, performance across different evaluated task-ranges is comparable, demonstrating CHT's preemptive property.

For T=5 on Omniglot, CHT outperforms even the MergedHT baseline (which has access to all task information from the start), suggesting that having more classes to jointly classify makes the learning problem harder for the original HT's image embeddings, particularly evident in tieredImageNet where MergedHT's performance falls below 60% even for just two tasks.
MAML++ performed well on the first task but was unable to retain knowledge for subsequent tasks due to catastrophic forgetting.
Pretraining-based methods and EWC were not able to learn sufficiently well even the first task, because they could not learn effectively from few examples.

Table 1 shows CHT achieves 87.2% on task 0 and maintains 69.3% by task range 0-4, far exceeding Pretraining, MAML++, and EWC at every task range, since CHT combines few-shot competence with resistance to forgetting that these baselines individually lack.

When tasks are drawn from different distributions and image domains, the task-agnostic ConstPN approach is expected to suffer in accuracy because it must find a single universal representation that works well across all image domains.
In contrast to ConstPN, CHT could adapt its sample representations differently for different detected image domains, potentially leading to improved performance under cross-domain heterogeneity.

Using a multi-domain generator spanning six datasets (Omniglot, Caltech101, CaltechBirds2011, Cars196, OxfordFlowers102, StanfordDogs), CHT outperforms ConstPN by close to 3 percentage points on combined tasks, a larger gap than observed in the single-domain Omniglot/tieredImageNet experiments, confirming CHT's superior adaptation to multi-domain task distributions.
Differential privacy obscures client updates with randomized noise, but stronger privacy requires larger noise magnitudes that significantly degrade model performance.
MPC-based secure aggregation protocols cryptographically ensure the server learns only aggregated results, but often incur substantial computational and communication overhead.
Motivated by the limitations of using DP or MPC alone, the paper proposes DDP-SA, integrating client-side local differential privacy with full-threshold additive secret sharing.
DDP-SA achieves formal (epsilon, delta) differential privacy at the client level while cryptographically hiding individual updates from both the server and all communication paths.
DDP-SA is designed with n clients and m intermediate servers to support scalability, achieving linear communication complexity and generalizing to arbitrary m.
Clients first perturb their gradients with calibrated Laplace noise, then encode the noisy gradients into additive secret shares distributed among intermediate servers.
Intermediate servers aggregate the received shares and forward only the combined result to the parameter server.
The parameter server reconstructs only the aggregated noisy gradient and updates the global model, never any client-specific contribution.
The two-stage protection mechanism ensures no single compromised server or communication channel can reveal any information about individual client updates.
Additive secret sharing splits a secret into shares such that each share is uniformly random and reveals no information about the secret on its own.

Under the semi-honest model, any strict subset of additive shares is uniformly random and independent of the secret, so an adversary controlling fewer than all servers learns nothing about any individual client update.

Lemma 1 formalizes that mutual information between the client update and any strict subset of its ASS shares is zero, and reconstruction probability decreases exponentially in the number of servers m under independent compromise.
Confidentiality fails only if an adversary controls all m intermediate servers or observes all share-carrying communication links simultaneously.
Theorem 1 states that DDP-SA, applying an (epsilon, delta)-LDP mechanism per client before ASS-based secure aggregation, satisfies (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy end-to-end.
The proof of Theorem 1 relies on post-processing invariance of DP, since ASS-based aggregation is a deterministic function applied to the noisy gradients.
Corollary 1 states that the privacy budget of DDP-SA equals that of the underlying LDP mechanism, since secure aggregation via ASS introduces zero additional privacy loss.
ASS provides information-theoretic security since any strict subset of secret shares is uniformly random and independent of the underlying secret.
Theorem 2 provides basic and advanced composition bounds for the cumulative (epsilon, delta) privacy loss of DDP-SA run over T training rounds.
The advanced composition bound gives a significantly tighter total epsilon than the basic composition bound when T is large (e.g., ~24.09 vs 100 for T=1000, epsilon=0.1).
To manage cumulative privacy loss across rounds, uniform allocation divides the total budget equally, while adaptive allocation assigns more budget to early rounds via exponential decay.
The intermediate server layer converts n client uplinks into m intermediate server uplinks, reducing the parameter server's ingress bandwidth from 4nd to 4md.
Because m is much smaller than n, DDP-SA improves scalability compared to LDP, enabling scalability to many clients and long training horizons.
MPC and DDP-SA upload 3m parameters per client since each gradient component is split into m secret shares, so communication cost scales linearly with m.

The computational overhead breakdown shows gradient clipping (scaling O(d)) dominates per-client per-round computation, accounting for over 92% of total time, more than secret sharing or noise addition.
DDP-SA incurs slightly higher communication and computation overhead than standalone LDP or MPC, but the overhead remains acceptable and controllable for practical settings.
DDP-SA achieves a higher test R2 (0.9666) than standalone LDP (0.9357), while both are slightly lower than No-Private/MPC (0.9999).
For a fixed target accuracy, DDP-SA can operate with a smaller privacy budget than LDP, indicating stronger privacy protection at equal utility.
MPC can be viewed as a special case of DDP-SA where the privacy budget is effectively infinite (no noise added) and clipping has no practical effect.
Because MPC is a degenerate special case of DDP-SA with no noise, DDP-SA can also provide stronger privacy protection than pure MPC.
Adding noise to client updates under LDP masks the contribution of individual records, mitigating membership inference attacks.
Perturbing gradients before aggregation hides fine-grained patterns that might reveal sensitive properties of training data, reducing property inference attack effectiveness.
Secure aggregation ensures model updates visible to the parameter server are aggregated and not attributable to any single client, making training data or label inference harder.

By combining local differential privacy with secure aggregation, DDP-SA mitigates a wide range of privacy inference attacks, including membership, property, training-data, and class representative attacks.

Adversarial examples are inputs perturbed by small, carefully crafted noise, and their transferability across models enables black-box attacks, making defenses challenging in practice.

While adversarial training is widely adopted to improve robustness, it is studied under white-box assumptions that ignore realistic conditions where attackers operate with different architectures or datasets.

Because AT is predominantly evaluated under unrealistic white-box, matched-distribution assumptions, this gap limits understanding of AT's practical value in deployment conditions where attacker and defender differ.
Deepfake detection is particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbation because it relies on subtle spatial and frequency artifacts, which adversarial perturbations can easily disrupt.

The general gap in understanding AT's real-world value, combined with deepfake detection's specific reliance on fragile spatial/frequency artifacts, motivates a systematic evaluation of adversarial training for deepfake detectors under realistic attacker-defender mismatch scenarios.
The DUMB framework formalized attacker-defender mismatch scenarios along dataset source, model architecture, and class balance axes.
DUMBer extended the DUMB framework to adversarially trained models, revealing significant gaps in robustness under transfer-based attacks.
The DUMB and DUMBer frameworks offer systematic evaluation protocols for transferability but have not yet been applied to deepfake detection.
Beyond the DUMB/DUMBer gap specifically, limited research more broadly has assessed adversarial training for deepfake detectors under transfer-based attacks and dataset shifts.

Because DUMB/DUMBer's systematic mismatch-evaluation methodology exists but is unapplied to deepfakes, and because deepfake-specific AT robustness under transfer/shift is otherwise underexplored, this work extends the DUMB/DUMBer methodology to the deepfake detection domain.
The DUMB taxonomy formalizes attacker-defender mismatch scenarios along three axes: Dataset soUrce, Model architecture, and class Balance.

The paper adopts a balanced class configuration throughout, simplifying the DUMB notation to the most practically relevant and interpretable four cases varying only dataset and model architecture: C1 (white-box), C3 (cross-model), C5 (cross-dataset), C7 (cross-dataset & cross-model).

Transfer-based attacks require no access to target parameters and only a single application, closely reflecting realistic threat scenarios, unlike query-heavy decision-based or score-based black-box attacks; this is the focus of the study's attack setting.

Attack Success Rate (ASR) measures the fraction of attacked samples misclassified after attack, and Attack Mitigation Rate (AMR, Eq. 1) measures the relative reduction in ASR after adversarial training, together quantifying both raw attack effectiveness and AT's protective benefit.

Combining the four mismatch cases, transfer-based attack focus, and the ASR/AMR metrics yields the full evaluation protocol: 5 detectors × 3 attacks × 2 datasets × 12 training strategies × multiple surrogate/test-set combinations, totaling 1920 evaluations (Section 3.5).

The main challenge of adversarial training lies in enhancing robustness to adversarial examples without significantly compromising accuracy on clean data, a trade-off highlighted in prior work and addressed by regularization approaches like TRADES.
Standard adversarial training typically relies on a single attack such as FGSM, PGD, or a variant, with evaluations usually restricted to white-box settings.

Relying on a single attack during AT provides robustness against that specific attack but is susceptible to catastrophic overfitting, which reduces the resilience of retrained models to unseen attacks.
To address single-attack overfitting, prior methods vary the perturbation budget adaptively or via curriculum, or use ensemble strategies combining multiple attacks such as PGD and FGSM in training.

Building on the known limitation of single-attack AT and prior diversity-based mitigations, this paper defines and tests eleven adversarial training strategies (single, dual, triple/ensemble, and surrogate-diversified) to assess whether increased diversity improves robustness specifically under the DUMB mismatch scenarios.

PGD consistently achieved the highest ASR in all settings, with near-perfect success in white-box (C1: 99.6%) and substantial transferability in cross-model (C3: 89.8%) and cross-dataset (C5: 65.1%; C7: 66.7%) cases (Table 1).

FGSM, while less effective than PGD, still showed significant transferability especially in white-box and cross-model settings, and FPBA, though especially effective against frequency-based detectors, had lower overall transferability than PGD (Table 1).

The ASR remains non-negligible, around 50%, in cross-dataset scenarios (C5, C7), indicating attackers do not require access to the defender's data distribution to significantly degrade detection performance.

Because attack success persists substantially even under severe architecture and dataset mismatch, transfer-based adversarial attacks are confirmed as a credible threat under realistic conditions, and PGD's especially high transferability highlights the limitations of defenses that focus solely on white-box robustness.
All AT strategies maintained high clean performance, with AUC exceeding 94% on FF++ and robust performance on Celeb-DF-V2, ranging from 81.9% to 82.9% (Table 2).

No catastrophic overfitting was observed in nominal performance, even when employing multi-attack or multi-surrogate training strategies, unlike the failure mode associated with single-attack AT described in Section 2.3.
The ensemble and surrogate-based AT strategies preserved nominal performance, with limited fluctuations compared to the Base (no-AT) baseline.

Because high AUC is preserved across all AT strategies and both datasets, this supports the practical deployment of adversarial training in real-world systems, satisfying the basic requirement that a defense not sacrifice nominal performance.
AT with a single strong attack such as PGD yields substantial ASR reductions in-distribution, e.g. reducing C1 ASR from 99.6% to 20.2% (Table 3).

Increasing diversity of adversarial examples brings further gains: Ensemble AT achieves the lowest C1 ASR (1.1%) and strong C3 reduction, and surrogate-based AT (PGD_surr, Ens_surr) generally outperforms single-attack counterparts, with an exception for FPBA in C1/C5.

Because broader exposure to adversarial perturbations during training reduces ASR further than single-attack AT, particularly and most pronouncedly in cross-model configuration C3, this confirms that diversity in AT enhances the model's ability to generalize to unseen attacks and transfer scenarios in-distribution.

The benefits of AT diversity diminish under cross-dataset (C5) and cross-dataset & cross-model (C7) conditions; even Ens_Surr, the most diverse strategy, yields only modest ASR reductions and remains above 50% ASR in some cases.

In certain cross-dataset configurations such as FGSM, FPBA, Ens, and Surr, negative AMR values are observed, indicating that adversarial training can inadvertently increase vulnerability rather than reduce it.

The authors hypothesize the observed negative AMR values can be attributed to models overfitting on the adversarial artifacts distribution seen during training, leading them to be less accurate on perturbations from other (unseen dataset) distributions.

The combination of diminished gains, near-50%+ residual ASR, and outright negative AMR under cross-dataset mismatch shows that the robustness conferred by adversarial training is highly sensitive to the alignment between training and evaluation distributions, revealing a critical limitation of AT alone.

Leave-one-out ensemble AT shows that omitting any single attack consistently increases ASR across all DUMB cases, with omitting FPBA (leaving PGD_FGSM) causing especially higher cross-dataset ASR (C5: 64.1%, C7: 66.2%), highlighting the unique value of frequency-domain-specific attacks in training coverage.

Surrogate-based AT strategies demonstrate that leveraging adversarial examples from multiple model architectures further enhances robustness versus single-surrogate counterparts, particularly cross-model and cross-dataset, but surrogate diversity alone cannot fully compensate for distributional shift between training and evaluation data.

DeepSeekMath uses an iterative pipeline: train a fastText classifier on a seed corpus (OpenWebMath), recall math web pages from deduplicated Common Crawl, discover math-related domains, manually annotate math URL paths, and add newly found pages back to the seed corpus.

After four iterations of data collection, the pipeline yields 35.5M mathematical web pages totaling 120B tokens, at which point collection is stopped because ~98% of data was already collected in the prior iteration.
Web pages containing 10-gram (or 3-gram for short texts) overlaps with English/Chinese evaluation benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, AGIEval) are filtered out of the training corpus.
DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B trained on the DeepSeekMath Corpus outperforms models trained on MathPile, OpenWebMath, and Proof-Pile-2 across GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, and BBH.

The DeepSeekMath Corpus is several times larger than prior math corpora and contains substantial English and Chinese content, improving performance in both languages, whereas prior English-centric corpora show limited or negative Chinese performance.

DeepSeekMath-Base 7B (initialized from DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B and trained on the corpus) achieves 64.2% on GSM8K and 36.2% on MATH, leading all open-source base models on 8 English/Chinese benchmarks.
DeepSeekMath-Base 7B is competitive with the much larger closed-source Minerva 540B model on mathematical benchmarks.

The comparable performance of a 7B model against a 540B model indicates that model scale alone does not determine mathematical reasoning capability; high-quality pre-training data is also a key factor.
Two-stage training with code tokens before math tokens significantly enhances the ability to solve GSM8K/MATH problems using Python compared to general-token pretraining.
Code training also moderately improves chain-of-thought (non-tool) mathematical reasoning and boosts the efficiency of subsequent math training.

Mixing code and math tokens in one-stage training mitigates catastrophic forgetting of coding ability but compromises non-tool mathematical reasoning, plausibly due to limited model capacity at 1.3B scale.
DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B and DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B were separately trained on MathPile and ArXiv-RedPajama arXiv corpora.
Training on arXiv-only corpora shows no notable improvement, and sometimes deterioration, across quantitative reasoning, multiple-choice, and formal math benchmarks.

PPO requires training a value function typically as large as the policy model, creating substantial memory and computational burden, complicated further because usually only the last token receives a reward score.
GRPO obviates the need for a separate value function by using the average reward of a group of sampled outputs for the same question as the baseline.
By removing the value model, GRPO significantly reduces the training resources required compared to PPO.
The group-relative way GRPO computes advantages aligns with the comparative nature of reward models, which are typically trained on pairwise/group comparisons of outputs to the same question.

Instead of folding a KL penalty into the per-token reward as PPO does, GRPO adds the KL divergence between policy and reference model directly to the loss, avoiding complications in advantage estimation.
Outcome-supervised GRPO normalizes the group's rewards and assigns the same normalized reward as the advantage to every token in an output.
Process-supervised GRPO scores each reasoning step and assigns a token's advantage as the sum of normalized rewards from subsequent steps, providing finer-grained supervision.

In iterative GRPO, the reward model is continually retrained on new samples from the policy (with a replay mechanism retaining historical data), and the reference model is periodically reset to the current policy.
GRPO is applied to DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B using ~144K chain-of-thought GSM8K/MATH questions, excluding other SFT data to isolate the effect of RL on out-of-domain benchmarks.
GRPO improves DeepSeekMath-Instruct from 82.9% to 88.2% on GSM8K and from 46.8% to 51.7% on MATH.
GRPO also improves out-of-domain performance, e.g. CMATH improves from 84.6% to 88.8%, despite RL training data being restricted to GSM8K/MATH.
DeepSeekMath-RL 7B surpasses all open-source models from 7B to 70B and the majority of closed-source models on the evaluated benchmarks.
SFT, RFT, DPO, Online RFT, PPO, and GRPO can all be described within a single gradient formulation composed of a data source, a reward function, and an algorithm producing a gradient coefficient.
Online RFT significantly outperforms offline RFT on GSM8K and MATH, with the advantage growing in later training stages as the policy diverges further from the original SFT model.

GRPO outperforms Online RFT because it adjusts its gradient coefficient based on the reward model's magnitude (differential reinforcement/penalization), whereas Online RFT uniformly reinforces all correct responses.
GRPO with process supervision (GRPO+PS) shows superior performance to GRPO with outcome supervision (GRPO+OS), indicating the benefit of fine-grained, step-aware gradient coefficients.
Across two rounds of iterative RL, performance improves further, with the largest gain observed at the first iteration.
Evaluating Maj@K and Pass@K for Instruct vs RL models shows RL improves Maj@K accuracy but not Pass@K accuracy on GSM8K and MATH.

Because RL boosts Maj@K but not Pass@K, the improvement is attributed to making correct responses more likely to surface from the TopK candidates (a more robust output distribution), rather than to an enhancement of the model's fundamental reasoning capability.
Traditional deep learning frameworks assume all pertinent training data is centralized under the governance of a singular, trustworthy entity.

In real-world industrial contexts, data is often distributed across multiple independent parties where a central trusted authority is impractical, and legal restrictions (CCPA, GDPR) plus business competition further limit data sharing.

Federated learning emerged as a promising collaborative learning infrastructure where participants retain data locally, training models locally and sharing only model parameters with a central server that aggregates and redistributes updates.

Even though raw data stays local, adversaries may still infer sensitive data from shared model parameters — raw data content can be inverted from parameters, or membership information can be inferred.

Methods based on homomorphic encryption or secure multiparty computation (MPC) require significant computational overhead and do not protect the final output of the computation, leaving them vulnerable to inference attacks.

Differential privacy (DP) is one state-of-the-art paradigm to mitigate privacy risks in FL; adding proper DP noise during local training or to uploaded parameters can prevent unintentional leakage (e.g., via membership inference attacks).
As the volume of publications on differentially private federated learning continues to grow, summarizing and organizing this research has become both urgent and challenging.
Despite existing surveys on DP-FL, they do not provide a comprehensive, technical, and systematic analysis of differential privacy within the federated learning context.
Existing taxonomies have not adequately considered the objects and level of privacy protection provided by various DP models in federated learning.

Prior classification approaches based on the presence of a centralized trusted server lack precision, because FL is inherently a composite framework (e.g., cross-silo clients may also maintain local servers), so characterizing scenarios lacking a trusted central aggregator solely as LDP is overly simplistic.
This gap motivates a new taxonomy of DP-FL based on the definition and guarantee of various DP models (DP, LDP, shuffle model) and federated scenarios, rather than server-trust assumptions alone.
The survey classifies works into Horizontal FL, Vertical FL, and Transfer FL based on how data is partitioned among participants, encompassing all federated learning scenarios.

Although most prior work on DP for FL has been conducted in Horizontal FL, as more privacy issues are exposed in vertical and transfer FL, research on DP models in those settings is becoming increasingly important.

For DP and the shuffle model, works are further categorized into sample-level and client-level based on the definition of neighboring datasets, corresponding to the protected objects (LDP lacks this neighboring-dataset concept).

Rigorous differentiation of DP models based on definitions and privacy guarantees clarifies the protection subjects of different DP models and enhances understanding of their associated implementation methods.
The main difference between DP and LDP lies in their definitions: DP relies on neighboring datasets as input, while LDP has no concept of neighboring datasets.

LDP can be derived from DP when the input datasets are taken to be single-record datasets, since any two single-record datasets are trivially neighbors; this makes LDP a stronger condition requiring the mechanism to satisfy DP for any two domain values.
LDP can comply with (imply) DP, but the reverse does not hold true.

The shuffle model adds a trusted shuffler between server and clients; each client satisfies LDP facing the shuffler, and the shuffled data (now forming a dataset with a neighboring-dataset concept) satisfies DP facing the server.

Thanks to anonymity from shuffling, each user's privacy benefits from both local randomization and randomness from other clients, yielding a smaller centralized privacy loss ε_c than the local budget ε_l — a phenomenon called privacy amplification, roughly O(√n) smaller.

Sample-level DP (SL-DP): two datasets are neighboring if they differ in a single sample; the goal is to bound the influence of any single sample/record on the learning outcome distribution, generally assuming a semi-honest (honest-but-curious) server, with independent per-client privacy budgets.

The most mainstream approach to implementing SL-DP is executing Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD) on each client: per-sample gradient clipping bounds sensitivity, then Gaussian noise scaled to the clipping bound is added to the batch-averaged gradient before the descent step.

Client-level DP (CL-DP): two datasets are neighboring if they differ in a single client/device; the goal is to limit the impact of any single client on the aggregation result distribution, generally assuming a fully honest server acting as data owner.

SL-DP and LDP are often confused because both assume a semi-honest server, but they differ: SL-DP has a neighboring-dataset concept requiring per-sample clipping across local iterations, whereas LDP's neighboring datasets degenerate to any two inputs, with sensitivity from directly clipping model parameters and privacy loss occurring only at upload time; LDP mechanisms generally achieve SL-DP protection but not vice versa (except the rare single-data-point case).

LDP and CL-DP-with-Secure-Aggregation both add local noise but at different scales (e.g., Lap(0, ε/Δf) for LDP vs. Lap(0, ε/(KΔf)) for CL-DP with K clients), so CL-DP-with-SA's local noise, though nonzero, provides far weaker local protection than true ε-LDP.
CL-DP as described requires the server to be trusted to correctly aggregate client updates, which is itself a strong assumption.

To eliminate reliance on a trusted central authority, recent studies combine DP techniques with secure aggregation: each client adds noise locally, encrypts, and sends to the server, which aggregates, so the aggregate noise level across clients ensures the encrypted model satisfies CL-DP.
Secure aggregation relies on modular arithmetic and cannot be directly compatible with continuous noise mechanisms (Laplace, Gaussian) traditionally used for DP.

This incompatibility motivated researchers to design discrete noise-addition mechanisms (binomial, discrete Gaussian, Skellam, Poisson Binomial) integrable with secure aggregation, each addressing limitations of the prior mechanism (e.g., binomial noise only achieves approximate DP; discrete Gaussian isn't closed under addition; Skellam's noise is unbounded requiring modular clipping bias; Poisson Binomial is unbiased and bounded).

LDP-HFL can be viewed as a mean estimation problem based on LDP, since each model parameter represents a high-dimensional continuous data point that each client perturbs locally before the server aggregates.

Directly applying LDP mean estimation to FL faces obstacles because model-parameter dimensionality is extremely high, and as dimension increases, the privacy budget allocated per dimension decreases, leading to exponential increase in statistical variance.

One family of solutions uses parameter shuffling (splitting parameters by layer and shuffling within each layer) to break cross-dimension associations, avoiding privacy-budget division across dimensions under the independence assumption — though this does not itself constitute the formal shuffle model's privacy amplification.

A second family selects or samples a subset of important dimensions (e.g., top-k by update magnitude) to perturb, rather than perturbing all dimensions, trading off convergence speed for reduced noise.
Referring to the HFL taxonomy, the shuffle model within HFL is divided into two classes: client-level (shuffle CL-DP) and sample-level (shuffle SL-DP).
In shuffle CL-DP, each user randomizes local updates with LDP, and the aggregated updates through shuffling satisfy DP; researchers typically set δ_l=0 for the local LDP budget.

In shuffle SL-DP, the neighboring-dataset definition for the resulting DP analysis is based on samples rather than clients; a straightforward approach perturbs each sample's update separately before aggregating and shuffling.
The amount of work on DP models in VFL and TFL is far less than in HFL, though as more privacy issues are exposed in VFL and TFL, research there is becoming increasingly important.

In VFL, parties share sample IDs but hold different feature spaces (one party typically holding labels); joint training poses privacy threats because both extracted features and gradient-derived label information can potentially be inferred by the respective other party.

Consequently, DP-VFL research splits into work protecting features (perturbing the feature extractor's output before transmission to the server) and work protecting labels (perturbing gradients or labels themselves, since the server/label-holder needs label access to compute gradients), with some work protecting both sides simultaneously.

TFL applies when clients (source domains) and a server (target domain) have limited or no overlap in features or samples; knowledge distillation is commonly used to transfer knowledge from local 'teacher' models to an unlabeled public/target dataset via aggregated predictions.

Because attackers can exploit teacher models' output predictions to attack original data, DP is incorporated into the aggregation of teacher predictions, originating with the PATE algorithm and its subsequent refinements (Gaussian-mechanism/RDP tightening, multi-client extensions, LDP variants without a trusted aggregator).

In graph-data FL, GNN message passing makes a node's embedding depend on both itself and neighboring nodes, so accurately measuring this dependency is crucial for determining sensitivity (which drives DP noise scale), but doing so is hard.

Methods addressing this either avoid direct dependency measurement by perturbing the graph structure/embeddings outside standard GNN training (at the cost of usability, since perturbation isn't tailored to GNNs), or explicitly measure node dependency level (e.g., bounding in-degree via sampling) and apply gradient perturbation via DP-SGD, at the cost of high sensitivity that grows with GNN depth.

A tight upper bound on convergence provides theoretical assurance of rapid convergence and enables analyzing how hyperparameters affect convergence speed, guiding tuning or new optimization algorithm design.
Compared to standard HFL, DP-HFL convergence analysis must consider the effects of clipping and noise addition, making it more challenging to obtain a relatively tight upper bound.

Existing convergence analyses for DP-HFL algorithms either make strong assumptions about the objective function/gradients (e.g., Bounded Gradient, Bounded Variance) or remain at a loose O(1/ε) bound, leaving tighter, assumption-light convergence analysis as an open future direction.

In many scenarios a client (e.g., a hospital) contains many users, and an individual user may contribute multiple samples/records (e.g., a patient with multiple medical records), which neither SL-DP nor CL-DP directly captures.

User-level DP is defined so that two datasets are neighboring if they differ in all samples from a single user, aiming to bound the influence of any single user's entire contribution on the learning outcome distribution.

Allowing users to contribute many samples (to protect minority high-contribution outliers) may introduce excessive noise, while restricting user contribution keeps noise lower but discards surplus data and introduces bias; this field remains underexplored in FL specifically.
The objects directly protected by DP-FL vary based on the DP model and neighborhood level used, yet privacy protection is commonly characterized by a single privacy budget ε across all of them.

Although many articles design algorithms for different DP models and levels, no article yet provides a comprehensive comparison among them, and definitions with the same nominal ε may have different real-world privacy effects due to their different protection objects.

Conducting practical attacks (membership inference, attribute inference, data reconstruction) or applying DP auditing technology to approach worst-case guarantees is proposed as a way to empirically quantify and compare privacy effects across DP models and levels.

While some prior work (Naseri et al.) compared SL-DP and CL-DP under a trusted server, the survey argues this comparison is not comprehensive enough since the two definitions have different security assumptions and protection objects and cannot be directly compared without accounting for that.

Federated fine-tuning of LLMs with DP has significant promise for privacy-preserving personalization, but faces substantial communication overhead from the iterative aggregation of model updates for a complex, large model.

Some strategies mitigate communication bottlenecks but cannot provide concrete guarantees for protecting training data privacy, motivating approaches (like DP-LoRA) that reduce communication cost while retaining formal DP guarantees by fine-tuning only a small set of low-rank parameters.

DPSGD's added noise, applied to the immense parameter count of language-model embedding layers, severely impacts learning ability — the curse of dimensionality — requiring solutions like public-data pre-training plus private fine-tuning, or knowledge distillation, to bypass adding heavy noise directly to high-dimensional private data.

The survey reviewed the definitions and guarantees of DP, LDP, and shuffle model, summarizing their relaxations/differentiation, plus commonly used properties, composition mechanisms, and perturbation methods.
The survey broke from the traditional server-trust-based classification and explored a new taxonomy grounded in DP definitions and guarantees.
Over 70 recent articles on DP-FL are discussed and clarified by protection target, covering not just Horizontal FL but also Vertical and Transfer FL.
Applications of DP-FL are summarized by data modality (graph, bipartite/recommendation, time series) and real-world scenario (healthcare, IoT, finance).
Based on the preceding discussion, 6 promising future research directions are proposed (convergence analysis, user-level DP, privacy auditing, LLM fine-tuning, cross-domain TFL, multimodal FL).
Recent trustworthy machine learning efforts emphasize that reliable systems in safety-critical deployments must be both robust to perturbations and uncertainty-aware.
Adversarial training has emerged as the dominant paradigm to improve robustness against imperceptible, often transferable adversarial perturbations.

When errors are costly, robustness alone is insufficient for risk-sensitive decision making; a system must also know when not to predict, a requirement naturally captured by selective classification, where the model can abstain on inputs it considers unreliable.

Selective behavior depends not only on accuracy under attack but on the integrity of uncertainty under perturbations: errors, especially adversarial ones, must be assigned high uncertainty so they can be rejected.

Robustness evaluations that primarily report robust accuracy can hide a damaging failure mode: a method may become harder to fool while simultaneously degrading uncertainty ranking, producing confident adversarial mistakes that bypass rejection and manifest as silent failures at practically relevant operating points.

Because robust accuracy alone can mask degraded uncertainty ranking, and selective classification has rarely been systematically analyzed alongside adversarial robustness, this motivates investigating adversarial training's effect on predictive uncertainty through the lens of selective classification.

Both robustness and uncertainty are highly sensitive to experimental confounders (architecture, augmentation, threat model, etc.), making it difficult to draw controlled conclusions about their trade-off.

The sensitivity of both robustness and uncertainty to uncontrolled confounders motivates introducing a unified benchmark that standardizes these factors and evaluates models as selective systems across clean, adversarial, and common-corruption regimes.

Across a broad set of state-of-the-art adversarial training methods evaluated under this standardized benchmark, robustness gains do not reliably translate to robust uncertainty, and several strong defenses improve adversarial accuracy while worsening risk-coverage behavior due to degraded uncertainty ranking.

Because the standardized benchmark reveals that existing SOTA adversarial training methods do not reliably preserve uncertainty quality under attack, this motivates developing a training objective that explicitly targets predictive uncertainty and regularizes the posterior under attack.

AT often induces a trade-off between clean and robust accuracy; TRADES addresses this by balancing clean classification performance with clean-adversarial prediction consistency, while MART, AWP, SEAT, and Generalist improve robust generalization through other example-aware or ensembling mechanisms, but none explicitly targets uncertainty quality.

Evidential Deep Learning parameterizes a higher-order distribution (e.g., a Dirichlet) to represent evidence over class probabilities, and despite known theoretical limitations (e.g., absence of strictly proper scoring rules for second-order distributions), EDL uncertainties are often well-ranked in practice for selective prediction and OOD detection.

Robustness and uncertainty are often studied separately despite being closely related; under adversarial perturbations even conformal and representation-distance uncertainty methods may become unreliable, and both conventional and EDL classifiers can produce overconfident adversarial errors.

Despite growing recognition that robustness and uncertainty interact, the specific effect of adversarial training on uncertainty ranking and selective performance remains comparatively underexplored in the literature.

Because prior AT variants target only accuracy-level consistency, EDL provides well-ranked but not adversarially-tested uncertainty, and the AT-uncertainty interaction is underexplored, this motivates a method that combines evidential (Dirichlet) uncertainty modeling with an adversarial training objective explicitly enforcing posterior-level robustness.
For input x, the network outputs a non-negative evidence vector eθ(x), parameterizing a Dirichlet distribution over categorical probabilities via concentration parameters α = eθ(x) + 1.

This induces a posterior predictive distribution Cat(π̄) with predictive mean π̄ = α/S used for classification, while the total concentration S = Σαc inversely quantifies model uncertainty, so the Dirichlet parameterization structurally separates the classification signal from the confidence signal.
Total predictive uncertainty is quantified as u(x) = H[Cat(π̄)] = -Σc (αc/S)log(αc/S) (Eq. 1), enabling a threshold-based selective rule that rejects predictions whose entropy exceeds τ.

Because the Dirichlet parameterization cleanly separates predictive mean (label) from strength (confidence), and total uncertainty is defined directly from the resulting posterior predictive entropy, this provides a principled basis for the selective rule gτ(x;u) = 1[u(x) ≤ τ] used throughout the paper.

Adversarial training addresses clean accuracy and robustness of the predicted label by minimizing worst-case classification loss over the ℓp-ball, but it does not explicitly enforce integrity of uncertainty; robust-accuracy gains can therefore coincide with degraded uncertainty ranking.

EV-AT regularizes uncertainty under adversarial perturbation via posterior-level robustness, aligning clean and adversarial evidential representations in log-parameter space (η = log α) to jointly stabilize the predictive mean and the evidence strength/concentration.

The evidential classification loss LEV combines the negative log marginal likelihood over the Dirichlet-Categorical model (Eq. 2) with a KL regularizer toward the uniform Dirichlet prior on non-ground-truth evidence, encouraging vacuity when evidence is weak (Eq. 3).

Unlike standard AT, which constructs adversarial examples by maximizing classification loss, EV-AT's adversary explicitly maximizes a discrepancy D between clean and adversarial log-Dirichlet parameters η via K-step PGD, directly stress-testing uncertainty integrity rather than only flipping the predicted label.

The robust evidence alignment loss LREA = D(η, η_adv) is minimized alongside LEV in the overall EV-AT objective L = LEV + β·LREA (Eq. 4), where β trades off clean evidential fitting against robust posterior alignment.

EV-AT instantiates the discrepancy D as the Improved Kullback-Leibler (IKL) Divergence, which measures drift directly in log-parameter space and yields stable gradients for both the evidence-targeted attack and the alignment objective.

Because LREA penalizes worst-case discrepancy in the full log-Dirichlet posterior rather than only logits, the EV-AT objective directly discourages confident adversarial errors by jointly limiting attack-induced changes in both the predictive mean and the evidence strength.

Logits alignment is a common robustness heuristic, but logits are not identifiable (e.g. additive shifts leave softmax unchanged) and standard alignment targets only a single classification vector, not the confidence structure needed for abstention.

In an evidential model, the Dirichlet posterior separates these roles: the mean π̄ determines the predicted class, while the strength S controls uncertainty, so aligning the (log-)posterior directly stabilizes both the predictive distribution and its confidence.
With η = log α, the predictive mean equals softmax(η) (Eq. 5), so constraining drift in η directly constrains drift in the predictive mean π̄.

Lemma 1 shows that if the ℓ∞ drift in η is bounded by ρ, then the ratios of perturbed to original αc, S, and π̄c are all bounded within multiplicative factors of e^ρ or e^(2ρ) (Eq. 6), formalizing that log-Dirichlet alignment jointly limits changes in class probabilities and evidence scale.

Lemma 2 shows that for any Dirichlet distribution, the maximum per-class posterior variance is upper-bounded by 1/(4(S+1)) (Eq. 7), so higher, stabilized strength directly limits posterior variance/precision.

Because the selective rule thresholds predictive entropy u(x) = H[Cat(π̄)], and η-alignment (via Lemmas 1-2) jointly stabilizes both the mean π̄ (which determines entropy) and the strength S (which governs precision), aligning in η-space is theoretically the appropriate target for robust selective behavior.

Lemma 3 (a Fannes-type entropy continuity bound, Eqs. 8-10) shows that if π̄_adv stays close to π̄ in total variation, the resulting uncertainty score changes by a bounded amount, and consequently the accept/reject decision gτ is provably unchanged whenever this uncertainty change is smaller than the margin to the threshold τ.
Across the standardized benchmark, no SOTA baseline dominates as a selective system: higher AutoAttack accuracy does not reliably imply lower adversarial AUGRC (Table 1).

Under Basic augmentation, IKL-AT and TRADES-AWP achieve the strongest AA accuracies among baselines yet remain comparatively weak in AUGRC under AA, indicating degraded uncertainty ranking under attack despite strong robust accuracy.

AT-AWP attains the best Clean/AA AUGRC among baselines under Basic augmentation despite lower AA accuracy than other baselines, revealing an internal robustness-uncertainty trade-off within existing methods.

Plotting average accuracy versus average AUGRC across methods shows a weak correlation: e.g. IKL-AT increases robustness over AT (69.90 vs 68.05) but yields worse uncertainty (8.00 vs 7.85), and AT-AWP matches AT's robustness while degrading uncertainty.

Among SOTA baselines on CIFAR-10/WRN-34-10, TRADES-AWP offers the strongest trade-off (Acc.avg=70.29, AUGRCavg=7.68), illustrating that no single baseline is uniformly best across the robustness-uncertainty space.

Under AA perturbations, retention and generalized-risk curves degrade more severely than under common corruptions, with failures concentrating at moderate-to-high coverage where many adversarial errors remain accepted, i.e. overconfident mistakes reflected in low coverage at fixed risk for baselines.

The weak accuracy-uncertainty correlation, internal trade-offs among baselines, and concentrated confident-error failures together confirm that under attack, uncertainty no longer reliably separates correct from incorrect predictions for existing SOTA adversarial training methods, leading to silent failures at practical operating points.
Averaged over augmentations, EV-AT improves Acc.avg from 70.29 (TRADES-AWP) to 71.84, and reduces AUGRCavg from 7.68 to 6.52, moving beyond the Pareto frontier formed by prior objectives (Figure 1a).
The Clean/AA improvement is consistent across all four augmentation regimes in Table 1, and extends to corruption shift, where EV-AT also achieves the best corruption accuracy and corruption AUGRC.

In selective operating point analysis, EV-AT reduces the clean-AA retention-gap and substantially increases coverage at fixed risk relative to strong baselines (Figure 5), directly addressing the confident-error failure mode identified in C7.

Compared with the strongest baseline IKL-AT, EV-AT consistently achieves higher accuracy and lower AUGRC under PGD-20, PGD-100, and AutoAttack, for both ℓ∞ and ℓ2 threat models (Table 2), indicating gains are not an artifact of weak attack evaluation.

Sweeping the ℓ∞ radius from 0 to 8/255, EV-AT remains consistently best across the full range, with gains persisting at both small and large budgets (Figure 6), indicating improvement beyond a single evaluation radius rather than overfitting to it.

Across architectures and datasets, EV-AT remains on or beyond the Pareto frontier in the Acc.avg-AUGRCavg plane (Figure 4), indicating the advantage is stable across model capacity and dataset choice rather than an artifact of a specific pipeline.

Because the robustness-uncertainty improvement holds across augmentations, attack strength/type, perturbation budget, architecture, and dataset, the paper concludes that EV-AT genuinely shifts the robustness-uncertainty Pareto frontier rather than exploiting a narrow or confounded evaluation setting.

Removing the robust evidence alignment term (β=0) collapses performance (Acc. 71.51→20.11, AUGRC 6.67→37.67), indicating the clean evidential loss alone is not robust and that posterior alignment prevents pathological evidence mismatch under attack (Table 3).
Removing AWP degrades performance (Acc. 68.46, AUGRC 8.21) relative to the full EV-AT, showing AWP contributes an additional gain that is not substitutable by the evidential/REA components alone.

Replacing the evidential clean loss with standard cross-entropy degrades the robustness-uncertainty trade-off (Acc. 69.56, AUGRC 7.88 vs. the full EV-AT's Acc. 71.51, AUGRC 6.67), confirming the evidential formulation itself contributes to the gains.

Aligning in α or in the Dirichlet mean π̄ substantially degrades the trade-off (Acc. 67.32/64.64, AUGRC 10.26/10.43) compared to aligning in η=log α (Acc. 71.51, AUGRC 6.67), empirically confirming the theoretical motivation in C6 for log-parameter alignment.

Using IKL as the REA divergence outperforms ℓ2 or KL divergence alternatives (Acc. 69.81/70.61, AUGRC 7.64/7.60 vs. IKL's Acc. 71.51, AUGRC 6.67), confirming the choice of discrepancy measure matters for alignment quality.

Sweeping β shows small values under-emphasize alignment (weaker robustness/selective performance) while overly large values cause over-regularization that harms both AA accuracy and AUGRC, with an intermediate value giving the best joint operating point (Figure 7).

Because removing or substituting any individual component (REA, AWP, evidential loss, alignment space, divergence choice) degrades the robustness-uncertainty trade-off relative to the full configuration, the ablations confirm that EV-AT's gains arise from the combination of its evidential objective, evidence-targeted adversary, and η-space alignment via IKL, rather than any single component in isolation.
Most existing causality-based fairness methods assume access to the ground-truth causal graph over an individual's features.
Lacking perfect domain knowledge forces solving the notoriously difficult problem of learning the entire causal graph structure from observational data.
Learning the full graph relies on restrictive functional assumptions about the data-generating process, whose violations can undermine fairness guarantees.
Recent methods leverage a CPDAG, identifiable from conditional independence relations, to relax the full-graph assumption.
Estimating a CPDAG remains challenging in high-dimensional settings, requiring many conditional independence tests whose errors can accumulate and undermine fairness guarantees.
Cluster CPDAG inference needs substantially fewer conditional independence tests than variable-level CPDAG inference because clustering reduces graph size.
Motivates the research question: can interventional fairness be achieved using a cluster CPDAG despite unknown within-cluster causal structure?
Prediction is interventionally fair if the interventional distribution of the outcome is invariant to interventions on sensitive features, holding admissible features fixed (Salimi et al. 2019).
Interventional fairness is a group-level notion defined via interventional distributions, distinct from individual-level counterfactual fairness.
Interventional distributions in the fairness definition can be identified using partial causal graph knowledge, formalized as a CPDAG.
Under acyclicity and no unobserved confounders, standard back-door adjustment can be applied to identify interventional distributions.
A cluster graph is built by grouping nodes of a variable-level DAG according to a partition; a directed edge exists between clusters if any variable-level edge crosses between them.
The resulting cluster graph is assumed to be a DAG, feasible via an admissible partition designed with domain knowledge.

Even under acyclicity, a cluster graph can entail different conditional independence relations among clusters depending on unspecified variable-level structure inside clusters (e.g., collider vs non-collider).
Anand et al. propose independence arcs (marg/cond/never) plus connection and separation marks to explicitly represent the within-cluster ambiguity.

A cluster CPDAG expresses a cluster Markov equivalence class using directed edges, independence arcs, and connection/separation marks common to all compatible cluster DAGs, plus undirected edges that vary.
CLOC (Anand et al. 2025) infers a cluster CPDAG without restrictive assumptions about within-cluster connectivity, motivating its use as the inference backbone here.
Because a cluster CPDAG represents multiple compatible DAGs, a single adjustment set Z cannot be identified for back-door adjustment.
The proposed solution is to enumerate adjustment sets Z1,...,ZM such that at least one is valid for the true cluster DAG.
Efficient enumeration methods for variable-level CPDAGs rely on graphical properties (e.g., chordality) that cluster CPDAGs lack.
A novel adjustment-set enumeration algorithm is developed that explicitly accounts for independence arcs and separation/connection marks.
First enumerate candidate parent sets of sensitive features A (definite parents plus possible-parent subsets of siblings satisfying Theorem 3.5).
If parent sets contain connection-marked clusters, iteratively augment each candidate set via Algorithm 1's queue-based propagation to achieve d-separation.

When Algorithm 1 cannot guarantee identifiability (FAIL), the cluster CPDAG is refined by splitting connection-marked clusters into singleton nodes and re-inferring, at worst reaching variable-level granularity.
It is uncertain which of Z1,...,ZM yields a valid adjustment for the true cluster DAG.
The unfairness penalty is defined as the maximum, over m, of the aggregated kernel MMD between interventional distribution pairs.
Naively computing this worst-case MMD requires O(M·NA^2·NXad·n^2) time, which is computationally prohibitive.
This prohibitive cost motivates developing efficient estimation strategies for the penalty function.
Pairwise MMD summation over sensitive-value pairs (a,a') is rewritten as a sum of MMDs to a barycenter (mixture) distribution, reducing O(NA^2) to O(NA).
The feature map of the MMD kernel is approximated with dRFF-dimensional random Fourier features, reducing per-MMD cost from O(n^2) to O(n·dRFF).
Combining inverse probability weighting with RFFs yields a weighted empirical estimator of the kernel mean embedding for each interventional distribution.
Combining barycenter decomposition and RFF approximation reduces overall worst-case MMD computation to O(M·NA·NXad·n·dRFF).
Since the max over m in the penalty is non-differentiable, it is approximated with the Mellowmax function to enable gradient-based training.
Excluding Oracle and Full, C-IFair achieves the best RMSE and unfairness across all synthetic settings (d=5,10,15; linear and nonlinear).
C-IFair achieves fairness closest to Oracle while maintaining high accuracy, despite Oracle requiring the unrealistic true variable-level DAG.
Unaware and No-DesCs exhibit high RMSE and unfairness, implying that simply discarding predictive features fails to remove indirect discriminatory effects.
ε-IFair and ℓ-IFair produce less fair predictions than C-IFair in high-dimensional setups (d=15), indicating inferred variable-level CPDAGs become unreliable there.
Cluster CPDAG inference is more reliable than variable-level CPDAG inference in high-dimensional setups, explaining C-IFair's relative advantage at d=15.
Varying penalty weight λ from 0 to 200 shows increasing λ reduces unfairness at the cost of higher RMSE, confirming C-IFair can flexibly tune the fairness-accuracy trade-off.
Excluding Oracle and Full, C-IFair achieves the best AUC and unfairness among all baselines on Adult, German credit, and OULAD datasets.
The real-world results underscore C-IFair's practical utility for real-world fairness applications.
Comparing inferred interventional distributions of Ŷ across sensitive-feature interventions on Adult shows C-IFair makes sufficiently fair predictions with respect to gender and race.
A graphical algorithm to enumerate adjustment cluster sets, at least one of which enables identification of interventional distributions for the true cluster DAG.
A learning framework that achieves interventional fairness by penalizing worst-case unfairness across adjustment cluster sets, using an efficient barycenter kernel MMD.
Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate a better fairness-accuracy trade-off than existing approaches.
Local DP assumes adversaries can observe all local updates, which requires injecting substantial noise and degrades utility.
Pairwise Network DP (PN-DP) relaxes Local DP by modeling only pairwise observability between connected nodes, rather than full observability.
PN-DP's relaxed observability assumption enables privacy amplification by decentralization, improving utility in decentralized learning.
Existing PN-DP analyses rely mainly on Renyi DP (PN-RDP), which often yields loose privacy bounds.
The paper introduces Pairwise Network f-DP (PN-f-DP), extending PN-DP with the f-DP formalism for tighter, lossless privacy accounting via a hypothesis-testing interpretation.
Unlike previous federated f-DP formulations, PN-f-DP captures additional privacy amplification arising from decentralization, random walks, and iterative communication.
Secret-based Local DP (SecLDP) considers user pairs that share secrets with neighbors and coordinate correlated noise injection to improve the privacy-utility trade-off under limited collusion.
The paper introduces Secret-based f-Local DP (Sec-f-LDP), generalizing f-DP to regimes with correlated noise and shared secrets.
Sec-f-LDP leverages shared secrets to incorporate correlated noise, achieving additional privacy amplification in structured collusion scenarios not addressed by standard Local DP.
The one-time snapshot observed by user j is a mixture distribution over first-visit times, since the model reaches j from i for the first time at a random step governed by the hitting time.
The paper leverages the joint concavity of trade-off functions to lower bound the privacy loss of the mixture mechanism by a convex combination of per-step trade-off functions.
Lemma 4.1 establishes a lower bound on the trade-off function of the single-observation mechanism as a weighted combination of per-step trade-off functions, weighted by hitting-time probabilities.
The paper defines the mixture weights based on the hitting-time distribution rather than matrix power entries (W^t)_ij, better capturing random walk dynamics and yielding tighter bounds.
The hitting-time weights are computed recursively via the Markov property, based on the transition matrix W.
Each per-step trade-off function is computed using the composition rule of f-DP to account for the cumulative privacy effect of local SGD updates.

For strongly convex and smooth loss functions, privacy amplification by iteration in f-DP is applied, using the contraction effect together with repeated noise injection to yield tighter trade-off functions (Lemma 4.2).
For general non-convex loss functions, the standard f-DP composition rule is used instead, yielding a more conservative bound (Lemma 4.3).
A Hoeffding-type concentration inequality for Markov chains is used to bound the total number of times node j is visited during training.

Theorem 4.1 combines the single-visit mixture bound with the Markov concentration bound on visit counts to yield the final user-level PN-f-DP guarantee for Algorithm 1, computable numerically though lacking closed form.
Converting the f-DP guarantees back into RDP yields improved bounds compared to prior work, primarily due to the more accurate modeling of communication timing via hitting times.
Record-level privacy considers datasets differing by a single record within one user's local dataset, rather than the entire user dataset.
In the record-level setting, each user computes a gradient from a random subset of local data, reducing the probability a given record is selected and amplifying privacy via sub-sampling.
Sub-sampling interacts with privacy amplification by iteration, making the record-level analysis more intricate than the user-level analysis.
Lemma 4.4 characterizes the record-level trade-off function using a sub-sampling operator applied to the per-step Gaussian trade-off bounds.
The record-level privacy guarantee is obtained by substituting the record-level trade-off function from Lemma 4.4 into Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.1.
The correlated-noise analysis models honest-but-curious collusion at level q, where a coalition of up to q users may pool information including shared secrets.
Algorithm 2 (DecoR) incorporates both independent Gaussian noise and pairwise correlated noise via shared secrets before mixing via the transition matrix.

Theorem 4.2 shows Algorithm 2 satisfies (mu, S)-SecGDP against colluding users, with mu expressed in terms of independent noise variance, correlated noise variance, collusion level, and the graph Laplacian's second eigenvalue.
Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show f-DP-based accounting yields consistently tighter (epsilon, delta) bounds than RDP-based approaches.
Tighter (epsilon, delta) bounds allow calibrating less noise for a given privacy level.
Requiring less noise for the same privacy guarantee leads to significantly improved model utility.
On a hypercube graph with 32 nodes, PN-f-DP yields noticeably smaller pairwise privacy budgets epsilon than PN-RDP across nearly all node pairs.
Even against a refined RDP baseline using exact hitting times rather than an upper bound, PN-f-DP consistently yields the smallest epsilon.

On MNIST classification and logistic regression tasks under an expander graph topology, the f-DP-calibrated method achieves consistently higher test accuracy than RDP-based methods across graph structures and privacy budgets.
On ring and torus topologies with logistic regression on the a9a dataset, Sec-f-LDP achieves a better privacy-utility trade-off than both SecLDP and local DP baselines.
Although privacy and algorithmic fairness are each rapidly growing research areas, their joint effect remains comparatively under-explored.
Prior empirical work indicates that differential privacy can deteriorate fairness in various settings.
Most prior works on joint DP-fairness lack rigorous theoretical guarantees on both fairness and excess risk control, and are typically developed under a single-server centrally-stored data setting.
The paper proposes a two-step algorithm, FDP-Fair, targeting demographic disparity constrained classification under federated differential privacy in a multi-server distributed setting.
In the special case where there is only one server, the paper further proposes CDP-Fair, a simple yet computationally-lightweight alternative to FDP-Fair.
Central DP (CDP) requires that the privacy mechanism's output distribution changes by at most a multiplicative eps and additive delta factor between neighboring datasets differing in one entry.
Federated DP (FDP) requires that, in the non-interactive setting, each server's transcript shared to the central server individually satisfies an (eps_s, delta_s)-CDP constraint.
Federated DP is defined by requiring the privatized transcript output by each individual server to satisfy central DP, extending CDP to the non-interactive distributed setting.
Demographic disparity (DD) of a classifier is defined as the difference in probability of predicting the positive label between the two sensitive groups.
The alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier minimizes misclassification error subject to the constraint that the absolute demographic disparity is at most alpha.
The alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier can be obtained by shifting the unconstrained Bayes decision rule through an adjusted threshold determined by a fairness parameter.
The paper's goal is to construct an estimator for the alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier under federated differential privacy constraints.
Step S1 of Algorithm 1 uses Gaussian mechanisms (univariate noise for scalars, Gaussian processes for functional outputs) to privately estimate class probabilities and regression functions.
Site-wise privatized estimators of class probabilities and regression functions are aggregated at the central server through weighted sums, yielding global estimators while maintaining FDP.
To estimate the private fairness threshold, the continuous optimization problem is approximated by discretising the search interval into a fine evaluation grid.
Each discretised candidate is reduced to evaluating tail counts via binary trees, where counts in dyadic intervals are organized hierarchically to enable efficient privacy budget allocation.
In the binary tree construction, changing a single data point affects at most one node per tree level, resulting in constant-order L2-sensitivity for the Gaussian mechanism.
Because the tree depth is selected to be logarithmic, only a logarithmic number of privacy compositions is required, unlike the polynomial compositions needed in standard discretisation approaches.
The combination of constant per-level sensitivity and logarithmic-depth composition leads to substantial accuracy improvement compared to standard private nonparametric discretisation approaches.
The resulting site-wise binary trees are aggregated at the central server via weighted averaging, with weights chosen according to the variances of the corresponding site-level estimators.

Aggregating Gaussian noise across different leaves of the binary tree means the evaluated empirical DD across grids is no longer guaranteed to be monotonically non-increasing, unlike the true DD function.
Algorithm 4 is introduced to fit, with high probability, a non-increasing sequence to the noisy DD evaluations while controlling the induced bias, restoring the structure needed for threshold search.
In the single-server case, the empirical demographic disparity function is monotonically non-increasing, as shown in Theorem 12.

Because the single-server empirical DD is monotone, the threshold optimization is equivalent to finding where DD first crosses the fairness level, allowing the DD curve itself (rather than the cutoff point directly) to be perturbed vertically with noise.

Algorithm 5 (CDP-Fair) estimates the adjusted threshold by adding one correctly calibrated Gaussian noise term directly to the empirical DD function, avoiding the more complex noisy binary tree procedure.
By ensuring each pointwise release of the DD function at a given threshold satisfies CDP, the induced release of the resulting cutoff point also satisfies CDP.
Under the stated assumptions, Algorithm 1 (FDP-Fair) is (eps,delta)-FDP and Algorithm 5 (CDP-Fair) is (eps,delta)-CDP.
The population demographic disparity of the CDP-Fair output exceeds alpha by an offset of order N^{-1/2} plus (N*eps)^{-1}.

Under additional conditions on server sample sizes and bandwidth, the population demographic disparity of the FDP-Fair output exceeds alpha by an offset of order rho, as defined via a combination of privacy and sample-size terms across servers.

The CDP-Fair offset term is determined by the high-probability bound on the deviation between the empirical and estimated DD at the threshold, capturing both sampling deviation and Gaussian noise variance.
The CDP-Fair offset combines the standard parametric rate N^{-1/2} for plug-in fairness estimators with an additional private parametric rate of order (N*eps)^{-1}.

The FDP-Fair disparity inflation of order rho is larger than the CDP-Fair inflation in (5), because privacy compositions across server communications preclude direct infinite pointwise evaluation of DD, unlike in the single-server CDP case.

The larger FDP-Fair inflation term is primarily driven by the discretisation error introduced by the noisy binary tree construction, corresponding to the estimation error of DD per evaluation grid point.
The absolute excess risk relative to the optimal fair classifier is bounded by the fairness-aware excess risk plus a disparity cost term.

Theorem 2 provides finite-sample fairness-aware excess risk bounds for Algorithm 1 under a chosen bandwidth and server weighting scheme, the first such guarantees for fairness-aware classification under FDP.
The excess risk upper bound decomposes into the intrinsic cost of classification, the cost of privacy in classification, the non-private cost of fairness, and the private cost of fairness.
When the fairness threshold parameter is zero (automatically fair regime), the excess risk bound recovers the minimax optimal rate for FDP non-parametric classification without fairness constraints.
The cost of privacy in the excess risk bound manifests as a reduction of the effective sample size from SN to SN^2*eps^2, along with a loss in exponent due to added dimension dependence.
When fairness constraints are active, additional terms quantifying the cost of fairness arise from the estimation error of the adjusted threshold, split into non-private and FDP-induced components.

The parametric rate inside the fairness-cost term highlights the importance of the binary-tree-based threshold construction, since a naive smoothing-based plug-in alternative would introduce non-parametric rates and yield strictly weaker guarantees.

Relaxing the fairness constraint (increasing alpha) yields a noticeable reduction in misclassification error while the fairness constraint remains active, until it becomes inactive and the error curve flattens.
Weakening the privacy constraint (increasing epsilon) reduces the excess risk for each fixed alpha, with performance converging toward the oracle benchmark as epsilon grows.
Under fixed privacy and fairness parameters, increasing the sample size N leads to uniformly smaller misclassification error.

When a fixed total sample size is distributed across more servers, the misclassification error of FDP-Fair deteriorates, since local per-server sample size decreases and cross-server aggregation introduces additional privacy-preserving noise.
When there is only one server, FDP-Fair performs comparably to CDP-Fair, yielding nearly identical misclassification errors and empirical disparities.

On the AdultCensus and Law School datasets, CDP-Fair and FDP-Fair successfully control empirical disparity below the target level while incurring higher misclassification error than non-private classifiers, with the gap narrowing as epsilon increases.

The standard measure of a CL model's stability is its 0-shot resistance to catastrophic forgetting, and plasticity is typically measured as performance on the most recently learned task, i.e. Average Task Accuracy.

Natural learners like humans often require warm-up via cued recall to switch context, and the rapid re-acquisition of seemingly forgotten concepts, known as the relearning effect, is well studied in humans and other animals.

A stable CL model may efficiently regain past performance after adaptation, an aspect not measured by existing forgetting/backward-transfer metrics, so 0-shot 'forgetting' may reflect retrieval difficulty rather than irrecoverable loss.

While mitigating forgetting is well studied, plasticity is often treated as an afterthought and measured only as the ability to learn a new task through direct optimization, ignoring that plasticity can itself improve as learning progresses via shared task structure.

0-shot forward transfer, an occasionally studied plasticity-related metric, is trivially zero when new tasks do not share the same outputs as learned tasks, and only measures generalization within shared domains.

An ideal metric for plasticity should measure within-task adaptation—how efficiently a model adapts to a new task with limited information—since this aligns better with natural learning and generalizes across tasks with differing inputs/outputs/difficulty.

The retrieval-based nature of 0-shot forgetting and the inadequacy of existing plasticity metrics together motivate a new evaluation paradigm: continuous evaluation with few-shot adaptation on every task at every checkpoint.

Backward Transfer/Average Forgetting F measures the average loss in performance on task Tt across later checkpoints (Eq. 1), with stability defined as σCL = −F, while plasticity ϕCL is the Average Task Accuracy measured immediately after optimization (Eq. 2).

The standard plasticity metric ϕCL is reactive—it only confirms that a stable method retains the ability to learn via gradient descent—so with a strong learner ϕCL is high irrespective of the CL method used, failing to capture real differences in adaptation ability.

Research on few-shot learning studies rapid adaptation to unseen classes via fine-tuning on a handful of examples, and LLMs use in-context learning to perform new tasks without optimization, both illustrating rapid task adaptation outside standard CL metrics.

The Learning Curve Area (Eq. 3) is, to the authors' knowledge, the only prior exploration of few-shot transfer in CL, but it is not a true measure of 'area'—it effectively measures average performance over 0-K shots rather than the rapidity of adaptation.

Because LCA aggregates average performance rather than capturing how quickly a model improves with additional shots, this motivates defining a new per-shot plasticity metric (SAUCE) that isolates the rapidity of adaptation.

Existing meta-CL strategies either modify the learner's architecture using meta-information across the task sequence, or use a meta-optimizer leveraging cross-task information, but obtain all meta-information from a buffer of already-learned past task examples (hindsight meta-learning).
Many existing meta-CL works only evaluate on short sequences (fewer than 10 tasks), and methods often do not scale well to longer sequences.
To the authors' knowledge, no meta-CL method optimizes for few-shot performance (forward or backward), despite this being a prevalent goal in the broader meta-learning literature.

The reliance on past-task buffers, poor scaling to long sequences, and absence of explicit few-shot optimization together motivate developing a foresight meta-CL method that meta-learns on new, forward-looking examples rather than only past ones.

In the 0-shot setting, methods that explicitly replay task examples or model outputs vastly outperform the SGD fine-tuning baseline on backward tasks, with SGD performance often close to random, indicating apparent catastrophic forgetting.

At k=5-shot adaptation, SGD recovers a significant amount of performance, even approaching the accuracy of methods that store and replay samples during training, across four common CL sequences (Figure 2).
The increase in performance with few-shot adaptation on previously learned tasks is significantly higher than any corresponding increase on tasks that have not yet been learned.

Because the backward-task-specific recovery outpaces gains on tasks never learned, this confirms the observed recovery is genuine rapid reacquisition of previously learned knowledge, rather than a generic benefit of any few-shot adaptation.

Because few-shot adaptation recovers most of the performance that training-time replay strategies preserve, test-time few-shot replay appears nearly as effective as training-time replay while incurring a much smaller overhead, since samples are only replayed once at evaluation.
In fine-grained per-checkpoint tracking over 20-task sequences, every method except MER maintains stability with no deterioration, but none shows significant improvement in stability over time.
Across every setting, the conventional 0-shot current-task accuracy ϕCL is roughly identical across CL methods, suggesting most methods lead to similar plasticity under this metric.
Examining 10-shot accuracy on forward tasks shows CL methods differ significantly in plasticity as expected from their differing inductive biases, unlike the flat 0-shot picture.

EWC, which promotes stability via weight-space regularization, shows strong plasticity on the short SEQ-MNIST-5 sequence but significantly loses plasticity on longer sequences, even with high cross-task structure as in ROT-MNIST-20.

AGEM makes task updates in the null space of prior tasks, giving high plasticity in sequences with low task overlap (STRUCT-CIFAR100-20) and low plasticity in sequences with high overlap (SEQ-CIFAR100-10), even on the same base dataset.
