SGD remains highly competitive with other methods on few-shot forward transfer, which is expected since it does not explicitly preserve stability and thus retains maximal plasticity.

Because 10-shot forward transfer reveals inductive-bias-driven plasticity differences (EWC's degradation, AGEM's overlap-dependence, SGD's competitiveness) that are invisible under the near-identical 0-shot ϕCL, few-shot forward transfer is established as a more informative plasticity measure.

Existing meta-CL methods optimize for stability with backward-looking meta-updates, motivating the question of whether few-shot learning-to-learn ability can instead be optimized as the model progresses forward through the sequence.
The standard CL outer loop trains a model many-shot sequentially on the task sequence via repeated application of the update operator UN across tasks (Eq. 4).

In a rolled-back setting at task t+L, foresight meta-learning uses up to k unseen examples from tasks Tt+1,...,Tt+L to meta-learn an initialization via MAML (Eq. 5) before training on the full task Tt+1 (Eq. 6), distinguishing it from hindsight meta-learning that uses only already-learned examples.

A sequential variant of foresight meta-learning composes updates across an explicit ordered sub-sequence of look-ahead tasks Tt+1→...→Tt+L within the inner loop (Eq. 7), rather than treating them as a single batch.

Combining the rolled-back setup, the MAML-based inner loop over unseen future tasks, and the parallel/sequential update variants yields a concrete foresight meta-CL method that explicitly optimizes forward few-shot performance, addressing the gap identified in the related-work critique.

Adding foresight meta-learning improves performance on forward tasks beyond the look-ahead window for most methods on each task sequence, with STRUCT-CIFAR100-20 as the exception due to lack of shared task structure (Figure 5).

The foresight procedure results in improved backward transfer even though it is only optimized in the forward direction, indicating the model's general ability to adapt may be improved rather than only its forward-specific performance.

On ROT-MNIST-20, comparing MAML, Reptile, and a look-ahead fine-tuning baseline as the inner-loop meta-learning algorithm shows second-order MAML generally outperforms the other strategies, though Reptile performs well when combined with ER.
On EWC, the weakest forward-transfer method identified in Section 3.3, foresight meta-learning is observed to add limited additional benefit.
The sequential foresight strategy performs similarly to the parallel strategy, with the authors hypothesizing that differences between the two would require studying longer task sequences.

A major consideration in few-shot evaluation is selecting an appropriate value of k, driven by the tasks, model, methods, and practical constraints on available examples, and no single k is clearly correct.

Aggregating performance across multiple values of k, as LCA effectively does, fails to capture an important aspect of plasticity: the rapidity of adaptation to increasing information, since two models with identical 0- and K-shot performance can differ greatly in how quickly they improve in between.

The Area Under the Performance-Adaptation Curve (AUAC) quantifies the cumulative absolute error over a set of adaptation strategies (Eq. 8), approximating early regret in learning under gradient-descent adaptation.
AUAC's numerical value is highly dependent on a model's 0-shot and K-shot performance, meaning it conflates overall performance level with the rate of adaptation.

To isolate the rate of adaptation specifically, SAUCE scales the worst-performing adaptation to error 1 and the best to 0, and scales by the adaptation range, producing a metric in [0,1] that measures relative improvement in performance with increasing adaptation (Eq. 9).

Backward per-shot plasticity is defined as aggregated SAUCE over backward tasks (akin to cued recall), and forward per-shot plasticity is the analogous aggregation over future tasks, measuring learning-to-learn ability at a given point in the sequence.
SGD remains the most plastic method by average SAUCE, consistent with its lack of additional inductive bias constraining adaptation.

Replay-based methods (ER, DER++), which perform very well in the few-shot setting overall, appear to reduce models' ability to rapidly adapt to new tasks compared to SGD and regularization-based methods, per SAUCE.

Because replay-based methods have a high performance ceiling but adapt less rapidly per shot, a practitioner facing very few adaptation examples may not want to choose a replay-based method despite its strong asymptotic few-shot performance.

Because this sample-efficiency trade-off between replay-based and other methods does not emerge with conventional plasticity metrics, its detection via SAUCE demonstrates the practical benefit of per-shot plasticity as an evaluation metric.

On STRUCT-CIFAR100-20 (no task overlap), AGEM shows the most rapid per-shot plasticity improvement and the best final plasticity, attributed to its inductive bias of partitioning task representations into orthogonal subspaces.

On every sequence except ROT-MNIST-20, adding foresight meta-learning not only improves average SAUCE performance versus non-meta counterparts but also shows a steady increase in plasticity over time, whereas non-meta methods show relatively flat adaptation rates.

Because the plasticity improvement from foresight meta-learning applies to both forward and backward per-shot plasticity, it cannot be attributed simply to the additional forward information provided by look-ahead examples, supporting a genuine learning-to-learn interpretation.

Federated learning is a distributed method where multiple devices collaboratively train a model under a central server's coordination without sharing underlying data, addressing centralized-data privacy concerns.

Devices in an FL network differ in storage, processing power, battery life, and connectivity, leading to communication bottlenecks that reduce training efficiency, making it important to minimize communication rounds and transmitted package size.

Despite not sharing underlying data, recent studies show sensitive information can be exposed through gradient analysis during training, e.g. Carlini et al. show credit card numbers can be revealed from RNNs trained on user language data.
Data size and distribution vary widely across devices due to local environment and usage patterns; this non-IID data generation process introduces bias, causing slow convergence or divergence.

To the authors' knowledge, no previous studies explored combining differential privacy and adaptive quantization on non-IID datasets at large scale (e.g., 1000 clients), despite both being key real-world FL challenges.

Static/probabilistic quantization methods reduce gradients to low-precision representations to cut communication, but require careful level selection to balance accuracy and quantization error, with 32-bit as the common baseline capping compression at 1/32.

AdaQuantFL dynamically adjusts quantization via stochastic uniform quantization; FedDQ uses descending quantization but assumes uniform client contributions and ignores data heterogeneity; FedAQ optimizes joint uplink/downlink quantization but ignores non-IID data and privacy.

JoPEQ uses static rather than adaptive quantization; MSPDQ-FL's dynamic quantization targets only submodel parameters; RQM focuses on privacy-accuracy trade-offs without adaptive mechanisms; Nguyen et al.'s framework lacks adaptive quantization and scalability analysis.

To overcome these limitations, the paper proposes a descending quantization strategy for both uplink and downlink using a novel client importance estimation mechanism for non-IID data, rigorously evaluated up to 1000 clients, addressing downlink optimization and heterogeneity gaps in existing approaches.

Differential privacy is a randomized method reducing the relation between input and output so a change in one input feature doesn't much change the output distribution, aiming to hide whether a specific sample was used in training.

The paper uses Laplacian-based DP, which is relatively underexplored in FL, chosen for its sharper privacy guarantees under l1-sensitivity, making it ideal for bounded updates in FL, versus Gaussian- or Binomial-based noise used elsewhere.

The method first applies Laplace noise to secure model updates, then applies adaptive quantization that reduces bit-lengths via client importance estimation, ensuring noise is effectively incorporated into the quantized updates.
The consecutive noise-then-quantize usage is designed to maintain a balance between privacy, accuracy, and communication cost, particularly under non-IID and large-scale FL settings.
A central server manages training via client selection, broadcasting, local update, aggregation (where quantization and DP are applied), and global update, using FedAvg to aggregate local models.
The FL objective minimizes the sample-weighted sum of local cross-entropy losses across clients, solved in a distributed manner with each client running SGD locally.

MNIST is partitioned naturally by its 1,000 users (power-law sample counts) with a 2-layer CNN (1.6M params); CIFAR10 uses a Dirichlet(alpha=0.5) partition among clients with a VGG7 model (300K params), simulating realistic non-IID heterogeneity.
Additional experiments use PAP-Smear, Chest X-ray Pneumonia, and BreakHisV1 with an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B0 model to test applicability to a real-world healthcare classification scenario.

The paper employs symmetric quantization (zero offset) with stochastic rounding, mapping a real value range to a signed b-bit integer range via a scale factor s, clipping out-of-range values to the nearest bound.

The stochastic rounding operation rounds a value down or up to its nearest integers with probability proportional to distance from those values, ensuring quantization error is uniformly distributed rather than deterministic.
The paper uses per-tensor granularity, sharing the same quantization parameters across each tensor in a layer, rather than the more expensive per-element granularity.

Because stochastic uniform quantization rounds probabilistically so the expected quantized value equals the original (as proven by Alistarh et al.), and Laplace DP noise is zero-mean, combining the two introduces higher variance but no systematic bias into model updates.
High quantization precision early accelerates loss reduction while later training needs fewer bits, so a descending schedule (following Qu et al.) is more efficient for FL than a fixed level.

A global bit-length scheduler uses cosine annealing over communication rounds to smoothly reduce precision from an initial bmax (e.g. 32 bits) to a final bmin (e.g. 2 bits), used directly for server-to-client (downlink) transmission.

A client importance score νi combines the client's dataset-size ratio to the largest client's dataset (|Di|/ntmax) and normalized Shannon entropy of its label distribution, weighted by λh, so larger and more class-balanced datasets score higher.

The client-based ("Dynamic") scheduler combines the cosine annealing schedule with client importance νi for uplink transmissions, while downlink uses cosine annealing alone, so higher-importance clients retain higher precision.

The high entropy indicates a balanced, multi-class dataset that leads to increased accuracy and easier convergence, so clients with higher entropy get less compression, contributing more to the global model.
During local training, gradient clipping bounds the l1-norm of gradients, restricting any single data point's effect on the update and enabling controlled noise addition for sensitivity analysis.

Client sensitivity Ξ_i^t is computed via a piecewise formula depending on the local Lipschitz smoothness λ_i, clipping bound ξ, learning rate η, and number of local epochs E, differing by whether λ_i=0, or λ_i>0 with E below/above a threshold E0.

Each client adds noise w_i^t ~ Laplace(0, Ξ_i^t·T_i/ϵ) to its trained weights before uploading, where sensitivity is scaled by T_i=PT/(NE), so noise magnitude is tied to both the DP budget and how much each client's updates could influence the global model.

Algorithm 1 combines FedAvg with adaptive quantization and DP: the server quantizes/broadcasts the global model each round, clients dequantize, train locally with gradient clipping, add Laplace noise, compute importance/bit-length, quantize their update, and the server dequantizes and aggregates.

With 100 clients, reducing the gradient norm ξ diminishes accuracy: ξ=100 causes a 6.67% CIFAR10 and 5.22% MNIST accuracy drop versus unbounded (ξ=∞), because increasing ξ generates more noise per Eq.(12), obscuring true gradients.
Because accuracy diminishes as ξ shrinks but privacy weakens as ξ grows, ξ=100 is selected to balance privacy and model stability in later experiments.

At ξ=100, decreasing total client count increases test accuracy (e.g. MNIST 95.06% at 50 clients vs 88.17% at 1000), because fewer clients means each has a larger, more diverse local dataset, improving local model convergence.

Across client counts and privacy budgets ϵ, lower ϵ (stronger privacy) reduces accuracy, and the accuracy gap widens as client count increases because per-client sample count ni shrinks, raising sensitivity-driven noise per Eq.(12).
With 1000 clients, convergence failures occur for ϵ≤10^3 on MNIST and ϵ≤10^5 on CIFAR10, motivating higher minimum privacy budgets (e.g. ϵ≥5×10^5) for CIFAR10 at that scale.
Across λh values, increasing the number of clients per round significantly raises total communicated gigabytes for both CIFAR10 and MNIST.

For large client counts (e.g. 1000), lower λh (favoring dataset size over homogeneity) slightly reduces communicated gigabytes; dataset size becomes more influential than homogeneity as per-client dataset size shrinks with more clients.

λh changes accuracy by at most 1.12% on CIFAR10 (at 200 clients) but up to 9.75% on MNIST (at 1000 clients), so λh=0.75 (or 0.5) is chosen as the value balancing accuracy and communication cost across both datasets.

Across all client counts, 8-bit quantization offers a practical balance between accuracy and communication, while 4-bit quantization introduces severe quantization error and training instability, especially with non-IID data.

The Cosine method reduces total communicated gigabytes by about 37.46% versus 32-bit; the Dynamic method achieves 49.54-52.64% reduction on MNIST and 43.45-45.06% on CIFAR10 across 50-1000 clients, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

At 1000 clients, the Dynamic scheduler achieves better accuracy and communication cost than Cosine on MNIST specifically, demonstrating the client-importance strategy's effectiveness at scale, while for CIFAR10 Cosine slightly edges out Dynamic on accuracy at a marginally higher cost.

On PAP-Smear, Dynamic cuts communication by 37% with F1 dropping only from 90.94% to 89.41%; on Pneumonia, Cosine cuts communication by 31% with near-baseline F1 (93.79% vs 93.99%); on BreakHisV1, Dynamic cuts communication ~39% with F1 dropping from 89.80% to 87.03%.

In some cases (e.g. PAP-Smear), 16-bit static quantization achieves higher F1/BACC than Cosine and Dynamic while also communicating less data, suggesting a fixed moderate bit-length can sometimes offer a better trade-off.

Because Cosine/Dynamic dynamically adjust bit-lengths, they may occasionally use higher precision during certain rounds than a fixed 16-bit setting, increasing communication overhead and introducing more performance variability from quantization-noise fluctuation.
Laplacian DP noise and quantization error interact and can amplify performance variability, so adaptive quantization's success depends on careful management of the noise-precision trade-off.

The paper contributes a global cosine-annealing bit-length scheduler, an entropy-based client-adaptive scheduler, and their combination with Laplacian-based DP, extensively evaluated across model architectures, client counts, privacy budgets, and non-IID vision and medical datasets.

The methods are easy to implement, the entropy calculation has linear time complexity, and they are adaptable to any problem without extensive modification, though the Dynamic scheduler's λh parameter may need fine-tuning.

The methods do not account for the quality of samples on clients, a potential limitation that could be mitigated with client/data valuation methods estimating each client's contribution to model performance.

Future work will refine adaptive quantization with more advanced client-importance estimation algorithms and investigate integrating secure multiparty computation to further strengthen privacy guarantees.
A series of recent works demonstrate that even minor perturbations to the input graph can significantly degrade GNN performance.
Many studies report substantial gains using differing experimental setups, making results difficult to compare and conclusions potentially misleading.

Mujkanovic et al. warn that the graph community has yet to learn the 'bitter lesson' from the vision community, where overlooking adaptive attacks and evaluation rigor once led to a flood of unreliable defense evaluations.
GNNs are often trained using attack-specific hyperparameters or fixed data splits, biasing reported results.
New attack models are frequently tested under more favorable conditions than their baselines, further biasing comparisons.
Evaluations commonly select target nodes in a way that underrepresents high-degree nodes, which are typically more resistant to attacks.

Because of biased hyperparameters/splits, favorable conditions for new attacks, and skewed target-node selection, reported improvements in the literature may reflect favorable experimental setups rather than genuine advances in method design.

These recurring evaluation issues motivate re-evaluating several widely used gray-box attacks under a standardized, robust evaluation framework to demonstrate how variations in evaluation protocol produce inconsistent or overstated findings.

Errica et al. and Shchur et al. standardize evaluation procedures and promote a reproducible experimental environment with rigorous model selection and assessment, focusing on graph classification and node classification respectively.

Shchur et al. have shown that the train/validation/test split of choice used in evaluation significantly impacts the performance ranking, drawing community attention to the necessity of using multiple splits.
Errica et al. and Shchur et al. focus on designing rigorous evaluation frameworks for GNN models generally, rather than on preventing biased estimates of adversarial attack performance specifically.
The Graph Robustness Benchmark focuses mainly on global evasion attacks and does not consider targeted attacks, poisoning scenarios, or the distinction between homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

By unifying the model-selection/assessment rigor of Errica et al. and Shchur et al. with an adversarial-attack-specific evaluation procedure, and by adding targeted evasion, poisoning, and homophily/heterophily coverage that GRB lacks, this paper's benchmark addresses the identified gaps in prior work.
Validation accuracy is often a biased estimator of generalization performance, and overreliance on it can lead to overfitting and inflated expectations of model quality.
In adversarial GNN literature, model selection and final evaluation are often conflated, undermining fair comparisons across attack strategies.

Because validation-based selection is a biased estimator and is often conflated with final evaluation in this literature, proper separation between model selection (choosing hyperparameters via validation) and risk assessment (estimating performance via held-out test splits) is essential to avoid misleading conclusions.

The proposed evaluation formalizes this separation: model selection for victim models (and surrogate models) is performed solely on clean, unperturbed data via validation performance, prior to attacking, ensuring an unbiased risk estimate (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
Most prior works follow the Nettack strategy for target node selection: 10 highest-margin nodes, 10 lowest-margin (but correctly classified) nodes, and 20 additional randomly chosen nodes.
The Nettack-style selection strategy ignores structural properties such as node degree, even though richer neighborhood context makes high-degree nodes harder to attack.
Because the standard selection criteria (margin, random) do not account for degree, this strategy may systematically underrepresent high-degree nodes, which are typically more resistant to attacks.

By underrepresenting the harder-to-attack, attack-resistant high-degree nodes, the standard target-selection strategy inflates measured attack performance and skews the resulting conclusions about attack effectiveness.

To correct this bias, a high-quality evaluation should select target nodes to include diverse structural types (not just margin and random criteria), explicitly incorporating node degree as a selection axis.
Seven widely cited attack methods (Nettack, FGA, SGA, GOttack, PR-BCD, PGD, and one more) are benchmarked, selected based on peer-review status, architectural diversity, and citation count.

Four vanilla GNN victim models (GCN, GSAGE, GIN, PNA) and nine defended victim models are evaluated, so attacks against vanilla models establish baseline vulnerability while defended scenarios test the effectiveness of robustness interventions.

The gray-box setting (attacker has training data/labels to train a surrogate, but not full model parameters) is adopted as it balances realism with the ability to diagnose vulnerabilities, and targeted attacks on a node subset are used since they are harder to detect in real systems.

Unlike prior work using fixed surrogates only, adaptive attacks directly optimized against defended victim models are also evaluated (e.g., PR-BCD adaptive vs. non-adaptive variants), simulating stronger adversaries.

A naive yet surprisingly effective baseline, L1_D-RND, which perturbs edges based on node degree and features rather than gradients or learned surrogates, is introduced to contextualize performance claims and enable basic sanity checks against complex new methods.

Diverse attacks/defenses, vanilla and defended victims, gray-box adaptive attacks, and a naive baseline together instantiate the rigorous evaluation criteria (model selection, multiple splits, diverse target nodes, vanilla and defended victims) called for by the preceding diagnostic sections.

At budget ∆=1, PR-BCD (NA) has the highest misclassification rate in only 4 of 12 evasion scenarios on homophily datasets, with L1_D-RND surprisingly yielding the highest rate for PUBMED and CITESEER when PNA is the victim.
When the budget increases (∆=2...5), Nettack demonstrates superior performance in 36 of 48 cases, while PR-BCD (NA) only remains best on CITESEER and CORA for GCN.

Poisoning attacks are significantly more effective than evasion attacks: at ∆=1 Nettack's average misclassification rate rises 4.72% from evasion to poisoning, and even the naive L1_D-RND baseline improves by 8.9% under poisoning.

GraphSAGE is the most resilient victim model in both evasion and poisoning attacks, with Nettack yielding the lowest average misclassification rate (44.8% evasion, 47.97% poisoning) against it compared to other victim models.

At budget 1, average misclassification rate is higher on heterophily (33.96%) than homophily (27.78%) datasets, but by budget 5 homophily datasets show the higher rate (52.21% vs 46.86%), indicating the first perturbation has greater impact under heterophily while later perturbations gain more under homophily.

Nettack is best on homophily datasets (rank 1.64) but drops to rank 5.48 on heterophily datasets, while FGA rises from rank 3.10 on homophily to rank 1.92 (best) on heterophily, and the naive L1_D-RND similarly reverses from worst on homophily (rank 6.27) to competitive on heterophily (rank 2.33).

On the moderately sized OGB-ARXIV dataset (under 200K nodes), only three of seven attack methods and two of four victim models could be fully evaluated within the 120-hour compute limit, despite ample GPU resources, underscoring a critical scalability limitation.

Because attack effectiveness rankings, the evasion-vs-poisoning gap, and scalability all shift substantially across budget, homophily/heterophily, and dataset scale, no single attack or ranking generalizes across settings, confirming that prior single-setting evaluations risk overstated or misleading conclusions.

Defense models substantially reduce misclassification rates on homophily datasets, with poisoning attacks generally easier to defend against than evasion; e.g. Nettack's average rate drops from 49.1% to 32.2% under evasion and from 53.6% to 23.56% under poisoning with defenses applied.

Among defense methods, GNNGuard is the most effective on homophily datasets, achieving average misclassification rates of just 5.01% (evasion) and 5.92% (poisoning) at ∆=1 across three datasets and seven attacks, with GRAND consistently second-best.

The naive L1_D-RND baseline achieves the highest misclassification rate in 19 of 45 defended evasion settings and 18 of 45 defended poisoning settings, despite lacking any optimization or model-specific tuning.

Because a simple degree/feature-based baseline frequently outperforms optimized, learned adversarial attacks against defended models, this raises doubt about how much genuine gain sophisticated attack methods actually provide over naive perturbation strategies.

Defenses are more effective on heterophily datasets than on homophily datasets: average misclassification rates under defense are substantially lower on heterophily ([16.08%,23.33%]) than homophily ([20.11%,40.82%]) across budgets, with the best defense (RUNG) reducing most heterophily attack rates to about 2%.

Despite its strong homophily performance, GNNGuard becomes notably fragile under heterophily, in one case pruning all edges on Chameleon and producing uniformly zero misclassification rates regardless of attack, an artifact rather than genuine robustness.

Because attack rankings against defenses, defense effectiveness, and even defense failure modes (e.g. GNNGuard's edge-pruning degeneracy) all vary sharply between homophily and heterophily graphs, and because a naive baseline frequently rivals sophisticated attacks, robustness conclusions cannot be generalized from a single dataset type or attack set, reinforcing the need for the standardized multi-setting evaluation this benchmark provides.

Using node degree as a selection criterion results in substantially lower attack success compared to margin-based or random selection, even in vanilla undefended settings, empirically confirming the earlier bias diagnosis.

All attack methods perform poorly on high-degree nodes, which exhibit misclassification rates of only 0.05 to 0.28 despite the complete absence of any defense, while low-degree and low-margin nodes remain vulnerable.

Because most attacks were developed and benchmarked on small graphs with low average degree, and scalability limitations prevented testing on larger, high-degree networks, the high-degree robustness gap remained undetected in prior evaluations.

Because low-degree/margin-biased evaluations miss the strong inherent robustness of high-degree nodes, such evaluations systematically overstate both the effectiveness of attack models and the fragility of GNNs, especially given that real-world networks tend to have much higher average degree.

Incorporating model selection into evaluation significantly alters attack outcomes: on CORA and CITESEER, model-selected victim models are generally more vulnerable (e.g. SGA's misclassification rate on GIN under poisoning differs by an average of 15.27% across budgets), while on PUBMED model selection sometimes yields more robust victims, particularly for GraphSAGE.

Because incorporating realistic model selection can substantially shift measured attack success in either direction depending on the dataset, the perceived effectiveness of adversarial attacks depends not only on the attack method but also on whether the victim model is realistically selected, so omitting this step can overstate or understate GNN vulnerability.

Oversmoothing occurs because GNN layers act as low-pass filters, so after many layers node representations become dominated by the principal eigenvector of the propagation matrix, converging to a uniform vector.
The rate of oversmoothing is governed by the spectral gap of the graph's propagation operator, and oversmoothing is inevitable for any fixed-spectrum graph as the number of layers grows.

Oversquashing describes information from distant nodes failing to reach a target node because messages must flow through a narrow cut/bottleneck, compressing exponentially many messages into fixed-size vectors.
Oversquashing is a structural phenomenon quantified by the graph's conductance or effective resistance; a graph with a bottleneck forces information squashing regardless of layer count.
Graphs that mitigate oversquashing (expanders, dense graphs) tend to have high connectivity, which accelerates oversmoothing.
Sparse, tree-like graphs resist oversmoothing but create severe bottlenecks that cause oversquashing.

Because oversmoothing- and oversquashing-mitigating graph properties conflict, this raises the natural question of whether graph structure can be optimized to strike an optimal balance between the two.

While heuristic rewiring methods (DIGL, SDRF) have shown empirical success, the fundamental computational complexity of the underlying graph optimization problems had remained unexplored prior to this paper.
A construction is needed that maps a graph H to a new graph G such that the conductance of G is small if and only if H has a small bisection, to enable reductions from Minimum Bisection.

There exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given H with n vertices, outputs a 3-regular graph G with 2n vertices such that H is an induced subgraph of G, and cut conductance in G is tightly related to cut size in H in both directions (upper bound via part 2, and a converse via part 3 with a balancing procedure).

The constants c1, c2, c3 in the Expander Embedding lemma can be made arbitrarily small or large by choosing a sufficiently strong or weak expander, allowing specific inequality conditions (e.g., c1 < 1/6, c2c3 < 1/2) to be satisfied.

Any Minimum Bisection instance (H, B) can be transformed in polynomial time into an equivalent instance with convenient bounds relating B to the number of vertices n (either B >= 2n and B = O(n), or n/2 <= B <= 2n), preserving the yes/no answer.
The worst-case bottleneck is captured by conductance phi(G), and the oversquashing loss is defined as the negative conductance, so maximizing phi(G) minimizes oversquashing.
GROC asks: given graph G, integer budget K, and threshold phi0, does there exist G' with symmetric-difference edge budget at most K such that the conductance of G' is at least phi0.
Given a candidate graph G', its conductance can be computed exactly via a min-cut/max-flow computation in polynomial time, so GROC is in NP.

Using the Expander Embedding and Instance Scaling lemmas, a Minimum Bisection instance (H,B) is transformed into a 3-regular graph G with K=0 and a threshold phi0 = 1 - c1(B+n)/n, chosen so that phi0 > 1/2 using the constant bound c1 < 1/6.
If H has a bisection with at most B edges, Lemma 2(2) gives a cut in G with conductance at most 1-phi0, which is less than phi0, so (G,0,phi0) is a NO instance.

If H has no bisection with at most B edges, assuming phi(G) < phi0 leads via Lemma 2(3) and the balancing procedure to a bisection of H with fewer than B edges, a contradiction; hence phi(G) >= phi0 and (G,0,phi0) is a YES instance.
Because Minimum Bisection reduces to GROC (with inverted YES/NO answers, invertible in polynomial time) and Minimum Bisection is NP-complete, GROC is NP-hard.
Since GROC is both in NP and NP-hard, it is NP-complete.
For a regular graph, the Dirichlet energy after L layers decays as E(X(L)) <= (mu2(P))^(2L) * E(X(0)), where mu2(P) is the second-largest eigenvalue of the propagation matrix.
Because the Dirichlet energy decay rate is governed by mu2(P), preventing oversmoothing requires minimizing mu2(P).
Since mu2(P) = 1 - lambda2(L), minimizing mu2(P) is equivalent to maximizing lambda2(L), the spectral gap of the normalized Laplacian.
GROS asks: given graph G, integer budget K, and threshold tau, does there exist G' with symmetric-difference edge budget at most K such that mu2(P_G') <= tau.

A certificate is the target graph G'; the edge-budget constraint is checked directly, and mu2(P_G') <= tau can be decided in polynomial time via root isolation (e.g., Sturm sequences) since the propagation matrix has rational entries and polynomial-bit-length algebraic eigenvalues.

Using the same Expander Embedding (with constants satisfying c1 < 1/48, 2c2*sqrt(3c1) < 1/2) and Instance Scaling lemma (part 1), a Minimum Bisection instance is transformed into a 3-regular graph G with K=0 and threshold tau = 1 - 2c1(B+n)/n - epsilon for a suitably small rational epsilon.
If H has a bisection with at most B edges, Lemma 2(2) and Cheeger's inequality give mu2(P_G) >= 1 - 2c1(B+n)/n > tau, so (G,0,tau) is a NO instance.

If H has no bisection with at most B edges, assuming mu2(P_G) > tau leads via Cheeger's inequality, Lemma 2(3), and the balancing procedure (using B >= 2n and c2*c3*sqrt(3c1) bounds) to a bisection of H with fewer than B edges, a contradiction; hence mu2(P_G) <= tau and (G,0,tau) is a YES instance.
Because Minimum Bisection reduces to GROS and Minimum Bisection is NP-complete, a polynomial algorithm for GROS would solve Minimum Bisection, so GROS is NP-hard.
Since GROS is both in NP and NP-hard, it is NP-complete.
Conductance phi(G) cannot be approximated within a factor of O(sqrt(log n)) unless P = NP.
The spectral gap lambda2(L) cannot be approximated within any constant factor for regular graphs.

These inapproximability results suggest that algorithms attempting to optimize graph structure for these measures under a limited edge-change budget will also be hard to approximate, though a formal proof for the rewiring problems themselves remains open.

SDRF (iteratively removing most-negative-curvature edges and adding highest-effective-resistance edges, total O~(n^3)) and DIGL (graph diffusion via personalized PageRank, O(n^2 log n)) are existing heuristic rewiring methods shown to run in polynomial time.

Because exact optimization of GROC and GROS is NP-hard/intractable while SDRF and DIGL run in polynomial time, the hardness results provide theoretical justification for using such heuristics rather than seeking exact solutions.

For regular graphs, mu2(P) = 1 - lambda2(L) and phi(G) lies between lambda2(L)/2 and sqrt(2*lambda2(L)), mathematically linking the oversmoothing objective (spectral gap) and the oversquashing objective (conductance).

This mathematical relationship reflects a tangible tradeoff: a graph with high algebraic connectivity (good for oversmoothing) tends to have high conductance (good for oversquashing), but the exact relationship is constrained by the spectral gap.

The NP-hardness results for both GROC and GROS show that optimizing either objective exactly is intractable in general, reinforcing that practical approaches must rely on approximations or heuristics.

A highly connected graph (e.g., complete graph) can simultaneously mitigate oversquashing (no bottlenecks) and oversmoothing (large spectral gap), but such graphs are often prohibitively dense for real-world applications.

Because dense graphs mitigate both issues but are often impractical, while sparse graphs may suffer from both, finding an optimal sparse graph that strikes the right balance is computationally challenging, justifying iterative heuristic rewiring methods like SDRF and DIGL.
Post-hoc explanation techniques approximate black-box behavior after training, but can be unreliable and susceptible to manipulation, raising faithfulness concerns.
Inherently interpretable models (decision trees, rule lists, rule sets, scoring systems) are easier to understand but may exhibit reduced predictive performance in complex settings.
This limitation motivated hybrid interpretable models, which combine an interpretable component with a black-box component via a gating mechanism assigning each example to one or the other.
By varying the proportion of examples assigned to the interpretable component (transparency), hybrid models realize different trade-offs between interpretability and predictive performance.

Even when hybrid models improve the aggregate accuracy-interpretability trade-off, they may distribute interpretability unevenly across individuals or demographic groups — a largely overlooked question.
A large body of fairness-in-ML work focuses on fairness criteria defined with respect to a predictive model's outputs, intervening via pre-, in-, or post-processing.

Fairness in explanation quality has been examined for post-hoc explanation methods (feature attribution, counterfactual explanations), revealing demographic disparities in properties like sparsity, robustness, and recourse cost.
Fairness in explanation quality and recourse fairness both fall under procedure-oriented fairness, evaluating whether externally-produced reasoning is equally reliable across groups.
In hybrid interpretable models, interpretability is not provided by a separate post-hoc method; it is allocated by the model itself through its gating mechanism.

Unlike prior work on explanation quality or recourse, ICD and ICA measure how interpretability itself is allocated via the routing decision, not the quality of an explanation produced after a prediction.

This distinction means ICD shifts attention from whether explanations are equally good to whether different individuals/groups are equally likely to receive interpretable decisions in the first place.
A hybrid interpretable model is defined by a triplet ⟨Ω, hs, hc⟩ where Ω is the interpretable region handled by simple model hs, and examples outside Ω are deferred to black-box model hc.
The transparency C_Ω of a hybrid model on a dataset is the proportion of examples covered by the interpretable region Ω, with 0 = pure black-box and 1 = single interpretable model.

In practice, existing hybrid interpretable models use a set of rules r as the interpretable component, where the rules' support simultaneously defines Ω; examples not captured by any rule are deferred to the black-box.
Several models can achieve nearly indistinguishable predictive performance while disagreeing on individual predictions — a phenomenon called predictive multiplicity.
The set of near-optimal models is formalized as the Rashomon set R(H, ε, S), those with loss within a factor (1+ε) of the reference model's loss.

Although models in the Rashomon set have comparable predictive performance, they can differ substantially on other desiderata, motivating evaluation across the whole set rather than a single arbitrary model.

Exact enumeration methods for constructing Rashomon sets exist only for specific simple hypothesis classes (rule lists, rule sets, decision trees) and scale poorly with ε and rule/feature counts; enumeration-free methods are similarly limited to particular model classes.

Building the exact Rashomon set is not tractable for black-box models, and even more so for hybrid interpretable models, whose interpretable component training often depends on a pre-trained black-box.

Consistent with prior work showing model-sampling/bootstrapping provides useful Rashomon-set approximations, the paper replaces the exact Rashomon set with a bootstrap-based approximation for estimating interpretability-coverage statistics.
The Interpretability Coverage IC_p of protected group p is defined as the fraction of individuals from p that fall within the interpretable region Ω.
Interpretability Coverage Disparity (ICD) is defined as the maximum pairwise difference in IC across protected groups, equivalently max IC_p minus min IC_p.
ICD depends only on the allocation of individuals to interpretable vs. black-box regions, not on the predictions made by either component, making it a procedural fairness notion.
ICD alone does not identify which groups are relatively advantaged or disadvantaged, since it only reflects the largest observed disparity, motivating reporting per-group coverage as well.
ICF(x) is defined as the fraction of models in the (approximate) Rashomon set for which example x falls within the interpretable region Ω.
ICA(x) = 1 - 2|ICF(x) - 1/2|, so ICA is high when x is assigned to the interpretable region for roughly half the Rashomon-set models and low when assignment is consistent.
Values close to 1 indicate high arbitrariness (unstable routing across the Rashomon set), while values close to 0 indicate consistent assignment to one component.
Because exact Rashomon-set construction is intractable for hybrid models, ICF and ICA are computed using the bootstrap-based approximate Rashomon set instead of the exact one.
Four state-of-the-art hybrid interpretable learning methods are evaluated: HyRS, CRL (heuristic, simulated-annealing based), and HybridCORELSPre/Post (exact branch-and-bound based).
HyRS and CRL optimize accuracy-transparency-sparsity trade-offs but do not provide optimality guarantees and cannot enforce a prescribed transparency level.

HybridCORELSPre/Post rely on exact branch-and-bound to explore rule prefixes, with HybridCORELSPost optimizing accuracy+sparsity subject to a hard transparency constraint, and HybridCORELSPre learning the prefix before the black-box.
Experiments use three datasets of varying size: COMPAS (recidivism), UCI Adult Income (earnings), and ACS Employment (employment status), each with Age/Gender/Race subgroups.

For each method/hyperparameter configuration, a reference model is trained plus 1000 bootstrap-resampled retrainings, yielding 1001 models per configuration (10,010 per method across 10 configurations), deduplicated and binned by transparency.

Within each transparency bin, unique models are filtered to keep only those satisfying the Rashomon parameter ε relative to the reference model, yielding the approximate Rashomon sets used for all downstream analyses.
Results reveal substantial ICD across nearly all experimental settings, confirming hybrid interpretable models can distribute interpretability unevenly, with values approaching 1.0 in several cases.
Within the same transparency bin, certain subgroups (e.g., African-American on COMPAS under HyRS) consistently receive lower interpretability coverage than others, not just larger variance.
In the lowest transparency bin most instances go to the black-box; in the highest bin most go to the interpretable component — both regimes are dominated by a single component.
Intermediate transparency bins (0.25-0.75) are where both components actively contribute to prediction, better characterizing the truly hybrid regime.
The largest ICD values occur in intermediate transparency bins, with ICD increasing from low to intermediate bins and then decreasing/stabilizing at higher bins.

Non-parametric pairwise (Mann-Whitney U, Holm-corrected) tests across adjacent transparency bins confirm the bell-like ICD pattern is frequent and statistically significant across datasets/methods, strengthening at larger ε.
Assignment arbitrariness (ICA) is generally limited in the lowest and highest transparency bins, where predictions are predominantly handled by a single component.
Substantially higher ICA emerges in intermediate transparency bins where both components contribute to prediction, consistently across all evaluated methods.
The consistent pattern across methods supports the hypothesis that hybridization itself amplifies assignment uncertainty within Rashomon sets.

The observed substantial ICD plus high within-Rashomon-set variability across transparency bins shows near-optimal models can induce very different ICD levels, motivating a predictive-multiplicity-based search for fairer models.

ICD is mitigated by incorporating a maximum ICD constraint η into the HybridCORELS branch-and-bound algorithms: a candidate best prefix is retained only if it satisfies the constraint, otherwise discarded.
The bounds and symmetry-aware data structures used in HybridCORELSPre/Post remain valid and tight under the added maximum-ICD constraint.
ICD mitigation applied during training consistently reduces both magnitude and variability of test-set ICD distributions across all sensitive attributes and transparency bins.
ICD mitigation produces no substantial change in the distribution of ICA, indicating it is effective at reducing group-level disparity but has limited impact on individual-level arbitrariness.

Mitigated models frequently show lower median EO/SP disparities and reduced variability, despite these algorithmic fairness metrics not being directly targeted during training, though improvement is not uniform across settings.

Enforcing ICD constraints results in only minor increases in rule count and largely comparable accuracy distributions, occasionally even slightly improving accuracy (suggesting a regularization effect).

As the maximum ICD constraint η is relaxed from strict to unconstrained, ICD magnitude and variability consistently increase across Rashomon models, while test accuracy remains remarkably stable throughout.

Bin-level analysis shows the largest EO/SP improvements from tightening η occur in higher-transparency bins, where interpretability coverage is greatest and the constraint most strongly affects routing (e.g., HybridCORELSPost's EO from ~0.25 to ~0.18 as η tightens from 0.25 to 0.05).
Combined with stable predictive performance across mitigation strengths, results show substantially lower ICD can be selected from the Rashomon set without sacrificing predictive accuracy.
ICD (demographic-parity-style group disparity) and ICA (predictive-multiplicity-based individual arbitrariness) are introduced as procedural fairness notions for interpretability allocation.

Extensive experiments across four hybrid methods show substantial ICD/ICA can arise on real-world datasets, with some individuals arbitrarily assigned and some groups systematically routed to the black-box.
Existing hybrid interpretable learning methods are extended to mitigate ICD, with the resulting impact on sparsity, predictive performance, and algorithmic fairness investigated.
LaMaTE decouples encoding and decoding from language modeling by using an LLM as the NMT encoder and leaving the NMT decoder unchanged.
Decoupling encoding and decoding confers modeling flexibility, allowing a deep complex encoder paired with a lightweight decoder.
The heterogeneous architecture (powerful encoder, lightweight decoder) is well-suited for MT, using a powerful encoder to understand input while generating translations at lower decoding cost.
LaMaTE achieves 2.4-6.5x inference speedups over baselines.
LaMaTE achieves a 75% reduction in KV cache memory footprint.
The function Dec_theta( , [c,x]) serves as a unidirectional encoder in LaMaTE.
Because both the LaMaTE encoder and decoder are unidirectional, the whole model can roughly be thought of as a hybrid language model: a large model for prefilling, a small model for decoding.
The LLM decoder may have a larger hidden size than the NMT decoder, creating a mismatch.
An adaptor is added to the output of the LLM decoder to reduce its dimensionality to match the NMT decoder.
A simple linear mapping adaptor falls short because LLMs are too big, making it difficult for untrained smaller models to use the transformed representations directly.
An adaptor with three components (layer fusion, MLP, EncStack) is designed to make better use of LLM outputs for the NMT decoder.
LLM layers are divided into K groups and their outputs fused via a learnable weighted sum plus layer norm (Hfuse).
Fusing outputs of intermediate layers (rather than only the final layer) forms a finer-grained output, a method found beneficial to deep-to-shallow architectures in prior NMT work.
A 2-layer MLP is placed after layer fusion to reduce hidden size from d1 to d2, matching the NMT decoder's hidden size.
A stack of Transformer encoder layers (EncStack) is used to learn bidirectional representations from the unidirectional adaptor output, added with small computational overhead.
Removing layer fusion causes a COMET drop of 0.24 and BLEU drop of 0.71 relative to full LaMaTE.
Removing EncStack causes a COMET drop of 0.30 and BLEU drop of 0.53 relative to full LaMaTE.
Fusing intermediate LLM layers provides a more informative representation than relying solely on the final layer.
The adaptor enhances the native representations of LLMs, rendering them more suitable for the NMT decoder.
Fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs is costly, making it generally favorable to use less labeled data.
Using less labeled data can lead to inadequate learning of the new parameters (adaptor and NMT decoder).
Extensive fine-tuning may cause the LLM to forget its original knowledge encoded in its parameters.
A two-stage training method is presented to perform more efficient learning for different types of parameters.
In stage 1, the LLM decoder is frozen while the adaptor and NMT decoder are pre-trained on a standard translation task.
Because the LLM decoder parameters are frozen in stage 1, only a forward pass through the large network is needed, avoiding the backward pass.
Avoiding the backward pass through the LLM makes stage 1 less computationally expensive than full LLM fine-tuning, enabling scaling to large datasets.
In stage 2, the LLM decoder, NMT decoder, and adaptor are fine-tuned together on various tasks using the ComMT dataset.
Training with only stage 1 (W/o S2) results in a substantial performance drop (COMET -2.25, BLEU -4.18).
Incorporating stage 2 while freezing LLM parameters yields improvements over stage-1-only but still falls short of full LaMaTE performance (COMET -0.16, BLEU -0.12).
The ablation results underscore the importance of both high-quality data and LLM parameter tuning in maximizing model performance.
There remains a notable gap in comprehensive, high-quality data resources tailored to developing universal translation models.
ComMT, a new comprehensive evaluation/training benchmark spanning five diverse translation-related tasks, is developed to generalize and evaluate LaMaTE.
ComMT comprises five tasks: General Translation, Document-level Translation, Domain Translation, Terminology-constrained Translation, and Automatic Post-editing.
ComMT's training set totals 239,661 samples across four languages (German, Czech, Russian, Chinese).
Llama3-8B was fine-tuned on ComMT and compared against WMT17-20 and TowerBlock datasets, evaluated on the WMT23 test set.
ComMT surpasses WMT17-WMT20 in both En->X and X->En directions.
ComMT excels in En->X but underperforms TowerBlock in the X->En direction.
The X->En discrepancy versus TowerBlock may be attributed to TowerBlock's larger dataset size and its inclusion of additional general task data predominantly in English.
LaMaTE surpasses NLLB-3.3B, NMT, and mT5-Large across all evaluated ComMT tasks.
This result highlights the potential of LLMs as high-capacity encoders, capable of producing more expressive and informative representations.
The enhanced representations from LLM encoding provide a solid foundation for the decoder, ultimately improving translation quality.
LaMaTE achieves comparable overall performance to Llama3-8B-SFT, a fully fine-tuned decoder-only LLM.
The comparability to Llama3-8B-SFT demonstrates that LLMs can serve as effective MT encoders, offering an efficient alternative to fine-tuning LLMs as direct generators.
Encoder-decoder models (mT5-large, LaMaTE) consistently exhibit lower off-target rate, unaligned source words, and unaligned target words than decoder-only models.
LaMaTE follows the encoder-decoder paradigm, which also helps mitigate misalignment issues as an added bonus.
The misalignment improvement is speculated to be attributable to the cross-attention mechanism in the NMT decoder, which allows direct token-wise interaction between target and source.
Cross-attention enhances source-target alignment, in contrast to LLMs relying on a single attention mechanism over concatenated source and target text.
Relying on a single attention mechanism to jointly process concatenated source and target text could potentially cause a loss of attention focus.
The Concat Decoder variant, which removes cross-attention, underperforms the standard decoder (COMET -0.80, BLEU -2.34).
The Prefix Decoder variant, which also removes cross-attention, underperforms the standard decoder (COMET -0.66, BLEU -1.47).
The standard decoder proves superior to the alternative cross-attention-free decoder designs.
Together with the misalignment findings, maintaining cross-attention in the decoder is argued to be particularly beneficial for translation tasks that demand strong alignment.
Increasing decoder layers significantly improves translation performance, particularly En->X, but decoding speed drops sharply as depth increases, with a 39% reduction from 8 to 16 layers.

Because decoder depth improves quality but sharply hurts speed while EncStack depth gives only modest gains with minimal efficiency cost, scaling the encoder offers a more effective trade-off between performance and computational efficiency than scaling the decoder.
Adding more EncStack layers leads to modest improvements in both translation directions, with relatively small gains compared to decoder variations.
Since EncStack operates only on the encoder side, its impact on decoding efficiency is minimal.
LaMaTE underperforms compared to mT5-large in low- and very-low-resource languages in the large-scale 99-language evaluation.
The low-resource underperformance is likely due to limited pre-training data for these languages in the Llama3-base model.
Using a model with stronger multilingual capabilities as the encoder could further improve performance on low-resource languages.
The NMT decoder in LaMaTE is intentionally lightweight relative to the LLM encoder.
Because the decoder is lightweight, it may become a bottleneck when generating translations into many target languages.
Expanding decoder capacity is essential for better performance given this potential bottleneck.
A more effective strategy might involve scaling the decoder's capacity with Mixture-of-Experts instead of adding more layers, boosting performance without compromising efficiency.
The approach requires pre-training the decoder's parameters using large-scale bilingual data in stage 1 because the decoder is randomly initialized.
The requirement to pre-train a randomly initialized decoder on large-scale bilingual data may not be the most efficient process.
Future work could explore initializing decoder parameters from the encoder or leveraging a small pre-trained language model to reduce the state gap between encoder and decoder.
Llama3-8B consistently outperformed XGLM-7.5B, Bloom-7B, Falcon-7B, and Qwen2-7B in 0-shot and 3-shot translation across En<->De/Cs/Ru/Zh.
Llama3-8B's superior cross-lingual performance suggests it possesses stronger multilingual capabilities.
Based on the evaluation results, Llama3-8B was selected as the backbone model for subsequent LaMaTE experiments.
LLMs exhibit broad capabilities, yet their inference remains opaque: decision factors are unobservable and generated explanations often lack faithfulness.
This opacity hinders adoption in high-stakes domains, risking confident hallucinations and biases in medicine and fictitious legal precedents that undermine accountability.
Attribution and attention-based explainability methods are primarily correlational, whereas faithful explanations require causal evidence.

Counterfactual methods using causal graphs over textual variables provide stronger causal evidence but typically remain local and input-centered: they quantify a given factor's causal effect but do not recover the model's high-level inference.
Mechanistic interpretability targets internal components like neurons and circuits, providing a valuable low-level science but is often misaligned with the explanations stakeholders actually need.
What remains missing is an applicable explainability method providing a global, causal account of how a model organizes human-interpretable concepts and reduces them to a prediction.
Prior work uses causal graphs, and sometimes LLMs, to recover causal graphs of external-world processes (concepts → text → prediction, graph usually assumed a priori).

Instead, this paper uses causal graphs to model LLM inference itself (text → concepts → prediction), providing a transparent view of how the model perceives and organizes high-level concepts to produce a prediction.
In this new setting, the graph is itself the explanation, and both the relevant concepts and their causal relations must be inferred rather than assumed in advance.

In mechanistic interpretability, causal graphs are defined over model-internal components (attention heads, neurons, residual-stream directions), abstracting away the complete computation to retain only components hypothesized to mediate a targeted behavior.

Causal graphs are also used to enable estimation of causal effects of high-level concepts on predictions (via counterfactuals, matching, adjustment), where the graph is usually assumed in advance and describes concepts → text → prediction.

The paper introduces a third utility: causal graphs describing the model's high-level reasoning (text → concepts → prediction), where the graph is the explanation and has received no prior attention in the literature.

COAT (Liu et al. 2024) also uses an LLM to propose concepts and applies causal discovery, but aims to recover real-world causal structures and focuses on local Markov blankets for causal effect estimation.

Because the goal is to characterize the model's internal reasoning rather than estimate a real-world effect, this work recovers the full graph from text to prediction rather than only a local Markov blanket, to capture the complete reasoning process.

Because observational data sparsely cover the model's internal decision space, this work introduces an MCMC-inspired counterfactual augmentation procedure to actively expand the concept space for more robust graph discovery.
A central challenge in causal discovery is data coverage: reliable structure learning requires a representative sample spanning diverse combinations of concept values.
In many domains, obtaining such coverage requires costly, impractical, or unethical interventions.

Because the mechanism under study is an LLM, the model itself can be prompted to generate counterfactual texts in which a targeted concept is altered while the remaining context stays stable, making the coverage bottleneck more tractable.
The MCMC-inspired algorithm iteratively proposes counterfactual chains and rejects unfaithful candidates, producing a denser, higher-quality concept space for robust causal discovery.
The method adopts Pearl's Causal Graph framework, relaxed to admit cyclic dependencies, acknowledging potential reciprocal influences among concepts an LLM uses internally.

A concept-extraction function ϕ maps input text x to a concept vector [l_c1,...,l_cn], where each l_ci is a categorical variable over subsets S ⊆ Y indicating which classes the LLM perceives concept ci to support (∅ = absent, Y = non-discriminative).
The LLM's inference process is represented as a directed graph G=(V,E) with V = {X} ∪ C ∪ {Ŷ}, capturing high-level causal flow from input text through LLM-perceived concepts to the prediction.
Three structural constraints are imposed: X has only outgoing edges (root), Ŷ has only incoming edges (sink), and the text's effect on prediction is mediated by the concept variables.
Given these constraints, the task reduces to recovering the concept set C and edge set E.

Ground-truth labels in D are replaced with the LLM's own predictions ŷ=f(x); all downstream phases use these predicted labels so the recovered graph reflects the model's perspective rather than dataset labels.
Discriminative Concept Discovery processes training data in small, class-balanced batches; for each batch, the model proposes new candidate concepts which are added to the accumulating concept set C.

Every ten batches, accumulated concepts are annotated and filtered, retaining only concepts whose assigned value maps to a strictly partial subset of classes (neither ∅ nor Y) in a fraction of examples exceeding threshold τ=1/|Y|.

This filtering removes concepts that are rarely expressed in text (providing little evidence for a text-to-concept edge) and concepts broadly aligned with all classes (providing little evidence for a concept-to-prediction edge).
After processing all training batches, test examples are annotated with concept vectors and the same filtering criterion is applied once more, yielding the final concept set C.

Rather than operating directly in the discrete concept space, the algorithm operates in raw text space: the LLM proposes a textual perturbation, which is mapped to a concept vector by ϕ and retained only if it induces the intended conceptual shift.
Operating in text space preserves linguistic coherence while allowing exploration of realizable regions of the concept space, i.e., configurations expressible by natural text.
Each original training example initiates an independent expansion process lasting K=11 steps, iterating through concepts and sampling a target class y* to determine a directional shift (MORE/LESS).

A proposal is accepted (akin to a Metropolis-Hastings test) if it achieves the intended target alignment for the targeted concept and the count of drifted non-target concepts is bounded by a small tolerance ϵ.

If a proposal fails either acceptance condition, the LLM is re-prompted with feedback on which criterion was violated, up to R=5 regeneration attempts per concept; if all fail, no sample is appended for that concept.

The MCMC-inspired expansion densifies the latent concept space by exploring combinations beyond the original dataset, stochastically exploring the valid concept manifold and providing richer support for causal discovery.

σ-CG (Forré and Mooij 2018) is chosen because it accommodates cyclic causal structures, which may arise in LLM inference and cannot be ruled out a priori, and it supports the discrete variables produced by the concept annotations.
σ-CG is applied to the expanded, annotated dataset D_mcmc, obtaining a directed graph G over the variables V.
As background knowledge, the algorithm imposes that ŷ is the unique sink node and enforces this constraint during edge orientation.
Because the goal is to recover a causal graph over the LLM's latent inference process, there is no ground-truth graph available for direct evaluation.

The learned graphs are evaluated via predictive fidelity: if a graph captures meaningful dependencies, direct causal parents should screen off indirect variables, making them more predictive of a node than other concept subsets.

For each target node, a multinomial logistic regression is trained to predict it from its graph-based parent set, compared via 10-fold CV to models trained on all other concept subsets that do not fully contain the parent set.
Graph-based predictors outperform the average alternative subset in every setting, across all models, datasets, and target types, indicating discovered parent sets capture relevant information.

In every setting but one, the causal-graph parent set ranks among the best predictors (Top-3) in a majority of CV cases, despite being compared against tens of alternatives, further strengthening the conclusion.

On the synthetic Disease Diagnosis dataset, extracted concepts are consistent across LLMs and successfully recover the ground-truth variables (specific symptoms) defining the dataset's generative causal graph.
The learned graphs reveal that different LLMs can follow different concept-level reasoning patterns: even when models rely on similar concepts, their causal topologies differ.

This model-specific structure is even more pronounced in naturalistic Sentiment Analysis and LLM-as-a-Judge tasks, where the extracted concepts themselves vary across models, suggesting models rely on different reasoning mechanisms.

These differences matter for deployment: choosing among models requires understanding not only their performance but also whether their underlying reasoning aligns with stakeholders' expectations and constraints.

Multi-chain diagnostics such as the Gelman-Rubin statistic are not directly applicable because the setting uses a single chain per instance; convergence is instead monitored via the empirical KL divergence over the combinatorial concept-state distribution across iterations.

A naive KL decrease is not sufficient evidence of convergence, since as the sample pool grows each new counterfactual carries diminishing marginal weight, mechanically reducing KL regardless of genuine stabilization.

To separate genuine convergence from this artifact, the empirical KL is bounded between an orthogonal-expansion upper bound (every new sample unseen) and a perfect-overlap lower bound (every new sample duplicates an existing one).

A desirable trajectory begins near the upper bound (actively discovering new valid concept states) and gradually approaches the lower bound (samples increasingly come from a stable, realizable region).
The empirical KL curve on Sentiment Analysis for GPT-OSS-20B follows precisely this desired trajectory.
Once the KL stabilizes, the Hamming distance between causal edge sets recovered across successive iterations drops to zero, suggesting additional augmentation no longer changes the learned graph.
The contribution of MCMC expansion is evaluated by comparing three data regimes: All Original, Original Seed (subset seeding the chains), and Seed + Counterfactuals.
The counterfactual-augmented regime achieves the highest predictive accuracy for both concept nodes and prediction across all models.
The MCMC-generated counterfactuals introduce concept-state combinations absent in the original data, enabling more accurate estimation of dependencies between concepts.
Consistent with the predictive fidelity evaluation, the causal graph's parent subsets outperform the average over all concept subsets in this ablation as well.
Together, these two patterns (counterfactual benefit and parent-subset superiority) demonstrate the necessity of the counterfactual augmentation stage.
A causal paradigm is introduced for global, concept-based explainability that maps LLM reasoning to causal graphs.
An MCMC-inspired data augmentation framework is proposed that generates counterfactuals to better cover the concept space, enabling robust causal discovery.
An evaluation protocol is developed for assessing both the structural stability and predictive fidelity of the resulting causal graphs, addressing the absence of gold-standard reasoning graphs.
Although accuracy is the most fundamental evaluation metric, it is insufficient to ensure reliability in real-world LLM applications.
Despite improved accuracy, deep neural network models, including LLMs, have been shown to be easily fooled by specific imperceptible input perturbations.

A lack of robustness may result in unintended biases, incorrect predictions, or overreliance on spurious correlations, raising reliability concerns in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, complex reasoning, code generation, and finance.
Because of the risks in high-stakes domains, a thorough and exacting assessment of LLM robustness that goes beyond conventional accuracy criteria is required.
The absence of standardized definitions and categorizations of robustness complicates cross-study comparisons, as research efforts differ in how they frame scope and components.

Pinpointing the root causes of non-robustness (data biases, unstable training dynamics, architectural limitations, inference inefficiencies) requires disentangling complex interactions across these factors.
While numerous mitigation strategies exist, their effectiveness often depends on addressing specific vulnerabilities, making it difficult to generalize solutions.
Evaluating robustness remains fragmented, with no unified metrics or benchmarks to holistically assess performance under diverse real-world conditions.
Existing literature on LLM robustness is scattered across domains, limiting cross-pollination of insights and hindering cohesive solutions.

The combination of definitional fragmentation, disentangling root causes, non-generalizing mitigations, fragmented evaluation, and scattered literature motivates this survey's comprehensive overview to unify perspectives and accelerate progress.
Robustness is conceptualized as the degree to which a model's output remains stable or correct when the input is perturbed or drawn from a test distribution different from the training distribution.

The survey's working definition is that LLM robustness is the model's ability to maintain consistent performance, reliability, and adherence to intended behaviour despite variations in inputs, contexts, or data distributions, encompassing resilience to noise, paraphrasing, distribution shifts, incomplete information, reasoning perturbations, instruction variations, and adversarial manipulations.

The survey delineates key dimensions of robustness: resilience to adversarial attacks, OOD generalization, sensitivity to prompt variations, handling noisy input, fairness under stress, consistency/reliability of outputs, and task-specific robustness, noting these categories overlap and interact.
A model prone to spurious correlations (an OOD issue) is often more vulnerable to adversarial attacks that exploit those patterns and more sensitive to prompt variations that shift these cues.
Enhancing consistency (e.g., reducing prompt sensitivity) can lower adversarial vulnerability.
Stronger OOD generalization reduces hallucination risks and may indirectly reinforce consistency.
Robustness to noise may also strengthen consistency.
Enforcing consistency too rigidly may limit adaptability to novel inputs, illustrating a trade-off between dimensions.
Alignment methods aimed at improving fairness may weaken OOD generalization, a phenomenon also known as the alignment tax.
OOD inputs can push models beyond their knowledge boundaries, increasing hallucination risks.
Overall, robustness requires balanced strategies, since over-optimizing a single dimension can undermine other dimensions.

Failures in robustness can be broadly categorized as stemming from data, model architecture, the training/learning process, or inference, spanning the entire lifecycle from data collection to deployment.

Instead of learning intended causal relationships, models learn to rely on simpler, superficial patterns (shortcuts) that correlate with correct outputs in training data but do not hold universally, causing performance collapse when such correlations are absent or altered.

Training data reflects societal biases and superficial annotation patterns (e.g., crowd-sourced shortcut labeling), which LLMs learn and amplify, perpetuating robustness failures across training, evaluation, and deployment.

Adversaries can inject malicious examples into training or fine-tuning data to create hidden backdoors triggered by specific inputs at inference time, often without noticeably degrading general performance.

Standard pre-training (next-token prediction) and fine-tuning (ERM) objectives primarily optimize average performance on the training distribution and may not explicitly encourage robustness to distribution shifts or perturbations, potentially encouraging shortcut reliance.
RLHF can cause the model to exploit weaknesses/biases in the reward model (reward hacking) and can amplify biases present in inconsistent or incomplete human feedback (bias amplification).
Improving alignment (helpfulness, harmlessness) can come at the cost of reduced performance on general knowledge benchmarks, worse calibration, or new vulnerabilities -- termed the alignment tax.

Fine-tuning can cause overfitting to fine-tuning-data-specific patterns (harming OOD generalization), high sensitivity to noise in instruction/preference data, and brittleness to instruction phrasing variations at test time.
Specific Transformer components, such as the self-attention mechanism, can be points of failure, and expanding model depth can particularly disrupt attention mechanisms.

Deployment modifications like quantization and pruning can induce information-loss cascades that significantly degrade robustness, with extreme cases like bit-flip attacks showing catastrophic sensitivity.

The algorithm used to select the next token (greedy, beam search, sampling) has a major impact on model performance and consistency, with deterministic vs. stochastic strategies offering different trade-offs and hyperparameters like temperature/beam width strongly affecting robustness.
LLM confidence scores frequently fail to accurately reflect true correctness likelihood, especially after RLHF fine-tuning (overconfidence), hindering reliable decision-making based on model outputs.

RAG systems' robustness depends heavily on the quality and relevance of retrieved context; inaccurate or noisy retrieval can significantly compromise final output quality, sometimes worse than no retrieval at all.

Mitigation strategies are categorized by deployment stage: pre-processing (data-stage interventions), in-processing (training/fine-tuning interventions), intra-processing (inference-time adaptations), and post-processing (output validation/filtering).

Pre-processing strategies (data augmentation, data filtering) intervene at the data stage before training/fine-tuning, aiming to prevent the model from inheriting or amplifying data biases and vulnerabilities.

In-processing strategies (adversarial training, regularization, alignment) integrate directly into the training/fine-tuning loop, actively guiding learning to develop more robust representations and counter training-induced non-robustness.

Intra-processing strategies (robust prompting, weight redistribution, modified decoding, inference-time adaptation) dynamically adjust how models interpret inputs or produce outputs during inference, addressing data/training/inference-related non-robustness without retraining, though not root causes in training data or parameters.

Post-processing strategies (output filtering/validation, LLM-as-a-judge) scrutinize, filter, validate, or transform generated text after generation but before delivery, catching harmful content, inaccuracies, biases, or outputs from attacks that bypassed earlier defences.

Overly strict data filtering to remove toxic content or bias can inadvertently harm general performance or erase valid examples from underrepresented groups, creating a data-quality-vs-quantity trade-off.

Adversarial training formulates an inner loop that maximizes loss via worst-case perturbations and an outer loop that minimizes loss on these examples, but scaling it to LLMs faces challenges: discrete-text gradient mismatches, high computational overhead, a robustness-utility trade-off, and attack-specific (non-transferable) robustness gains.

Alignment techniques (SFT, RLHF, DPO variants) contribute to robustness against attacks eliciting harmful/biased content, but introduce challenges: over-sensitivity to prompt phrasing causing unnecessary refusals, failure to anticipate post-alignment vulnerabilities, reward hacking, and high computational/data requirements.

Intra-processing strategies are cost-effective (avoiding retraining) and adaptable to emerging risks, but because they act at inference time, they do not address root causes in the training data or model parameters.

Using an LLM to judge another model's outputs enables scalable assessment of bias, safety, and factuality, but judge evaluations can be inconsistent due to prompt sensitivity and inherent biases, and judge models themselves can be manipulated by adversarial stylistic cues.
Effective robustness evaluation requires combining complementary metrics across multiple dimensions, since no single metric tells the whole story.
Metrics like Accuracy/F1 Drop, Attack Success Rate, and Compliance/Refusal Rate quantify how much performance or safety degrades when moving from clean to challenging (adversarial/noisy) conditions.

Metrics like OOD Accuracy/F1, ID-OOD Performance Gap, and OOD Detection (AUROC, Energy Score) assess how well models perform on and detect distribution-shifted inputs, using benchmarks such as BOSS, ANLI, Dynasent, and WANLI.

Metrics like Semantic Consistency, Consistency Rate, Response Consistency, and LLM-based Consistency Score assess whether outputs remain stable under paraphrasing, sampling variation, or answer-choice reordering.

Expected Calibration Error and its OOD-shifted variant assess whether a model's predicted confidence reliably reflects actual correctness likelihood, which is particularly important given RLHF-induced overconfidence (linking to P33 in C3).
Fairness metrics (e.g., FLEX-derived measures) evaluate whether disparities in ASR, refusal rate, or accuracy across demographic groups emerge specifically under bias-inducing adversarial prompts.

Metrics like FactScore, FEWL, SelfCheckGPT-style consistency checks, and Hallucination Rate Increase (HRI) measure factual correctness and how much hallucination tendency increases specifically under stress conditions relative to standard conditions.

Studies using benchmarks like BOSS show the ID-OOD performance gap can vary in complex, non-monotonic patterns depending on model scale, training steps, and task type, indicating that improving ID performance does not always guarantee better OOD performance.

Adversarial benchmarks primarily focused on inducing misclassification or safety failures can inadvertently trigger hallucinations, since attacks that manipulate reasoning or push models into unusual states via jailbreaking may cause factually incorrect outputs as a byproduct.

The field is trending toward benchmarks that are dynamic (generating test cases on-the-fly, e.g., ODE, DyVal) and LLM-free (avoiding reliance on potentially unreliable LLM judges, e.g., AMBER) to improve reliability and validity of robustness evaluation.
Larger models are not inherently more robust; scaling trends for robustness often show weak or inconsistent patterns.
Despite safety alignment, models remain susceptible to sophisticated jailbreaking attempts and can deteriorate sharply under minor distribution shifts or input perturbations.
Many promising defences (adversarial training, complex inference-time checks) are computationally expensive and may not scale efficiently to trillion-parameter models.

Aggressively optimizing for robustness often negatively impacts general capabilities or clean-task performance, exemplified by the RLHF alignment tax; balancing the two remains a critical ongoing challenge.

Current evaluation lacks comprehensive benchmarks covering multiple robustness dimensions simultaneously and subtle failure modes, and evaluating generative-task robustness remains harder than classification-task robustness.
