Further evidence for the clarity interpretation comes from the correlation of confidence scores across the two independent committees in the original experiment (0.39±0.072), suggesting confidence tracks a real, paper-intrinsic property rather than pure reviewer idiosyncrasy.

Searching for similar titles with the same contact author, the authors tracked 680 of 1,264 rejected papers, finding 177 only on arXiv, 76 as unaffiliated PDFs, and 427 published at other identifiable venues (many at top-tier ML venues like AAAI, AISTATS, ICML).
For rejected papers, correlation between quality score and citation impact was ρ=0.22±0.038, a weak but real correlation, in contrast to the null result for accepted papers.
Among rejected papers are some with hundreds to thousands of citations; the most highly cited rejected paper has more citations than all but two of the accepted papers.

Together, the null correlation among accepted papers and the weak positive correlation among rejected papers suggest reviewers are better at judging which papers are weak (in terms of eventual impact) than at judging which are strong.

Reviewers are picking up on at least three different components of a paper: 'quality' (uncorrelated with citation impact in its upper range), 'impact' (weakly correlated), and 'clarity' (inferred via confidence, more strongly correlated).
The 'Quality' score may be conflating separate ideas since reviewer instructions indicate rigour is also a component of the quality score, alongside novelty and other criteria.

There is an inconsistency between the 'Qualitative Evaluation' instructions, which are neatly partitioned into Quality, Clarity, Originality, and Significance, and the 'Quantitative Evaluation,' which collapses these into a single score.

Some of the subjective variance in scoring may arise from different reviewers placing different implicit weightings on quality, clarity, originality, and significance when producing a single combined score.

For future conferences, the authors suggest scores be separated (e.g., clarity, rigour, significance, originality individually), with final rankings determined by a program-committee-agreed combination rather than left to individual reviewer discretion.

As the ML community has grown, researchers are becoming less familiar with each other's individual contributions, creating a risk that publication counts at 'top-tier' venues become a proxy for researcher quality.
For early-career researchers who have had less time to establish themselves, this publication-count proxy will be highly sensitive to inconsistency in reviewing processes.

With rising commercial interest in ML, 'top-tier' conference publication has also begun to be used in corporate performance review processes, which are often even shorter-term and thus even more sensitive to reviewing inconsistency.

Given the demonstrated inconsistency in the reviewing process, the paper concludes the community should place less onus on the notion of 'top-tier conference publications' when assessing individual researcher quality.
Twelve leading AI companies published or updated Frontier AI Safety Frameworks in 2025, each containing safety claims, many of which are consequential and used to justify release decisions.

The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index reports an average sector score of 40/100 (down 9 points year-over-year for weighted-average flagship developers), with six major developers at zero on model-information disclosures and no developer adequately reporting train-test overlap.

Independent measurement-theory work shows attack-success-rate comparisons in red-teaming are often founded on apples-to-oranges comparisons or low-validity measurements, with measurement choices rather than attack quality often driving reported differences.
Frontier models can generate strategic-dishonesty responses that fool every output-based jailbreak monitor tested, rendering benchmark scores unreliable.

The 2026 International AI Safety Report concludes that reliable pre-deployment safety testing has become harder to conduct and that models now distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts and alter their behaviour accordingly.

The result of rising claim consequence alongside declining transparency is an evidential inversion: in most of ML, more consequential claims carry stronger disclosure/rerunnability norms, but in frontier AI safety the relationship is often inverted.

A frontier AI safety claim is a published assertion about the safety, controllability, or societal-risk mitigation of a highly capable general-purpose model or frontier deployment, where the assertion is liable to inform public governance, standards, or procurement decisions.
A model is anchored as frontier if it exceeds the EU AI Act's systemic-risk training-compute threshold of 10^25 FLOPs or California SB-53's 10^26 FLOPs threshold.

Regardless of compute, a paper is also in scope if it presents evidence of emergent dangerous capabilities (CBRN uplift, autonomous cyber-offence, self-replication, or strategic-deception capability).
The capability-based backstop closes the principal gaming pathway of training a small but dangerously capable model under the FLOP gate, without requiring reviewers to second-guess training compute.

To prevent authors avoiding the capability anchor by simply not claiming emergence, the trigger is textual rather than interpretive: a paper is in scope if it reports any evaluation of CBRN uplift, autonomous cyber-offence, self-replication, or strategic-deception capability, regardless of headline finding.

The defining feature separating in-scope from out-of-scope claims is that the claim is normative (asserting the model is safe enough or adequately mitigated) rather than merely descriptive (e.g., a benchmark score) that authors do not use to license a deployment conclusion.
A claim is normative (and in scope) if the paper's abstract, conclusion, or policy implications argue for a deployment decision, threshold crossing, or mitigation adequacy.
The operative test for whether a claim is liable to inform governance is what the claim is reasonably likely to be used for, not what the authors intend.

Across the five principal claim types (harmlessness evaluation, alignment reduction, red-team summary, controllability, risk-card summary), the disclosure gap (missing prompt sets, withheld reward models/pipelines, unpublished protocols and thresholds) is concentrated where claim consequence is highest.

Frontier AI safety claims justify release decisions, regulatory compliance, and public assurances, yet the artefacts needed to evaluate them may themselves be sensitive, producing partial transparency without scientific reproducibility.

Current practice (e.g., Anthropic's RSP public risk reports with redactions and external reviewers, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework external evaluators, METR's cross-policy analyses) shows reproducibility is not impossible, but is currently optional, fragmented, and unstandardised.

The Claude Mythos Preview release -- with a public technical report, updated RSP risk assessment, and independent AISI/CETaS evaluations -- still has redacted risk-report sections, internally-reliant capability evaluations, and structurally unavailable third-party reproducibility, illustrating the gap even under the most cooperative disclosure regime currently observable.
Prior work argues that black-box access is insufficient for rigorous AI audits, supporting the case that current disclosure practices fall short of enabling genuine evaluation.

The ASR low-validity finding, the jailbreak-monitor-fooling finding, and the harder-pre-deployment-testing finding are each measurement-validity findings; reproducibility is the standard mechanism by which such distortions are identified and corrected.
Because reproducibility is the standard mechanism for correcting measurement distortions, the present proposal applies that mechanism specifically to frontier safety claims.

NeurIPS has already established the ML Reproducibility Checklist (2019), the mandatory ethics statement (2020), the Datasets and Benchmarks track (2021), and the Position Paper Track (2025), each subsequently adopted by ICML, ICLR, and ACL.

Given this track record of NeurIPS setting field-level norms that are later adopted elsewhere, requiring reproducibility standards for frontier safety claims is presented as the natural next extension of that pattern.

System cards for major frontier models cite NeurIPS-published research, alignment benchmark papers are NeurIPS-family, and dominant alignment methods (RLHF, Constitutional AI, DPO) were published at or around NeurIPS.
Because frontier safety claims already draw scientific legitimacy from NeurIPS-adjacent publication, NeurIPS should require an evidentiary standard commensurate with that legitimacy.

The proposal is presented as direct continuity with, and operationalization of, five accepted 2025 NeurIPS position papers on AI policy leadership, post-hoc refutation tracks, ASR measurement validity, clinical AI monitoring standards, and a six-pillar view of rigor.

ACM's artefact-review badging framework distinguishes available, reviewed, and validated statuses rather than requiring a binary release/trust choice, and proprietary artefacts may be shown to reviewers without public release -- offered as the model for the paper's own graduated disclosure proposal.

NeurIPS should require a claim inventory for any paper making frontier AI safety claims, where authors list each claim, state its scope, identify required artefacts, declare a requested disclosure tier, and specify relevant uncertainty sources.

The framework defines T1 (public release, when it does not materially raise risk, supporting full ordinary empirical support), T2 (controlled/confidential review when public release would create material risk, supporting strong but qualified support), and T3 (restricted, when even confidential review is infeasible, supporting only limited contextual use).

The critical design principle for T3 is that if authors cannot share artefacts even confidentially, the associated claim does not disappear from the paper, but it loses the right to function as a strong scientific warrant -- it may appear as context but not as basis for threshold-crossing or release-justifying conclusions.

Because authors might misclassify a claim's tier to reduce disclosure burden or avoid scrutiny, tier selection is reviewable at submission (ordinary reviewers checking tier-claim-form consistency) and at Phase 2 (a confidential panel that can downgrade T2 classifications).

A single domain-matched reviewer may sign a public adequacy statement in place of the full panel for T2 claims whose artefacts contain no CBRN-uplift, cyber-offence, deception, or systemic-risk-threshold content, while the full 5-7 person panel is required whenever such categories are present, preventing mission creep on the highest-impact claims.

The claim inventory must include a scope statement specifying the evaluated system (checkpoint type), evaluation environment, pipeline components present, and applicable uncertainty (distribution shift, judge-model error, evaluation-awareness effects).
A failure to adequately specify the scope statement makes the corresponding claim scope-limited regardless of which disclosure tier was assigned.

Because the pool of qualified frontier-safety reviewers is small and partially overlaps with the labs being audited, panel membership is restricted to unaffiliated academics and AI Safety Institute personnel, with fixed three-year terms, mandatory five-year recusal on prior collaboration, and auditable access logs.

Because NeurIPS lacks existing secure infrastructure for T2 review at scale, the pilot is bounded to at most five papers per cycle and hosted via a federated colloquium of national AI Safety Institutes, independent evaluators, and trusted academic secure-review labs, with host selection based on claim domain.

NeurIPS adds a five-question frontier safety claim section to the author checklist; the gating question (S1) takes minutes for most papers, and full claim inventories are required only when S1=Yes, using existing ordinary reviewers under extended ethics-review guidelines with no new confidential infrastructure required.

NeurIPS pilots a small confidential panel (5-7 unaffiliated academics and AISI personnel, fixed three-year terms, five-year COI recusal), bounded to at most five papers per cycle, receiving T2 artefacts under NDA-equivalent confidentiality with auditable access logs, producing a public adequacy statement while ordinary reviewers continue assessing scientific contribution.

Accepted papers receive a visible disclosure label (Publicly Reproducible, Confidentially Reviewed, or Restricted Claim); graduated sanctions apply for non-compliance (revision request, claim-strength reduction, or desk rejection plus senior-PC referral); NeurIPS publishes aggregate tier statistics; ICML and ICLR are invited to co-adopt.

Because Tier 2 controlled review is capacity-constrained, it should begin only as a bounded pilot after the Year-1 baseline (claim inventory, scope statement, claim-strength labelling) has been tested in practice, minimizing the risk of a serious proposal failing due to premature scale.
The most important safety evaluations cannot be released because doing so creates safety risks, making a reproducibility mandate incompatible with responsible safety evaluation.

The three-tier framework addresses this directly, since T2 and T3 do not require public release; the relevant precedent is confidential expert review (medical ethics boards, classified peer review, coordinated vulnerability disclosure), and NeurIPS assesses evidentiary status of claims, not model safety certification.
Frontier AI labs can publish through corporate or government channels; NeurIPS legitimacy is not a precondition for governance impact.

In practice labs submit significant technical work to NeurIPS because peer review confers legitimacy that other channels do not, and regulators distinguish peer-reviewed from non-peer-reviewed findings, so governance-relevant claims made at NeurIPS should meet a governance-relevant evidentiary standard.
Stricter standards would push frontier labs toward non-peer-reviewed channels instead of complying.

Current frameworks already assume mixes of public reporting, redaction, and trusted-actor disclosure, so the proposal simply asks labs to map existing practice onto a conference-standard format or accept narrower claims; inability to satisfy even T2 is itself informative about the claim.
Reproducibility presupposes a fixed evaluation context, but frontier safety operates under distribution shift, adversarial prompting, and deployment mismatch.

The mandatory scope statement addresses this by explicitly scope-limiting claims about deployment made from offline evaluation; reproducibility does not eliminate deployment-context uncertainty but makes that uncertainty traceable, which is the precondition for reducing it.
The confidential panel is vulnerable to conflict-of-interest capture and to leakage of sensitive artefacts.

The response to capture/leakage risk is governance rather than abandoning the framework: restricting the panel to unaffiliated academics and AISI personnel, fixed terms, five-year COI recusal, auditable access logs, and public tier rationales, following precedent already operating in Anthropic's external-review design.

Most large-scale fMRI decoding studies focus on either isolated concepts or holistic stimulus reconstruction, leaving open how to decode high-level relational meaning between multiple visual concepts.

The paper asks whether decoding predicate-driven concepts (e.g., holding) can be improved by explicitly accounting for their constituent arguments (e.g., person and baseball-bat) and their representations across brain regions.
Naturalistic images and videos often involve multiple interacting concepts, making them well-suited for probing how to decode entities and their relations from neural activity.

Motivated by the need for compositional supervision, the paper proposes fMRI-QA datasets (BOLD5000-QA, CNeuroMod-QA) pairing fMRI recordings with structured queries about corresponding visual stimuli.
Linear models lack the capacity to capture interactions between multiple interacting components in fMRI decoding.

Large neural decoders with language model backbones tend to encode stimuli holistically without explicitly modeling modular concepts or their relations, leading to coarse alignment between neural activity and language.
Because neither simple linear models nor purely end-to-end neural decoding models can capture compositional concept interactions, neither is found sufficient for solving the fMRI-QA task.

To address the insufficiency of linear and purely end-to-end models, the paper proposes a neuro-symbolic approach that integrates the compositionality of symbolic systems with the expressivity of neural networks.
From this paradigm, the paper proposes NEURONA, a neuro-symbolic framework integrating symbolic reasoning and compositional execution with fMRI grounding across brain regions.

Unlike the LEFT framework's original visual domains where candidate entities (e.g., object proposals) are specified a priori, fMRI has no canonical notion of entities analogous to objects in a scene; relevant neural representations must be inferred.

To address the lack of canonical entities, NEURONA jointly evaluates hypotheses over candidate neural entities derived from parcellated fMRI signals and learns how these entities should be composed for decoding.

To make differentiable program execution compatible with the uncertainty over neural entities, NEURONA introduces execution semantics that replace hard selection with a soft, role-conditioned aggregation mechanism guiding predicate grounding.

Fine-grained fMRI signals are mapped to P functional networks using a functional atlas (e.g., Yeo-17), yielding parcel-level embeddings that define candidate neural entities onto which concepts may ground.
Unary concepts (e.g., person, baseball-bat) are scored over entity embeddings using a linear projection, producing concept-specific grounding logits over parcels.

Relational concepts (predicates like holding) are scored over parcel pairs by augmenting entity embeddings with learnable parcel features, concatenating pairwise embeddings, and applying a learnable transformation and linear classifier.

For concept classification queries, guided unary and relational similarity scores are computed by combining subject/object unary groundings with unary and relational answer-candidate similarity tensors, then summed into a final score for answer selection.

The paper defines five hypotheses about how concepts may be grounded: single-region (H1), multi-region co-activation (H2), subject-guided (H3), object-guided (H4), and full argument-guided multi-region (H5).

Because NEURONA is modular, it can explicitly test guided grounding by conditioning predicate representations on their arguments rather than treating each concept independently, enabling comparison of the five grounding hypotheses.
NEURONA consistently outperforms prior works (linear, UMBRAE, SDRecon, BrainCap) across both BOLD5000-QA and CNeuroMod-QA, achieving a 47% relative improvement over the strongest prior method.
NEURONA demonstrates significant gains specifically on queries about actions and positions, which involve precise relational reasoning over subject and object roles.
The gains on relational queries highlight the strength of the neuro-symbolic framework, which explicitly grounds neural activity using predicate-argument structure to answer relational queries.
Evaluation splits with disjoint training and testing queries, with no overlapping entity-relation combinations, force models to generalize compositionally.
NEURONA achieves the strongest performance across both datasets on unseen compositions, while prior methods show significant degradation, often falling to near-chance levels.

Language model-based baselines retain slightly better generalization performance than other baselines due to their use of pre-trained language models carrying general linguistic priors, but still perform well below NEURONA since they lack explicit concept grounding.
The generalization results suggest that NEURONA learns meaningful groundings that support robust generalization to novel decoding queries via systematic recombination of concepts.

Allowing concepts to ground to combinations of regions (multi-region, unguided) does not yield consistent gains over single-region grounding in overall accuracy, especially in vocabulary classification tasks where both overfit to frequent labels.
Guiding multi-region grounding using subject and/or object arguments of relational concepts consistently outperforms unguided multi-region baselines.
Object-guided grounding is generally more effective than subject-guided grounding among the guided variants.
Using both subject and object arguments together yields the best performance, notably on action and position queries requiring precise relational reasoning.

These ablation results suggest that while multi-region grounding expands the representational space, explicit structural guidance based on predicate-argument dependencies is crucial for accurate and generalizable decoding.

There is no ground truth for intermediate concept groundings, motivating the introduction of a consistency metric measuring whether the same concept tends to ground to similar regions across different fMRI-QA instances.
NEURONA achieves significantly higher grounding consistency scores than a multinomial null model that randomly assigns region groundings while preserving total sample counts per concept.
The significantly higher consistency of NEURONA's groundings compared to the null baseline suggests its learned groundings are reproducible across stimuli rather than arising from chance.

Qualitative analysis shows the same predicate (e.g., hold or look) can be best decoded from different regions depending on the object, e.g., holding(person,kite) uses Control B while holding(person,surfboard) relies on Somatomotor B and Control A.

This pattern of predicate groundings varying with object identity is consistent with the paper's quantitative results on guided grounding, suggesting predicate decoding benefits from argument-dependent modulation.

EEG and MEG offer millisecond-level temporal resolution but poor spatial localization, whereas fMRI provides rich spatial detail but suffers significant temporal lag, despite both stemming from the same underlying neural processes.

Despite their shared neural origins, extreme discrepancies between electromagnetic and metabolic signals have traditionally confined EEG/MEG and fMRI to isolated analysis pipelines, hindering holistic interpretation of brain activity.

Although a unified analysis of these complementary modalities could theoretically unlock a holistic view of brain dynamics, current frameworks lack the capability to bridge this 'frequency gap' effectively.

Most recent brain foundation models aim to learn task-agnostic neural representations and therefore do not explicitly incorporate task-specific or stimulus-level contextual information, so the rich structure of evoking stimuli is underutilized during representation learning.

Because external sensory stimuli provide the ground truth needed to align brain signals with high-level semantic concepts, integrating them as contextual input is crucial for raising the ceiling of decoding performance.

The combination of the electromagnetic/metabolic frequency gap and the underuse of stimulus context motivates NOBEL, a neuro-omni-modal brain-encoding LLM designed to bridge both gaps within a shared semantic space.

NOBEL conceptualizes brain signal decoding as a multi-modal alignment problem, leveraging a strong LLM to integrate heterogeneous data sources via a modular encoding strategy projecting diverse signals into a shared semantic space compatible with the LLM.

For fMRI (metabolic) signals, a dual-path strategy is implemented to explicitly disentangle task-agnostic physiological state information from task-specific semantic information, since these two types of information have very different signal properties.
The task-agnostic path uses a universal encoder (based on NeuroSTORM) to process raw 4D voxel input and capture universal physiological features.

Because semantic representations vary significantly across different stimulus domains (e.g., viewing an image vs. watching a video), a set of task-specific encoders is instantiated, one per stimulus domain, to extract high-level semantic content from GLM beta weights.
Each encoding branch (voxel and per-domain beta) is followed by a modality-specific 3-layer MLP aligner with GELU activation, mapping heterogeneous features into the LLM's input token space.
The combination of task-agnostic and task-specific fMRI paths allows NOBEL to simultaneously leverage global physiological context and precise, stimulus-aligned semantic details.

Neuronal activity generates electrical currents in the cortex that produce secondary electrical and magnetic fields measurable by EEG and MEG respectively, so despite measuring different physical quantities, EEG and MEG arise from the same underlying neuronal current sources.

Exploiting this shared biophysical origin, NOBEL adopts the BrainOmni backbone as a single unified encoder to extract common temporal-spectral representations from EEG/MEG input, rather than treating them as separate domains.
The resulting electromagnetic tokens from the unified EEG/MEG encoder are mapped into the LLM's semantic space through their own modality-specific three-layer MLP aligner.
To ground neural representations in perceptual context, distinct encoders are used for different stimulus modalities (visual, audio) to process raw media inputs into stimulus tokens.

The LLM-input token sequence is dynamically constructed by concatenating the user prompt with the aligned tokens of whichever modalities (stimuli, EEG/MEG, task-specific beta, task-agnostic voxel) are present for a given input, using indicator functions to omit absent modalities.
Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is used to efficiently adapt the pre-trained multimodal LLM backbone, freezing its original parameters and injecting trainable low-rank matrices into the attention layers.
NOBEL leverages Qwen2.5-Omni as its backbone, directly inheriting its visual and auditory encoders, which are thus already aligned with the LLM's semantic space.

Decoding subtle, stimulus-evoked perceptual information via fMRI beta weights is significantly more difficult than extracting global physiological meta-information, due to the low signal-to-noise ratio of the beta-branch features.
Directly mapping these noisy, high-dimensional beta features to the LLM space often leads to optimization instability and poor semantic grounding.

To address this instability, a targeted pre-alignment strategy is implemented for the fMRI beta branch prior to joint multimodal training, inspired by MindEye2's approach of prioritizing alignment with the LLM's already-robust sensory features.

The output features of the beta encoders and the corresponding frozen stimuli encoders are projected into a shared low-dimensional latent space, with a contrastive objective maximizing similarity between brain-signal embeddings and their ground-truth stimulus embeddings.

MixCo-style neural feature mixing is additionally adopted during pre-alignment, interpolating neural representations and stimulus embeddings as cross-modal regularization, to mitigate the limited sample size in fMRI datasets and improve generalization.

This pre-alignment process effectively utilizes the high-quality visual/audio representations as semantic anchors to stabilize the fMRI beta features before they are projected into the LLM input space.

Only after this cross-modal correspondence is established via pre-alignment are the pre-aligned features projected into the LLM input space via the MLP aligners, at which point the framework proceeds to unified omni-modal instruction tuning across all modalities.

During joint instruction tuning, all decoding tasks are formulated as brain-to-text generation problems, optimized with the standard autoregressive next-token-prediction loss over the target text response.

To mitigate optimization instability caused by extreme heterogeneity of input signals, a modality-aware batch sampling strategy ensures all samples within a single training batch belong to the same modality.

Conventional baselines are specialized models trained/optimized exclusively on single datasets for isolated tasks, while NOBEL is a unified, omni-modal foundation model integrating heterogeneous signals within a shared semantic space -- a structurally harder task.

Despite the generalist-vs-specialist disadvantage, NOBEL consistently outperforms established discriminative baselines such as ST-Transformer and SPaRCNet across the majority of EEG and MEG benchmarks.
NOBEL exhibits competitive performance even against the current state-of-the-art BrainOmni, and surpasses it specifically on AD65 (81.3%) and TUAB (82.4%).
Surpassing BrainOmni on some benchmarks suggests the potential of the generative LLM-alignment framework for aligning high-frequency electromagnetic features with the rich semantic space of an LLM.
On gender classification across ABIDE-I, Neural Processing, and XP1-2, NOBEL achieves 89.2%, 83.6%, and 78.8% respectively, consistently surpassing both NeuroSTORM and SWiFT baselines.

The consistent gender-classification improvement suggests the unified framework effectively captures global phenotypic traits, potentially benefiting from the regularization provided by the LLM's semantic space to generalize better across subjects.
On the HCP benchmark (perturbed brain area classification and stimulus amplitude regression), NOBEL matches the high precision of the NeuroSTORM encoder.

Matching NeuroSTORM's precision on HCP confirms that the model successfully retains the underlying encoder's capabilities, and that the alignment/projection process preserves the precision required to perceive subtle, low-level fMRI information.
In fMRI-only decoding, NOBEL achieves 74.6% accuracy on HAD video classification (competitive with a specialized MLP baseline) and a Rouge-L score of 29.7 on NSD image captioning.

The MindEye2 baseline for NSD captioning is reported only on a single-subject split, whereas NOBEL is evaluated in a multi-subject setting, which is more challenging due to heterogeneous functional topography across subjects, yet NOBEL still achieves high linguistic correspondence.
Because stimuli and fMRI reside in distinct modalities, existing baselines struggle to process them concurrently for the stimuli-input cross-modal verification setting.

By aligning omni-modal signals within the LLM's semantic space, NOBEL is able to effectively analyze the relationship between sensory input and neural response, something existing single-modality baselines cannot do.
NOBEL achieves 62.8% accuracy on HAD and 92.7% on NSD for the task of determining whether a specific image/video triggered the recorded fMRI signal.

The high accuracy on NSD indicates the model has learned a precise alignment between visual features and their corresponding cortical representations, enabling it to verify the causal link between stimulus and brain activity.

To validate synergistic capability, NOBEL is evaluated on paired datasets (LEMON, Nat-View, SMN4Lang) where cross-modal EEG/MEG-fMRI recordings are available, integrating electromagnetic signals with metabolic maps.
Across all paired benchmarks (LEMON, Nat-View, SMN4Lang), NOBEL's joint EEG-MEG+fMRI model consistently outperforms the best-performing single-modality baseline.
On the Nat-View dataset, the EEG-only branch yields below-chance performance (16.7%), likely because the task relies heavily on spatial features that scalp-EEG fails to capture.
Rather than being hampered by the weak EEG-only branch, the joint model utilizes fMRI information while extracting subtle temporal cues from EEG, pushing final Nat-View accuracy to 92.8%.

Because the joint model's performance on Nat-View far exceeds what either modality alone (or a naive average) could achieve, these results validate that NOBEL's LLM backbone acts as a semantic integrator that aligns millisecond-level EEG-MEG dynamics with voxel-level fMRI topology, rather than merely averaging separate encoder outputs.

Bayesian meta-learning methods formulate the goal of meta-learning as amortized variational inference of the posterior distribution over task-specific parameters in a multi-task setting, maximizing an ELBO that balances likelihood fit against a KL regularization to a prior.

VERSA employs an NN-based meta-model to directly predict the Gaussian posterior of the agent NN's task-specific weights from a small context set, but this direct approximation of NN weights is limited in scalability due to the large dimensionality of the weights, so it only considers weights for the single softmax output layer.
VERSA does not utilize any task-specific prior, so its conditional posterior could collapse into a deterministic one while training with Monte Carlo approximation.

Neural Processes (NPs) instead model the conditional posterior via a latent representation used as a second input to the likelihood, offering an alternative efficient way to transfer conditional task information.

Follow-up studies indicate NPs often suffer from under-fitting and posterior-collapsing behavior, conjectured to be partially inherent to their original variational formulation since the posterior relies on the whole task data during training but generalizes poorly at test.

It is well known in the broader VI literature that highly flexible NN-based likelihoods can neglect the latent representation during variational inference, contributing to the posterior-collapsing behavior also observed in this paper's own NP experiments.

The scalability limitation and prior-less collapse risk of VERSA, together with the under-fitting/collapsing behavior of NPs, motivate designing a new type of NN-based conditional posterior model that can bypass both failure modes.

Variational Dropout (VD) models the variational posterior via dropout regularization, using a Gaussian approximation of Bernoulli dropout that provides a fully factorized, tractable posterior over NN parameters and allows learning independent per-parameter dropout rates rather than one fixed global rate.
The dropout posterior in conventional VD becomes fixed once trained and is unable to express a conditional posterior according to multiple different tasks.

NVDPs extend VD by defining a conditional dropout posterior over each layer's parameters where the task-specific dropout rate P^t_{k,d} (rather than a fixed rate) determines the mean and variance of each independent Gaussian, with the deterministic parameter theta shared across tasks as the common structure.

The context set for a task is summarized via a permutation-invariant set representation (the mean of per-example features), which is fed into a meta-model that predicts the task-specific dropout rate.

The meta-model predicts logit vectors that, via a temperature-scaled sigmoid, yield low-rank components of the task-specific dropout rate: a row-wise, a column-wise, and a layer-wise term, whose product forms the full per-parameter dropout rate.

Because the product of Bernoulli random variables is itself Bernoulli, the multiplicative combination of row/column/layer dropout components can be interpreted as a low-rank product of Bernoulli experts approximating the task-specific dropout rate.

Because the meta-model only needs to predict the low-rank row/column/layer components rather than the full weight posterior, its complexity is O(L(K+D+1)) compared to VERSA's O(LKD) for directly modeling the full NN weight posterior, greatly reducing the complexity of approximating high-dimensional task-specific weights from few context examples.

An important requirement in the conventional VD framework is that the analytical derivation of the KL term between posterior and prior should not depend on the deterministic NN parameter theta, allowing constant optimization of the ELBO with respect to all independent variational parameters.
The conventional VD approach of using a log-uniform prior is known to be an improper prior, since the KL divergence between the posterior and the log-uniform prior is infinite.

The impropriety of the log-uniform prior can yield a degeneration of the dropout posterior model to a deterministic one, and additionally the conventional VD prior does not support task-dependent regularization.

NVDPs introduce a task-specific variational prior approximated using the same conditional dropout posterior form but conditioned on the whole task dataset rather than just the small context set, i.e., p(phi^t) is approximated as q(phi^t | D^t).

This choice is motivated by prior analytical results in amortized VI showing that the optimal prior maximizing the VI objective is the variational posterior aggregated over the whole dataset, so a posterior conditioned on the larger whole-task set is hypothesized to be much closer to this optimal prior than one conditioned on only a small context subset.

The KL divergence between the context-conditioned dropout posterior and the whole-task-conditioned variational prior is derived analytically and is independent of the shared parameter theta, satisfying the necessary condition to be usable as a prior in the VI optimization.
Although developed alongside NVDPs, this variational-prior formulation is general enough to be adopted by other latent-variable-based conditional posterior models such as NP variants.
Combining the conditional dropout posterior (Eq. 2) and the task-specific variational prior's KL term (Eq. 4) yields the full ELBO objective for NVDPs over the multi-task dataset.

Using the stochastic gradient variational Bayes (SGVB) reparameterization trick, the random task-specific weights are expressed as a deterministic differentiable transformation of i.i.d. noise, making them differentiable with respect to theta and the predicted dropout rates.

Because the transformed weights and the dropout rates (deterministically computed by the meta-model) are differentiable with respect to all variational parameters (theta, psi, omega, tau), the resulting minibatch Monte Carlo ELBO estimator can be optimized end-to-end via stochastic gradient descent.
In practice, a local reparameterization trick is further utilized to reduce the variance of the gradient estimators during training.
NVDP achieves the best LL scores compared with all baselines (NP, NP+VP, NP+CNP, NP+CNP+VP) in both the fixed-variance and learned-variance likelihood settings on the GP regression dataset.

NVDP records high reconstructive log-likelihood (RLL, indicating low under-fitting) on observed context points and excellent predictive log-likelihood (PLL, indicating low over-fitting) on the unseen target points.

Because NVDP achieves both high RLL and high PLL simultaneously, this indicates the conditional dropout posterior approach can simultaneously mitigate under-fitting and over-fitting compared with the other baselines.

When the variational prior (VP) is applied to NP or NP+CNP, PLL scores increase by meaningful margins in all cases, demonstrating that the variational prior approach can independently reduce over-fitting of latent-representation-based conditional posterior models.

Visualizing sampled functions shows NP has high variability but fits context data poorly, NP+CNP fits context data well but loses epistemic uncertainty (posterior collapse), while NVDP captures function variability well while also fitting observed context points better than NP.

In the active learning experiment, each model sequentially selects additional context data points with maximal variance across sampled regressors, starting from one random point followed by 19 variance-guided selections.
NVDPs outperform the other models in log-likelihood improvement across selected points, especially with a small number of additional points, showing steady improvement with less over-fitting.

Because active learning selection quality depends directly on the accuracy of the model's variance estimates, NVDP's superior active-learning performance demonstrates that its dropout-based uncertainty estimation is more accurate than the baselines'.
NVDP achieves the outperforming log-likelihood scores compared with all other baselines on MNIST, CelebA, and the MNIST-trained-to-Omniglot-tested generalization setting.
Interestingly, NVDP (trained only on MNIST) also achieves the best results when evaluated on the entirely unseen Omniglot dataset, among all compared models.

NP generates variable but poorly-fitting samples with few context points, NP+CNP achieves crisp reconstruction but with almost no sample variability due to posterior collapse, while NVDP achieves comparable reconstruction quality while retaining a reasonable amount of variability.

Because NVDP both fits the complex image function space well and generalizes strongly to the entirely unseen Omniglot dataset, this implies NVDP captures more general knowledge applicable to new unseen tasks, beyond simply fitting the training distribution better.
On Omniglot and MiniImageNet few-shot classification, NVDP achieves higher predictive accuracy than the other model-based meta-learning approaches CNP and VERSA.

NVDP's classification accuracy on Omniglot is comparable with state-of-the-art optimization-based meta-learning approaches such as MAML and Meta-Dropout, despite NVDP being a model-based (instant-inference) rather than optimization-based approach.
NVDP also records good classification accuracy on the more complex MiniImageNet dataset, consistent with its strong Omniglot results.

LLMs fabricate quotations, invent sources, and produce confident well-formed but ungrounded claims; this has surfaced in legal filings, news, code repositories, and technical documents, often where readers lack time/expertise to verify.

Researchers increasingly use LLMs to rephrase paragraphs, restructure arguments, summarize related work, and assemble bibliographies, so a rough title or partial memory can become a polished BibTeX entry in seconds.

The resulting manuscript still looks scholarly (claims supported, references alphabetized), but what has changed is the underlying chain of evidence, lowering the cost of placing a fabricated or misattributed reference into the record.
Checking an arbitrary technical claim in a paper's body is essentially an open automated fact-checking problem: claims are subtle, context-dependent, and even expert reviewers may disagree.
Citations differ: a reference names a work and authorship record that either exists and matches, or does not, making the bibliography checkable in a way surrounding text is not.
This checkability property motivates asking a pointed, tractable question of the published record: how often do accepted papers contain hallucinated citations?

A citation is both a social gesture (crediting prior work) and a pointer giving readers enough information to recover the cited artifact from the public record; LLM-assisted authoring can quietly destabilize the pointer role.
Fabrication: the cited work does not exist at all — no indexed artifact matches the title, and the listed authors never produced anything matching it.
Author-identity corruption: a real paper exists, but the citation assigns it to a substantially different set of authors.

Fabrication and author-identity corruption are treated as two faces of one phenomenon and both counted, because from a reader's perspective the reference fails to point to the work it claims to credit either way, leaving an unverifiable intellectual debt.

Minor name variants, spelling mistakes, and venue/year/publication-status changes (e.g., preprint to proceedings) are not counted as hallucination unless author evidence no longer matches at a substantial level.
The measure makes no claim about whether the surrounding text was LLM-generated or whether the cited result is true; it asks only whether the bibliography points to a real work by the named authors.
Zhao et al. audit 111M references across 2.5M arXiv/bioRxiv/SSRN/PubMed papers, but their corpus is dominated by preprints rather than camera-ready proceedings.

GhostCite audits 2.2M citations across 56,381 AI/ML and security-venue papers (2020-2025), finding 1.07% of papers carry an invalid citation and 76.7% of surveyed reviewers report not checking references; it is less conservative in selecting candidates and needs more manual filtering.

This study differs from Zhao et al. by auditing camera-ready proceedings rather than preprints, and from GhostCite on precision, paper-level structure (affected-paper prevalence, high-count tail), and reported per-paper cost.

Studies like Naser (11.4-56.8% hallucination rates across models/domains under direct prompting) characterize models in isolation, whereas this work measures what survives peer review into the archival record.

Reading the convergence of this and other independent, concurrent measurements (Zhao et al., GhostCite, Ansari, Sakai et al., GPTZero disclosures) is taken as evidence that the citation-hallucination phenomenon is real and growing.

The corpus includes only accepted papers whose camera-ready PDFs are openly accessible via OpenReview or official proceedings pages, excluding author-hosted substitutes, to ensure every analyzed manuscript is tied to a controlled publication record.

RefChecker extracts bibliographies from PDFs (primary input here), parsing fields (title, authors, year, venue, DOI, arXiv ID, URL) using LLM-assisted parsing (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) or GROBID fallback, preserving the original string for auditability, then normalizing fields to absorb harmless formatting variation.

Each normalized reference is checked against multiple bibliographic sources (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, CrossRef, DBLP, ACL Anthology) because coverage and metadata quality vary significantly across venues, years, and publication types; disagreements are preserved rather than treating one source as absolute ground truth.

A reference is escalated when unverifiable, when author overlap falls below a 60% default threshold (for 3+ author references), when a DOI/arXiv ID resolves to a different work, or when a cited URL fails/misdirects; minor year/venue variation alone does not trigger escalation.

Escalated references are sent to an LLM with web-search capability, constrained to find a dedicated source page (not merely another paper repeating the citation); if found, RefChecker re-verifies cited metadata against that source before clearing or retaining suspicion.

LLMs help parse noisy bibliographies and perform targeted searches, but the final decision is constrained by external evidence (database matches, identifiers, discovered pages, re-verified metadata); this design reduces but does not eliminate model risk (missing obscure sources, over-trusting low-quality pages).

Of the three-layer label system (final status, issue value, hallucination verdict), only references with a positive hallucination outcome after re-verification (LIKELY, surviving metadata re-check) are counted in the aggregate hallucination measurements; errors, warnings, suggestions, and unverified cases inform triage but are not automatically counted.

Across the 48,095-paper, 2,614,992-reference corpus, the reference-level likely-hallucinated rate stays below 1% in essentially every venue-year (e.g., 2025: 0.38% ICLR, 0.54% ICML, 0.68% NeurIPS, 0.81% USENIX Security on all references).

A sub-1% rate sounds negligible for one bibliography, but a full proceedings contains thousands of papers and hundreds of thousands of references (e.g., ICLR 2025: 221,281 references across 3,703 papers), so even a small rate reaches a large absolute number of flagged references and distinct papers (835 flagged references, 692 papers for ICLR 2025 alone).
At the paper level, at least one likely hallucinated reference appears in 18.7% of ICLR 2025, 23.3% of ICML 2025, 26.2% of NeurIPS 2025, and 34.9% of USENIX Security 2025 accepted papers.

Requiring at least two academic-paper-like likely hallucinated references (a more conservative, false-positive-resistant threshold) still yields 1.9% (ICLR), 3.4% (ICML), 5.1% (NeurIPS), and 4.8% (USENIX Security) for 2025 — roughly one in twenty accepted papers at NeurIPS/USENIX Security.

The post-ChatGPT trend does not show clearly at the raw reference-level rate (where false-positive noise dominates), but sharpens once focus shifts to papers with several likely hallucinated references, which are far less likely to be false positives.

Among affected papers in 2025, exactly one likely hallucinated reference accounts for 87% (ICLR), 81% (ICML), 74% (NeurIPS), and 65% (USENIX Security), arguing against framing affected papers as generally compromised manuscripts.

Despite the single-reference majority, a visible tail of papers carries 5+ hallucinated citations in a single bibliography, with USENIX Security 2025 showing 34.6% of affected papers with ≥2 and 2.0% with ≥5, and NeurIPS 2025 showing 1,545 affected papers, 407 with ≥2, and 30 with ≥5.
The more failures a single bibliography accumulates, the less plausible it is that every one is a false positive, so 5+-reference papers are the cases the authors can most safely call genuine.

Papers with 5+ flagged references are rare on a paper-rate basis (≤1%, often zero pre-2022) but contribute a disproportionate share of all flagged references (e.g., 11.7% at USENIX Security 2024, 9.6% at NeurIPS 2025), so even a tail-only check would intercept a non-trivial fraction of hallucinated citations.
The single-paper maximum observed is 20 (NeurIPS), 13 (ICML and USENIX Security), and 8 (ICLR) — a bibliography with 20 likely hallucinated references is not a borderline case.

A natural objection is that the measured rates reflect ordinary bibliographic drift (e.g., an arXiv year instead of venue year, a transliterated name, an outdated URL) rather than genuine hallucination.

Across every venue family, likely hallucinated references decompose into three identity-level failure buckets — unresolved references, multi-field failures, and substantial author-list mismatches — with ordinary venue/year/publication-status drift logged separately and never entering any rate.

Joining hallucination counts to mean reviewer rating for the OpenReview-covered subset (22,764 papers) shows the difference between clean (0 hallucinated refs) and affected (≥1) papers is almost negligible: Δ=+0.02 ICLR, +0.005 ICML, +0.04 NeurIPS — if anything affected papers rate marginally higher.

Slicing by acceptance tier instead of rating shows posters affected at 20.4%, spotlights at 23.5%, orals at 20.3% — acceptance into the most selective tier does not lower hallucinated-citation prevalence.

Across 14 research areas with ≥100 papers, affected-paper prevalence sits in a narrow 15.5%-25.7% band; the problem cannot be reduced to a particular community's authoring practices, though LLM/foundation-model researchers appear slightly less prone (16.1%), possibly from more careful reference checking.

Accepted ICLR 2023 papers (mean rating 6.61) are affected 16.0% of the time; rejected papers (mean rating 4.67, nearly two points lower) are affected 16.9% of the time — a negligible integrity gap despite a large assessment gap.

Because a paper judged much weaker by reviewers is not, in expectation, much more likely to carry hallucinated citations, the hallucinated-citation rate is driven by authoring practice rather than overall paper quality.

Together, these results show reviewers' rating signal carries essentially no information about whether a paper's bibliography survives verification — the signal exists in the published record but is invisible to the process deciding what gets published.
Recent ICLR 2026 and ICML 2026 policies explicitly listing hallucinated references as desk-rejection grounds are responding to precisely this invisibility of the signal to ordinary review.

The single most consistent lesson from the audit is that manual inspection is needed: across manually verified references, most flags were not hallucinations but mangled author strings, truncated titles, or PDF-extraction corruption.

The flags that survived scrutiny shared a sharper property: no corresponding work could be found, or a real title was bound to an unrelated authorship record — illustrated by cases where no source anywhere matches a well-formed cited title/authors, and where a real title (e.g., 'Compressive Transformers...') is bound to a wrong author list.

Documented false-positive patterns include an editor's name miscounted as a coauthor, a title fragment parsed as part of the author field (e.g., 'Jimmy Ba Adam'), and two genuinely distinct real papers sharing an identical title where the tool matched the wrong one.

Deciding how much author-list divergence counts as fabrication is hard: on a two-author reference a single wrong name already crosses a 'half the names' cutoff, yet one wrong name is exactly what an ordinary copy-paste slip produces; the kind of difference (transposition vs. genuinely different person) matters as much as its size.

At this resolution, metadata alone almost never separates an erroneous copy-paste from deliberate or machine-generated fabrication, so the tool's output remains a set of candidates requiring human verification and final decision.
To further check results, authors of accepted papers with at least five likely hallucinated references were contacted directly and shown the tool's output for their paper.

Across responses, authors consistently attribute citation hallucinations to errors introduced during bibliography construction (often LLM-based generation/reformatting not subsequently verified, sometimes specifically at the camera-ready stage) rather than intentional fabrication.

Other authors clarify that cited works were real but had corrupted metadata (author lists, titles, venues), while a smaller subset disputed certain flags as false positives (e.g., webpage references or valid but misidentified papers).

No response claimed deliberate fabrication; where errors were acknowledged, authors uniformly reported correcting the citations and, in several cases, proactively notifying program chairs or updating public versions.

Read together, these responses match the paper's framing of the failure as an unchecked, machine-completed reference that no pipeline stage was responsible for validating, rather than deliberate misconduct.
In one venue-scale scan, auditing 3,703 accepted papers and 221,281 references cost approximately $157, or roughly four cents per paper.
At this price, verification can be run at submission (to inform review) and again at camera-ready (to catch revision-introduced references) without materially affecting a conference's budget.

The practical implication is not a manual gate but a standardized check folded into submission infrastructure: run the tool at submission/camera-ready, surface only failing references with supporting evidence and the search trail, and let a human confirm or dismiss each flag.

This design is motivated by respect for reviewers' workload, since reviewing is voluntary and already strained by rising submission volumes, and manually resolving every reference is neither reasonable nor scalable.

Even though the underlying signal is real and large enough to matter, and desk-rejection policies are a reasonable deterrent, flags should inform an evidence-backed, human-reviewed process giving authors a chance to justify or correct before punitive action, given cases like not-yet-indexed works.

A conservative, externally auditable notion of hallucinated citation is defined, based on non-existent works and substantial author-identity mismatch, explicitly excluding ordinary venue/year/publication-status drift.
RefChecker, a scalable open-source reference-verification pipeline combining multiple authoritative bibliographic sources with deep web-search re-verification, is built.
A large-scale audit of likely hallucinated citations is conducted across accepted papers from top AI and security venues.
The audit shows likely hallucinated citations survive peer review and appear in camera-ready proceedings, including award-winning papers and papers with multiple failures in one bibliography.
The post-ChatGPT increase, paper-level prevalence, error composition, and high-count tail are quantified, and conference-scale auditing is shown to be performable at low cost.
LLMs like GPT, BERT, and LLaMA demonstrate remarkable performance largely due to self-supervised learning, training models to predict parts of input from other parts without human annotations.

SSL approaches like DINO, iBOT, and BEiT extend these ideas to vision, mostly using large Transformer (ViT) architectures and learning global representations by solving auxiliary tasks like predicting similarities between augmented views.
While effective for image classification and matching, these global-representation methods often struggle to capture the compositional structure of objects in scenes.

Methods like CutLER typically identify only a single dominant foreground region and struggle to isolate multiple objects without costly iterative training, while Slot Attention/SlotCon produce structured representations via implicit grouping but lack explicit hierarchical organization and instance-level decomposition.

Current methods tend to produce whole-scene representations with limited capacity for structured object understanding, even though an image contains objects, parts, and spatial relationships that a meaningful representation should reflect at local, intermediate, and global scales.
Fine-tuning these SSL models for dense prediction tasks often demands substantial computational resources and extensive annotated data, making deployment challenging in resource-constrained settings.

An SSL approach based on a new ProtoScale module is introduced, designed to overcome these limitations by progressively constructing a structured visual representation combining semantic abstraction, instance separation, and hierarchical organization.

The approach builds on the intuition that an effective representation should be able to (i) group pixels by semantic meaning, (ii) identify distinct instance parts, and (iii) organize them coherently into complete objects.
Object detection is chosen as the evaluation task because it offers a good balance between local and global scene complexity for testing this hypothesis.
Unlike SOTA methods that rely on disruptive cropping strategies, the full scene context is preserved across views to ensure instance consistency while maintaining spatial structure.
A lightweight hybrid CNN/Transformer encoder is adopted to reduce computational cost and improve feature scalability.

Unlike traditional downstream pipelines based on Mask R-CNN (which rely on NMS post-processing and are often less efficient), a DETR-like architecture is adopted for a fully end-to-end, NMS-free formulation better aligned with evaluating structured object-centric representations.

Contrastive methods (SimCLR, MoCo) maximize similarity between two views' representations in latent space; DINO extends this with a teacher-student EMA framework leading to spontaneous emergence of structured patterns like foreground/background.
Their primary goal is to encode an entire image as a global vector, suitable for image-level tasks like classification but falling short for dense prediction.

Object-discovery methods (MOST via clustering, CutLER via iterative supervised loops) are effective at discovering salient regions but remain limited by initial pseudo-label quality and often focus on a single dominant object per image.
Dense SSL methods (DetCon, SoCo) learn features preserving spatial coherence and local consistency, but do not explicitly structure objects.

Slot Attention assigns pixels to abstract instances via iterative attention; SlotCon combines semantic grouping with contrastive learning for object-centric representations — but ProtoScale extends SlotCon's formulation by modifying semantic grouping and explicitly modeling hierarchical relationships between instances.

Most recent SSL methods rely on pure ViT architectures, which are computationally expensive and whose patch-based processing fragments the input, limiting the ability to capture small or occluded objects.

Contrastive methods yield effective global/local representations but lack grouping; latent slot models offer encouraging directions but still fall short on hierarchy, modularity, and generalization — this gap is what ProtoScale's modular, hierarchical, shared-prototype grouping mechanism addresses.

Both student and teacher networks share the same encoder architecture but differ in input processing and training role; the teacher's parameters are updated via exponential moving average (EMA) of the student weights and serves as a stable label generator.
Training encourages student predictions across all views to align with the teacher output using three loss terms, promoting view-consistent grouping, tightly integrated with the ProtoScale module.

Both models share a multi-scale encoder extracting feature maps at three spatial resolutions, enabling ProtoScale to operate simultaneously at fine, intermediate, and global scales, helping discover small object parts, full objects, and global scene structure in a unified representation.

The teacher processes a single globally augmented image (random cropping, zoom out, horizontal flip, photometric distortions), serving as the stable training target and base input for generating student views.

The student is exposed to four distinct views from a different transformation pipeline (Gaussian blur, random spatial masking, color jitter) designed to be spatially coherent, preserving object layout and relative positioning while introducing appearance variability.
SOTA methods relying heavily on random cropping strategies disrupt the spatial distribution of objects and degrade dense prediction performance.
By adopting a strategy that preserves full scene context across views instead, instance consistency is promoted without compromising the underlying spatial structure.
Unlike previous SSL methods, a hybrid CNN/Transformer encoder inspired by RT-DETR is employed, processing multi-scale features extracted from a ResNet backbone.
The lowest resolution feature map is passed through a full self-attention transformer, capturing long-range spatial dependencies and providing coarse guidance on where the model should focus.

The resulting low-resolution attention is progressively fused with intermediate and high-resolution convolution features through top-down and bottom-up fusion paths, relying on CNN local precision to determine what is present in the identified regions.
This hybrid design enables accurate dense representation while reducing the computational cost associated with full-resolution attention.

ProtoScale consists of three sequential components: semantic clustering per feature map, aggregation into shared instance-level prototypes across the batch, and a hierarchical module inferring relationships between instances.

At each encoder scale, spatial features are fed into a semantic grouping module computing softmax dot-product attention between 256 learnable semantic prototypes and spatial features, each prototype aggregating features into semantic queries via weighted attention.

A centered Gaussian prior (μ=0.5, σ=0.7) is applied to attention maps to reduce collapse and bias toward generic representations (encouraging local-structure focus), and a set of auxiliary prototypes R, excluded from the loss, absorb noisy activations to stabilize learning.
While semantic grouping isolates regions, it fails in crowded or occluded scenes, motivating a differentiable instance grouping stage.

Instance grouping introduces shared latent prototypes I_k learned across the batch; each semantic slot is softly assigned to 32 learnable instance prototypes, scaling the corresponding attention map before summation over semantic prototypes, trained with consistency and sparsity regularization to encourage specialization and spatial diversity.

Beyond instance-level attention, ProtoScale models object relationships via a relation (affinity) matrix between instance prototypes, predicted by a shallow MLP with sigmoid activation; thresholding low-affinity pairs at 0.5 lets the model merge overlapping/related instances, capturing part-whole and object-group structure.
The student is trained via a weighted objective L_total = λ_sem L_sem + λ_inst L_inst + λ_hier L_hier, with (λ_sem, λ_inst, λ_hier) = (1, 2, 1) found to yield the best experimental results.

Each loss term includes a KL-divergence term computed between corresponding student and teacher attention maps, chosen to encourage matching the entire probability distribution rather than only the highest-probability regions.
All modules operate at three spatial scales, enabling rich object-centric reasoning across fine, intermediate, and global resolutions.

SSL encoders are typically evaluated via downstream fine-tuning using Mask R-CNN, but this work adopts RT-DETR, an end-to-end detection pipeline without NMS post-processing that achieves significantly better performance than Mask R-CNN.
Because RT-DETR does not support instance segmentation, evaluation focuses exclusively on object detection as the downstream task.

A set of strong SSL baselines (DINOv1, DINOv2, iBOT, TEC, SlotCon) are selected, with each method's encoder backbone attached to a shared projection module outputting multi-scale features, integrated into the same student-teacher method for fair comparison under identical training configurations; a fully supervised RT-DETR baseline is also included as reference.

COCO (high scene diversity) and UA-DETRAC (high object density) are used, with class labels redefined into a fine-grained 17-class taxonomy and images filtered to those containing at least two such classes, yielding 50,022 combined training and 5,555 combined validation images.

Evaluation varies fine-tuning epoch count and the proportion of labeled training data (always testing on the full validation set), reflecting realistic conditions where high computing infrastructure and large annotated datasets are often unavailable.

ProtoScale significantly outperforms current SOTA SSL approaches and the supervised RT-DETR (random init) baseline, consistently achieving higher performance even versus models pretrained on much larger datasets (ImageNet-1K, LVD-142M).
ProtoScale, pretrained for only 35 epochs on COCO, outperforms methods like SlotCon which requires up to 800 pretraining epochs to achieve competitive results.
The method demonstrates strong performance specifically on small and medium objects, even with fewer fine-tuning epochs.
DINOv2 slightly outperforms ProtoScale on large objects, likely due to the strong generalization capabilities of transformer architectures trained on a massive 142-million-image dataset.

Different training-set fractions (10%, 30%, 50%, 70%) are used to simulate low-resource scenarios, comparing the two best-performing methods (ProtoScale and DINOv2) for robustness under varying data availability.
Although overall performance decreases relative to 100%-data fine-tuning for both methods, results show ProtoScale requires less labeled data to achieve competitive performance.
ProtoScale consistently outperforms DINOv2 on small and medium objects across the tested data fractions, while DINOv2 performs slightly better on large objects.
The performance advantage is achieved despite ProtoScale using only about 12 million parameters, compared to DINOv2's ViT-Small encoder's approximately 21 million parameters.
An SSL approach is proposed that combines semantic grouping, instance-level clustering, and hierarchical reasoning to build structured visual representations without any annotations.
ProtoScale, a modular grouping module operating at multiple spatial scales, is introduced, capable of organizing pixels into instances and instances into structured groups.
Full scene context is preserved across views by avoiding disruptive cropping, improving consistency in dense prediction tasks.
A lightweight hybrid CNN/Transformer encoder, adapted from RT-DETR, is leveraged to balance feature precision and reduce computational overhead.

The proposed approach is validated through downstream object detection experiments, comparing against SOTA methods and evaluating under realistic constraints of small annotated datasets and limited training epochs.
LLMs have catalyzed NLP advances but encounter challenges such as hallucination and the need for domain-specific knowledge, and cannot promptly update their knowledge.
Recent methodologies integrate information retrieved from external resources with LLMs, substantially enhancing their performance across NLP tasks.

Existing surveys on RAG are limited in scope: some do not cover all relevant domains or lack developmental timelines, some introduce retrievers and generators independently limiting insight into their interaction, and some focus narrowly on text generation with limited illustrative detail.

Existing surveys on RAG only address NLG-oriented retrieval augmentation, neglecting that NLU tasks also necessitate external information, leaving a scarcity of comprehensive surveys spanning the full spectrum of NLP.

This survey addresses the gap by covering both Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Retrieval-Augmented Understanding (RAU) under the unified concept of Retrieval-Augmented Language Models (RALM), aligning generation work with NLG and the rest with NLU.
RALM is defined by the basic architecture y = F(x, z), where x is the input, z is the retrieved message, and F is a language model or data processing function.
In sequential single interaction, a retriever finds top-K relevant documents z for input x, and the language model then receives x and z to generate output tokens.
Researchers discovered that a single retriever-LM interaction is insufficient for long dialogue generation and solving multi-hop problems.

To address the insufficiency of single interaction, a method with multiple interactions between retriever and language model was proposed, where the LM generates output first and the outputted content is used for subsequent retrieval steps.
The strictly sequential flow of information (retriever-to-LM or LM-to-retriever) may not be optimal in all domains and may be less extensible.

As an alternative to sequential structures, researchers proposed a parallel interaction structure where the retriever and language model work independently on the input, with the output determined by weighted interpolation of their respective outputs.
Sparse retrieval's main advantage is simplicity, allowing easy integration into existing indexing systems due to fewer dimensions, and it is easier to generalise and more efficient.

Simple term matching methods (TF-IDF, BM25) became insufficient to meet retrieval demands, motivating the use of machine-learning-based sparse vector representations that capture semantic essence rather than exact term overlap.
The emergence of deep learning techniques significantly transformed retrieval, driving growing interest in dense retrieval methods that sacrifice some comprehensibility for enhanced accuracy.

The dual encoder architecture, comprising two networks that independently generate dense embeddings for queries and documents, is the common design for dense retrieval models, favored for its high accuracy and suitability for RALM.

Knowledge distillation is a technique for gradually filtering and streamlining a large retrieval database to make it more suitable for a user's query, transferring data from larger pre-trained models to smaller ones.

Internet retrieval offers a plug-and-play approach well-suited to open-domain generalisation without requiring real-time database updates, but the presence of irrelevant or harmful web information can significantly reduce RALM effectiveness without proper screening.

As researchers gained better understanding of individual retrieval techniques' strengths and weaknesses, they increasingly combined them into hybrid approaches to improve effectiveness and robustness of the RALM architecture.

AutoEncoder language models introduce an independence assumption during pre-training that means correlations between predicted [MASK] tokens are not considered, and the [MASK] marker creates inconsistency between pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

Because AutoEncoder language models are highly generalisable, unsupervised, and naturally incorporate contextual semantic information, self-encoding models are commonly used in RALM architectures for natural language understanding tasks.

AutoRegressive language models predict the next word based only on preceding words (left-to-right modelling), making them well-suited to generative NLG tasks like dialogue generation and machine translation.
Because of their left-to-right generative advantage, AutoRegressive language models are a popular choice for NLG tasks in the RALM field.

The Transformer encoder-decoder architecture divides input into source and destination sequences processed by encoder and decoder respectively, enabling parallel computation and significantly increasing training and inference speed.
Retrieval can produce documents that not only fail to provide helpful information but can also compromise the quality of the language model output, motivating research on retrieval quality control.

An instruction-tuning approach updates the query encoder using a generalised supervised retrieval training target, enabling the retriever to produce more contextually relevant results consistent with LLM preferences.

Inspired by the instruction-tuning approach to retrieval quality, SELF-RAG proposes a more sophisticated model trained on an instruction-tracking dataset, retrieving and selecting outputs via fine-grained self-reflection.

A further method improves on SELF-RAG by designing a correction strategy that classifies retrieved information into CORRECT, INCORRECT, and AMBIGUOUS categories to address inaccurate retriever results.
The RALM architecture initially used a single document for retrieval augmentation, but performance significantly improved when the number of retrieved paragraphs was increased.

Because increasing retrieved paragraphs improved performance, Fusion-in-Decoder was proposed: keeping the retriever unchanged, encoding related documents individually, then connecting them for decoder output.
An improvement on FiD constrains the information flow from encoder to decoder and tunes source pointers to improve topmost source accuracy.
Knowledge distillation was applied to the FiD model (FiD-KD), using cross-attention scores from a sequence-to-sequence reader to obtain synthetic targets for the retriever.
The KNN-LM approach linearly interpolates an extended neural language model's predictions with K-nearest-neighbours in the pre-trained LM embedding space.
It was proposed that not all generated tokens need to be retrieved; a lightweight neural network can be trained to aid KNN-LM in adaptive retrieval, improving efficiency.

RETOMATON, an unsupervised weighted finite automaton built on the datastore using saved pointers and clustering, is more effective than the adaptive retrieval approach in improving accuracy while requiring no additional training data.
REALM used masked language training in pre-training and included a retriever trainable end-to-end, targeting only the QA task with a frozen retriever during fine-tuning.
Unlike REALM, RAG used an already-trained retriever (DPR) and only employed BART for partial end-to-end training.

Building on REALM's approach with an unsupervised pre-training and supervised fine-tuning pipeline, subsequent work found that using end-to-end trained retrievers resulted in significant performance improvement across tasks.
Exceedingly simple prefix attacks can diminish the relevance and accuracy of RALM output and even alter the retriever's retrieval strategy, revealing poor robustness as a limitation.

In response to prefix-attack vulnerability, Gradient Guided Prompt Perturbation (GGPP) is proposed as a method to perturb RALM and detect such perturbations by prompting the internal state of the perturbed model.

When using the Internet as a retrieval tool, the quality of sources can vary widely, and merging this data without proper consideration can introduce noise or misleading information, contributing to poor retrieval-result quality.

The persistent uncertainty that retrieval outcomes fully align with the LM, and the noise introduced by variable-quality Internet sources, motivates the proposed future direction of improving retrieval quality via better datasets and re-ranking techniques.
Some existing RALMs require extensive model changes and complex pre-training/fine-tuning, increasing time and space overhead and reducing scalability as retrieval scale grows.

The overhead limitation motivates proposed future solutions such as plug-and-play intermediate modules, greater use of Internet retrieval, and in-context learning to reduce the cost of improving language models.

Unlike robotics simulators or game environments with explicit machine-readable success criteria, desktop applications rarely expose clear, machine-readable indicators of task completion; objectives are typically implicit, visually grounded, and unstructured.
Applying reinforcement learning to GUI-based environments remains fundamentally constrained by the absence of reliable, scalable reward signals.
Prior work often relies on brittle, task-specific heuristics (e.g., DOM element checks in web environments) or manually annotated success labels to supply a reward/success signal.

Brittle heuristics and manual success labels fail to scale across different applications, operating systems, and task distributions, substantially limiting generalization beyond narrowly defined settings.

Defining task success internally within the computer-use agent itself introduces additional reliability concerns, since the agent's own perception and reasoning are imperfect and are exactly what RL aims to improve.
The lack of a scalable and reliable reward mechanism remains a central bottleneck for effective RL fine-tuning of computer-use agents.

State-of-the-art desktop agents achieve success rates of only around 60% on OSWorld and approximately 40% on macOSWorld, highlighting a significant gap between current capability and practical deployment.

Autonomous evaluators based on Vision-Language Models can achieve high accuracy and generalize across diverse applications, but inevitably introduce noise via false positives (labeling unsuccessful executions as completed) and false negatives (failing to detect success).
Naively using evaluator outputs as reward signals can introduce bias and lead to unstable reinforcement learning.
The paper models the autonomous evaluator's feedback as a noisy binary reward channel, characterized by false-negative rate e+ and false-positive rate e-.
