The non-uniform advantage (ETTh2 MSE exception) indicates different synthetic priors may capture different aspects of real-world temporal dynamics, so results are interpreted as encouraging rather than conclusive evidence.

Existing studies mainly focus on simulating human dialogue; non-verbal behaviors like item clicking in recommender systems, though implicitly exhibiting user preferences, have not been deeply explored.
The gap between universal language modeling and personalized behavior modeling, plus LLMs' incomprehension of user-item relations, is a main reason non-verbal behaviors are underexplored.

Verbalizing interaction records into natural language text to prompt LLMs struggles to capture underlying behavioral patterns, since semantically unrelated items (e.g., diapers and beer) can be behaviorally correlated in ways that confuse LLMs.

Prior agent-based recommendation studies (e.g., RecAgent) mainly characterize user-side behaviors using universal LLMs, neglecting the effect of item-side modeling in the two-sided interaction process.

AgentCF is proposed as an agent-based collaborative filtering approach that considers both users and items as agents, collaboratively optimized together, inspired by collaborative learning in traditional recommenders like BPR and NCF.
Both user and item agents are equipped with memory modules maintaining simulated preferences and tastes, including intrinsic features and acquired behavioral information.
User agents are equipped with short-term memory (recently updated preference text) and long-term memory (a pool of historical preference texts) to reflect dynamically changing preferences.
Item agents are equipped with a single unified memory module recording their characteristics and adopter preferences, since item information is relatively stable through time.

User agents are presented with a contrastive pair of a positive and negative item candidate and tasked with selecting an item and providing an explanation, analogous to the forward computation of models like BPR.

To increase discrimination difficulty, a negative item with high popularity is sampled and placed before the positive item in the selection list, deliberately introducing popularity and position bias.

Based on the disparity between an agent's decision and real-world interaction records, user and item agents are prompted to reflect on and adjust their memories in a mutual manner, serving as the 'backward update' analogous to gradient-based learning.
The memory of the negative item agent is not modified during reflection, because LLMs tend to over-complain about the negative item's drawbacks despite it possibly being attractive to other users.

Because memory of both user and item agents is updated for each interaction record, item memory becomes injected with adopter preferences, which propagate to subsequent users interacting with that item (and vice versa for users), implicitly modeling collaborative filtering.

User and item memories serve as language-based parameters (embeddings); the selection process corresponds to forward preference evaluation and collaborative reflection corresponds to backward parameter update, with reflection acting as a 'semantic gradient'.
AgentCF outperforms other baselines in most scenarios, highlighting the effectiveness of collaborative learning for simulating personalized agents.
The performance of the basic AgentCF-B variant, acting as a collaborative filtering recommender, demonstrates the efficacy of preference propagation in modeling the collaborative filtering idea.
Retrieving user agents' specialized preferences toward candidates (AgentCF-B+R) enables more personalized inferences.
In sparse interaction cases (Office dataset), incorporating user historical interactions to enable LLMs as sequential recommenders (AgentCF-B+H) achieves better performance.
AgentCF achieves comparable performance to traditional recommenders trained on full datasets in sparse scenarios, despite being trained on only ~0.07% of the complete dataset.

Existing tuning-free methods (Pop, BM25, LLMRank) exhibit unsatisfactory performance, with LLMRank falling significantly behind traditional models despite using ChatGPT with user historical interactions.

Without autonomous interaction (directly providing real interaction records to agents), performance drops, showing that comparing autonomous interactions to real-world records generates more comprehensive feedback for reflection.
Without user agent memory updates (representing users by raw historical interactions), performance declines, showing simple verbalized interaction text cannot reflect underlying user preferences.

Without item agent optimization (representing items by identity information only), performance also declines, highlighting the effectiveness of behavior-involved item-side modeling for capturing two-sided relations.
An LLM prompted by user historical interactions (LLMRank) is influenced by both popularity bias and position bias, tending to select popular and higher-positioned items.

AgentCF, although inevitably affected by popularity and position bias, performs with enhanced stability compared to LLMRank, confirming it ranks candidates based on personalized preferences rather than general knowledge alone.

Continuous optimization across steps enables user agents to align their preferences with real users, leading to an increasing number making correct choices on initial attempts before optimization at each step.
Around 95% of user agents can make correct choices after collaborative reflection, highlighting its effectiveness.
User agents can read and write reviews about items, simulating user-user social behaviors where test users read reviews from other user agents before deciding.

Simulated user agents show a growing inclination to purchase items after positive reviews, refrain from purchasing after negative reviews, and trust reviews from users with similar preferences, akin to real-user behavior.
New item agents are prompted to interact with and learn from popular item agents with extensive interaction records, warming up cold-start items by estimating adopter preferences.
The item-item interaction process enhances propagation of collected user preferences to new items and improves their ranking performance compared to using cold-start memory alone.

Even interactions with item agents that differ in identity information can alleviate the cold-start problem to some extent, implying new item agents comprehend the relationship between identity information and personalized memory rather than simply replicating other agents' memories.

A seed user agent is initialized with special preference descriptions not spontaneously emerging during normal optimization, then agents autonomously interact and optimize memories to observe propagation.

Through continuous interactions, an increasing number of user agents with similar behaviors to the seed user express similar preferences, but the proportion gradually decreases as interaction scope expands, indicating information decay consistent with real-world diffusion principles.

Due to the continuous stream of user interactions and feedback in web-based systems, recommenders increasingly rely on contextual multi-armed bandits (CMABs), which encode users and items as feature vectors, select an item to recommend, and update incrementally from feedback.

Most CMAB research has concentrated on four aspects: the underlying model consuming user state, the exploration strategy, the inference procedure for producing recommendations, and reward modeling for learning and evaluation.

Current literature often neglects the state representation — the contextual encoding of user interaction history (one-hot vectors, item metadata summaries, or more commonly embeddings) — with most CMAB studies treating it as a given design choice rather than investigating its impact.

The paper investigates the impact of different embedding-based state representations derived from matrix factorization models on the performance of traditional CMAB algorithms, hypothesizing that this seemingly minor design choice substantially influences final performance.

The paper presents the first large-scale empirical comparison of state representations in contextual multi-armed bandits, evaluating six recommendation datasets, two matrix factorization models, three representation strategies, and three CMAB models, systematically varying both embedding method and representation formulation to isolate their impact.
The study shows that the choice of bandit algorithm often results in minor performance differences compared to the substantial impact of the selected context representation strategy.

The paper identifies a prominent gap in the literature: while much research emphasizes new algorithms, reward modeling, and evaluation methods, the design of the environment's state representation remains largely overlooked.

Content-based CMAB context uses user demographic information and item metadata, useful for cold-start and explainability, but such features are not always available and are often subject to noise and inconsistencies, limiting applicability.

Due to content-feature limitations, a common strategy represents users and items via latent embeddings capturing preferences and characteristics in a shared latent space, exemplified by warm-up ALS initialization, Latent Contextual Bandits, BanditMF, and deep-learning healthcare recommenders that concatenate learned embeddings as bandit input.

Many existing recommenders using item/user embeddings as context rely on offline pre-trained embeddings that remain static during online interactions, simplifying modeling but potentially failing to capture evolving real-time dynamics.

To address the static-embedding limitation, studies like COFIBA (dynamic user clustering with LinUCB), Alternating Linear Bandits (continuously retrained MF embeddings), and Khosravi et al.'s work explore evolving user states and their representation.

Even accounting for dynamic embeddings, the vast majority of studies pay limited attention to how item/user feature vectors are obtained and state representations constructed, treating context as given without describing how to build it.

Studies emphasizing state representation — dynamically learned variable-sized embeddings (He et al.), bandit-based denoising and diffusion-enhanced contrastive learning for sequential recommendation (Feng et al., Cui et al.), and knowledge-graph embeddings (Gan and Kwon) — demonstrate that state-representation decisions can outweigh algorithm choice in impact.

Interaction logs are ordered by timestamp; the first 50% of interactions form historical data for model initialization (with a 10% slice for hyperparameter tuning and the remainder for learning embeddings and warming up CMABs), while the second half is dedicated exclusively to online evaluation (Fig. 1).

Embeddings are generated in a single non-incremental pass and kept static (not dynamically learned) to prevent effects related to temporal drift and model coupling, deliberately isolating the influence of state representation for a controlled comparison.

Since the static embedding space was generated in a single pass, unseen test-set items lacked vector representations; interactions involving those items were excluded to avoid the cold-start issue and ensure consistent evaluation.

In the online stage, test data is processed in 10 equally-sized chronological windows; in each window, models generate ranked recommendations, observe actual user choices, and update their linear predictors with the new feedback.

Matrix factorization models approximate the interaction signal between a user and item as the dot product of a user feature vector and an item feature vector in a shared d-dimensional latent space (Eq. 1), learned by minimizing a loss over observed interactions.

Implicit Alternating Least Squares (ALS) and Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) were selected as embedding models; both leverage historical user-item interactions but differ in optimization objective — ALS uses confidence-weighted feedback while BPR optimizes a ranking-based loss — and both are well-established, efficiently trainable baselines.

For both MF models, hyperparameters (latent factors d, learning rate, regularization strength, training epochs) were tuned on the validation split of warm-up data, selecting per-dataset the configuration yielding the best NDCG@20 (Table 2).

The simplest strategy represents the state solely by the static user embedding p_u; it is the most personalized representation available but remains unchanged throughout online evaluation, yielding stable but non-diversified recommendations and failing to capture behavioral drift in dynamic environments.

This strategy computes the user state as the average of embeddings of all previously consumed items (Eq. 2), dynamically adapting to behavior changes while maintaining fixed dimensionality, but losing the sequential order of interactions.

To preserve sequential information, this strategy concatenates the embeddings of the h most recent consumed items in FIFO order (Eq. 3, zero-padded if fewer than h items exist), explicitly encoding interaction order but increasing computational/memory complexity linearly/quadratically with h, making it the most computationally expensive strategy tested.

Different embedding models lead to significant performance variation with no single algorithm consistently outperforming the other; ALS achieved up to 22x better results than BPR on BestBuy, while BPR outperformed ALS by 47x in specific MovieLens-100k scenarios.

Holding CMAB algorithm and aggregation function fixed, ALS attained the best overall score in 61% of experiments, with BPR thriving in the remaining 39%, showing alternating dominance across datasets and contexts.
A Friedman test comparing ALS and BPR embeddings across all results revealed no statistically significant difference (chi-squared_r=2.67, p=0.102), consistent with the alternating dominance pattern.

Although expected to generally underperform (and indeed generally the worst among BPR approaches per Table 4), the static user-embedding strategy achieved the best and second-best results on BestBuy and outperformed item concatenation for both BPR and ALS on MovieLens-100k.
Contrary to the prior assumption that concatenation would be superior due to preserving item-consumption ordering, other (simpler) strategies surpassed concatenation in 41% of experiments.

A Friedman test comparing the three aggregation strategies found significant differences (chi-squared_r=16.26, p=0.00029, 99% confidence); a post-hoc Nemenyi test (critical difference 0.5522) showed Item-averaged and Concatenated embeddings are statistically superior to User embeddings with 95% confidence, with no significant difference between the two item-based methods.

The performance of LinUCB, LinGreedy, and LinTS using the same state representation is generally very similar, typically differing only in the fourth decimal place, with only a few notable exceptions such as Delicious and MovieLens-100k under item concatenation.

Across all datasets, switching from a lower-quality embedding representation to a more effective aggregation method or embedding model resulted in substantially larger performance gains (up to 47x) than changing the underlying bandit algorithm.

Synthesizing the RQ1-RQ3 findings, both the embedding algorithm and the aggregation strategy significantly impact recommendation performance, but no single combination consistently dominates across datasets, underscoring the need for domain-specific, tailored evaluation.

Because state-representation quality generally has a stronger effect on results than the specific bandit algorithm, future work should prioritize optimizing embedding-based context representations alongside algorithmic improvements rather than focusing predominantly on new bandit algorithms.
Existing vision encoders for robotics face a fundamental bottleneck: robotic datasets lack the scale necessary for large-scale pre-training.

Prior work circumvents data scarcity using internet-scale image/language data or egocentric human video, but neither paradigm learns from paired vision and action data that downstream visuomotor control policies require.
Robot trajectories, the most direct source of paired vision-action signal, are not available at pre-training scale.
The unavailability of robot trajectories at scale motivates extracting action signals from abundant human video instead.
CAIP treats human hand poses from large-scale egocentric video as a proxy for end-effector actions, since this representation aligns naturally with downstream robot action spaces.
CAIP is introduced as a vision encoder that learns a unified action-image representation through a contrastive objective.
CAIP's architecture consists of three encoders: vision (ViT-L/16), language (24-layer transformer), and action (lightweight 4-layer transformer), initialized from SigLIP 2 where applicable.
The vision encoder retains the full patch sequence without global pooling, so text tokens can attend to spatially localized features in the next step.
Language tokens attend to image patch features to produce text-grounded visual features, then a learnable query token attends over these to produce a single text-conditioned image embedding.
The action encoder is a lightweight 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, processing an action sequence and extracting a CLS token as the action embedding.

A SigLIP-style sigmoid contrastive loss aligns text-conditioned image embeddings with action embeddings, treating each pair independently as binary classification rather than requiring global batch normalization.
Hand poses are represented as 42 keypoints (21 per hand including wrist), each expressed as an SE(3) transform following the MANO hand convention.
Actions are formed by emulating end-effector delta control: the action at offset i is the relative SE(3) transform between the pose at time t and time t+i, for i=1,...,T (T=64).
CAIP trains on 32,041 hours of annotated human egocentric data (lab and in-the-wild) plus ~88 hours of tabletop humanoid manipulation data for embodiment diversity.
CAIP achieves the highest average success rate at 76% across six real-world manipulation tasks, outperforming the strongest baseline (SigLIP 2, 43.4%) by over 30 points.
CAIP attains the top success rate on five of the six manipulation tasks.

Baselines do not exhibit consistent behavior: encoders competitive on one task (e.g., MVP on Dispense Soap, DINOv2 on Pour) degrade significantly on others, suggesting non-manipulation-centric representations suit some tasks over others.
In contrast to baselines, CAIP maintains strong performance across all tasks, indicating that action-centric contrastive pre-training produces generalizing representations.
CAIP outperforms the larger SigLIP 2 SO400M baseline despite being initialized from the smaller SigLIP 2 ViT-L backbone, isolating the performance gain to action-centric pre-training.
CAIP consistently outperforms all baselines, including the strongest (DINOv2), by a substantial margin across the full data-efficiency curve on held-out action classification.
Zero-shot retrieval with CAIP, despite requiring no in-domain supervision, exceeds the linear-probe performance of every baseline up to 16 samples per class.
These results suggest CAIP's learned representations transfer effectively to unseen data and capture semantically meaningful structure for action understanding.
CAIP achieves the highest success rate under every lighting and distractor perturbation, despite all policies being trained only on unperturbed demonstrations.

CAIP outperforms Qwen3.5 ViT by roughly 20-30% and degrades far less than MVP under perturbations, making it the most robust encoder in absolute terms despite Qwen3.5 ViT retaining a larger relative fraction of its (much lower) original performance.

Scaling the vision encoder across ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-SO400M shows increasing scale leads to substantial performance improvements, with ViT-B to ViT-L yielding the largest gain of over 30% on average.
Based on the scaling ablation, ViT-L is selected as the primary vision encoder, providing the best trade-off between performance, model size, and inference speed.
Existing contrastive learning approaches incorporate subject and signal attributes but do not incorporate clinical knowledge, nor handle missing metadata.

Clinically validated risk scores translate complex physiological factors into interpretable values that guide clinical actions, and can be leveraged as contextual information for contrastive pretraining.
CLEF introduces a novel contrastive learning approach that uses an established clinical risk score to adaptively weight negative pairs.
CLEF includes an explicit mechanism to handle missing metadata when computing risk-score-based similarity.
Negative pairs contribute unequally to representation learning; a weighting term Wik adjusts the relative importance of negatives according to similarity to the positive.
For a negative pair, dissimilarity Di,k is defined from the squared difference in risk scores, normalized and bounded within [α, 1].
A multiplier Mik is assigned to negative pairs based on the number of missing metadata variables, functioning as a reliability adjustment.
The weight matrix combining dissimilarity and missing-metadata reliability is defined as the Hadamard product of D and M.
The clinically-guided contrastive loss Lw uses the weight matrix W to adaptively weight negative pairs in the batch-averaged contrastive objective.
The dissimilarity alignment loss computes MSE between cosine similarity of embeddings and their corresponding weight, encouraging clinically similar signals to map to nearby embeddings.
The final CLEF objective combines the clinically-guided contrastive loss and the dissimilarity alignment loss with equal weighting.
When many metadata variables are missing, Mik moves the weighting closer to uniform SimCLR-like behavior, preventing uncertain risk differences from unduly influencing the contrastive objective.
During pretraining, one of the 12 leads is randomly selected per sample with stochastic augmentation, so the model is collectively trained across all leads.
Because CLEF is not restricted to a specific lead during pretraining, it can be fine-tuned to any target lead, supporting cross-device use.
Pretraining CLEF exclusively on the downstream task's lead yields further AUROC improvements over pretraining on all 12 leads, approaching the performance of supervised ECGFounder.
CLEF outperforms the best baseline across both leads, achieving average AUROC improvement of 3.1% on lead I and 4.8% on lead II.
CLEF variants differ by only 0.3%, 0.0%, and 1.4% on average in AUROC across leads I and II, unlike ST-MEM and KED which favor lead I.
CLEF performs particularly well on form/rhythm/arrhythmia pattern identification tasks, improving AUROC by 5.9% (lead I) and 8.5% (lead II) over strongest baselines.

CLEF underperforms supervised ECGFounder on lead I (its trained lead) but outperforms it on lead II, since ECGFounder's performance drops on the untrained lead while CLEF maintains performance across leads.
CLEF outperforms SimCLR, BYOL, and MoCo self-supervised pretraining methods, with 100 of 117 instances outperformed by CLEF.

Initializing the best-performing baseline (KED) with its pretrained weights and further applying the clinically-guided pretraining objective improves AUROC on nearly all downstream tasks by 3.0% on average.
Without the missing-metadata handling term M, performance of all CLEF models degrades on the majority of tasks, with AUROC decreasing by 1.9% on average.
The AUROC decrease from removing missing-metadata handling is larger on wearable datasets (4.0% drop) compared to lead I clinical datasets (1.1% drop).

Although CLIP achieves remarkable zero-shot performance, its image and text alignment is imperfect: CLIP models tend to encode images and texts into different feature clusters even after sufficient training on massive datasets, a phenomenon termed the modality gap.

Prior work shows the modality gap largely affects downstream task performance, especially fine-grained classification, and that CLIP models often fail to retrieve localized objects and attributes in images from corresponding captions.

Existing pre-training modifications (auxiliary self-supervised losses, shared encoder weights/feature maps) reduce the modality gap but require training from scratch on million-scale datasets like LAION-400M, incurring heavy computational costs across multiple GPUs, and such pre-trained models are often not published.

Fine-tuning methods (prompt tuning, adapters) require much smaller datasets and less compute than pre-training, but degrade the general zero-shot transfer performance because their primary goal is improving target-task performance.

The paper proposes a post-pre-training phase between pre-training and fine-tuning, aiming to mitigate the modality gap and enhance zero-shot transfer performance of off-the-shelf pre-trained CLIP models using only small datasets and modest compute (e.g., a single GPU and COCO Captions).

Directly minimizing the gap between image and text features (naive alignment loss) corrupts the feature space's uniformity on the hypersphere, an important property of contrastive representations that indicates how much input information is preserved.

Post-pre-training with contrastive loss causes catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge in pre-trained CLIP models, driven by overfitting due to restricted mini-batch sizes far smaller than those used in original pre-training.

Because naive alignment destroys uniformity and contrastive post-pre-training induces catastrophic forgetting, an effective post-pre-training method must reduce the modality gap without sacrificing uniformity or retained knowledge.

A naive loss minimizing the L2 distance between image and text feature vectors (Eq. 2) improves alignment of positive pairs but destroys hypersphere uniformity by forcing changes to the feature distribution, degrading validation performance as shown by prior work on alignment/uniformity trade-offs.

Instead of directly matching paired features, RaFA refines image and text features to follow a shared prior distribution (e.g., standard Gaussian) by minimizing the L2 distance between each feature vector and a random reference vector sampled from the prior, shared across the image-text pair (Eq. 3).

By using a shared random reference vector per pair, RaFA indirectly minimizes the modality gap, gradually aligns features to the shared prior, and the randomness helps avoid overfitting to the small post-pre-training dataset and reforms model capacity.

To retain past knowledge, a baseline strategy penalizes the post-pre-training model with a knowledge distillation loss where the frozen pre-trained CLIP model acts as teacher, minimizing a batch-wise KL-divergence between teacher and student softmax outputs over image-text similarity matrices (Eqs. 4-7).

Although minimizing the standard self-distillation loss retains past knowledge, it strongly enchains the model's parameters to the pre-trained ones, which was found to interfere with RaFA's feature-alignment objective.

To reconcile RaFA with knowledge retention, HyCD modifies the teacher output by alpha-blending an indicator function for correct image-text pairs with the teacher's similarity output (Eq. 8), letting the model learn the correct pairing directly while referencing the teacher's relative knowledge on other pairs.

Using the blended hybrid targets, the HyCD loss is computed as the average of image-to-text and text-to-image KL-divergence losses (Eqs. 9-10), enabling the model to both retain past knowledge and learn new alignment knowledge.

CLIP-Refine optimizes model parameters by jointly minimizing the sum of RaFA loss and HyCD loss (Eq. 1); equal contribution of both losses was empirically found to achieve the best performance, avoiding the need for additional balancing hyperparameters.

While HyCD alone improves generalization performance of pre-trained CLIP models, combining it with RaFA achieves larger improvements by minimizing the modality gap without losing past knowledge, per the algorithmic procedure in Algorithm 1.

Methods adding auxiliary losses (cyclic consistency, fine-grained token similarity, self-supervised augmentation, supervised contrastive, LLM-augmented text) or sharing encoder weights/discrete token spaces require large-scale datasets like CC12M and LAION-400M, incurring high computational costs on multiple GPUs.

Prompt tuning (CoOp/CoCoOp), visual prompt tuning, unified visual-textual prompt tuning, shared low-rank adapters, and mixup-based feature-space refinement (m2-mix) succeed in reducing the gap on target datasets, but do not intend to improve zero-shot transfer performance, unlike CLIP-Refine's objective.

In contrast to both prior lines, CLIP-Refine improves generalization performance of off-the-shelf pre-trained models using only small datasets (Flickr8/30K, COCO Caption) with a single GPU, is cooperative with any pre-trained model, and can still be followed by fine-tuning to further boost target performance.

On 12 zero-shot classification datasets, post-pre-training with plain contrastive loss (Contrastive, m2-mix) largely degrades top-1 accuracy for all datasets compared to the pre-trained baseline (Table 1).

Since Self-KD does not show degradation, the contrastive loss's degradation is attributed to catastrophic forgetting caused by a much smaller mini-batch size (512, single GPU) than at original pre-training (32,768, hundreds of GPUs), limiting negative samples and causing overfitting.

In contrast to contrastive-loss baselines, CLIP-Refine impressively improves zero-shot classification performance for all datasets, with ablations showing the gain comes from combining HyCD with RaFA (Table 1).

HyCD combined with the naive alignment loss (HyCD+Lalign) resulted in the worst performance among baselines, confirming that naively minimizing the image-text feature gap leads to generalization degradation (Table 1).
On COCO2017-Val and Flickr8K/30K retrieval, CLIP-Refine achieves the best performance with an even larger margin over baselines than observed in classification tasks (Table 2).

Unlike in classification, Contrastive and m2-mix baselines improve text-to-image (T→I) retrieval over the pre-trained model while degrading image-to-text (I→T) retrieval, indicating asymmetric overfitting between modalities.

This asymmetry is explained by images having continuous-valued pixel representations with high degrees of freedom (prone to overfitting on limited negative samples in small batches), while discrete-token text representations have limited degrees of freedom and can learn new knowledge while retaining the past; since zero-shot classification is itself an I→T task, this also explains the classification degradation in P21.
CLIP-Refine successfully prevents the overfitting in I→T retrieval and greatly improves performance in both I→T and T→I directions, unlike the contrastive-loss baselines.

Among all methods, HyCD+Lalign achieves the best modality gap and alignment scores, but significantly degrades the uniformity score, indicating that directly minimizing the naive alignment loss destroys the feature space well-constructed by CLIP pre-training (Table 3).

In contrast to HyCD+Lalign, CLIP-Refine consistently improves all three scores (modality gap, alignment, uniformity), suggesting that minimizing both the image-text gap and preserving uniformity is important for generalization performance, consistent with prior alignment-uniformity theory (Table 3).

Because CLIP-Refine penalizes features to follow the shared reference distribution N(0,I), whose samples tend to be uniformly distributed on the hypersphere, it naturally achieves a good balance of alignment and uniformity while reducing the modality gap.

PCA visualization shows the contrastive model enlarges the modality gap, HyCD+Lalign gathers image/text features into the same cluster but distorts each modality's feature distribution, while CLIP-Refine reduces the modality gap while keeping the shape of the pre-trained per-modality feature distributions (Fig. 3).

Using the uniform distribution U(0,1) as the RaFA prior does not show large improvements in zero-shot performance or uniformity score, likely because samples from U(0,1) do not concentrate on the hypersphere the way N(0,I) samples do, possibly collapsing uniformity gains (Table 4).

Among Gaussian priors using pre-trained feature statistics, the prior based on text feature statistics N(mu_txt, sigma_txt^2) yields the largest zero-shot classification improvement, indicating that aligning image features toward text-feature statistics is particularly effective, consistent with the I→T retrieval gains observed in Sec 4.2 (Table 4).

Varying variance magnitude beta in zero-mean Gaussian priors shows performance depends on sufficient randomness; N(0,I) (beta=1) achieves the best overall balance of zero-shot accuracy, alignment, and uniformity, emphasizing the importance of randomness in RaFA (Table 4).
Testing Flickr8K/30K, COCO Caption, CC3M, and CC12M as post-pre-training datasets, most CLIP-Refine models outperform the pre-trained baseline on zero-shot classification and retrieval (Table 5).

CC3M and CC12M, despite being larger, are inferior to COCO Caption, likely because they contain mismatched and noisy image-text pairs, whereas COCO Caption's higher-quality captions better support modality alignment.

Filtering out low-quality image-text pairs via CLIP-Score-based filtering (DataComp) on CC3M/CC12M yields significant performance improvements, indicating caption quality is crucial and that CLIP-Refine is scalable given high-quality data (Table 5).

Evaluated on ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, OpenCLIP ViT-H/14, OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14, SigLIP ViT-SO400M/14, and DFN ViT-H/14, CLIP-Refine stably improves the pre-trained baseline's zero-shot classification and retrieval performance across all models (Table 6).

The consistent improvement across model scales suggests that even bigger and stronger pre-trained models still suffer from the modality gap, and modifying it with CLIP-Refine helps improve generalization performance regardless of scale.

Across varying mini-batch sizes in post-pre-training, plain contrastive-loss post-pre-training underperforms the pre-trained baseline at feasible (small) batch sizes, likely due to large discrepancy from the pre-training batch size (32,768) causing forgetting in negative-pair predictions (Fig. 4).

CLIP-Refine always outperforms the contrastive-loss baseline and successfully improves over the pre-trained baseline across all feasible mini-batch sizes, showing that HyCD prevents knowledge forgetting even with small mini-batches and few negative pairs (Fig. 4).

Fine-tuning only a linear classification head on ImageNet while freezing post-pre-trained backbones, CLIP-Refine outperforms both the pre-trained and contrastive-loss baselines, showing the method generates useful representations even for downstream fine-tuning (Table 7).

Contrastive language-image pre-training enables ViTs to achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance and become de facto vision encoders for MLLMs, but pre-training a single ViT-L/14 on LAION-2B requires 1.2x10^5 A100 GPU hours, exceeding $500,000.

Mixed-precision training, system-level optimizations, mask image modeling, input token reduction, loss optimization, and data-efficient designs all share the common underlying viewpoint of optimizing the training of individual models, despite belonging to different research lines.

VFMs are typically pre-trained as a family of architecturally similar models with varying sizes, and family size shows an ever-growing trend driven by demand for specialized model sizes and broadening parameter ranges from larger models.

The ever-growing family size trend creates a dilemma for pre-training model families: affording escalating pre-training costs from ever-growing family size, or compromising deployment flexibility by limiting the number of model sizes offered.

Faced with this dilemma, the paper poses the central question of how to achieve pre-training acceleration that scales efficiently with family size, motivating a reexamination of the standard pre-training pipeline.

From the micro view, main pre-training costs stem from large models in the family; computational complexity expands around 4x when selecting a larger ViT variant, and training ViT-H/14 costs over 80x more than training ViT-B/32.

From the macro view, inefficiency stems from individual training: models are trained using the same objectives, datasets, and protocols, yielding common knowledge within the family, but this is ignored, making traditional individual training highly repetitive and redundant.

The paper hypothesizes that both the micro (large-model cost) and macro (redundant training) bottlenecks can be simultaneously addressed by redefining the training pipeline to enable knowledge reuse from small to large models within the family.

Models within a family are organized in ascending order of size to form a model chain, a pre-training sequence starting with the smallest model pre-trained individually in the standard manner, then each subsequent model leverages inverse knowledge transfer from its predecessor (Fig. 2).

The model chain eliminates the isolation of individual training by ensuring each model inherits knowledge from its strongest predecessor, drastically reducing the prohibitive pre-training costs of larger models while maintaining performance comparable to individual training.

Beyond per-model efficiency gains, the chain design unlocks training efficiency that scales favorably with family size; e.g., the ViT-T->ViT-S->ViT-B->ViT-L chain reduces training costs by an additional 20% versus ViT-B->ViT-L, since the extended chain's smaller models converge in far fewer epochs, making the total overhead of the first three models smaller than training ViT-B from scratch.

Inverse knowledge transfer enables a knowledge relay along the model chain where each intermediate model first serves as a student learning from its predecessor, then as a teacher guiding its larger successor, differing from traditional KD in that the teacher-student size relation is inverted and intermediate models serve dual roles.

Effective relay requires addressing different forms of knowledge representation: a model's knowledge is statically encoded in the parameter space, while exhibited dynamically in the feature space across different samples.

Weight initialization and feature distillation are tailored for knowledge reuse in the parameter space and feature space respectively, and their synergy ensures efficient knowledge transfer relay with speedups increasing progressively along the chain (Fig. 1).

Net2Net first proposed reusing small model weights to initialize larger models via function-preserving transformations, and NetExpand advanced this using SVD-based width expansion and EMA depth scaling; similar LLM-pretraining approaches were found generally less effective.

Vanilla KD and FitNet use large teacher logits/features to supervise smaller students, with further techniques on feature transform/selection/ensemble; collaborative learning approaches (ONE, DML) instead perform online ensemble or bidirectional distillation between same- or similar-sized networks.

FLIP accelerates CLIP via random patch masking; data-efficient CLIP methods (DeCLIP, ALIP, LaCLIP, MLLM-A, DreamLIP) reduce required data scale via improved supervision/captioning, but all target single-model training efficiency.

In contrast to weight-reuse, KD/collaborative-learning, and single-model CLIP acceleration lines, CoM-PT focuses on accelerating the training pipeline at the model family level, with the novel objective of scaling efficiently with family size.

For block-block width differences, parameters of the smaller teacher are directly inserted into the larger student with remaining parameters randomly initialized; for layer-layer depth differences, weights of each layer are duplicated and indexed as the succeeding layer (Fig. 3, Step 1).

Since empirical results (Table 4a) reveal the model chain itself drives primary efficiency gains, simplicity is prioritized and both inverse weight initialization and feature distillation are implemented using vanilla approaches rather than sophisticated designs.

Inverse feature distillation applies a feature transform to project student features into the teacher's feature space, minimizing an L2 loss between transformed student features and teacher features (Eq. 1), balanced against the task loss via coefficient α to ensure the distillation loss remains smaller than the task loss.

Given a model chain, adding a smaller model before the first model, or inserting a medium-sized model between two chain members, can further accelerate convergence of subsequent models, provided the benefit outweighs the additional training cost.

The smallest model size should be selected based on pre-training data scale — compact enough to maximize efficiency, yet with proper capacity to fit the data distribution, guaranteeing lossless training acceleration and a robust foundation for the chain.

Intermediate model variants are obtained by expanding their teacher's size; expansion ratios of 2x-4x yield considerable efficiency gains, with larger factors (4x) minimizing overall training cost and smaller factors (2x) maximizing acceleration ratio.

Training epoch allocation along the chain decreases linearly as model size increases exponentially under the premise of achieving lossless training acceleration; a linearly decreasing schedule is initialized and validated/relaxed based on the first network pair's outcome.

LaCLIP, a strong data-efficient CLIP variant with a neat formulation, is selected as the baseline and boosted using stronger text augmentation, expanding each image-text pair to 16x more text variations with 4 subcaptions randomly selected per iteration.
The text-to-image contrastive loss is computed over M augmented positive text pairs per image (Eq. 2), and combined by duality with the image-to-text loss to form the overall task loss (Eq. 3).

The overall training loss sums the task loss and the averaged inverse feature distillation loss over visual and text teacher-student feature pairs (Eq. 4), applied alongside inverse weight initialization, requiring no modification to the baseline method due to CoM-PT's simplicity.

Early CLIP studies standardized 32 epochs on large-scale datasets, and follow-up data-efficient methods adopted the same setting, but the paper empirically reveals models remain far from convergence with only 32 epochs on smaller datasets like CC3M.

Evaluation across 32-256 epochs on CC3M shows performance steadily improves up to 128 epochs, establishing 128 epochs as the standard baseline; for Merged-15M, 64 epochs is set to account for its 5x larger data scale (Fig. 4).

Compared against original LaCLIP and MLLM-A (leading contrastive-loss-only approaches), the paper's baseline outperforms both (Table 1), establishing a solid foundation for validating the performance-lossless property of CoM-PT.

Models pre-trained with CoM-PT generally exceed the baseline on three zero-shot benchmarks, especially for the largest model; e.g., Swin-L on CC3M surpasses baseline by 0.29%/0.88%/1.72% on ImageNet-1K/VTAB+/COCO (Table 2).
In the rare cases where performance slightly falls below baseline, differences remain within the defined 0.5% lossless threshold, ensuring family-level lossless acceleration is maintained.

The individual acceleration ratio (in MACs and GPU hours) increases with model size, reaching around 7.5x at ViT-L, meaning the total family training cost is lower than training the largest model alone (Fig. 5, Table 2).

The accumulated acceleration ratio in GPU hours is slightly lower than in MACs because smaller models have lower GPU utilization, causing disproportionately longer training time; still, CoM-PT achieves 4.10x/3.80x acceleration for ViT/Swin on CC3M and 2.37x for ViT on Merged-15M.

Models trained with CoM-PT outperform baselines across all five open-vocabulary segmentation datasets (average improvements of 5.64%/6.14% for ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16) and across vision-language benchmarks after LoRA-based fine-tuning (Table 3).

For fine-grained datasets ADE-847 and PC-459, the gain from CoM-PT exceeds 3x over baseline, suggesting the acceleration stems from both faster convergence and genuinely better representation capability, not just faster training.

With inverse weight initialization alone (no chain relay), independently trained ViT-S/ViT-B need 1.3x/5.1x more epochs to approach CoM-PT performance, showing IWI alone loses acceleration efficacy as model size increases (Table 4a).

Because IWI alone degrades with scale, the knowledge transfer relay provided by the model chain plays the pivotal role in accelerating the training pipeline, assisted by both components of inverse knowledge transfer applied at each step.

Table 4(b) shows both inverse weight initialization and inverse feature distillation individually improve zero-shot IN-1K/COCO performance over the baseline, with the combination of both components yielding the best performance.

Further analysis reveals IWI primarily accelerates early training, whereas IFD provides sustained benefits throughout training, explaining why combining both components in inverse knowledge transfer yields synergistic gains.

By interpolating performance curves across epochs, required training epochs for ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-L to match baseline decrease in a roughly uniform manner (23.45, 18.28, 12.34 epochs respectively), even as model size grows exponentially along the chain (Fig. 8).

Reducing default training epochs on CC3M from 128 to 64 and 32, the overall acceleration ratio stably sustains above 4x, validating that CoM-PT's efficacy does not rely on longer training epochs (Fig. 9a).

Across pre-training data scales from 22.0M to 206.8M image-text pairs, acceleration ratio first sharply decreases then stabilizes around 2.8x from 103.4M to 206.8M pairs, with extrapolation to 2B scale maintaining above 2.3x acceleration (Fig. 9b).

Knowledge Distillation lets compact students inherit teacher knowledge for efficient inference, but does not alleviate training burden since students are usually distilled on the entire dataset under teacher guidance, incurring significant training cost.

An emerging line of research points to reducing the number of samples participating in distillation (data pruning) as a way to retain competitive performance while cutting training cost, with Baruch et al. re-evaluating classical pruning methods and Chen et al. introducing a KD-specific pruning method using teacher cross-entropy loss within a medium-difficulty window.

High-fidelity trajectory-based difficulty metrics (EL2N, Forgetting, AUM) are computationally prohibitive for KD because they need training-time statistics not available from pretrained teachers, while cheap CE-loss scoring is an unreliable difficulty indicator since over-parameterized networks can overfit even hard/mislabeled samples, producing weakly discriminative losses.

Even with reliable scores, conventional sampling strategies (top-k, fixed-cutoff stratified sampling, window-based selection) impose a fixed selection region that cannot adapt to varying data distributions and teacher-student dynamics across KD settings, limiting performance.

To overcome both obstacles, the paper proposes IF-Beta (Influence Function based Beta Policy), which unifies influence-function scoring with a learnable probabilistic pruning policy parameterized by a Beta distribution.
The student is trained by minimizing a weighted combination of standard cross-entropy loss and a KL-divergence distillation term between teacher and student predictive distributions (Eq. 3).

Most existing pruning methods follow a two-stage pipeline of estimating a per-sample score (difficulty or uncertainty, typically requiring training dynamics) and then selecting a subset via heuristic rules (top-k, stratified cutoff, sliding window) under a given pruning ratio.

Influence functions estimate how a model's predictions would change if a training point were removed, expressed via the gradient and inverse Hessian of the loss at the optimal parameters (Eqs. 4-6), but were historically considered impractical due to high computational cost and unreliable estimation quality in deep networks.

Building on recent advances showing that optimizing toward a flat validation minimum stabilizes influence estimation, the teacher model is fine-tuned on the validation set using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (Eq. 8), enforcing local flatness of the loss landscape.

Under the FVM condition, the influence of a training sample on the validation set is computed using gradients and the Hessian of the SAM-tuned teacher (Eq. 9), approximated via a diagonal Fisher Information matrix in place of the full inverse Hessian for practicality at scale.

Spearman rank correlation experiments (Fig. 1) show IF-FVM consistently aligns more strongly with established difficulty metrics (EL2N, AUM) than CE-loss or IF-LiSSA baselines, validating it as a computationally efficient yet robust score estimator for KD pruning.
CCS's optimal cutoff ratio varies significantly between KD and non-KD settings, making pre-defined hyperparameters non-transferable (Figs. 2a-2b).
Replacement experiments show that introducing randomness into BWS's selection window actually improves performance, revealing that its fixed-window design is suboptimal (Fig. 2c).
The threshold-shift and fixed-window limitations of CCS and BWS underscore the need for an adaptive, learnable sampling strategy beyond rigid heuristic-based selection.
Precomputed IF-FVM difficulty scores are mapped via rank-to-percentile normalization onto [0,1], with smaller normalized values corresponding to more difficult samples.
Each sample's selection probability is parameterized using a Beta distribution over the normalized score (Eq. 10), with learnable parameters ϕ jointly controlling the shape parameters α and β.

The Beta Policy is a Beta-distribution-based categorical distribution over binary mask vectors conditioned on ϕ and pruning ratio r, constrained to a fixed number of selected samples (Eqs. 11-12), yielding the pruned subset.
The continuous, flexible Beta density over the sample space (Fig. 3) contrasts with the rigid, uniform sampling over predefined support sets used by CCS and BWS, enabling more adaptive selection.

Finding the optimal Beta Policy is formulated as a bilevel problem: the outer objective minimizes expected validation loss over policy-sampled masks, while the inner objective trains the student on the sampled subset via the KD loss (Eqs. 13-15).
Naively differentiating the bilevel objective yields a gradient requiring implicit differentiation through the inner optimum, which is computationally prohibitive for deep networks.

By exploiting the Beta Policy's probabilistic formulation, an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (Theorem 1, Eqs. 17-18) is used instead, eliminating the need for implicit differentiation and enabling SGD updates of ϕ (Eq. 19).

Although the outer loop is efficiently optimized via policy gradients, the inner-loop optimization remains costly since it would require retraining the full student network to convergence for every policy update.

The KD structure is leveraged by replacing the full student with a surrogate: a trainable linear classification head attached to frozen teacher features, reformulating the student model as a linear map over frozen features (Eq. 20).
The inner-loop objective becomes optimizing only a single linear classifier on the subset (Eq. 21), which is efficient and keeps overall bilevel optimization computationally negligible in overhead.

The general bilevel formulation applies to both KD and standard supervised classification by swapping the inner KD loss for a standard CE loss, enabling IF-Beta to serve as a general-purpose data pruning framework.

Across CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet under KD, IF-Beta consistently outperforms all baselines including DUAL (which needs partial retraining) and Medium-Difficulty (retraining-free) across all pruning ratios (Fig. 4).

IF-Beta enables students trained on a pruned subset to surpass full-data distillation performance, e.g., 70% retained on CIFAR-10 (95.69% vs 95.50%), 90% on CIFAR-100 (79.53% vs 79.38%), and 50% on ImageNet (74.02% vs 73.54%).
The ability to surpass full-data performance with fewer samples suggests some samples actively impede student generalization, and pruning them yields a cleaner, more informative training signal.
IF-Beta is further validated with ResNet-50/101, WideResNet, and ViT-Base teachers, consistently outperforming all retraining-free baselines across settings.

Under severely constrained iteration budgets, IF-Beta with 50% data pruned achieves 90.80% (CIFAR-10), 67.31% (CIFAR-100), and 60.70% (ImageNet), all exceeding full-data baselines and consistently beating random pruning (Table 1).
The consistent margin over random pruning demonstrates that IF-Beta's gains are not solely from a favorable training regime induced by fewer samples but stem from effective sample selection itself.
Including the pruning process cost, IF-Beta reaches or surpasses full-data students' final performance using less time across CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet (relative costs 0.806x-0.915x) (Table 2).

Distilling ResNet-34 into MobileNet on ImageNet, IF-Beta achieves the best accuracy (71.20%) while requiring only 19.24 hours, less than half the cost of the full-data Baseline (39.86h) and Medium-Difficulty* (36.98h) (Table 3).

The efficiency gains stem from three factors: reduced data volume (70% subset), no repeated teacher queries per epoch, and a higher-quality subset preserving distillation effectiveness even under one-shot teacher logits.

Evaluated under Relational KD, FitNets, and Attention Transfer objectives on CIFAR-10/100, IF-Beta consistently outperforms both Random pruning and Medium-Difficulty across all losses, pruning ratios, and datasets (Table 4).

Consistent benefits across diverse training budgets, distillation objectives, and teacher-student pairs suggest that careful data curation is a universally effective and complementary strategy for improving efficiency and effectiveness of KD, potentially mattering more than algorithmic specifics.
To isolate the contribution of the sampling policy, CCS and BWS are combined with the paper's IF-based scores (IF-CCS, IF-BWS), which do not require retraining.

Across CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet at multiple pruning ratios, IF-Beta consistently outperforms both IF-CCS and IF-BWS (Table 5), demonstrating that the learnable Beta Policy provides clear advantages over fixed-threshold and fixed-window selection even when using the same underlying scores.

With the inner objective replaced by standard CE loss (per P25), IF-Beta remains competitive and consistently outperforms other baselines across all pruning ratios on CIFAR-10/100 in the standard supervised pruning setting (Fig. 5).

Thanks to the FVM property, a generic ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 can replace an in-domain pretrained model to compute IF scores when no in-domain pretrained model is available, avoiding retraining costs while still yielding competitive pruning performance (Table 6).
Using a generic pretrained model for scoring means IF-Beta can completely avoid any retraining cost while still providing strong pruning quality in the standard (non-KD) data pruning setting.

Flow- and diffusion-based generative models map noise to data via optimal transport or iterative noising/denoising, and while effective for generation and as priors for inverse problems, they do not explicitly capture the unconditional data score, only the score of smoothed manifolds at different noise levels, leaving the measurement likelihood intractable on these noised manifolds.

Because flow/diffusion approaches shuttle between noised and data distributions without a tractable likelihood, existing methods (e.g., DPS approximating an intractable integral with a single sample, D-Flow differentiating through simulated trajectories) resort to crude approximations and lack a direct way to navigate the data manifold in search of the optimal solution.

Energy-based models (EBMs) learn a scalar function E(x) defining an unnormalized density exp(-E(x)), explicitly retaining likelihood information usable for conditional generation and additive priors, and enabling direct curvature-based analysis (e.g., local intrinsic dimension) unlike diffusion models — but practical EBMs have historically suffered from poor generation quality due to training instabilities like mode collapse.

To overcome instability, many EBM methods resort to time-conditioned ensembles, hierarchical latent ensembles, or cooperative training with separate generator networks, requiring significantly higher parameter counts and training complexity.

The paper proposes Energy Matching, a two-regime training strategy combining flow matching's efficient long-range transport with EBMs' explicit likelihood modeling, learning a single time-independent scalar potential without auxiliary generators, time conditioning, or additional networks.

The Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme, the basis of many recent generative models, describes discrete-time evolution of a probability distribution along trajectories minimizing a sum of transport cost (Wasserstein distance), potential energy, and an entropic internal-energy term weighted by a temperature-like parameter ε(t) (Eq. 1).

Departing from most literature treating ε as constant, the paper considers ε(t) dependent on time and studies the behavior of the JKO objective as t→∞, using a linear schedule that keeps ε=0 before a threshold time τ*, then linearly increases to εmax (Eq. 3).

Analyzing the JKO objective via its first-order optimality conditions yields a coupling equation relating transport displacement, the potential gradient, and the entropic score term, which must hold for all OT-coupled point pairs (Eq. 4).
When ε(t)=0 (i.e., t<τ*), the optimality condition simplifies to a pure OT flow-like regime where displacement is governed solely by the potential's gradient (Eq. 5).

As t becomes large and the distribution approaches equilibrium (x≈y for coupled points), the optimality condition simplifies to show the equilibrium distribution is proportional to exp(-Vθ(x)/εmax), i.e., an EBM with energy E(x)=Vθ(x)/εmax.

Combining the OT-flow insight (P9) and the EBM-equilibrium insight (P10), the paper proposes learning a single time-independent scalar potential Vθ(x) whose Boltzmann distribution matches the data distribution, transported via two regimes: near-zero ε for rapid deterministic OT-like movement away from the manifold, and ε≈εmax for stable Boltzmann diffusion near the manifold (Eq. 6).

The method constructs a global velocity field -∇Vθ(x) carrying noise samples to data samples via geodesics in Wasserstein space, computing an OT coupling between empirical noise and data mini-batches (using the POT solver), guaranteed to yield a transport map T under uniform empirical distributions of equal cardinality.

For each data point, an interpolation along the OT geodesic is defined, with constant velocity (xdata - T(xdata)); the flow-like loss L_OT trains -∇Vθ(xt) to match this velocity, interpretable as flow matching under an irrotational (gradient-field) constraint consistent with OT's irrotational velocity fields.

Because the later contrastive phase requires high-quality negative samples, training begins with Phase 1, optimizing only L_OT via mini-batch OT coupling and interpolation sampling, ensuring stable initial mixing before the contrastive phase begins.

Near the data manifold, Vθ(x) is refined using a contrastive divergence loss (following Hinton) that contrasts the potential's value at real data samples against its value at negative samples drawn from the induced equilibrium distribution, with a stop-gradient on the negative-sample path.

Negative samples are approximated using an MCMC Langevin chain, with half the chains initialized from real data and half from the noise distribution, so Vθ forms well-defined basins around high-density regions while also shaping regions away from the manifold.

The overall training combines the OT loss and the contrastive divergence loss weighted by a dataset-specific hyperparameter λ_CD, following the linear ε(t) schedule to balance the deterministic flow-like regime away from the manifold and the stochastic Boltzmann regime near equilibrium (Algorithm 2).

Evaluated against diffusion models, flow-based models, EBMs, and diffusion+EBM ensembles on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32x32, Energy Matching outperforms state-of-the-art EBMs, reducing FID score by more than 50% (Tables 1-2), while using a comparable or smaller parameter count (50M) than some baselines.

Energy Matching achieves FID scores that compare favorably to flow-matching and diffusion models, and to complex diffusion+EBM ensembles, despite using a single time-independent scalar field without auxiliary generators or time-conditioned EBM ensembles.

For recovering data x from noisy measurements y=A(x)+w, the posterior factorizes into a measurement-fidelity term and the learned EBM prior exp(-Eθ(x)) where Eθ(x)=Vθ(x)/εmax (Eq. 7), obtained directly from the Energy-Matching-trained potential.

Samples from the posterior are drawn via a Langevin update starting from random noise, combining the prior gradient, a measurement-fidelity gradient term weighted by ζ, and an optional interaction energy term between multiple simultaneously sampled chains (Algorithm 3).

An additional interaction energy term W(x1,x2) can be incorporated to encourage diversity between simultaneously generated samples, giving high probability to pairs that lie far apart in a specified region of interest, encouraging exploration of posterior edges rather than only its modes.

Applying the interaction-energy-augmented posterior to a CelebA 64x64 inpainting task, the method reconstructs two distinct high-fidelity completions from a partially observed face, with the interaction term encouraging the two reconstructions to differ specifically within the region of interest while preserving overall fidelity (Fig. 2).

Using the latent-space representation of VLGPO, an Energy-Matching Langevin sampler with an inference-time tunable repulsion term is applied to designing AAV capsid protein segments targeting a desired fitness (predicted viral packaging efficiency), evaluated on medium and hard benchmark splits.

The inference-time repulsion term allows explicit control over designed-protein diversity, enabling a flexible trade-off between fitness and diversity that results in high fitness scores alongside substantially improved sequence diversity compared to flow-based, score-based, and other non-likelihood baseline methods (Fig. 3).

Recent diffusion-based LID estimation methods examine the learned score function, but since diffusion models do not learn the score exactly at the data manifold (t=1), their estimates become unreliable there, forcing reliance on approximations near but not on the manifold.

Because EBMs explicitly parametrize the relative data likelihood, the Hessian matrix of the learned potential at a data point can be computed and spectrally decomposed; the count of near-zero eigenvalues (within a threshold τ) reflects the number of flat directions, revealing the local intrinsic dimension directly on the data manifold.

Energy Matching's Hessian-based LID estimates achieve the strongest Spearman correlation with PNG compression rate on both MNIST (0.877) and CIFAR-10 (0.901) compared to ESS, FLIPD, and NB baselines (Table 3), attributed to relying on fewer approximations by computing exactly on the manifold rather than near it.
The structural misalignment between sparse terminal rewards and the sequential nature of agentic trajectories underlies training pathologies.
In the absence of intermediate feedback, model outputs grow monotonically to the length limit as token-level coverage becomes a proxy for task completion.
The agentic structure degrades from coordinated tool-use dialogues into verbose single-turn monologues.
Response explosion and multi-turn collapse are causally linked: shifting to monologues lengthens responses, which further discourages multi-turn interaction.
On-policy distillation, effective for single-turn reasoning, fails in agentic settings because teacher policies become stale faster due to combinatorial trajectory complexity.
Standard GRPO assigns a uniform advantage estimate to all tokens in a multi-turn sequence, failing to credit specific turns and causing unstable convergence.
HealthcareAIGym implements a 5D reward function combining accuracy, procedure, safety, format, and coherence, with default weights (0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10) plus optional assertion weight.
Agents prioritize structural correctness over clinical utility, a problem addressed by the safety-severity taxonomy and coherence checks in the 5D reward.
The 5D reward incorporates procedural quality but remains fundamentally episode-level, necessitating denser regularization during training.
Turn-level Truncated On-Policy Distillation (TT-OPD) is proposed as a self-distillation framework using a gradient-free EMA teacher for dense, outcome-aware KL regularization at every turn.
The teacher is updated solely via exponential moving average (α=0.995) every 5 steps, with a periodic hard-copy fallback every 30 steps.
The teacher receives correctness-dependent hints (reinforcing or corrective) inserted at the prompt-response boundary but hidden from the student's observed context.
A cosine-shaped length-controlled reward discourages monotonic response length growth as responses approach the max length.
TT-OPD sustains controlled response lengths (5.7-9.3K tokens) compared to GRPO oscillation (7.7-10.8K tokens) and unchecked explosion without length control.
TT-OPD preserves multi-turn structure with tool-use frequency stable at 7.0-7.4 turns throughout training.
TT-OPD achieves the best performance on 10 of 18 benchmarks with an average +3.9 pp improvement over the non-RL baseline.
Periodically replacing the teacher with the student's weights causes catastrophic KL collapse, dropping abruptly at each copy event and destroying the distillation gradient.
Without a stable reference distribution from KL collapse, accuracy declines monotonically (56.9% to 49.3%).
Under periodic teacher reset, multi-turn tool use collapses from 7.65 to 5.52 turns per episode.
Replacing periodic resets with EMA teacher updates eliminates KL collapse entirely, allowing smooth teacher drift and continuous KL growth.
Without outcome-aware conditioning, turns still erode from 7.82 to 6.23 because the KL target does not encode good multi-turn behavior.
Adding outcome-conditioned hints without length constraints causes responses to grow monotonically toward the max length, eventually collapsing accuracy via truncation.
Adding cosine length-controlled reward to EMA plus outcome hints resolves response explosion and enables sustained non-monotonic convergence to 61.1% accuracy with stable turns.
RL improves procedural competence but does not transfer to text-based QA benchmarks due to format-reward dilution.
Multi-turn agentic evaluation introduces systematic overhead on knowledge-recall benchmarks, e.g., MMLU drops from 83.8% (text logprob) to 60.6% (Base+AR).
TT-OPD recovers +4.9 pp over Base+AR on MMLU (65.5% vs 60.6%), suggesting RL partially compensates for agentic evaluation overhead.
GRPO leads on knowledge-intensive long-form QA tasks (KQA-Golden 65.3%, KQA-Silver 64.9%), suggesting higher peak training accuracy translates to better factual recall in open-ended settings.
Vanilla GRPO achieves strong training accuracy (+9.4 pp), reaching a higher peak of 62.0% at step 55.
GRPO shows response length oscillating between 7.7K-10.8K tokens throughout training.
GRPO suffers from training instability evidenced by significant oscillations in response length and prolonged convergence periods.

Existing CF methods build the embedding function with descriptive features only (e.g., ID and attributes), without considering user-item interactions, which are only used to define the training objective.
The lack of explicit encoding of collaborative signal, latent in user-item interactions, means resultant embeddings may not sufficiently capture the collaborative filtering effect.
When embeddings are insufficient in capturing CF, methods have to rely on the interaction function to make up for the deficiency of suboptimal embeddings.
High-order connectivity in the user-item interaction graph is a natural way to encode collaborative signal, e.g., paths like u1←i2←u2 indicate behavioral similarity.
NGCF is proposed to integrate the bipartite user-item graph structure into the embedding process by propagating embeddings on the graph, explicitly injecting collaborative signal.

The message from item i to user u encodes both the item embedding and the element-wise product of item and user embeddings (ei⊙eu), making the message dependent on the affinity between them, unlike conventional GCNs that use ei only.

The coefficient pui is set as the graph Laplacian norm 1/sqrt(|Nu||Ni|), interpretable as a discount factor reflecting how much a historical item contributes to user preference and decaying with path length.
First-order propagation aggregates neighbor messages plus a self-connection message (mu←u=W1*eu) via LeakyReLU to refine user u's representation, retaining original feature information.
By stacking l embedding propagation layers, a user (or item) receives messages propagated from its l-hop neighbors, recursively formulated using representations from the previous layer.

Stacking multiple embedding propagation layers seamlessly injects collaborative signal into representation learning, e.g., capturing the path u1←i2←u2←i4 explicitly in the third-layer representation of u1.
The layer-wise propagation rule can be expressed in matrix form using the Laplacian matrix, enabling efficient simultaneous update of all user and item representations without node sampling.
Representations from different propagation layers are concatenated to form the final user and item embeddings, since different layers emphasize messages passed over different connections.
The final user and item embeddings are used to estimate preference via inner product, emphasizing the embedding function rather than a complex interaction function.
Compared to MF, NGCF uses only 2Ldldl-1 more parameters, an almost negligible additional cost since L is usually smaller than 5 and dl is much smaller than the number of users/items.
NGCF adopts message dropout (randomly dropping outgoing messages) and node dropout (randomly blocking nodes and discarding their outgoing messages) to prevent overfitting.
Setting L=1 and disabling the transformation matrix and nonlinear activation, NGCF reduces to a form that recovers SVD++ (and FISM as another special case) under specific coefficient settings.
NGCF consistently yields the best performance on all three datasets, improving over the strongest baselines by 11.68%, 11.97%, and 9.61% recall@20 on Gowalla, Yelp2018, and Amazon-Book respectively.
By stacking multiple embedding propagation layers, NGCF explicitly explores high-order connectivity, unlike CMN and GC-MC which only utilize first-order neighbors.

Compared with PinSage (which uses only the last layer's output), NGCF considers multi-grained representations from different layers, demonstrating that different propagation layers encode different information.

NGCF's improvement over HOP-Rec indicates that explicitly encoding CF signal in the embedding function achieves better representations than HOP-Rec's approach of enriching training data via random walks.
NGCF and HOP-Rec consistently outperform all other baselines across user groups of different interaction sparsity levels.

Exploiting high-order connectivity greatly facilitates representation learning for inactive (sparse-interaction) users, since collaborative signal can be effectively captured even with few direct interactions.

Improvements achieved for the most inactive user groups (e.g., 8.49% for <24 interactions in Gowalla) are more significant than for the most active groups (e.g., 1.29% for <1014 interactions), verifying embedding propagation particularly benefits inactive users.

NGCF-2 and NGCF-3 achieve consistent improvement over NGCF-1 (first-order neighbors only) across all datasets, attributed to second- and third-order connectivities capturing collaborative user similarity and collaborative signal respectively.
Further stacking a fourth propagation layer (NGCF-4) leads to overfitting on the Yelp2018 dataset, with only marginal improvements on the other two datasets, suggesting three layers are sufficient.

NGCF-1 is consistently superior to NGCF-1-SVD++, NGCF-1-GC-MC, and NGCF-1-PinSage variants, with improvements attributed to the representation interaction term (eu⊙ei) functioning like an attention mechanism.

When concatenating all layers' outputs, NGCF-1-PinSage and NGCF-1-GC-MC achieve better performance than the original PinSage and GC-MC, emphasizing the significance of the layer-aggregation mechanism itself.

Node dropout offers better performance than message dropout (e.g., on Gowalla, p2=0.2 yields recall@20 of 0.1514 vs. message dropout's 0.1506), since it makes representations robust against both edge and node influence.
NGCF exhibits faster convergence than MF across all three datasets, since indirectly connected users and items are involved when optimizing interaction pairs in mini-batches.
Representations from NGCF-3 exhibit discernible clustering in t-SNE visualization, meaning items consumed by the same user tend to form clusters, unlike MF representations.

For the same users analyzed across MF and NGCF-3 visualizations, embeddings of their historical items tend to be closer under NGCF-3, qualitatively verifying that embedding propagation injects explicit collaborative signal.
Pruning a pretrained MoE model to a target architecture provides a significantly better initialization than training the same architecture from scratch, under matched training tokens.
The Pruned + KD Loss model achieves an average benchmark score of 73.45.
The Random Init + KD Loss model achieves an average benchmark score of 61.66.
The pruned architecture recovers 86.5% of the teacher's performance (73.45 vs. 82.68) despite being 3.4x smaller.
Pruned initialization yields considerably faster convergence and lower language modeling (LM) loss than random initialization.
The combined Pruned + KD recipe achieves the lowest training loss among the compared initialization/objective setups.
Different one-shot expert compression methods converge to similar final performance after large-scale continual pretraining (400B tokens).
No single one-shot pruning or merging method establishes consistent superiority across all downstream tasks.
A partial-preservation expert merging strategy is proposed, retaining half of the target experts intact and merging the rest into selected merge bases.
The partial-preservation expert merging strategy improves downstream performance across most benchmarks compared to full merging.
Expert compression requires balancing pretrained expert specialization preservation against consolidation of discarded experts.
Combining next-token prediction knowledge distillation (NTP KD) with a standard language modeling (LM) loss outperforms pure KD.
Adding LM loss to KD improves knowledge-intensive benchmarks such as MMLU (74.16→74.93) and MMLU-Pro (50.97→51.44).
Multi-token prediction (MTP) distillation is proposed, extending the distillation objective beyond single tokens.
Integrating MTP KD into NTP KD or a joint objective improves performance on several knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
MTP KD yields substantial efficiency gains for speculative decoding across pretraining and SFT stages.
MTP KD consistently improves the multi-token acceptance rate from acc_1 to acc_4 across benchmarks.
The gains from MTP KD are often larger for longer accepted token sequences.
Three progressive, two-stage distillation/pruning schedules are compared: depth-first, width-first, and joint.
Progressive pruning strategies consistently outperform one-shot compression under an identical token budget.
Staged capacity reduction provides a significantly smoother optimization trajectory for knowledge transfer.
The depth-first progressive model is officially designated as SlimQwen due to superior overall performance.
MMLU improves from 75.86 (one-stage) to 77.39 (depth-first) and 77.14 (width-first).
More fine-grained stage partitions do not provide additional benchmark performance gains.
Depth pruning directly drops the last N layers of an L-layer model.
Width pruning reduces hidden dimension using importance scores derived from RMSNorm activation statistics on a calibration dataset.
Expert importance is quantified using frequency-based, soft-logits, and router-weighted output activation (REAP) criteria.
Discarded experts are merged into their nearest retained neighbor using importance score as scaling factor.
Qwen3-Next-80A3B is compressed to a 23A2B model (~4x compression) via the proposed pruning and distillation recipe.
The compressed 23A2B model retains competitive downstream performance across MMLU variants, BBH, GSM8K, coding, and Chinese benchmarks.
Pre-trained neural networks that jointly model column names and table entries must be fine-tuned to bring benefits, lacking the convenience of popular foundation models in text or vision.
Existing table foundation models come with sizeable computation costs and cannot easily be reused or combined with other architectures; Kim et al. (2024) report times 200x slower than XGBoost.
TARTE is introduced as a foundation model that transforms tables to knowledge-enhanced vector representations using strings to capture semantics.
TARTE yields representations that facilitate subsequent learning with little additional cost, unlike prior models where benefits come mainly from fine-tuning rather than pre-training.
TARTE models a row as a set of column(E)-cell(X) pairs, mapping column names, numerical, categorical, and datetime values to the same dimension using a language model and datetime converter.
TARTE avoids the graph structure used in CARTE, which creates a bottleneck limiting information flow between inputs in self-attention layers.
By avoiding the graph structure, TARTE keeps all column relations in a single attention mechanism, providing better context to capture data semantics.
TARTE is trained as a shallow architecture of three layers, reflecting that the input works in a column-level setting prone to oversmoothing with deeper architectures.
YAGO4.5 includes relatively little numerical information compared to downstream tables and lacks diversity in relational information, especially for numerical triples.
TARTE enriches YAGO4.5 with numerical facts (numbers and dates) from the more comprehensive but noisier Wikidata to address its numerical information shortcomings.
