DG-PRM extracts reward criteria with a judge function over positive/negative output pairs, filters them with an automated validator, embeds them (BAAI/bge-en-icl, d=4096), and organizes them by incremental hierarchical clustering (BIRCH) into a tree of coarse parent and fine child criteria, merging criteria with cosine distance below xi=0.25.

For each step, DG-PRM selects relevant parent criteria from the tree using a window of the previous mu=20 steps, generates fine-grained evaluation aspects, and matches child criteria whose cosine distance to an aspect is at most zeta=0.2, scoring each selected criterion.

DG-PRM computes the Pareto-optimal set over candidate steps given multi-criteria scores and forms preference pairs where Pareto-optimal steps dominate dominated ones, optimized with a step-wise DPO-style loss.
DG-PRM selects about 3.7 reward criteria per step on average (1.5 coarse and 2.3 fine); QASC needs only coarse-grained criteria while specialized ChemistryQA needs more fine-grained ones.

Pareto-based filtering improves accuracy over randomly pairing the highest-scoring sample, by 1.79% to 4.02% (e.g. ARC-c 90.63% to 94.65%), and over half of sampled steps are used for pair construction.

On PRMBench, DG-PRM improves R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on PS tasks from 45.6% to 62.4%, and improves DeepSeek-R1 overall from 69.5% to 76.5%, a new state of the art with a sensitivity average above 80%; generative models beat discriminative PRMs.

DG-PRM boosts win rates on MT-Bench and Arena-Hard near human annotation, and on QASC, StrategyQA, ChemistryQA and ARC-c improves models at all sizes (1.5B-32B), even surpassing human annotation on StrategyQA; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B beats human performance on QASC and StrategyQA.
In out-of-distribution settings ORM and Critic Direct drop sharply (sometimes below baseline) and Critic CoT drops on ChemistryQA, while DG-PRM generalizes well by selecting relevant rewards.
DG-PRM matches Critic CoT accuracy with only 30% of the training steps, attributed to Pareto selection of representative positive and negative samples.

Compared with Critic CoT-SC(50), DG-PRM needs about half the compute while achieving 4.8% higher overall PRMBench performance; reward-tree construction costs about 7,000 input and 3,000 output tokens per sample, far below manual annotation, and the tree is reusable.

Repeatedly inserting certain tokens into sentences changes text-embedding sentence similarity, e.g. appending 'lucrarea' to an unrelated sentence raises its Sentence-T5 similarity to a reference sentence.

Anomalous tokens primarily pull pairwise sentence similarity toward the mean pairwise similarity of the model's token embeddings (about 0.8 for ST5-base), rather than always increasing it; normal tokens like 'and' have a much smaller impact.

A token t is sticky if, for all sentence pairs and all insertion operations (prefix, suffix, random) with n insertions, inserting t brings the pair's similarity within a threshold epsilon of the mean token similarity u.

The Sticky Token Detector filters sentence pairs to those with similarity below u, removes undecodable and unreachable tokens, shortlists the top 2% of tokens by sticky score on sampled pairs, then validates shortlisted tokens against the definition on all filtered pairs with an adaptive threshold.

The sticky score combines the total positive and negative similarity changes, their frequencies, and the token's similarity to the sentence; hyperparameters chosen by ablation are n=8 insertions and k=5 sampled pairs.

STD finds 868 sticky tokens across 40 checkpoints of 12 text-embedding model families evaluated on MTEB STS datasets; sticky tokens make up 0.4% to 5.3% of shortlisted candidates, or 0.006% to 1% of vocabulary.
About 7% (64) of sticky tokens are special/control tokens ([CLS], [SEP], [MASK], [PAD], </s>) and unused tokens like <extra_id_27> frequently appear, e.g. </s> appears in 12 T5-based checkpoints.
About 22% (191) of sticky tokens contain non-English characters such as Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic and combining/math symbols, suggesting limited non-English coverage in pre-training.

Sticky token counts do not consistently correlate with model or vocabulary size (Spearman rho=0.127, p=0.706 for T5 models; sentence-t5-xl has 34 but xxl 22; gte-Qwen2-7B has 103 while GritLM-7B has 17), and models in the same family often share sticky tokens.

Inserting sticky tokens degrades MTEB clustering and retrieval much more than normal tokens (paired t-test, p=0.017, Cohen's d=0.41); for ST5-base SciFact falls 41.5% (45.76 to 26.76) and NFCorpus 52.3%, versus about 2.6% and 0.56% for normal tokens.
Lightweight models degrade catastrophically (sentence-t5-base Biorxiv clustering 23.11 to 15.02, -35.0%) while larger models like UAE-Large-V1 stay robust (SciFact 73.91 to 72.63, -1.7%).
In ST5-base, attention weights on appended sticky tokens concentrate in high-value ranges (>0.4) in intermediate layers, whereas normal tokens have a smoother Gaussian-like distribution.

The Wasserstein distance between sticky and normal token attention patterns is moderate in early layers (1-6), grows in mid-to-late layers (6-12) and peaks at the final layers, so small irregularities are progressively amplified.

Instruction-tuning may heighten LLMs' dependence on user inputs, making them follow external information even when it conflicts with their parametric knowledge, which can produce hallucinations from user-provided misinformation.
Prior studies on knowledge conflicts mostly identified that LLMs accept contradicting evidence, without investigating the direct impact of instruction-tuning as a cause.

Misinformation Susceptibility Rate is the percentage of questions answered correctly closed-book (parametric knowledge) for which the LLM, given misinformation, selects the incorrect option aligned with the misinformation.

Misinformation is presented as part of a single user turn (STQ), in a separate assistant-role turn (APD), or in a separate user-role turn (UPD), with the same system prompt and final user question 'What is the correct answer?'.

Experiments use Farm questions from BoolQ, NQ and TruthfulQA that GPT-4 answers closed-book, with misinformation supporting an incorrect option, on GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 (instruct and base).
Except for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, all instruction-tuned models have higher MSR in UPD than APD across all datasets, so misinformation is accepted more when presented through the user role.

Across all models and datasets, UPD has higher MSR than STQ (typically 5-8 percentage points, averaging 22 points for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3), so separating misinformation into its own user turn increases susceptibility.

STQ vs APD gives mixed results across models: some (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) have lower MSR in APD than STQ, showing they disregard the assistant role, while others (Mistral, Qwen2.5) show slightly higher MSR in APD.
All four base models rank APD highest in MSR consistently across the three datasets, and three of four (not Qwen2.5-7B) rank UPD above STQ, so base models weight the assistant role most.

After instruction-tuning, three of four open-source models (not Qwen2.5-7B) drop APD in MSR ranking and show UPD as the highest, so instruction-tuning reduces reliance on the assistant role and increases the user role's influence.

The high user-role susceptibility of instruction-tuned LLMs is not merely a pre-training byproduct but a direct result of instruction-tuning, since it aligns the model more closely with user instructions.

As misinformation length increases (adding second and third paragraphs), the UPD-APD MSR gap mostly narrows and sometimes reverses (e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct), so models revert toward the base-model pattern.

Adding a misinformation warning to the system prompt on NQ reduces average MSR by 69.1 points for GPT-4o and 20.1 for GPT-4o mini, but leaves open-source models nearly unchanged, and does not change the relative ranking across scenarios (except Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct).
The Fisher diagonal is widely used as a measure of parameter sensitivity in applications such as pruning, sparse training, continual learning, task similarity and model merging.

Computing the Fisher diagonal requires per-example gradients on sampled labels, often done with a batch size of one, and needs training data that may be unavailable; this hinders adoption, e.g. Fisher Merging is absent from mergekit.
Adam-style optimizers maintain an exponential moving average of squared gradients, available for free at the end of training.

The joint (empirical) Fisher is a square of aggregated gradients rather than a sum of squares, which gives theoretical motivation for relating the squared-gradient accumulator to the Fisher diagonal; joint and standard Fisher coincide (Lin et al. 2024).

The accumulator averages over a long EMA history (time constant about 10,000 steps for beta2 = 0.999), including gradients at old parameters, so it is a biased estimate of the joint empirical Fisher and needs rescaling when magnitudes matter.
The Squisher uses the squared gradient accumulator in place of the Fisher diagonal, directly where only relative parameter importance matters and with a rescaling term where magnitudes matter.
Across six settings spanning five applications, replacing the Fisher with the Squisher had little impact on performance and consistently outperformed Fisher-free baselines.
Computing the Squisher takes under 0.1 seconds in all settings (under 1 second for EWC), versus substantial time to compute the Fisher.
In continual learning, using the squared gradient accumulator without tuning the rescaling term lambda gives suboptimal results.
Squisher performance can degrade when fine-tuned models are not fully trained, since the accumulator has seen too few steps; beta2 = 0.95 degrades performance while the default 0.999 is best.
Explicitly squaring the sum of per-example gradients (turning off the moving average) gives results close to the Fisher, suggesting the joint Fisher is a useful approximation.

WER treats all lexical errors equally and measures only verbatim recall, ignoring how transcription errors propagate to semantic understanding and task completion; two transcripts with identical WER (29%) can differ drastically in meaning.
End-to-end voice LLMs bypass explicit ASR transcription, so WER-based evaluation does not apply and there is no unified metric comparing cascaded and end-to-end systems.
SpeechIQ evaluates LLM-Voice at three levels from Bloom's Taxonomy: Remember (WER), Understand (hidden-state similarity of LLM responses), and Apply (multiple-choice QA accuracy).

The Understand score prompts an LLM (LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct) to give a one-word background and one-word summary of the speech, and takes the lower of the cosine similarities between last-layer hidden states for ASR transcript and ground-truth transcript.

For each speech sample, 3 questions with 5 choices (including 'None of the above') are generated by GPT-4o from the ground-truth transcript, filtered so GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-flash answer them correctly, and answered 5 times with majority vote.

SIQ combines the three levels via per-sample discrimination weights (inter-model variance), global standardization, and inverse-variance dimension weights, converted to an IQ-like scale SIQ = 100 + 15 * Score.
On WER, Canary is best, GER (Whisper-v2 5-best + GPT-4o) increases WER relative to plain ASR, and all cascaded ASR models outperform all end-to-end models including Gemini-1.5.
Similar-size end-to-end models have much lower QA accuracy than cascaded ones, scaled-up end-to-end models (Gemini-1.5, Baichuan-omni) do best, and GER improves downstream reasoning.
Single ASR models lead on WER but lose their lead on higher-level intelligence; GER gives stable SIQ improvements and ASR+GER+LLM reaches the best SIQ (e.g. 108.64 for Whisperv2+GPT-4o+Qwen2-7B).
On human rankings of 10 models over 9 examples, SIQ_all has Spearman rho 0.952 (p=0.00002), higher than WER (0.770), SemDist (0.721), LLM-S (0.624), BLEU (0.806) and SIQ_rm (0.830).

With the same foundation LLM, cascaded variants outperform end-to-end models on all three levels, notably Qwen2-Audio and Salmonn at the Apply level (e.g. Salmonn accuracy 60.3 vs 87.3 for Whisper+Vicuna), suggesting multi-modal training may sacrifice reasoning ability.
QA that most LLM-Voice models fail identifies annotation errors: only 26 of 800 samples needed human review, and 17 were confirmed truly unanswerable, forming an unanswerable set.

On the unanswerable set, answering anything other than 'None of the above' counts as hallucination; LLaMA3-8B-Instruct hallucinates much more (41.2% cascaded, 70.6% in its end-to-end variant Desta2), explaining Desta2's unexpectedly high apply accuracy.
Hallucination of a foundation LLM is inherited by its multimodal variants, making foundation model selection and hallucination reduction important in multimodal training.

Using Gemini-1.5-flash as ASR with a cascaded LLM lowers apply accuracy (96.6 end-to-end vs 95.1 cascaded) while the small Qwen2-Audio gains slightly (83.9 to 84.2); humans reach 99.27 apply accuracy despite 53.67 WER, suggesting higher intelligence benefits higher-order levels even with imperfect transcription.
Most existing multi-agent systems are manually designed, requiring human effort for complex codebases and iterations of polishing, and target only specific scenarios.
SPP, AutoAgents and EvoAgent design a system per specific case and lack generalization; SPP and AutoAgents lack tool use; ADAS and Symbolic-Learning need many iterations and external data.
Linear, decentralized-debate and orchestrator structures have limited ability to trace back to fix errors or misunderstandings from previous steps.

A linear structure is an FSM with one transition per state and no traceback or verifier; decentralized debate has limited traceback to the first state; an orchestrator system is an FSM with a shared condition verifier.
An FSM with a customized condition verifier per state and unconstrained transition conditions maximizes flexibility and is well suited to automatic design.

Given a task-type description, MetaAgent designs the needed agents, summarizes states for the possible situations, and gives each state a task-solving agent, instructions, a condition verifier and listener agents.

At deployment the task-solving agent's output is checked by the condition verifier against transition conditions; if one matches the system moves to the next state, which can be an earlier state to allow traceback, and the output is saved as memory.
The initial FSM design often has excessively long chains of information transfer and task solving that hinder performance.
MetaAgent traverses each pair of states and uses an LLM to decide mergeability, eliminating trivial states, without needing external data or many iterations.
MetaAgent scores 0.86 on Trivial Creative Writing and 0.60 on GPQA (Diamond), above Direct, CoT, CoT-SC, llm-debate, Self-Refine and SPP (0.79 and 0.45), surpassing prior prompt-based SOTA by 9%.
On ML Bench, MetaAgent beats all auto-designed frameworks, is SOTA on Titanic and House Prices, second-best elsewhere, and reaches 97% of the best human-designed system's average performance.
On software development tasks MetaAgent passes 50% more checkpoints than the human-designed MetaGPT and outperforms other auto-designed frameworks.
Disabling tool use lowers performance on Trivial Creative Writing and GPQA (Diamond), showing the search engine helps.
Systems without traceback often fail due to unresolved bugs, e.g. a tester cannot relay a bug back to the programmer.
Removing the optimization causes a sharp performance drop, with failures from excessively long text in bad cases.

MetaAgent achieves higher or comparable performance at relatively lower token cost than other methods, and its task-level design is cheaper and more broadly applicable than case-level design such as AutoAgents.
Common supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) practices significantly degrade the confidence calibration of open-source LLMs (Fig 1, Fig 2).
Label smoothing mixes the target distribution with a uniform distribution using rate beta, acting as a regularizer that makes the model less confident on all samples.
Across Llama, Gemma and Mistral models fine-tuned on Tulu3 and evaluated on MMLU, label smoothing reduces calibration error with negligible effect on downstream accuracy.
The calibration benefit of label smoothing diminishes for smaller Llama3 models (1B, 3B) compared with the 8B model, and is much less visible for large-vocabulary LLMs.

A theoretical result links the lower bound of model output entropy to the hidden size D and vocabulary size |V| through the distribution of the final hidden state, limiting the ability to become overconfident.
Temperature scaling (T>1 divides logits) and logit softcapping change the logit scale and hence the entropy bound, allowing models to become overconfident so label smoothing's benefits re-emerge.
With a large vocabulary, cross-entropy requires materializing an N x |V| logit matrix that dominates the memory footprint of training.
Existing memory-efficient cross-entropy implementations avoid computing the full logit matrix by using only the target row of the classifier head, and so cannot support label smoothing.
The proposed kernel supports label smoothing with over 75% less peak memory than Liger Kernels, and trails compiled torch by under 10 ms while using about 7% of its memory.
The kernel matches Cut-Cross-Entropy with under 0.5% overhead on the forward pass and under 1% for combined forward/backward.
With beta=0.1, label smoothing consistently lowers ECE and RMS calibration error on MMLU, HellaSwag and ARC-Easy across Alpaca, Tulu3Mixture and OpenHermes SFT, while preserving accuracy.
Manually preparing OOD training data incurs substantial human and time costs, and some OOD data distributed outside the ID boundary cannot be collected in the real world.
Automated pipelines that generate OOD data are therefore needed to reduce labor when creating auxiliary outlier datasets.

DreamOOD samples from low-likelihood regions of a text-conditioned latent space, but with no explicit relation between low-likelihood regions and decision boundaries it cannot guarantee generated images lie on decision boundaries.
Outliers generated near ID decision boundaries are informative and help the classifier refine its boundary between ID and OOD data.

BOOD trains an image encoder with a class-embedding alignment loss against CLIP text embeddings of class names, producing a text-conditioned latent space compatible with the diffusion model input space.

The minimum number k of gradient-ascent (sign-gradient, step size alpha) perturbation steps needed to change the classifier's prediction serves as a proxy for an ID feature's distance to the decision boundary, d(z,y)=k bounded by K.
BOOD selects as ID boundary features those whose distances lie in the smallest r% of the distance set.
Selected boundary features are perturbed along the gradient ascent direction until the prediction switches, then for c additional steps, to yield OOD features around the decision boundary.
The synthesized OOD embedding replaces the class token embedding in the text prompt of a diffusion model to generate pixel-space OOD images.
The OOD detector is regularized with a binary logistic loss that treats ID samples as positive and synthesized OOD images as negative.
On CIFAR-100, BOOD lowers average FPR95 from 40.31% to 10.67% (29.64% decrease) and raises average AUROC from 90.15% to 97.42% (7.27% improvement) over DreamOOD.
BOOD also surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods on the ImageNet-100 benchmark.

Ablation shows both boundary-feature identification and OOD feature perturbation are essential: decoding selected ID features directly, or perturbing randomly chosen features, performs worse than full BOOD.
Documents have narrative or logical flow, so the meaning of each chunk depends heavily on its surrounding context, creating a need for context-aware embeddings.

Embedding models must compress a chunk into one vector, so longer chunks raise the chance of critical information loss; applications built on long-chunk embeddings often underperform those using short chunks.

On the book plot retrieval task, with the same total returned text (5k/10k/25k tokens) and the same embedding model (Jina or NV-Embed), recall consistently decreases as documents are segmented into longer chunks.
Situated embedding conditions a short chunk's embedding on its broader context, so the model only needs to integrate context relevant to the target chunk, easing the capacity limit.

Adding situated context to chunks significantly degrades the recall of all tested existing embedding models (M3, Jina-v3, E5-Mistral, GTE-Qwen2, NV-Embed-v2, Qwen3-Embedding) on NDP-v1, even though the context is within their claimed context windows (e.g. Jina-v3 Recall@10 53.33 chunk-only vs 15.68 with context).

Replacing situated context with GPT-4o-generated situated summaries yields much smaller degradation or slight gains for M3, Jina, E5 and Qwen3, indicating the baselines partly fail to situate a chunk within long contexts.

Training data is built from ~1.6M (1,614,007) query-chunk pairs of user book notes (Douban, ~100 popular books), treating the note as query and its anchored text as the chunk, since notes reflect contextual understanding.

The situated model learns the residual over a baseline chunk-only embedding model (query q~ = qb + qs, chunk c~ = cb + cs), with a margin loss over 10 negatives, to prevent shortcut use of ambiguous chunk-only clues and encourage context use.
SitEmb-v1-M3 (1B) with situated context reaches Recall@10 of 50.85 on NDP-v1, exceeding chunk-only M3 (42.55) and outperforming models up to 7B parameters.
SitEmb-v1.5-Qwen3 (8B) with book-note data reaches Recall@10 of 68.98 on NDP-v1, above voyage-context-3 (60.46) and Qwen3-Embedding chunk-only (51.58).
Including NDP books in NarrativeQA-based training gives no measurable gain on NDP-v1 (Recall@10 68.98 w/ vs 69.60 w/o), so book overlap does not drive results.
SitEmb performance on NDP-v1 is stable across situated context lengths from 512-800 to 8192-12800 tokens.

On the full book plot retrieval task (7 books, 1,394 queries), SitEmb-v1.5-Qwen3 improves by over 10% when trained on QA data and over 15% on QA+SA data, and both exceed voyage-context-3 (Recall@10 63.03 for QA+SA vs 51.39).

Training the same residual architecture on chunk-only M3 (Res-M3) does not improve over M3 (SA), and removing residual learning degrades SitEmb-v1-M3, indicating gains come from using contextual information.
On Recap Snippet Identification, SitEmb-v1.5 (QA+SA) is best (F1@5 38.9 vs 37.9 for Qwen3), while models trained without context usage drop slightly.

SitEmb-v1.5 (QA) outperforms its no-context counterpart on story understanding tasks (NarrativeQA, InfBench MC, DetectiveQA, NoCha) except on LongStoryQA, and substantially beats out-of-box Qwen3 especially at top-3 and top-5.
On DetectiveQA, SitEmb (QA) has the highest answer-evidence recall (top-3 42.5) and SitEmb (QA+SA) the highest clue-evidence recall (top-3 26.9), reflecting semantic association ability.
LLMs in the legal domain tend to produce hallucinations, text inconsistent with authoritative sources such as case law and statutes, which is risky because law requires strict adherence to sources.
RAG with regular decoding struggles to effectively integrate retrieved context, so outputs can diverge from the provided context.

Context-aware decoding methods like CAD amplify the influence of context by adjusting logits (contrasting probabilities with and without context) but do not explicitly enforce faithfulness to the context.
Legal texts often follow templatized structures and verbatim phrases, motivating token copying from context.

CoCoLex stores the hidden states of all context tokens with their next tokens, computes L2 distance to the current hidden state, converts it to similarity exp(-dist), and aggregates over the top-k most similar context vectors into a copy distribution over the vocabulary; it is training-free and needs no additional forward passes.
The model's confidence lambda_t = exp(-normalized entropy of its next-token distribution), smoothed with a running average over a past window, so lower entropy gives higher confidence.
CoCoLex's final distribution is p = lambda_t * p_model + (1 - lambda_t) * p_copy, so high confidence relies on the model and low confidence shifts to copying.

CAD and AdaCAD improve correctness and faithfulness on short-text CUAD but reduce fluency and coherence, and on ObliQA, AQuAECHR and CLERC they lower correctness and faithfulness (AlignScore) while improving only ROUGE, so they struggle on long-form generation.

CoLex (static-weight copy interpolation) improves faithfulness and correctness over regular decoding, CAD and AdaCAD, with larger gains in long-range tasks, and keeps fluency and coherence comparable to regular decoding.

CoCoLex further improves correctness and faithfulness over CoLex and improves fluency and coherence relative to CoLex, with results mostly statistically significant (e.g. CLERC Mistral Cor-AS 58.12 vs 54.94 CoLex vs 42.38 regular; Wilcoxon, 95%).

On 25 AQuAECHR questions rated by a legal expert on a 5-point scale, CoCoLex scores higher than Regular and AdaCAD on correctness (4.64), faithfulness (4.44), fluency (4.96) and coherence (4.92), and AdaCAD underperforms Regular on faithfulness (3.84).
The legally pre-trained Saul-7B underperforms the generalist Mistral-7B because it struggles to synthesize provided context, but copy-based decoding substantially improves Saul.
Retrieving and concatenating passages can disrupt semantics through improper chunking, degrading answer accuracy.

CoCoLex+ extends copying to hidden states of the entire document (encoded in overlapping chunks, each token keeping the state from the chunk with most autoregressive context) while keeping only top-k passages as textual context.

CoCoLex+ consistently outperforms CoCoLex in correctness on CLERC and AQuAECHR for both models (e.g. CLERC Saul Cor-AS 44.91 vs 34.95) while keeping fluency and coherence comparable, though AQuAECHR Saul passage faithfulness slightly declines.
Combining AdaCAD with CoCoLex improves results where AdaCAD beats regular decoding (CUAD both models, CLERC Saul) and decreases them where AdaCAD underperforms (CLERC Mistral, AQuAECHR both).
By the fundamental problem of causal inference, the outcome of the same unit cannot be observed both with and without treatment, so counterfactual outcomes are unobservable.
Ground truth causal queries often cannot be observed due to the fundamental problem, confounding and selection bias, so the community relies on expensive expert knowledge or experimental studies.

RCTs are expensive, time-consuming, often ethically infeasible, suffer non-random dropout and limited generalizability, and do not provide the diverse covariate coverage needed to train Causal ML models.
Because real ground truth is scarce, evaluations of Causal ML methods rely predominantly on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.
Researchers' design choices, often made to favor their own methods, bias synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments and limit comparability across studies.
Synthetic data can include only features researchers know how to model, so unknown unknowns are excluded.
Synthetic experiments are often derived from overly simplistic models such as additive noise models and lack sufficient realism to encourage practitioner adoption.
Curth et al. (2021) showed that making the IHDP treatment effect linear, with covariates unchanged, significantly shifted relative method rankings.
On IHDP, RealCause's point-estimate ATE error is 0.17 (true ATE 4.02), but over 20 seeds the mean error is 0.38 +/- 0.39 (up to 1.77), and over 100 realizations it is 0.95 +/- 1.36 (up to 9.45).

Applying segmented-linear or sinusoidal noise transformations that violate the diffeomorphism assumption did not significantly increase CausalNF's counterfactual RMSE, which reflects method-friendly synthetic choices rather than general robustness.
On a non-identifiable counterfactual example, CausalNF consistently converges to one of two SCMs sharing the same observational distribution, giving consistently biased errors when the other is true.
Synthetic data is the only reliable source of ground truth for causal queries and allows full control over noise, confounding and structural complexity, enabling rigorous controlled experiments.

Because researcher freedom biases results, all design choices (causal models, queries, training data, generation algorithm and induced distribution) must be explicitly stated so experiments are reproducible and the domain of validity is clear.

Evaluation should go beyond aggregated accuracy within the identification domain, including behavior outside the identification domain, since behavior under assumption violations is difficult to predict.
Standardized evaluation frameworks should be developed to improve comparability, replicability and documentation of data generation processes and assumptions.
LLMs form a task vector in intermediate layers during in-context learning, and factual-recall ICL follows a residual vector arithmetic f(x_query) = a_f + b_query, analogous to Word2Vec arithmetic.
In GPT2-medium embeddings, answer vectors align more strongly with the task vector than query vectors do, so x + task vector approximately equals y (Fig 1).
The theory models word embeddings with high-level task concepts, low-level concepts and irrelevant concepts, where the task vector is the high-level concept component.

Existing ICL theories overlook the residual stream or treat it unnaturally, rely on linearized attention or squared/hinge losses, and lack a theoretical account of why QA training data enables factual recall.

Nonlinear transformers with softmax attention, MLP, layer normalization and residual connections trained by gradient descent on cross-entropy loss can perform factual-recall ICL via vector arithmetic despite non-convexity (Thm 3.2).

When training and testing on word-label ICL data, the transformer fails to reliably retrieve the high-level task vector; the output becomes a hybrid vector contaminated by low-level features (harmful memorization), as in Fig 2(d).

Models trained on QA data learn the task vector, achieving arbitrarily small test error on both word-label ICL and QA-ICL prompts, because low-level features b_k are absent from QA data (Thm 3.2, Prop 3.3, Fig 3).
The trained transformer can approximately retrieve the task vector solely from demonstration pairs without requiring a query word.
The retrieved intermediate vector can be added to any query sharing the co-task concept to give the correct answer with test loss at most epsilon.

A QA-trained model generalizes to unseen dictionaries (new conic combinations of task vectors with new orthogonal features) and to prompts with multiple co-task concepts (fewer than 4) and varied length (Prop 3.4).
With multiple co-task concepts in a prompt, the model forms a softmax-weighted convex combination of task vectors, resembling Bayesian model averaging.
Simulations with K=2, K'=100, d=3000 show the QA-trained model avoids the persistent constant test error (0.2) of the ICL-trained model (Fig 2-3).
Standard vision systems store knowledge in weights via gradient descent, which raises concerns about interpretability, privacy and bias and makes adding or removing data difficult.
Perception with visual memory retrieves k-nearest neighbours from a database of reference embeddings, so knowledge can be added or removed by editing the memory without retraining a classifier.
The feature embedding model in prior visual-memory work is itself trained on real data, so knowledge and perception are not fully separated and removing data from the embeddings is hard.
The embedding model (ViT-S, DINO objective) is trained only on procedural data generated by simple code (OpenGL shaders), so all real-world data enters only through the visual memory.
Combining procedural embeddings with visual memory gives perfect control over all real-world data, enabling efficient unlearning and privacy analysis with respect to all real images.
Extracting mixing masks from Shaders images with K-Means (Shaders KML) increases diversity, and applying Mixup on top yields Shaders KML Mixup, a new state of the art among procedural processes.
On NIGHTS human visual similarity, the best procedural model reaches 82.4% alignment with humans, within 0.9% of a Places-trained model; white-box metrics like PSNR/SSIM barely beat chance.
With visual memory, the best procedural model beats the Places model by 15% on Flowers102, 8% on CUB200 and 1% on Food101, and is within about 10% on ImageNet-1K.
Procedural models achieve zero-shot and in-context semantic segmentation, with R2 on COCO within 10% of models trained on real data.

Procedural models have never seen real objects, so visually distinct parts of one object (e.g. bike wheel centre and spokes) get dissimilar representations, causing wrong memory matches that explain the remaining gap to real-data models.
Unlearning is done by removing samples from the memory; privacy guarantees can be computed, with less than 0.6% of training images non-private and a roughly linear accuracy-privacy trend.
The procedural model matches faces by appearance and expression on CelebA without training on faces, and matches or exceeds the original MedMNIST result on 7 of 10 datasets.
Client data in federated learning are non-IID, causing divergent local optimizations that degrade global model convergence and generalization.
Prior convergence analyses of FedAvg under non-IID data rely on convexity, bounded gradient dissimilarity or bounded gradients, which are hard to satisfy in practice.

For multi-layer overparameterized networks trained with FedAvg and GD, the model divergence caused by data heterogeneity is bounded and decays as O(n^{-1/2}) in the network width n, without convexity or gradient-boundedness assumptions (Theorem 1).

The heterogeneity term zeta = O(n^{-1/2}) slows the convergence rate and leaves nonzero convergence error, but as n approaches infinity zeta tends to 0 and the impact of data heterogeneity vanishes (Remark 2).
As width goes to infinity, both global and local FedAvg models stay within O(n^{-1/2}) of their first-order Taylor linearizations and have constant global and local NTKs (Theorem 2).
In the infinite-width limit with small learning rate, the linear global model has closed-form parameters and outputs through training (Theorem 3).
Infinite-width FedAvg and centralized GD yield identical model parameters and outputs under matched iterations, hence the same generalization performance.
On non-IID versus IID data, the test accuracy drop shrinks as width grows: FNN1/2/4/16 drop 17.4%/9.5%/6.3%/2.0%, CNN1/2/8/32 drop 44.9%/26.7%/5.1%/2.4%, ResNet1/2/4/16 drop 44.6%/29.1%/18.7%/14.8%.
With learning rate eta0/n, the convergence rate and final accuracy of FNN32 and CNN32 are nearly identical for IID and non-IID data, while FNN1 and CNN1 show a noticeable gap.
Increasing width diminishes variations in global and local NTKs and model parameters; sufficiently wide networks show nearly constant NTKs and parameters (lazy training).
The outputs of the global and local models stay nearly identical to their linear models for FNN512 but visibly differ for FNN16.
Experiments comparing overparameterized FedAvg with centralized learning show the same generalization behaviour, confirming Theorem 3.
Training language models with AdamW at large batch size shows clear performance degradation, requiring additional training tokens to reach comparable generalization.
During large-batch training with AdamW the max attention logit in attention layers increases sharply, exceeding values seen in small-batch training.
An inflated max attention logit yields overly sharp (near one-hot) attention distributions that limit the expressive ability of attention layers.
LAMB's weight-wise trust ratio reduces max attention logit in the first self-attention layer of GPT-2 but not in the medium (12th) layer.
There is a large disparity between max norms and l2 norms of query/key weights, so l2-norm-based trust ratios cannot effectively limit the maximum of W_Q/W_K.
MERIT computes the trust ratio with the max-norm, giving larger updates to extreme weight values and limiting spikes in max attention logit.
Query/key weight values show high similarity within rows (multi-head attention) and within columns (outlier dimension phenomenon).
LAMB's weight-wise trust ratio is inaccurate because extreme values in one row/column can harm training stability of other rows/columns.
MERIT computes row-wise and column-wise max-norm ratios and sets the element-wise ratio to the max of them, bounded below by the weight-wise ratio, with element-wise update clipping to 1.
MERIT's design successfully suppresses the rapid increase of max attention logit in the middle self-attention layers where LAMB fails.
On OpenWebText with GPT-2 small/medium/large, MERIT achieves lower validation loss than LAMB, AdamW, Lion and Sophia-G, with gaps widening as model size grows.
MERIT enables a 6k batch size with no degradation versus the standard batch size (480) at 48B training tokens, allowing larger batches than LAMB and AdamW.
Validation loss (GPT-2 small/medium): AdamW 3.470/3.172, LAMB 3.355/3.068, maxLAMB 3.304/3.040, MERIT 3.280/2.982.
Removing element-wise clipping weakens MERIT's gains, and using the weight-wise ratio as a lower bound significantly improves generalization.
Softmax attention has inductive biases that suit some tasks better than others, and it is computationally expensive in runtime and memory.

The attention scoring function takes a dot product of low-dimensional queries and keys, equivalent to a bilinear form with a rank-r matrix where the head dimension r is much smaller than the embedding dimension D.
The low-rank scoring function loses token information for tasks with intrinsically high-dimensional inputs; for example it cannot represent s(x,x')=x^T x'.
Prior work shows one full-rank attention head can significantly outperform low-rank multi-head attention in in-context linear regression after controlling for model size.

Block Tensor-Train (BTT) and contiguous Multi-Level Low Rank (MLR) matrices have high rank while remaining parameter- and compute-efficient, and replace the low-rank product in the attention scoring function (Bilinear BTT, Bilinear MLR).
On in-context regression with input dimension 128, standard 8-head attention cannot learn the task even at model width D=512, while 1-head attention (r=D, full rank) learns it at D=512.
Bilinear BTT with 8 heads is full rank and learns the in-context regression task at only D=256.
At fixed width D=256, both Bilinear MLR and Bilinear BTT attain lower regression error than 1-head or 8-head attention when controlling for training compute.
Standard attention scores every token pair with the same function and weights, and each token can attend to the whole context, which is expensive for long contexts.
Real-world datasets often exhibit locality, meaning a token's semantics depend most strongly on nearby tokens.

Using contiguous MLR for the attention score matrix gives nearby tokens higher-rank interactions and distant tokens cheaper ones, saving FLOPs compared to standard attention while keeping high-quality scores for neighbours.

With 6-layer character-level transformers on OpenWebText (T=1024, r=64, D in {256,384,512,768}), 8-level MLR attention (rank split 32|8|6|4|4|4|4|2) outperforms standard attention at all widths throughout training, giving a better scaling law.
When controlling for compute, MLR attention outperforms sliding window attention (window 128) and a Global+SWA hybrid across model widths.
Replacing T5 attention in Chronos with 6-level MLR attention (rank split 32|10|8|8|4|2) yields slightly lower validation loss with fewer FLOPs for embedding dimensions 128 to 512.
On the ETT dataset, MLR attention increasingly outperforms standard attention in oil temperature prediction as the forecast horizon grows.
Self-attention in diffusion transformers (U-ViT, DiT) has quadratic complexity in token count, which causes latency across denoising steps.
Prior token-reduction methods for diffusion (ToMeSD, Token Pruning, ToFu) rely on GPU-inefficient primitives such as sorting and scattered memory writes.
When paired with optimized attention such as FlashAttention in diffusers, the overhead of earlier merging logic dominates computation time and prevents practical speedups.
ToMA formulates destination-token selection as a submodular optimization problem solved with a GPU-optimized facility location algorithm, choosing a diverse and representative token set.
ToMA merges non-destination tokens into destinations via an attention-like linear transformation and unmerges them via an inverse transformation, using GPU-friendly matrix multiplications.

Because facility-location destinations cover largely disjoint source sets and low attention temperature sharpens the softmax, the merge matrix rows are near-orthonormal, so the transpose approximates the pseudo-inverse and is used as the default unmerge.
Latent tokens exhibit spatial coherence, so merging can run in parallel within non-overlapping local tiles.
Over a 10-step window, more than half of destination tokens are reused, so ToMA reuses destination sets and linear merge/unmerge weights across consecutive steps and layers to amortize overhead.
ToMA reduces total generation time by 24% for SDXL-base and 23% for Flux.1-dev with negligible quality change (DINO delta < 0.07).

ToMAtile gives the best DINO score but is slowed by memory copying, ToMAstripe is faster but slightly lower quality, and ToMAonce is fastest but has the worst quality; ToMA's default locality-aware variant balances them with up to 24% speedup.
On SDXL ToMA achieves the fastest generation time (up to 28.5% improvement) with competitive quality, while ToMe is slower due to sorting and ToFu shows unstable quality.
In split inference the client model maps private input x to an intermediate representation (IR) h = fc(x) that is sent to a cloud server, so an adversary can try to reconstruct x from h.
Existing data reconstruction attacks mostly target small CNN classifiers (e.g. ResNet18); the privacy risks of vision transformers and foundation models in split inference are largely unexplored.

DRAG reconstructs inputs by performing guided diffusion on a pre-trained latent diffusion model's image prior, using DSG-based guidance from the distance between fc(x) and the target IR, gradient clipping with Adam, and self-recurrence to handle non-convex fc.
DRAG++ initializes DRAG with a coarse reconstruction from an auxiliary inverse network trained on public data, noised at a small timestep t = sT.
On CLIP-ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 without defenses, DRAG consistently outperforms rMLE, LM and GLASS at deeper split points, while rMLE and LM are competitive only at shallow split points.
On CLIP-ViT-B/16, DRAG++ gives higher LPIPS and DINO scores than the inverse network alone and DRAG at split points beyond layer 3, with only a slight MS-SSIM loss relative to the inverse network.
DRAG and DRAG++ also reconstruct out-of-distribution aerial images from the UCMerced LandUse dataset.
Input data can still be reconstructed by DRAG from CLIP-ViT-B/16 layer-12 IRs protected by DISCO (Config III) and NoPeek (Config VI), including against adaptive attacks.
Under token shuffling and 50% token dropping on CLIP-ViT-B/16 layer 12, rMLE and LM fail to reconstruct images.
A 2-layer MLP token-position classifier reaches 21.40% top-1 accuracy (average L1 distance 2.34) on ImageNet-1K, enabling reordering by the Hungarian algorithm.
Under shuffling, GLASS and DRAG reconstructions degrade, but some images still retain key features of the original inputs.

In extreme multilabel classification the linear classification head, rather than the encoder, dominates parameters and memory; with embedding dimension 768 and 3 million labels the weights alone take about 8 GiB, and about 32 GiB with gradients and optimizer states.
Renee computes classifier gradients directly without materializing the loss, which reduces activation memory and enables end-to-end training that beats negative-sampling approaches.

Renee's mixed-precision training keeps a full-precision parameter copy, a second FP16 copy of the classifier weights that persists for the whole step, and upcasts classifier gradients to FP32, inflating memory.

Classifier-input gradient accumulation over the label dimension often overflows the FP16 range while classifier-weight gradients do not grow with label count, making Renee's training unstable and sensitive to encoder and label-space size.
Renee's peak training memory is 39.7 GiB at 3 million labels, because the FP16 weight copy (4 GiB), gradients (4 GiB) and their FP32 upcast (8 GiB) stack up.
ELMO uses BF16 instead of FP16 to avoid overflow because BF16 has the dynamic range of FP32, removing the extra high-precision copy of classifier gradients.
Replacing 32-bit optimizer weights with BF16 weights stops training progress because round-to-nearest cancels updates smaller than half the gap to the next representable number.
ELMO uses Kahan summation for the encoder optimizer and stochastic rounding for the classifier optimizer to compensate for BF16 rounding error.

Classifier weights can be trained in pure FP8 (E4M3) without loss scaling or mixed precision as long as gradients stay in BF16; 3 exponent bits suffice and mantissa degradation below 6 bits is recovered by stochastic rounding.

Chunking the classifier update (3 to 8 chunks), decoupling encoder and classifier updates, and fusing classifier gradient computation with the optimizer step in a Triton kernel avoids storing classifier gradients and reduces peak memory.
ELMO needs only 10.3 GiB (BF16) or 6.6 GiB (FP8) of peak memory for a 3-million-label model versus 39.7 GiB for Renee, a 4x-6x reduction.
ELMO's precision is comparable to Renee and competitive with existing XMC baselines on most public datasets despite pure low-precision training.
The largest public XMC dataset has 3 million labels, so recent large-scale experiments used proprietary data.
The authors curate LF-Paper2Keywords-8.6M from DBLP-Citation-network V14, using paper titles and abstracts with keywords as 8.6 million labels.
Other XMC baselines do not scale to 8.6 million labels, while ELMO's low-precision training yields significant memory and computational savings on it.

Traditional steering uses fixed steering strengths, chosen by costly, model-specific ad hoc hyperparameter sweeps, which leads to understeering (insufficient change) and oversteering (unnecessary, potentially detrimental change).
MERA identifies steering directions with linear error-estimation probes p(h)=w^T h trained to predict the LM's error E(a) from activations, rather than with contrastive pairs.

Minimising ||v||^2 subject to p(h+v) <= alpha gives the closed form v* = lambda* w with lambda* = max(0,(alpha - w^T h)/||w||^2), so steering is applied only where predicted error exceeds alpha and its strength grows with the predicted error.

Extracting activations at the exact token position of the generated answer performs at least as well as, and often better than, the last position for probe RMSE across most model families (Llama and Gemma).
Sparse autoencoder representations show no signal of improved probe performance over original activations and impose high compute costs, so MERA uses original activations.

The threshold alpha* is chosen on a separate calibration set to maximise the accuracy gain among candidates whose gain exceeds epsilon + b(delta,K,N), with b = sqrt(log(2K/delta)/(2N)) from a Hoeffding bound and Bonferroni union bound.
With i.i.d. samples, P(Delta_cal(alpha*) > epsilon) >= 1 - delta, so MERA either provably improves performance or abstains entirely (lambda*=0) when no candidate threshold is valid.

Across models and datasets MERA improves accuracy over both unsteered models and existing steering approaches in all settings, reducing errors across error percentiles and yielding more corrective transitions with fewer degradations than baselines.
Contrastive steering alone is unreliable and sometimes reduces accuracy, but with MERA it consistently improves, turning -0.05 SPI into +0.52 on Yes/No and -0.09 into +0.21 on MMLU-HS.
Without MERA, the base probe steering is too weak (+0.00 SPI on MMLU-HS and SMS Spam); with MERA it becomes the best-performing method, improving SPI by +0.64 on Sentiment and +0.53 on Yes/No.
Existing CRL algorithms often exhibit persistent constraint violations during training, limiting their use in safety-critical scenarios.
Function-approximation noise breaks the zero-mean assumption under a minimization objective, causing underestimation of the cost value, so high-cost states appear deceptively safe (Fig 2).
Underestimating the cost value in high-cost regions leads agents to over-explore unsafe states and produces frequent constraint violations during training even when a safe optimal policy exists.

Underestimation encourages exploration and overestimation discourages it, so in high-cost regions overestimation helps prevent unsafe exploration, and the challenge is to shape the bias rather than remove it.
MICE stores previously explored unsafe states (positive extrinsic cost) from the previous iteration's policy, embedded by random projection, to identify high-cost regions.
The intrinsic cost is the kernel-similarity-based pseudo-count of the current state visiting high-cost regions in memory, normalized for stability.
The extrinsic-intrinsic cost value function adds the intrinsic cost to the target, raising the cost estimate and mitigating underestimation in high-cost regions.
A balancing intrinsic factor beta, updated from the previous update's estimated bias, raises the intrinsic cost when underestimating and lowers it when overestimating.
A trust-region objective keeps the updated policy close to the policy that generated the memory, so stored unsafe states stay relevant and the intrinsic cost reflects the updated policy's risk.
The extrinsic-intrinsic cost admits constraint bounds (Theorem 4.3), and the MICE update has a worst-case constraint violation bound tighter than CPO's (Theorem 4.4).
Under assumptions similar to TD3 and Double Q-learning, the extrinsic-intrinsic cost value function converges to the optimal Q_C (Theorem 4.5).

On Safety Gym and Safety MuJoCo, MICE significantly reduces constraint violations while maintaining policy performance similar or superior to baselines, matching Saute and SimmerPID's constraint satisfaction with better return (Figs 3-4).
Validation shows MICE mitigates underestimation, its estimation bias approaches zero, and its cost value converges to the true value (Fig 5).
Replacing the memory-driven intrinsic cost with fixed constants (3, 5, 15) reduces return, and a larger constant (5 vs 3) does not necessarily reduce violations (Fig 6a,b).
On SafetyPointGoal1-v0, MICE adapts to cost thresholds 0, 15 and 25, enforcing compliance even at threshold 0 (Fig 6c,d).

Expectation-based constraints in CRL only guarantee compliance on average, so even when the expected cost satisfies the threshold, extreme tail events can cause frequent constraint violations (Fig 1a).
WCSAC approximates the cost distribution with a Gaussian that fails to capture tail behaviour, and QCPO's quantile constraint neglects the high variance and the exploitation of extreme samples.
Extreme reward samples reveal how to achieve task goals and extreme cost samples highlight critical constraints, but they are rare, making tail modelling high-variance.

By the Pickands-type theorem, the conditional excess distribution above a high threshold converges to a Generalized Pareto distribution, so the cost tail can be modelled by a GPD (Theorem 3.1); a GPD fits better than a Gaussian (Fig 1b, Fig 7).
Constraining the mu-quantile of the cumulative discounted cost, q_mu <= d, implies P(C <= d) >= mu.
EVO fits a GPD to peaks C > q_mu and sets the risk boundary q_(mu+nu) = q_mu + GPD quantile, treating samples beyond it as extreme, giving an EVT-based optimization objective.
Each sample's replay priority p = omega_r + omega_c sums its quantile levels under the reward GPD and cost GPD, so lower-probability high-value samples are replayed more often.
Reweighting stored off-policy samples by pi/pi_0 augments extreme samples and reduces the variance of the GPD fit.

EVO's quantile objective gives an upper bound J_C(pi_k+1) <= d - (GPD quantile term) that is tighter than the expectation objective in CPO, guaranteeing strict constraint satisfaction at a zero-violation exploitation range nu_0 (Theorem 4.1).
When mu is set by the expected cumulative cost, EVO has a smaller constraint violation probability than the expectation-based objective (Theorem 4.2).
The EVO quantile estimator has variance negatively correlated with sample count and lower than quantile regression methods, so more extreme samples via resampling reduce variance (Theorem 4.3).

On Safety Gymnasium with infeasible initial policies, EVO converges rapidly to the feasible domain and maintains zero constraint violations while matching CPO's return and beating Saute and WCSAC (Fig 3).
On Safety MuJoCo tasks with feasible initial policies, EVO maintains zero violations throughout training, while WCSAC shows significant violations (Fig 4).
Replacing the EVT-based objective with a constant quantile constraint achieves safety only by diminishing performance (Fig 5a,b).
Removing extreme prioritization degrades optimization, showing it exploits the learning signal in extreme samples (Fig 5).
Removing off-policy importance resampling for GPD fitting worsens constraint satisfaction due to inaccurate tail modelling (Fig 6).
Larger GPD fitting sample sizes generally improve constraint satisfaction, and EVO stays strong with as few as 10 samples in SafetyPointCircle1-v0 and above 20 in SafetyPointGoal1-v0 (Fig 8).
Adversarial training (AT) with multi-step attacks like PGD generates strong examples but requires substantial computation and long training time.
Fast adversarial training uses single-step attacks, allowing only coarse exploration of the adversarial space, and often suffers catastrophic overfitting, where robustness to PGD drops dramatically.
The paper aims to improve FAT robustness through a new loss function rather than stronger inner maximization, keeping training short.
Using convexity of cross-entropy w.r.t. logits, the AT loss is upper-bounded by L(f(x)) + (f(x+d)-f(x))^T grad_f L(f(x)) + (||H||_2/2)||f(x+d)-f(x)||^2 (Lemma 1).
The Hessian norm of the cross-entropy loss w.r.t. logits satisfies ||H||_2 <= 1/2 (Lemma 2).
The QUB loss is L_QUB = L(f(x)) + (f(x+d)-f(x))^T grad_f L(f(x)) + (1/4)||f(x+d)-f(x)||^2, usable by simply replacing the loss in existing AT methods.
The first term of QUB, loss on clean samples, drives standard accuracy.
The second term approximates d^T grad_x L(f(x)), the loss increment under perturbation; minimizing it dampens loss change and flattens the loss landscape.
The third term, the squared change in logits under perturbation, limits the effect of adversarial examples on the output, as in earlier works such as TRADES.
Because grad_f L = softmax minus one-hot is closed-form and lives in R^C, the second QUB term needs no extra backprop and less memory than input-sized d^T grad_x L.
Because of its worst-case nature QUB yields larger gradients than the AT loss, and using it throughout can cause excessive regularization that degrades standard accuracy.
QUB-decreasing linearly transitions from QUB loss to AT loss over training (L_total = (1-lambda_t) L_QUB + lambda_t L_AT, lambda_t = t/T) to balance robustness and generalization.
Except for FGSM-RS, all baseline AT methods improve in robustness when QUB loss is applied (Table 1, CIFAR-10 ResNet18).
QUB-static achieves better robust accuracy than QUB-decreasing for most methods, but at larger standard accuracy cost, sometimes outweighing the robustness gain (e.g. Free-AT).
QUB-decreasing achieves comparable or improved robust accuracy and better standard accuracy than QUB-static in many settings.
Combining QUB with FGSM-RS can degrade performance, because FGSM-RS's low-quality perturbations make QUB enforce smoothness in non-informative regions.
QUB adds slight training time over baselines but FAT with QUB remains cheaper than multi-step PGD-AT and TRADES.

Loss-landscape visualizations show smoother landscapes with QUB (Fig 1), and the average dominant Hessian eigenvalue is smaller (Fig 2), with sparsity analysis in Fig 4, supporting the flattening explanation.
Aligned LLMs exhibit safety vulnerabilities after fine-tuning, even on benign data or a small amount of malicious data.
Methods that align safety during fine-tuning (e.g. VLGuard, Lisa) increase training complexity, need extra compute, and can inhibit general capabilities.
RESTA restores safety by adding the safety vector to a fine-tuned model, but the safety vector contains components that suppress general capabilities, so the merged model's general ability drops.
The safety vector is delta_safe = theta_safe - theta_unsafe, obtained by harmfully fine-tuning a safety-aligned model to get an unsafe model and inverting the parameter delta.
The inverse safety vector consists of a low-rank safety drift component opposite to the safety direction and a general suppression component that impairs general-task performance.
The safety regions of LLMs are sparse and low-rank and isolated from the directions of general capabilities, and safety drift directions of safety vectors share a common low-rank subspace.

LSSF performs SVD on standardized linear-layer activations of the safety-aligned model on a harmful-query calibration set (128 PKU-SafeRLHF samples) and uses the left singular vectors to build an orthogonal low-rank projection matrix P(r).

The safety singular value entropy, based on squared singular values, determines the retained rank r as the smallest rank whose entropy ratio H_r/H_n exceeds threshold eta, adapting the rank to the safety information density of each layer.
A scaling factor alpha_i, decreasing linearly from alpha_1 for the largest singular value, weights the singular vectors to strengthen drift along the main safety directions.
LSSF restores safety by adding alpha*P'(r)*delta_safe to the downstream fine-tuned model's parameters, counteracting the safety-direction offset while minimally affecting task and other directions.

Adding safety principal components to Llama3.1-8B-Instruct raises refusal on AdvBench/DoAnythingNow while MBPP, GSM8K, BBH, MMLU and IFEval stay close to the base (e.g. BBH 68.20 vs 68.29), whereas SFT on jailbreak data drops BBH to 31.42 and IFEval to 45.79 (LoRA setting).
Compared with DARE, merging safety principal components causes less disruption to general ability (full fine-tuning BBH 68.52 vs 20.03; IFEval 81.88 vs 45.87).

In LoRA SFT on AG's News and Yahoo Answers, LSSF reaches near-perfect refusal rates (AdvBench 1.00 on Qwen2.5-7B for AG's News; 0.99-1.00 elsewhere) while keeping classification accuracy close to NA-SFT (e.g. 0.92 vs 0.91 on AG's News Qwen2.5).

In Medical QA full SFT, LSSF achieves refusal rates up to 0.99 while retaining BLEU/ROUGE-L (e.g. 0.42/0.50 on Qwen2.5-7B), whereas on Llama3.1-8B the baselines VLGuard, RESTA and Lisa lower BLEU/ROUGE-L by more than 0.2.

Baselines vary widely in safe refusal rate across harmful query datasets, especially in the LoRA scenario (e.g. NA-SFT refusal on AdvBench is 0.09 vs 1.00 for LSSF on Qwen2.5 AG's News), and RESTA lowers downstream accuracy (Yahoo Answers ACC 0.25 on Qwen2.5).

Lowering the entropy ratio eta makes the low-rank principal-component matrix smoother with values toward zero; the method selects a structured subnetwork rather than suppressing individual delta parameters.
Increasing eta gradually improves the safety of the merged model; for eta > 0.8 the refusal rate approaches 1.0 with BLEU only slightly affected.
Increasing the left-singular-vector weight alpha raises safety; for alpha > 2.5 safety is close to the safety model with BLEU only slightly affected (eta=0.5).

Conditional flow matching trains v_t(x,theta) against a conditional vector field per data sample, and L_CFM equals the FM loss up to a constant independent of theta, so it is an unbiased estimate of the marginal field.
Even when CFM regresses the vector field, the divergence gap |div v_t - div u_t| can be substantial, producing significant errors in the learned probability path and likelihood estimates (Fig 1).
The error eps_t = p_t - p_hat_t satisfies a continuity-type PDE with initial value 0 and a forcing term L_t = -p_t[div(u_t - v_t) + (u_t - v_t).grad log p_t] (Proposition 3.1).
The solution of the error PDE (Corollary 3.2) shows that minimizing the divergence gap is as important as reducing the vector-field discrepancy for learning an accurate probability path.
Under mild assumptions, TV(p_t, p_hat_t) <= (1/2) L_DM(theta) for any t, so p_t = p_hat_t when L_DM is zero (Theorem 3.3).
The marginal divergence loss cannot be minimized directly because the divergence of the marginal vector field is unavailable.
The conditional divergence loss L_CDM upper-bounds L_DM and gives TV(p_t, p_hat_t) <= (1/2) L_CDM (Theorem 4.1).
Minimizing L_CDM alone gives no guarantee of proximity between v_t and u_t because its two terms can cancel and the loss cannot reach exactly zero.
Flow and divergence matching trains with L_FDM = lambda1 L_CFM + lambda2 L_CDM, directly controlling the gap between vector fields and between their divergences.
L_FDM is computationally cheaper than controlling higher-order quantities such as the gradient of the divergence, and an efficient variant uses stop-gradient and Hutchinson trace estimation.
On a 1D Gaussian mixture with a 3-layer MLP on VP path, FDM (lambda2=0.2) learns the probability path closer to the data than FM (lambda2=0) (Fig 2).
On the checkerboard test set FDM improves likelihood over FM for both OT (2.53 vs 2.38) and VP (2.46 vs 2.34) paths (Table 1).
On CIFAR-10 FDM(OT) improves NLL from 2.99 to 2.85 and FID from 6.35 to 5.62 over FM(OT) (Table 2).
FDM improves FM with Linear and Dirichlet probability paths for promoter DNA sequence generation, with and without guidance (Tables 3-4).
FDM outperforms FM and diffusion on event-guided trajectory sampling, with lower KL divergence between event-constraint histograms (Table 7), without hurting estimation of p(E).
FDM improves latent FM on KTH and BAIR video prediction, keeping high visual quality in later frames where FM loses motion details (Tables 8-9, Fig 6).
Early fusion builds retrieval units (fused blocks) independently of the query, often including query-irrelevant passages that distort similarity between fused blocks and queries.
Late fusion retrieves single table segments or passages that may be only partially relevant, risking retrieval of a wrong table with overlapping terms (e.g. Grammy award tables).
Early fusion relies on predefined entity-linking relationships that fail to capture query-dependent links needed to answer the query.
Prior approaches rely on semantic similarity and so may fail to retrieve rows or passages requiring multi-hop or column-wise aggregation reasoning.
Table segments and passages are formalized as two node sets of a bipartite graph; an early-fusion fused block is a star centered on a table-segment node and a late-fusion evidence chain is an edge.

HELIOS retrieves a bipartite subgraph by indexing offline-fused edges with ColBERTv2 multi-vector embeddings, using edges as a unit between star graphs and nodes to cut irrelevant context while avoiding partial information.
HELIOS expands the candidate graph at node level with beam search (b=10) to find query-relevant edges missed by offline entity linking.
HELIOS has an LLM reason over the expanded graph decomposed into smaller star graphs, enabling aggregation and multi-hop selection while reducing hallucination risk.
On OTT-QA dev, HELIOS beats COS by 19.0% average answer recall (42.6% at k=2), 39.9% nDCG@50 and 12.2% Hits@4K.
On OTT-QA, HELIOS gets dev EM/F1 of 59.3/65.8 and test 57.0/64.3, above COS (56.9/63.2 dev, 54.9/61.5 test).
Edge-based retrieval outperforms star-graph and node-based retrieval by 6.9% and 12.4% on average AR, and by 20% and 43.7% on nDCG@50.
Removing query-relevant node expansion lowers AR by 2.1% on average, nDCG@50 by 4.2%, EM by 4.2% and F1 by 4.1%.
Removing star-based LLM refinement drops AR@2 by 5.5% and nDCG@50 by 1.1%, with the effect mainly on small k and logical-inference queries.
Prompting the LLM with individual star graphs instead of the full graph improves nDCG@50 by 12.4% (41.8 for the full-graph setting).

Mainstream attribution and feature-visualization methods associate neuron activation with the presence of concepts: attribution highlights present input features and feature visualization finds inputs that maximize activation.
A neuron z_j encodes the absence of a concept if inserting the concept into the input decreases its activation, i.e. f_j([x,C=1]) < f_j([x,C=0]) (Definition 2.1).

A neuron encoding the absence of a concept can be constructed with negative weights from neurons encoding its presence plus a source of positive potential, so DNNs can implement such neurons (Proposition 2.2).
Standard target attribution only highlights concepts present in the input, and concepts whose absence is informative are typically not present in images of the target class, so they cannot appear.
Feature visualization through maximization cannot visualize concepts whose absence is encoded, since maximally activating inputs contain minimal amounts of inhibiting concepts.

Counterfactual explanations operate between samples or classes and implicitly delete content, so they cannot tell whether a prediction relies on presence of a class concept or absence of a competing one.
Computing the attribution for class t on inputs from other classes (non-target attribution) makes concepts whose absence is informative appear, with negative attribution indicating inhibition.
Finding the input that minimizes a neuron's pre-activation reveals the patterns that inhibit it, i.e. the concepts whose absence the neuron encodes.

In a synthetic Hassenstein-Reichardt detector, Integrated Gradients and highest-activating patches explain the neuron encoding both directions faithfully but only highlight the left-to-right motion for the neuron encoding presence of one direction and absence of the other.
The proposed modifications reveal the missing inhibitory signal in the Hassenstein-Reichardt detector, with right-to-left motion receiving negative attribution (Fig 3e).

A small CNN trained to classify green-pixel presence learns an output that encodes absence of green via a negative weight from the green channel and a positive weight from the red/blue channel, matching the mechanistic construction.
On the toy CNN, standard methods fail to show the green pixel's causal role, while non-target attribution and minimization highlight the green pixel for the absence-encoding output (Fig 4).
In VGG19, ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16, inserting least-activating patches strongly suppresses channel activations while random patches have little effect (Table 1).
Inserting logical-NOT patches from Mu and Andreas (2020) or the most activating patches decreases activation no more than random patches, so they target presences or a different notion of NOT.

Channels that encode presence of concepts of a class often simultaneously encode absence of concepts of closely related classes, e.g. Border Collie vs. Leonberger, aiding fine-grained discrimination and robustness (Fig 6).
On a synthetic ISIC bias where all benign samples have colorful patches, a model with no debiasing overfits to them and fails when the patches are absent or the association is inverted (Table 2).
Presence debiasing with existing attribution priors reduces the bias but still fails on malignant samples with inserted patches, indicating bias from the absence of colorful patches.
Presence+absence debiasing gives the highest average accuracy in both setups without the training bias, comparable to a model trained without bias (Table 2).
Biases can arise from concept absence as well as presence, so effective debiasing must account for both.
Regret-based methods for zero-sum matrix games produce policies that generally do not converge, and the average policy used as a proxy is hard to compute for practical (e.g. neural network) policies.

Prior work (Cai et al. 2023; Dong et al. 2024) obtained only O(T^{-1/8}) exploitability-gap rates for last-iterate convergence with bandit feedback, against a known lower bound of Omega(T^{-1/2}) from K-armed bandits.
The best attainable rate for last-iterate convergence of uncoupled learning with bandit feedback in matrix games was an open question.

For any p in (0,2], no uncoupled learning sequence with unobserved opponent actions can achieve Lp last-iterate convergence faster than T^{-1/(2+p)} on all 2x2 games, i.e. Omega(T^{-1/4}) for L2 (Theorem 5.1).

In some 2x2 games a minimax policy makes all of the other player's actions equivalent so they cannot learn, while a policy converging to it only slows learning, so convergence to the minimax policy is detrimental to learning.
For p in (2,infinity], norm monotonicity yields the Omega(T^{-1/4}) lower bound for Lp last-iterate convergence (Corollary 5.3).
Guaranteeing last-iterate convergence is strictly harder than average-iterate convergence, which attains O(T^{-1/2}).

Algorithm 1 uses a shared random seed to synchronize players, playing the current profile of an anytime algorithm A on exploration steps and its output on exploitation steps, with exploration probabilities p_t summing to infinity.
If A has output convergence rate g, Algorithm 1 achieves an Lp last-iterate rate f_t built from p_t and g (Lemma 6.1).
Using EXP3-IX with p_t = t^{-p/(2+p)}, Algorithm 1 attains Lp last-iterate rate O~(t^{-1/(2+p)}), matching the lower bound up to constant and log factors (Theorem 6.2).
The first algorithm still needs average-policy computation (since it relies on A's output) and requires synchronizing the two players, so it is not practical.
Algorithm 2 runs mirror descent steps on a KL-regularized game L_tau with an unbiased loss estimate (instead of IX estimation), requiring no average policy.
With tau = ((A+B)/T)^{1/4} sqrt(2/(log A + log B)) and eta_t = 2/(tau(t+1)), Algorithm 2's final output has ||EG||_2 of order ((A+B)/T)^{1/4} sqrt(log(AB)), i.e. optimal O(T^{-1/4}) (Theorem 7.2).
The regularization in Algorithm 2 depends on the horizon T, so the rate is only guaranteed near the final output and not anytime.
Algorithm 3 (doubling trick with synchronized instances) gives an anytime L2 last-iterate bound of order ((A+B)/t)^{1/4} sqrt(log AB) log t, i.e. O~(T^{-1/4}) (Theorem 8.1).
Algorithm 3 shares the weakness of requiring the two players to synchronize which instance to play.
Without extra assumptions there are infinitely many joint distributions consistent with source data, so assumptions linking source and target are needed to identify the target joint distribution.

Existing latent-representation DA methods rely on restrictive assumptions such as independent latent variables, invariant label distributions or exponential-family distributions, or lack identifiability guarantees for the target joint distribution.
The label's Markov blanket (parents, children, spouses) is the minimal predictive set for the label, so a natural approach is to learn a representation of it.
Assumptions 1 and 2 require latent variables' and label's distributions to vary sufficiently across source domains, which makes recovery of latent representations feasible.

Under sufficient changes and faithfulness, modelling the generative process with the minimal number of edges in the learned Markov network recovers a representation that is an invertible transformation of the true Markov blanket (Theorem 1).
Because P(Y|Zmb) changes across domains and Y is unavailable in the target, the joint P(Zmb,Y) is not identifiable in the target domain from Markov blanket representations alone.
Under Assumptions 1-3 and faithfulness, the learned Markov blanket can be partitioned into subspaces that are invertible transformations of the true parents, children and spouses of Y (Theorem 2).
Assumption 3 requires that the intimate neighbors of Y's parents, children and spouses lie only within their own group.
With Zpa, Zch, Zsps disentangled, P(Y|X) in the target domain is determined by P(Y|Zpa) and P(Zch|Y,Zsps) in the target (Proposition 1 and Corollary 1).
Assumption 4 confines domain-specific conditional distributions P(Zch|Y=vc,Zsps) to a q-dimensional manifold, so each domain is characterized by mixture weights.
Under Assumptions 4 and 5 (linear independence), the target distributions P(Zch|Y,Zsps) and P(Y|Zpa) are identifiable, giving identifiability of P(Y|X) in the target domain (Theorem 3, Remark 1).
GAMA uses VAEs for (theta_Y, Zpa)->Y and (theta_ch, Y, Zsps)->Zch, with a Gumbel-Softmax VAE for discrete Y, plus a classifier; domain parameters theta are learned for the target during training.
GAMA trains with Lall = Lcls + l1 Lvae,Z + l2 Lvae,Y + l3 Lvae,Zch + l4 Lch + l5 LY, with beta1 and beta2 set to 1.
GAMA achieves the best performance in most Office-Home sub-tasks, surpassing the strongest baseline iMSDA by 1% on average (Table 1).
GAMA achieves better average accuracy than the best baseline on PACS, with 98.8% on the Photo domain (Table 1).
On Office-Home, removing the VAE losses (GAMA-vae) hurts, and the theta-related VAEs further improve accuracy over GAMA-theta (Table 2).
GNNs rely on the underlying graph structure, so even small structural perturbations can drastically degrade their performance.
Defending against attacks requires balancing accuracy on clean data and robustness to adversarial attacks; prioritizing one can harm the other.

The adversarial training objective decomposes into an accuracy term over nodes unaffected by perturbation (weighted by lambda) and a robustness term over affected nodes (weighted by 1-lambda), with the attack budget epsilon controlling lambda (Theorem 3.1).
Adversarial training and robust GNN architectures couple accuracy and robustness in a single model, limiting achievable robustness because higher robustness comes at significant accuracy loss.

Existing purifiers rely on predefined heuristics (Jaccard pruning, SVD low-rank) or on classifier-derived edge representations, which lack adaptivity and fail to capture structural differences between clean and adversarial edges.

The accuracy objective is assigned to a standard GNN classifier trained on the clean graph, while a separate purifier is trained self-supervised to reconstruct the clean graph G from randomly sampled perturbed graphs G' with a large budget, independent of node labels.
Single-step purification that prunes or keeps edges by fixed criteria makes abrupt, discretized changes, limiting precise recovery under complex or heavy perturbations.

Under the local Lipschitz assumption induced by the self-supervised objective, iterative purification G(t+1)=G(t)+alpha*dG(t) converges linearly to a stationary point for any step size alpha in (0,1] (Theorem 3.3).
The paper empirically estimates the local Lipschitz constant of the one-step purifier on test graphs from 100 random perturbed adjacency pairs to support Theorem 3.3.

Standard GAEs stack static GNN layers that smooth local variations (making adversarially connected nodes similar), suffer oversmoothing for higher-order information, and use proximity-based decoders that reconstruct spurious connections.
GPR-GAE encodes nodes with multiple Generalized PageRank filters whose learnable coefficients weight different adjacency powers, capturing diverse multi-scale structure without oversmoothing.
Edge embeddings are computed from concatenated node embeddings and decoded into directed link scores, which are averaged over both directions for undirected graphs.
GPR-GAE is trained with L = L_restore + delta*L_sym, a restoration loss over original edges and injected negative edges plus a symmetry loss, with delta balancing them.

At test time the adjacency is iteratively updated with step size alpha until ||dA||/||A|| <= tau, and the final continuous (non-discretized) adjacency is passed to the classifier; the paper uses alpha=1, tau=1/1000 and at most 5 steps.
Classification accuracy improves with each purification step and converges consistently across all alpha values under the termination condition (Fig 2).
Under adaptive attacks GPR-GAE attached to vanilla classifiers achieves higher robustness than vanilla, self-trained, adversarially trained and robust GNN baselines (EvenNet, SoftMedianGDC).
Against PRBCD with epsilon=0.5, adversarially trained GPRGNN reaches 48.5% test accuracy, and GPR-GAE with vanilla GPRGNN improves on this by 15.7 percentage points.
GPR-GAE preserves clean accuracy and works as a plug-and-play defense module compatible with GNN classifiers.
Traditional OCR-then-text retrieval (BM25, DPR) adds computational overhead, introduces recognition errors, and misses crucial visual context.
Parsing-free visual retrievers (e.g. DSE, VisRAG) outperform text-based methods in visual-rich scenarios but struggle with semantic details in text-rich scenarios such as web-page retrieval.
Text-based methods model linguistic semantics but overlook layout and graphics, while purely visual methods preserve visual context but struggle with fine-grained language understanding.
Unveil's visual-textual dual-encoder model feeds the VLM the document image plus its OCR text (prompt ' What is shown in this image?') and uses the end-of-sequence token embedding as representation.
Hybrid models combining text-based and visual-based scores give intermediate results, can fall below text-based models alone in web-page retrieval, and cost inference from both models.
The Unveil visual-textual model consistently achieves the highest performance across all retrieval scenarios, surpassing text-based, visual-based and hybrid methods.

The visual-only student is trained with representation alignment, soft label distillation from the teacher's score distribution, and adaptive re-weighting that upweights documents with high teacher-student KL divergence, under Ltotal = sum w_i (L_align + L_soft).
The distilled visual-only Unveil exceeds text-based and visual-based baselines and approaches the teacher's performance while requiring no text input at inference.
Ablation shows removing adaptive re-weighting, representation alignment or soft-label distillation each degrades performance, with removing representation alignment causing significant degradation.
t-SNE of 200 ChartQA documents shows student representations become much more aligned with the teacher's after distillation and cosine similarity between them increases.
Teacher performance improves as input OCR text length grows from 0 to 3096, with a large jump from 0 to 512 and diminishing gains from 2048 to 3096, but longer text raises inference cost.
Human evaluation is still considered the gold standard for long-form generation where automated metrics work poorly, and increasingly also meta-evaluates LLM-judges.
