Current human evaluation procedures lack standardization and operationalization, limiting validity, robustness, comparability and reproducibility.

The authors define 20 binary reportable criteria covering task definition, annotation operationalization, annotator information, and data analysis and interpretation, developed over four iterative codebook rounds.
From 9.1k+ *CL papers (2023-2025), over 1,800 study long-form generation with human evaluation; 356 were sampled and 284 manually annotated in full.
Most papers report evaluated dimensions (98%), number of annotators (77%) and number of samples (85%), but other criteria are reported far less often (Fig 1).
Only about 50% of papers give justification for the evaluation dimensions or the task guidelines shown to annotators.
Payment information is reported in 29% of papers, IRB determination in 11%, statistical metrics in 9%, and none use power analysis for sample size.
Among papers with more than one annotator only 51% report inter-annotator agreement (46% overall).
Long-form generation papers rose from around 30% to 50% in 2025, but the proportion of all papers with human evaluation stayed around 20%.
Half of manually annotated papers use LLM-judges, and 20% of these use them for other dimensions without human evaluation.
Papers using both LLM-judges and human evaluation for the same dimensions rose from 4% in EMNLP'23 to 30% in EMNLP'24 and 12% in EMNLP'25, without evident reporting improvement.
Authors should report the core reportable criteria for reproducibility, which can be done succinctly in a short passage.
Because human evaluation increasingly serves as the standard for assessing LLM-judges, weak protocols introduce error downstream, demanding greater rigor and documentation.

Most existing LLM creativity metrics are tightly coupled to specific tasks, rely on curated answer sets, hand-crafted rubrics or human annotation, and are therefore subjective, resource-intensive and hard to scale.

Creativity requires both novelty (divergent thinking) and usefulness or appropriateness (convergent thinking); without convergent evaluation, diverse but incoherent outputs would be misleadingly perceived as creative.

Semantic entropy (SE) computed over semantic-class probabilities of n=10 sampled next-step continuations, clustered by bi-directional entailment, is used as a reference-free measure of divergent creativity, since in open-ended tasks probability spread across distinct ideas reflects exploration rather than error.
Existing multi-agent judges such as ChatEval append the full discussion history each turn, so token cost grows with each round, making them prohibitively expensive at benchmark scale.

The proposed judge uses Problem, Solution and Criterion agents that store insights as retrievable fragments in a vector database and retrieve only the k most relevant fragments per turn, with confidence-based stopping, cutting token usage by about 63% versus ChatEval.

The benchmark evaluates 300 problems per domain on MacGyver, HypoGen and BookMIA stepwise: at each step the model samples n=10 continuations to compute SE, then greedy decoding continues the solution, whose final result is scored by the convergent judge.

Step-level SE correlates strongly with the number of unique idea categories (TTCT flexibility), increases with sampling temperature, and is negatively correlated with average pairwise cosine similarity of candidates.
On 50 MacGyver problems SE reaches Cohen's kappa 0.56 with human judgments of divergent creativity, above cosine similarity (0.49), Self-BLEU (0.35), Distinct-1 (0.37) and Distinct-2 (0.34).

Solution-level SE (mean over steps) is positively rank-correlated with LLM-judged novelty of final solutions, where the novelty judge was validated against human rankings (Spearman 0.80 on 30 MacGyver solutions).

The retrieval-based judge reaches accuracy comparable to individual human annotators on MacGyver and BookMIA (50 solutions each), outperforms single-agent baselines and ChatEval, and cuts computational cost by over 60%.
Larger and more recent LLMs (e.g. GPT-4o, LLaMA 3.1 70B over GPT-3.5, LLaMA 3.1 8B) and reasoning models (R1-70B over Llama 3.3) score higher on convergent creativity.
SE remains largely stable or sometimes decreases as models become larger or more recent across LLaMA generations (8B to 405B) and Vicuna sizes (7B to 33B).
Spearman correlations between SE and convergent metrics are consistently weak across models and domains, so the two dimensions are empirically separable and possibly independently optimizable.
The absence of strong negative correlation between SE and task fulfilment supports that SE in open-ended generation captures distributional breadth rather than hallucination or incorrectness.
VLA models are typically assumed to receive English instructions, and their robustness to multilingual instructions has been largely unexplored.

LIBERO is translated into ten languages (English plus Chinese, French, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, Portuguese, Arabic, Thai, Vietnamese) via Google Translate, checked by humans and back translation, and used to evaluate OpenVLA-OFT and pi0.5.
Success rates of VLA models drop by 30-50% under non-English instructions compared with English.

Language deviation from English representations varies strongly across execution steps; certain steps are strongly language-dependent and dominate task failure while others are largely language-agnostic.

Gradients of the predicted action with respect to language versus visual tokens on English executions give a ratio r_t that locates language-sensitive steps, and high-r_t steps coincide with larger non-English deviations.

Averaging language shifts over all steps weakens correction where differences are largest, and indiscriminate alignment perturbs language-agnostic steps and propagates errors in closed-loop execution.

The method retrieves K nearest English reference representations by cosine similarity, triggers alignment only if a fraction >= tau of neighbors lie in the top-p% language-critical steps, and aligns using a similarity-weighted reference.

Gradient-guided step-wise alignment consistently improves multilingual success rates over the no-intervention baseline for both OpenVLA-OFT and pi0.5, without language-specific tuning, while EN-CoT gives limited and inconsistent gains.
Aligning only at language-critical steps outperforms aligning at random steps or at all steps under the same alignment mechanism.
Among 100 sampled multilingual failures, 53% first fail at the Navigate primitive and 18% at Grasp, indicating errors in instruction-to-visual grounding and target selection.
Fine-tuning OpenVLA-OFT with Chinese instructions on language-critical steps (50% of steps) beats random 50% step selection and recovers a large fraction of full fine-tuning gains with fewer updates.
Step-wise intervention introduces negligible additional inference latency.
Existing dLLM post-training randomly masks tokens and optimizes the masked positions, which does not match the actual inference dynamics of dLLMs and causes a training-inference mismatch.
Blockwise SFT and left-to-right masking impose externally defined decoding orders, although under bidirectional attention token dependencies emerge dynamically rather than following positional order.

In dLLMs (Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, MATH-500 queries, final layer) attention is sparse, with diagonal self/neighbour patterns and a few hub columns, and each token attends to largely the same context tokens across denoising steps.

Tokens that allocate more attention to already-unmasked tokens (higher valid attention score S) show greater probability stability, i.e. smaller probability drops during later denoising, showing a positive S-vs-delta-P correlation.
Choosing among masked tokens with probability above 0.9 the one with highest S beats the max-probability baseline on MATH-500 at lengths 128/256/512 (21.2 vs 16.8, 16.2 vs 13.8, 15.2 vs 13.0).

AGDO derives a denoising order by starting from prompt tokens as unmasked, repeatedly selecting the top-n tokens by valid attention score S and recomputing S, so tokens are denoised only after attention-supported context exists.
The influence score I_k of a token is the total final-layer attention it receives from other tokens, and high-I tokens act as attention hubs with disproportionate influence on generation.
AGDO-SFT masks only the tokens assigned to each denoising step along the attention-guided order and weights the cross-entropy loss by (1 + gamma*I_k).
AGDO-RL applies the attention-guided order within GRPO and adjusts the advantage as A' = A + sign(A)*delta*I, amplifying updates for attention-central tokens.
On Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, AGDO-SFT averages 36.0% versus 34.4% for blockwise SFT, with a 3.0% gain on Minerva.
AGDO-RL outperforms RL baselines, e.g. 18.3% on LiveBench versus 15.2% for diffu-GRPO, with more sustained and stable accuracy growth during training.
With gamma=0 (no influence weighting) AGDO-SFT still beats blockwise SFT by about 2% on MATH500, isolating the benefit of the attention-guided denoising order; gamma=100 gives the best result.
On LLaDA-8B-Instruct (GSM8K, MATH500) AGDO outperforms d1-LLaDA, wd1 and LLaDA1.5 and improves faster than Diff-GRPO.

Contrastive VLMs like CLIP struggle with compositional understanding (object relations, attribute-object binding, word order), partly due to single global-vector optimization and not exploiting compositional information in image-text pairs.
Hard-negative approaches are costly, noisy, bias models toward superficial patterns, and can induce oversensitivity, ranking semantically equivalent captions incorrectly.

MACCO masks compositional concepts in one modality and reconstructs them using the full features of the other (masked text plus full image predicts concept words; masked image plus full text predicts patch pixels), without constructing hard negatives.

A parameter-free global-to-local injection averages each local token with the global CLS feature, compensating for the causal text encoder's lack of future context and CLIP's weak local patch supervision.
The Masked-augmented Cross-Modal Alignment loss adds masked texts or images as soft negatives in the cross-modal contrastive objective.
The Masked-augmented Intra-Modal Regularization loss contrasts masked features with their full counterparts within each modality to prevent masked-feature collapse and stabilize training.
MACCO's total loss is L_MCA + l1*L_MIR + l2*L_MLM + l3*L_MIM, fine-tuned from CLIP ViT-B/32 on about 110k MSCOCO pairs, with predictors discarded at inference so the CLIP architecture is unchanged.

MACCO-CLIP achieves state-of-the-art results across ARO, SugarCrepe, VL-Checklist, VALSE and What's-up, gaining over CLIP 14.4% (ARO-Relation), 5.8% (ARO-Attribute), 21.9% (ARO-Order) and 8.3% average on SugarCrepe.

MACCO-CLIP beats CLIP-FT (+8.8% ARO-Relation, +26.9% ARO-Order) and CLIP-CAE (+4.1% SugarCrepe Relation, +4.8% VL-Checklist Relation), attributed to explicit modeling of entity-relation/attribute dependencies.
Adding MACCO to NegCLIP and CE-CLIP yields further gains, e.g., +3.1% and +1.9% on VL-Checklist Relation.
MACCO-CLIP loses only 1.5% zero-shot and 0.4% linear-probe average accuracy versus CLIP on 11 classification datasets while raising compositional average from 61.2 to 67.7.
In SentEval probing, CLIP-FT degrades on three tasks while MACCO-CLIP improves on all four, and it improves SICK-R over CLIP-FT and CLIP-CAE (+4.8% Pearson).
MACCO-CLIP caption embeddings are significantly more similar to relation and attribute phrase embeddings than those of CLIP and CLIP-FT.
On the Hard Positive benchmark MACCO-CLIP beats CLIP-FT on all subsets, with a 4.6% gain on the SWAP augmented accuracy.
Ablations show both text and image reconstruction losses help, each auxiliary loss helps alone, MCA and MIR combine best with masked modeling, and global-to-local injection improves results.
Multilingual retrievers are typically developed and evaluated with monolingual or cross-lingual queries, so mixed-language query behavior is largely untested in standard benchmarks.
LLM-generated word-level code-switching does not guarantee successful generation and requires a separate generation for each mixing ratio, making ratio-controlled study resource-intensive.

Language-mixed queries are represented as a convex combination (ratio lambda, then L2-normalized) of the two monolingual query-translation embeddings, giving precise ratio control without repeated LLM generation.

Experiments use BGE-M3 on mMARCO with 35 language pairs from 13 languages, a filtered set of 1,484 long queries, and three document settings (L1-only, L2-only, L1+L2), giving 105 groups scored by nDCG@10.

On EN-ZH, embedding mixing matches word-level mixing trends in all three document settings (no new interior peak on EN+ZH) and attains higher nDCG, since it avoids word-mixing noise from generation variability and tokenization/LID errors.
Optimal embedding-level mixing ratios beat the best monolingual endpoint in 88/105 groups (83.8%), with mean gain +0.70, range -0.34 to +2.92, and 66/105 reliably positive.
The largest gain is EN-AR on AR documents (+2.9203 at lambda*=50) and the most negative is EN-ZH on EN+ZH documents (-0.3359 at lambda*=10).
When English is absent from the index all groups have positive gain (average +0.95), whereas with English documents gains cluster near zero (mean -0.04) so pure English queries are best.

Adding English to ZH queries improves ZH-document retrieval (+1.72 at lambda*=50), but adding ZH to EN queries consistently worsens English-document retrieval, so English overrides document-query similarity.
For every one of the 13 non-English document languages, English yields the largest mixing gain among tested partner languages, by a large margin.
The authors hypothesize English acts as a universal anchor because web-corpus imbalance gives the English subspace the most robust representations.

Without English-in-documents effects (44 non-English settings), typological distance has a moderate negative correlation with gains (Spearman rho=-0.405); script, family and resource effects are weak.
Gain is negatively correlated with the better endpoint's score (rho=-0.607), driven by English-document settings (rho=-0.684), weak when English is excluded (rho=-0.117).
Patterns hold across model families and Qwen3 scales; scaling raises monolingual scores and shrinks gains but English remains the strongest partner and mixing does not help English retrieval.
For English-inclusive indices systems should default to pure English queries, while for non-English indices embedding mixing is an effective test-time augmentation to improve recall.
In FL with heterogeneous data, local models overfit their own distributions, and even transferable features can be distorted during aggregation, misaligning them with global objectives.

Regularization, normalization and correction methods align local updates with the global model but neglect generalization, while FedSAM and FedAlign improve local generalization but do not preserve coherent objectives during aggregation, letting generalization become distorted.

Features with higher gradient signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR) yield larger OSGR and contribute more to generalization (Proposition 2.1/Theorem 2.1 from Liu et al.), motivating GSNR-based approaches in domain generalization.
Directly tracking GSNR in FL is typically infeasible due to communication and computational bottlenecks and the distributed nature of gradient collection.

Conjecture 1: large weights indicate well-learned (strong) features and small weights indicate weaker features needing more training; weight size correlates positively with GSNR, so global weight magnitudes serve as a proxy for feature strength.

FedCONST applies client-consistent linear convex constraints derived from the global model's weight magnitudes, keeping well-learned features close to the global model during local updates and emphasizing under-learned ones.

Local updates are projected with P_w=(I-pp^T) to be orthogonal to the global parameter direction p=w^k/||w^k||, and centering is enforced; under these constraints, updates to larger-weight features are no larger than to smaller-weight ones (Theorem 3.1).

Because the constraints are linear, convex and shared across clients, the averaged global update also satisfies them, (w^k)^T Delta w^k = 0 and 1^T Delta w^k = 0 (Eqs 20-21), preserving the generalization effect after aggregation.
Features whose gradient updates are in the top 10% have larger weight magnitudes and larger GSNR than the bottom 10%, supporting the weight-as-feature-strength conjecture (Fig 5).
FedCONST achieves a higher GSNR on global-model features than vanilla FedAvg, indicating improved generalization (Sec 4.3.3).
FedCONST reduces gradient variance relative to FedAvg while increasing drift diversity, meaning local training is stabilized yet clients still make sufficiently large updates (Fig 3).
Constraints produce a more convex loss landscape (Table 2), steering away from saddle points, and increase client consistency (Fig 4).

On CIFAR-10 FedCONST surpasses existing algorithms in all settings and is commendable on CIFAR-100, consistently exceeding others in cross-device settings; applying the constraints to alignment or local-generalization algorithms also improves them (Table 1).
Gradient-alignment DG methods push gradients toward a dominant direction that is itself often driven by spurious features, inadvertently reinforcing undesired correlations.

Most DG studies overlook imbalanced parameter updates caused by differing convergence speed or generalization capacity, so a small subset of parameters dominates optimization (Fig 1 for SGD, Adam, SAM).
Dropout based on Gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio suppresses overly predictive parameters but does not adjust update magnitudes by each parameter's contribution to generalization.

The One-Step Generalization Ratio R(Z,n) measures the ratio of test-loss to training-loss reduction from one update; it depends on each parameter's gradient magnitude and gradient alignment across the data distribution, and higher OSGR indicates better generalization.
If each parameter j applies a preconditioner p_j, the OSGR can be rewritten accordingly (Corollary 3.2), making OSGR adjustable through preconditioning.
GENIE rests on the conjecture that uniformly distributed OSGR across parameters indicates better generalization.

GENIE preconditions gradients with a factor p_j based on GSNR (variance clipped by tanh), adds noise scaled by 1-tanh(1/sigma^2) to the gradient, and applies a Bernoulli random dropout mask after preconditioning.
A one-step PAC-Bayes analysis shows balanced OSGR from preconditioning corresponds to a tighter generalization bound (Theorem 3.6).
Under Theorems 3.8-3.10, GENIE's average gradient norm converges at O(T^-1/2), the standard non-convex SGD rate (Theorem 3.11, Remark 3.12).
On five DG datasets GENIE outperforms Adam by 5.69%, SGD by 6.36% and SAM by 4.37%, with notable gains on VLCS and TerraIncognita (Table 2).

GENIE outperforms other optimizers even at 5,000 iterations, with lower overhead than SGD and Adam and on average 1.3x faster training than SAM, which needs two sequential gradient computations per step (Table 3).
On PACS, full GENIE improves accuracy 4.9% over ERM with Adam, and preconditioning alone improves it 3.8% (Table 6).
On VLCS, GENIE achieves an average OSGR closer to 1 than prior optimizers during training (Fig 4), consistent with the generalization analysis.
Different retrievers require different optimal query formulation strategies, but most agentic RAG work assumes a uniform single search engine.
Contriever is trained on Wikipedia span pairs and prefers document-style queries, BM25 is sparse and prefers keyword queries, and Qwen3-Embedding performs better with question-like queries.
The query rewriter policy is trained with GRPO using nDCG@10 of the retrieved documents against the ground-truth passage as reward, chosen over recall to reward ranking the correct document highly.

On RAGBench, RL-trained rewriters improve every tested retriever, e.g., Contriever average nDCG@10 from 45.5 to 56.3 (direct), BM25 from 45.0 to 56.9 (explore), Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B from 61.5 to 64.1.
Zero-shot on BEIR, the learned rewriter raises Contriever's average from 28.84 to 34.98, whereas Gemini-2.5-Flash rewrites reduce performance even with a Contriever-specific prompt.
On FinAgentBench, the rewriter improves Contriever (6.43 to 7.39), BM25 (8.17 to 9.02), all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (6.69 to 7.17) and Qwen3-Embedding (9.10 to 10.81).
RE-MMD measures the distance between distributions of successful queries across retrievers, split into semantic (intent) drift and structural (formulation) drift.

Semantic RE-MMD is typically below 2.0 while structural RE-MMD is often above 20.0, largest between sparse (BM25) and dense (Contriever) retrievers, so transfer failures are stylistic rather than about information need.
Query formulation policies optimized for one retriever generally do not transfer reliably to others.

Three prompt levels were compared: general (five candidate strategies, retriever unknown), exploratory (retriever and its training described), and specific (human-prescribed strategy, e.g., hypothetical documents for Contriever, keywords for BM25).

For Contriever, the exploratory prompt starts strongest but collapses early (around step 200) onto a keyword strategy, while the specific prompt enforcing hypothetical documents reaches the best final performance; the general prompt improves slowly.

For BM25, exploratory prompts outperform specific ones and both far exceed general prompts; the rewriter infers keyword queries early, plausibly because BM25 is well documented in LLM pretraining data.

Explicit human expert guidance helps RL when the model lacks knowledge of a retriever's optimal strategy, whereas exploratory prompts suffice when pretraining already captures the retriever's behavior.
Increasing the rewriter to 14B breaks the performance plateaus of the 4B and 8B models, with larger models exploring more diversely (lower initial reward, better final policies).
Under exploratory prompts the 14B model discovers statement-style rewrites: 'Being white and Latino' reaches nDCG@10 0.965 versus 0.542 for the question-style 'Can someone be both white and Latino?'.

A two-turn branching rollout samples M first-turn actions and N second-turn completions each (e.g., 4x4), estimating first-turn value by Monte Carlo averaging and isolating the second-turn learning signal because the shared first-round reward cancels in the advantage.
The 4x4 branching strategy significantly outperforms independent 16x1 rollouts in training stability, preventing the collapse seen in the independent baseline.
Increasing the number of retrieval steps improves query formulation because the model can use documents from earlier steps to refine later queries.

It is unclear whether factual retrieval is continuous accumulation across layers or a discrete state at which the entity representation can elicit the attribute, and the transformations the entity undergoes are largely unmapped.

A minimal attribute computation path is a subset of layers applied to the entity representation that suffices for the model to produce the target attribute and in which no layer can be removed without hurting the computation.
The lock operation (copying a layer's entity output to all higher layers) identifies the earliest layer l_attr after which no further computation on the entity tokens is needed.

The isolate operation feeds the clean entity embedding only through candidate path layers and passes counterfactual activations through the remaining layers, so a layer is non-essential if the prediction survives its replacement.

An iterative greedy search extends a path prefix by skipping as many layers as possible while remaining valid, yielding a minimal path; relaxing the upper bound to the last layer yields alternative minimal paths.
On 2,000 CounterFact prompts, attribute computation completes in early-to-mid layers, with average l_attr of 4.61 (LLaMA 3.1 8B) and 7.97 (Qwen3 8B).
Almost all paths contain more than two layers (mean length 5.91 LLaMA, 7.97 Qwen), and 33.1% (LLaMA) and 78.6% (Qwen) skip at least one layer, so no single layer retrieves a fact.
Non-identical alternative functionally-equivalent paths exist in 80.1% (LLaMA) and 82.7% (Qwen) of cases.

Alternative paths are longer (mean 9.47 LLaMA, 10.47 Qwen), use bigger jumps (mean skip 6.46 and 10.4 layers) and end deeper (mean l_attr 13.93 and 18.06), while the primary path is the most compact route.

Combining a primary-path prefix with an alternative-path suffix gives a working distinct path for 35.4% of LLaMA prompts and 32.8% of Qwen prompts, showing layer roles are not one-to-one across paths.

Overwriting the l_attr representation with a counterfactual disrupts prediction in over 94% of cases, but injecting it alone into higher layers restores the attribute for only about 56% of LLaMA primary paths, so intermediate path layers are also needed.

Longer paths rely on inter-token transfer: 50.1% of LLaMA primary paths (avg length 7.4) and 80.6% of alternative paths need a propagating layer, versus shorter paths when not required; Qwen shows the same pattern.
Factual knowledge computation is distributed and redundant: no single layer or range is responsible for a given fact, and the same fact can be computed via multiple paths.

Because attribute computation needs multiple transformations of the entity representation, editing succeeds by intervening at a necessary transformation stage rather than where the knowledge is localized, which may explain the localization-editing mismatch.
LLMs in few-shot settings still underperform fully supervised small models such as fine-tuned BERT on NER and are slower at inference, and prior ICL-for-NER work mainly explored few-shot settings.

NER is cast as conditional generation with an XML-style tagging format (entity spans wrapped in typed tags) and k demonstrations, either randomly sampled and fixed, or retrieved per test instance with BM25.
On MIT-Movie, MIT-Restaurant, CoNLL2003 and WNUT2017, F1 improves consistently as the number of in-context demonstrations increases up to 500.

Retrieval-based ICL improves rapidly and plateaus around 100 examples (about 50 on CoNLL2003), while random sampling improves more gradually, and the gap between them narrows to comparable results at 500 shots.
In nearly all cases (except LLaMA3.1-70B on MIT-Restaurant), many-shot ICL matches or exceeds BERT-FT trained on the full training set using only hundreds of demonstrations and no parameter updates.
Many-shot ICL requires long prompts and repeated calls to large models at each prediction, which is costly at inference time.
Many-shot In-Context Annotation (ICA) uses about 100 human-labeled examples as fixed demonstrations to have an LLM annotate 2k unlabeled sentences, then trains a BERT-based NER model on the output.

ICA is refined by self-consistency (majority voting over three outputs), self-correction (a second prompting step), and Error-Aware Refinement (EAR, three correction prompts for common NER errors: spurious, missing and type errors), applied to low-confidence sentences.

On five low-resource CrossNER domains, ICA outperforms data augmentation baselines and SOTA low-resource NER methods by an average absolute F1 of about 10 points, with competitive results with far less human effort.
EAR consistently outperforms the other refinement variants across all domains, giving an average gain of 1.79 F1 over standard ICA.
Self-correction and EAR also help when applied directly to ICL-MS inference, but ICA still outperforms ICL-MS with EAR by 2.95 F1 while allowing efficient BERT deployment.
Annotating 0.5k to 5k sentences with ICA+EAR, BERT performance rises rapidly over the first 1.5k-2k sentences and plateaus after about 2.5k.
With 0 to 300 human-annotated seed examples, performance rises significantly up to about 75-100 and then flattens, so about 75-100 examples are enough for strong ICA.
Larger, more capable annotators give better downstream NER: GPT-4o is best, followed closely by DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen-72B, while Qwen-7B lags widely, especially on Literature.

Most LLM value evaluations are itemwise and behavioral, so they do not recover how a model organizes competing values as a whole; models that look similar itemwise may prioritize morals differently once trade-offs are unavoidable.

Humans (N=35) and 12 LLMs from four families sort the same 140-item, theory-grounded (Schwartz, Moral Foundations) moral Q-set into a nine-column forced distribution; for LLMs strict full rankings are elicited and deterministically mapped to Q-sort buckets.

By-person factor analysis (PCA plus Varimax) of the 35 human Q-sorts gives a stable three-factor solution: Empathic Protection (F1, 22 sorts), Civic Decency (F2, 8) and Liberty & Accountability (F3, 5).
Leave-one-out re-estimation gives very high factor stability (mean Spearman F1=0.997, F2=0.981, F3=0.950), so the structure is not driven by any single participant.

For each LLM and temperature, an LLM item geometry is built by PCA over replicate-by-item bucket scores (n=10 replicates); conditions with rank below k=3 are flagged degenerate and geometry metrics left undefined.
Structural alignment with the human geometry is quantified by Procrustes similarity (phi) and RSA-based Spearman correlation (rho) between item-item distance matrices.
Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-8B are fully stable (r_stab=rho_stab=1.000), Gemini-2.5-Pro is highly stable (0.997 at T=0), but GPT-5.1 is much less stable (r_stab=0.473, rho_stab=0.484 at T=0).

At T=0 DeepSeek-V3 has the highest Spearman rho (0.176, phi 0.371), GPT-5.1 the highest phi (0.372, rho 0.105), and Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro are weakly aligned (rho -0.012/-0.033); model recency gives limited guidance.
Raising temperature from 0 to 0.7 lowers DeepSeek-V3 alignment (phi 0.371 to 0.234) but raises DeepSeek-V3.1 (0.139 to 0.198) and GPT-3.5-Turbo (0.277 to 0.341).
Gemini-2.5-Pro is extremely stable yet weakly aligned while GPT-5.1 is less stable but more aligned, so reliability and validity are distinct properties.

Alignment is heterogeneous across Schwartz regions: within one LLM some regions preserve human local trade-offs while others show weak or negative correspondence, so a single scalar can mask local mismatch.
Across non-degenerate conditions rank-based and bucket-based results are strongly consistent (Spearman 0.855 for phi, 0.846 for rho), so results are not driven by rank-to-bucket post-processing.
The priority-profile baseline is weak (median rho_best=0.143, max 0.332) and tracks geometry scores only loosely, so the framework captures trade-off organization rather than average endorsement.

Multimodal CoT should be applied selectively: it is generally effective on reasoning tasks but can introduce side effects on perception tasks such as visual grounding, knowledge VQA and object counting.
CoT improves performance by 6.1%, 2.9% and 4.9% on mathematical, scientific and multi-image reasoning respectively, consistently across almost all models.
For logical and algorithmic reasoning, which rely more on visual information, larger models benefit from CoT while smaller models often show limited or negative gains.

Existing open-source multimodal reasoning models show only limited gains over their base models across diverse tasks, possibly because RLVR training concentrates on math at the expense of broader reasoning.
Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking shows substantial and consistent gains across reasoning tasks, with a 24.7% improvement in algorithmic reasoning.
A large proportion of CoT errors come from visual reasoning failures, with over 80% in logical reasoning tasks due to incorrect reasoning over visual information.
On probes (math probes 93.0% and logical probes 88.5% verified accurate), models score about 20% lower on visual than textual reasoning probes.
Original task performance correlates more strongly (higher Pearson r) with visual probe accuracy than textual probe accuracy, so visual reasoning is the key bottleneck of current MLLMs.
Reflection in multimodal CoT splits into visual reflection (reconsidering the visual input) and verbal reflection (reconsidering its own reasoning).
Verbal reflection rises and peaks mid-way through the CoT, while visual reflection steadily declines over time.
Despite visual reflection, models show limited ability to abstain from answering when critical visual information is missing, indicating shallow visual reflection.
During long CoT, models (e.g. Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking) allocate disproportionate attention to reasoning tokens while progressively neglecting visual tokens, which may constrain visual reflection.
Prior MEE methods adopt diverse task formulations and evaluation protocols on the M2E2 benchmark, hindering fair comparison, and no standardized evaluation scripts exist for multimedia events.
MEE evaluation suffers from inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions and overly relaxed evaluation settings, plus test data leakage.
Studies optimize on differing numbers of samples (e.g. 75k vs 100k SWiG images) by adding dev sets of external datasets as training data.
Most reported scores apply post-processing that uses M2E2 ground-truth annotations to adjust textual ED predictions, which does not reflect real-world conditions and is often not clearly specified.
Some studies use refined SWiG-to-M2E2 verb mappings (73 verbs instead of the original 67), so performance differences reflect data engineering rather than modeling.

Many works restrict test predictions to sentences or images with at least one event, reducing sentences from 6167 to 1086 and images from 1014 to 391, and event-coreference-based evaluation uses only 309 image-text pairs (192 sentences, 203 images).
Ignoring trigger offsets lets arguments match any same-type event in textual EAE and lets incorrect predictions count as correct at sentence level in multimedia ED.
Many-to-many IoU-based matching lets multiple predictions match one gold visual argument, rewarding recall-oriented models; the authors propose one-to-one bipartite matching.
Some works train on VOA images and captions that include test documents of M2E2, causing information leakage even without ground-truth annotations.
Oracle trigger refinement and verb refinement give up to +13.9 F1 (textual ED) and +7.0 F1 (visual ED), whereas adding dev sets gives at most +1.3 F1.
Restricting to event-containing samples raises ED F1 by up to +27.8 (textual) and +30.0 (visual) and EAE by up to +14.5, mainly via higher precision, and does not reflect real-world conditions.
Ignoring trigger attachment changes textual EAE by up to 6.4 F1, and many-to-many visual matching with overlapping detector categories can add up to +8.0 F1.

Evaluating only samples with multimedia events gives up to +21.2 F1 for threshold-based coreference methods, and gold image-text coreference gives the highest scores, overestimating real-world performance.
StrictEval is a more rigorous framework that removes these pitfalls and uses predicted rather than gold coreferences and full test sets.

Under StrictEval, reevaluated recent methods show large degradation, with multimedia ED and EAE dropping by up to 56.8 and 33.6 F1, because precision falls when neither subset selection nor gold coreference is used.
Cross-modal event coreference resolution remains the largest challenge in a realistic setting, and minor implementation choices can dominate reported gains.
Small open-source MLLMs suit web agents for cost and privacy but have weak planning ability and limited cross-website generalization.

Coarse high-level exploration tasks are misaligned with their trajectories (e.g., task requires over 4.5 stars but trajectory reaches 4 stars) and lack stricter constraints that only real exploration of a partially observable site can reveal.

PEEU has two stages: planning tree exploration (the model autonomously sets goals from a homepage and explores to build an exploration tree) and planning experience utilization (extract atomic experiences from before/after observations, then aggregate them into hindsight-aligned, more strictly constrained high-level tasks).
Retrieval-based prompting with the same experiences fails for small models (7B Atomic/Trajectory-Prompt 3.7% vs base 7.8%; 3B 0.0%), while PEEU-GRPO training reaches 19.9% (7B) and 11.1% (3B).
With 2k trajectories on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, PEEU-SFT reaches 30.6% overall on unseen websites versus 19.0% for Coarse-SFT and 21.7% for Atomic-SFT, and exceeds Qwen2.5-VL-32B (22.7%).
PEEU's gains hold across 3B and 7B models and 0.1k and 2k trajectories, e.g., 7B 0.1k PEEU-GRPO 19.9% vs Atomic-GRPO 10.0%.
The Task Decomposition Hierarchical Analysis Framework defines low, mid and high task levels and studies ID bottom-up, ID top-down and OOD multi-level generalization.
Models trained on low-level tasks reach 80.5% (3B) and 89.6% (7B) Step SR on low-level tests but only 9.1% and 18.8% on in-domain high-level tests.
Coverage of good in-domain multi-level generalization is 44.8% (3B) and 51.9% (7B) when trained on high-level tasks, versus 3.2% and 9.1% for low-level training.
Out-of-domain coverage is 33.8% (3B) and 37.8% (7B) for high-level training, versus 18.9% and 25.7% for low-level training.
Full softmax attention costs O(N^2) in computation and memory, limiting practical context length.

Sparse and linear attention (sliding window, Mamba) cut cost but have local windows or fixed-size states that constrain retrieval across distant positions, degrading tasks needing precise long-range recall.
Sparse attention patterns in LLMs are highly context-dependent, so selectively retrieving relevant information needs dynamic, context-adaptive attention.

MATCH splits the context into fixed-size chunks (length U), retrieves top-K chunks by bi-encoder (Sentence-BERT) dot product, reranks them with a cross-encoder, and keeps the top-k (K > k) to balance speed and precision.

MATCH unmasks retrieved token positions in the attention mask (alongside causal and sliding-window masks), so the sparse-attention KV cache stays constant-size and retrieved positions are fixed regardless of sequence length, making memory constant with context length.
During decoding, retrieved raw inputs are fed as auxiliary inputs and their KVs recomputed at each layer once per decoding chunk, then cached in a fixed-size temporary cache for reuse.
On MQAR, MATCH matches full attention and, at sequence length 512, stays near-perfect while other sparse baselines (StreamingLLM, Strided, Random) degrade toward random guessing.
On MAD in-context retrieval tasks, MATCH raises average performance for Hymba from 64.0 to 92.4 (U=2) and for SWA from 59.9 to 89.4, a 45-50% boost.

On LongBench, MATCH consistently improves overall average across sparsity levels and models, with up to +15.1 on synthetic tasks, and is mostly on par with or better than RAG using the same retrieved content.
On Needle-in-a-Haystack (8K-128K), MATCH outperforms the sparsified baselines Qwen3 and Phi-3 at all context lengths, especially at 32K-128K.

Replacing the retriever with random indices (Qwen3, 80% SWA, k=8) underperforms both MATCH (34.1 vs 37.0 avg) and the sparse baseline, so gains come from relevant retrieved context, not extra KV pairs.
With 50%-sparsified Qwen3 and k=8, MATCH reaches the highest LongBench average (43.4), beating StreamingLLM and FlexPrefill, with the lowest TTFT and decoding memory at 32K.
At 90K tokens MATCH has TTFT of 4.98s (68% below full attention's 15.88s, close to SWA's 4.62s) and 32% less memory than full attention (18.72 vs 27.67 GiB).
Prior work on logical fallacies in LLMs focuses on identifying or classifying fallacies; robustness of LLMs when passively targeted by fallacious persuasion is largely unexplored.
Debate frameworks such as LOGICOM use non-absolute, controversial topics, so they cannot distinguish a genuine logical failure from a shift between equally valid stances.
Every LoFa item is a question with a unique, scientifically verifiable answer, so a cognitive shift is measurable as a transition from a correct to an incorrect state.

LoFa adapts the Farm dataset (questions from Natural Questions, TruthfulQA and BoolQ, all derived from Wikipedia) into about 2000 structured MCQ/Boolean items, and uses 10 fallacy types merged from prior taxonomies into two categories: Distraction/Distortion and Flaws in Reasoning/Evidence.

Each item is tested in three steps: baseline knowledge check, false-claim resistance screening on the standalone false claim, and a fallacy-driven attack of up to three rounds with a cognitive check after each argument.

LFR@k is the share of valid instances (correct at Step 1 and not accepting the bare false claim at Step 2) that avoid an incorrect answer after the k-th fallacy attack, separating fallacy-induced failures from knowledge gaps and simple misinformation susceptibility.

LLMs resist Flaws in Reasoning/Evidence fallacies (Hasty Generalization, Slippery Slope, Circular Reasoning) better than Distraction/Distortion fallacies; Equivocation and Straw Man are most effective, and Llama-3.1-405B reaches LFR@3 of only 29.4% on Equivocation and 57.0% on Straw Man (Finding I, Table 4).
GPT-4 shows cognitive deference to fabricated authoritative cues, with LFR@3 of 39.2% on Appeal to Authority, likely a side effect of RLHF prioritizing context adherence.
Average LFR@3 for Llama-3.1 rises from 59.75% (8B) to 70.38% (70B) to 77.17% (405B), with diminishing returns for some fallacies such as Slippery Slope (75.38%, 87.04%, 88.07%) (Finding II).

A model family has a consistent pattern of strengths and weaknesses across fallacies at different scales, so scale acts as an amplifier on an architecture-determined profile rather than correcting its vulnerabilities (Finding III, Fig 6).

In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct failures, layers 0-19 are semantically unrelated to the answer, layers 20-25 collapse onto null tokens like 'None' or 'neither' (a cognitive void), and layers 25+ converge on the fallacious answer (Sec 6.1, Fig 7).
Chain-of-thought improves GPT-4's average LFR@3 by 7% to 13% for most fallacies (largest 13.16% for Straw Man) but decreases it by 1.87% for Appeal to Authority.
Most open-source VLAs decode actions from only the current observation and instruction (a Markovian assumption), discarding motion trends and object permanence under occlusion.
Naively extending context windows or using video transformers with dense spatio-temporal attention incurs prohibitive compute, quadratic scaling, large memory and high latency for real-time control.

MIRTH compresses history into fixed-length memory via a workspace hub (K exponential moving averages at different decay rates, mixed with motion-statistics) and a short-horizon hub (attention over the last w frames), fused by a per-patch sigmoid gate; token count stays fixed regardless of history length.

Prior VLAs map inputs directly to actions (no interpretability or planning) or use hand-crafted discrete action-language supervision, which is costly to annotate and suffers the many-to-one problem where diverse descriptions map to the same motion.

MIRTH inserts m learnable reasoning tokens between context and action tokens, trained with InfoNCE contrastive losses that pull their representation toward both the action representation and the context representation, without text supervision.
Scalar-wise quantization of continuous actions needs an autoregressive chain of tokens per action dimension, causing high decoding latency that limits control frequency.

MIRTH uses one action token per full action vector (shortening the action sequence by 1/NF) and decodes the whole trajectory in parallel with a two-layer projection head in a single forward pass, trained with an L1 loss.
MIRTH exceeds 98% on LIBERO spatial, goal and object suites and reaches 95.3% on LIBERO-Long (average 98.1%), versus OpenVLA-OFT's 94.5% on Long and 97.1% average.

On the LeRobot platform, MIRTH's advantage over baselines widens as task difficulty increases, especially on abstract-instruction reasoning tasks, while maintaining throughput comparable to or above lighter baselines such as OpenVLA.
On LIBERO-Long, removing the workspace hub drops success by 1.3%, removing the short-term hub by 0.9%, and removing both (single-frame) by 2.1%.
On LIBERO-Long, removing the MI loss reduces success by 0.8% and removing the reasoning tokens entirely by 1.4%.
Linear probes on MIRTH's features give much lower MAE than on OpenVLA for normalized state (0.11 vs 0.32) and velocity (0.04 vs 0.15), showing the hubs encode motion dynamics.
Randomly shuffling the order of history frames in the short-term hub drops LIBERO-Long success from 95.3% to 88.0%, showing the model exploits sequential structure.
t-SNE of reasoning embeddings shows clusters by task semantics (e.g., container-opening vs pick-and-place) without task-ID supervision.
On LeRobot failure episodes MIRTH recovers 12.1% of the time versus 8.7% without reasoning tokens and 5.2% for single-frame OpenVLA.

Data referencing errors (DREs) are failures to faithfully locate and cite information from the input; for tables they split into Incorrect Citation (wrong values, confused rows/columns, fabricated content) and Omitted Information (missing required rows/values).
Tables contain many similar rows and columns, which makes models prone to referencing the wrong data even when they parse the table structure correctly.
A Sonnet-3.7 LLM-as-a-Judge that sees the ground-truth answer and judges response segments split at reflection tokens like 'Wait' detects DREs with 92.67% accuracy on manual inspection.
DREs occur across models from 1.7B to 20B, across table formats (JSON, CSV, Markdown) and across tasks (QA, claim verification, table-to-text); e.g. Llama4-Scout has a 46.48% DRE rate on WTQ.
Reasoning models with self-reflection still show DRE rates of 5.71%-46.04% on WTQ, and prompting Qwen3-8B to cite accurately leaves a 12.50% DRE rate and does not improve accuracy.

Incorrect responses contain DREs far more often than overall (e.g. DRE-in-Incorrect 46.89% vs 14.04% DRE rate for Qwen3-8B on WTQ), yet many correct answers also contain DREs, so accuracy alone misses them.
Selecting sampled responses with minimal DREs using the critic beats the average accuracy of all samples, and majority voting on the critic-filtered subset beats majority voting alone.
Segment-level rejection sampling, resampling a segment until the critic accepts it (max 8 retries), improves accuracy by up to 11.96% without changing the generator.
DREs are largely avoidable rather than fundamental limitations, since a DRE-free response can often be obtained simply by resampling.
A lightweight Qwen3-4B-Instruct critic is trained with SFT warm-up followed by RLVR on Qwen3-8B responses from the WTQ training set.
Critic-4B reaches 78.16% overall F1 versus 69.51% for untrained Qwen3-4B-Instruct, generalizing to other datasets (TableBench, FinQA) and other models.
Rejection sampling with Critic-4B consistently raises accuracy and lowers DRE rate for larger generators, though less than the stronger Sonnet-3.7+gt critic.

Sparse and delayed rewards in long-horizon agent tasks cause trajectory neglect, where the agent loses focus on the task goal and interaction history at intermediate steps, producing low-quality actions.
Step-level methods such as GiGPO and EMPG optimize all steps indiscriminately and lack a mechanism to locate the outlier steps caused by trajectory neglect.

Shannon entropy of step-level action distributions conflates inherent state complexity with agent confidence, because a high-entropy step may simply reflect a complex state with many plausible actions.

Normalized entropy Hn is the z-score of a step's mean token entropy within the group of actions taken at the same anchor state across sampled trajectories, which decouples state complexity from model confidence.
Outlier steps are those whose Hn lies outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR] over the training batch, so outliers are located without a manual threshold.
On ALFWorld and WebShop test sets, outlier steps (by normalized entropy) cluster at negative step-level advantage while inliers have higher advantage.
Outlier steps have lower trajectory attribution scores than inliers, so the model's focus on the trajectory is significantly weaker at outliers.

The trajectory-aware reward is the KL divergence between the policy's action distribution under the full prompt and under a trajectory-blind prompt with goal and history masked out; higher values mean the action depends more on the trajectory.

The trajectory-independent penalty is the KL divergence between the policy and the reference policy on the masked prompt, guarding against reward hacking and mode collapse when raising the trajectory-aware reward.

STAPO adds a selective term, gated by the outlier mask, of alpha times the trajectory-aware reward minus gamma times the trajectory-independent penalty to a GiGPO-style two-level (episode and step) advantage group-based RL objective.
STAPO outperforms all baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, reaching 96.9% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and raising WebShop success from 65.0% (GiGPO) to 69.0% with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.
Localizing outliers with normalized entropy beats raw Shannon entropy in the ablation (ALFWorld 92.2 vs 89.6, WebShop 69.0 vs 67.2).
Masking both goal and history for the reward beats masking only history or only goal, and history-only beats goal-only, so history is more critical than goal.
Applying the penalty selectively at outlier steps beats a standard global KL penalty, and raising the global KL coefficient degrades ALFWorld from 88.3% to 84.6%.
Compared to GiGPO, STAPO yields trajectories with a significantly lower proportion of outlier steps, and performance is negatively correlated with outlier proportion.
Training Llama3.1-8B-Instruct on WebShop gives GiGPO a flat zero success rate because no sparse outcome reward is found, while STAPO's trajectory-aware reward still provides a learning signal.
Preprocessing-based debiasing, which removes or alters stereotypical content in training data, is widely used because it is simple and imposes no inference-time cost.

Debiased Wikipedia corpora target six demographic groups across gender, race and religion, used for pre- and post-training of TinyBERT and GPT-2 under three strategies (removing stereotypical sentences, removing group mentions, swapping group references) at 100% and 5% data scale (12 settings), evaluated with StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs.
Stereotype scores for the targeted group typically decrease toward 50 relative to the base model for both TinyBERT and GPT-2 with broadly stable language modeling score (Sec 4).
Using only 5% of Wikipedia, pre- and post-training still consistently reduce stereotype scores for targeted groups (Sec 4, App A).
Stereotype scores for non-target groups, including across categories, sometimes move away from 50, i.e. stereotyping or counter-stereotyping increases (Sec 5).
Debiasing for females reduces stereotypes toward males, whereas debiasing for males increases stereotypes toward females (Fig 1a, Fig 2a-b).
Spillovers depend on the debiasing method, complicating a simple explanation by changes in the distribution of stereotypical training examples.

Side effects occur across three preprocessing strategies, pre- and post-training, reduced data scale, and encoder and decoder architectures, and a larger decoder-only model shows the same phenomenon on one post-training slice (Sec 7).
Standard evaluation benchmarks frequently fail to surface these side effects.
Attention-rollout patterns of mitigated models stay highly consistent with base models, with maximum distances PD 0.0061, SD 0.3029, JSD 0.0925 and AS 0.2235 (Sec 6, Fig 5).

Because side-effect cases (e.g. GPT-2 DG-female lowering stereotypes for Christians but raising them for Muslims) show tiny rollout shifts, side effects are not well explained by changes in semantic information routing as captured by attention rollout.
Data-level debiasing used in isolation is unreliable and unsafe since interventions helping the target group can unpredictably harm others; side-effect-aware diagnostics should be reported.

Prior work on LLM context sensitivity (knowledge conflicts, persuasive framing, pragmatic phenomena) lacks a systematic understanding of how form, tone and other aspects of an expression of belief (EoB) affect context integration.

The paper proposes a typology of 19 EoB types over four linguistically motivated dimensions: form, evidentiality, epistemic stance and tone, each varying how content is expressed while holding semantic meaning constant.

EoBench contains 65,778 EoBs built from 3,462 PopQA-derived semantic tuples (unique-answer facts, 15 relations) each paired with a sampled conflicting object and expressed in each of the 19 EoB types.
18 LLMs from Llama3, Qwen3 and Gemma3 are evaluated, spanning 1B-30B parameters and base vs instruction-tuned variants.
Context-following rate (CFR) is the fraction of valid responses that follow the context rather than prior memory, CFR = #C / (#C + #M), estimating P(Y=C | Y in {C,M}).
Averaged over models, child-directed, imperative, formal, appeal-to-authority, supposition and emotional EoBs are ranked significantly more context-following than a random baseline.
Averaged over models, counterfactual, belief-report, weak-epistemic-stance and interrogative EoBs are ranked significantly less context-following than a random baseline.

Base models are generally as or more susceptible to contradictory context than instruction-tuned counterparts across most EoB dimensions; Qwen3-8B is an exception, with its instruct variant agreeing with in-context belief 18.1% more.
For Llama3 and Gemma3, CFR tends to decrease as model size increases (clearly for Gemma3 from 1B to 30B), while Qwen3 instruct models stay relatively stable with high CFR.
Llama3 models have relatively low CFR compared with similarly sized Gemma3 and Qwen3 models, so model family is an important factor in agreeability to context.
The disparity in CFR between EoB dimensions tends to increase with model size for Gemma3, Qwen3 Instruct and (from 3B to 8B) Llama3 Instruct.

Remote-sensing agents built on general-purpose LLMs are domain-agnostic, so they struggle with concepts like NDVI, BSI or land-surface temperature, producing brittle tool-use trajectories with cascading errors such as premature termination or wrong tool invocation.
Expert-authored workflow templates are labor-intensive to build and maintain and act as external references rather than letting agents internalize corrections from execution failures.
Without domain knowledge, reflecting agents often misdiagnose failures and fail to turn errors into reusable experience.
The expert-curated knowledge base has a three-level hierarchy of 3 geoscience domains, 12 sub-domains and 64 atomic analytical tasks, each encoded as a Task Card (title, definition, suggestion).

Stream A retrieves the top-1 Task Card by combining sentence-embedding cosine similarity with lexical bonuses for task title, domain keywords and card content (alpha=0.2, beta=0.08, gamma=0.1, threshold 0.2), compensating for geoscience terms underrepresented in embeddings.

A label-free symbolic critic flags failed trajectories using heuristic rules: missing or malformed answer tags, empty responses, invalid option letters, refusal or incompleteness signals, and hedging language indicating guessing.

Reflections distilled from failed tool-use traces are stored per instance and the most recent one is retrieved by instance-indexed lookup in the next round, giving precise negative constraints and historical fixes.
On EarthBench, RSMeM consistently improves Any-Order, In-Order, Exact-Match and Wise-Score tool-use metrics across backbones, including DeepSeek-V3.2, Kimi-K2 and Qwen3-8B.
RSMeM raises DeepSeek-V3.2 accuracy by 6.07 points (to 57.89%) while token overhead rises only from 6.23% to 6.97%.

HKG mainly improves planning (on DeepSeek-V3.2, AO 77.27%->79.50%, IO 55.02%->56.51%), while FAR mainly improves trajectory robustness (Wise-Score 0.0408->0.0763 on Qwen3-8B); the full system peaks at 42.11% on Qwen3-8B and 57.89% on DeepSeek-V3.2.
Across evolution stages on DeepSeek-V3.2, EM rises from 25.85% to 27.01% and Experience Density from 55.72 to 57.69, indicating distillation into more concentrated corrective knowledge.
RSMeM outperforms flat embedding retrieval (+16.33 pp accuracy over Simple RAG) and the Reflexion reflection-only baseline across four backbones.

In a Landsat thermal case, treating brightness temperature BT10 as land-surface temperature derailed downstream steps; refinement distilled a semantic constraint (LST must be emissivity-aware) and a procedural constraint requiring a complete consistent pipeline.

Embodied multi-agent credit assignment is exacerbated by partial noisy egocentric multimodal observations with sparse, delayed rewards, and by open systems where agents enter or leave mid-task, violating fixed-agent-set assumptions.

Credit assignment methods like QMIX and COMA already degrade under insufficient feedback, and prior LLM-based credit assignment relies on simplified environments, handcrafted rules and strong assumptions.

MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment as rank aggregation: each agent's credit is a latent contribution score inferred from pairwise comparisons of which agent contributes more, replacing absolute with relative estimation.

An LMM, prompted as a referee with task context, agent-image mapping, comparative reasoning and JSON output, compares egocentric observations of active-agent pairs in both orders (to mitigate position bias), skipping when fewer than 2 agents are active.
The comparison matrix is aggregated with a Bradley-Terry model by MLE into per-agent contribution scores, which handles noise and yields cardinal values for smooth rewards.

Scores are softmax-normalized into a potential (zero at terminal states) and used for potential-based reward shaping with weight rho, preserving policy invariance while the scores evolve during training.

If the comparison graph is connected, with probability at least 1-n^-2 the MLE error to the latent preference is bounded by C0*sqrt(n log n / K)/sqrt(n) with K comparisons, so more comparisons filter out LMM noise.
If the LMM's latent preference equals true Shapley values, MARS-RA scores are consistent estimators of them up to a translation constant, an idealized interpretive lens rather than a practical claim.

MARS-Bench in ManiSkill3 has three tasks (Pass Gate, Herd Sheep, Collect Ball) with 2-4 agents, egocentric pixel observations, sparse rewards, and battery depletion that removes and later respawns agents, creating open agent counts.
All baselines (MAPPO, QMIX, COMA, SQDDPG, SAMA, V-GEPF) stay below 50% success on MARS-Bench while MARS-RA keeps success above 47% on all three tasks and exceeds 70% on Herd Sheep.
LMM pairwise judgments are consistent, with a 3-cycle rate of 8.95% versus 25.00% for random and held-out 3-way NLL of 0.41 versus 1.10 for random.
The LMM Score variant, which has the LMM directly output contribution scores, shows oscillation and weaker performance than rank aggregation, even though LMM spatio-temporal inference helps.
Performance rises with LMM comparison accuracy (Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1 above 70%; Qwen3-VL 2B/4B/8B above 43%) and number of queries, with gains from more queries larger for lower-accuracy LMMs.
MARS-RA is comparable to SAMA on five Overcooked tasks and remains effective on 10-agent Pistonball, suggesting benefit beyond small teams and MARS-Bench.

Human translators use fast intuitive processing (System 1) for familiar content and slow deliberate reasoning (System 2) at Rich Points such as ambiguous terminology, complex syntax or cultural disparities, whereas MT systems translate all inputs uniformly.

SFT-trained LLM translators operate purely in System 1 and struggle with Rich Points and out-of-domain data, while large reasoning models and CoT prompting apply the same long reasoning pattern regardless of input difficulty.

Applying RL directly to a base model leads reasoning traces to collapse to shallow patterns of at most 100 tokens regardless of KL setting, with the top three templates accounting for about 73% of traces on Zh-En.
RL after CoT SFT produces longer reasoning but cannot control when it is needed, giving verbose, redundant traces even for simple inputs.

General-CoT performs poorly in-domain because its reasoning lacks domain grounding, defaulting to generic translations, while adding explicit domain reasoning (Domain-CoT) largely restores in-domain quality (e.g. 56.53 to 62.65 on Hard samples), though it still applies the same strategy regardless of difficulty.

TwT's cold-start builds ~7k difficulty-adaptive traces: DeepSeek-R1 generates domain-aware CoT, GPT-4o rates difficulty via Rich Points (sentence complexity, vocabulary rarity, grammatical divergence, contextual nuance) and rewrites Easy inputs into concise System 1 checks and Hard inputs into full System 2 deliberation, followed by SFT.
The RL stage uses GRPO with a hybrid reward combining BLEU and COMET translation quality with a repetition penalty to optimize adaptive reasoning behavior.

Evaluated on 15 benchmarks, TwT-7B and TwT-14B outperform much larger SOTA reasoning models in translation quality while reducing token usage by 32-60% (32% vs OpenAI-o3-mini, 60% vs Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking); in-domain TwT-14B averages 66.62 vs DeepSeek-R1 65.40 and GPT-5 66.05.

TwT-7B averages 66.25 on five OOD test sets versus 63.58 for SFT-Parallel-7B, and TwT-Gemma-2-9B-IT trained on 27K examples beats Tower-Plus-9B trained on 286K by +8.19 across seen and 59 unseen languages.
On Easy inputs TwT cuts token usage by 33% while gaining +6.4 quality over General-CoT, and on Hard inputs it gains +6.7 quality points.

Removing adaptive CoT raises reasoning length from 278 to 748 tokens with comparable quality, removing the SFT stage causes degradation and length collapse to 62 tokens, and only the full pipeline reaches the best score (64.77); removing the repetition penalty gives only a slight drop.
TwT resolves over 94% of the redundant reasoning steps found in the SFT-with-RL baseline, including 97.2% of Low-Density Long Descriptions and 87.3% of Over-Segmentation issues.
TwT yields consistent improvements across three backbones (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B).
Logit- and sampling-based uncertainty metrics focus on final output distributions, capture mainly aleatoric ambiguity, and can give high confidence while internal reasoning is unstable.

Existing mechanistic UQ methods (SAPLMA, Lookback Lens, DoLa, ICR Probe) merge memory and context signals into unified representations, obscuring conflicts between parametric memory and contextual cues that signal failure.
FFNs act as key-value memories for parametric knowledge while multi-head self-attention routes contextual information.

DUD runs a clean pass, a corrupted pass (Gaussian noise added to input embeddings, Total Effect TE = mean drop in token probability), and patch runs that restore only the Attention or only the FFN output at each layer.
Each module's layer-wise restoration score (probability recovered divided by TE) forms a 2L-dimensional dynamic profile used as the feature vector of the DUD-Probe.
Across datasets, restoration scores in early layers (0-5) fluctuate strongly between correct and incorrect predictions for both Attention and FFN, indicating encoding-phase routing instability.
In late layers (20-28) FFN restoration scores collapse while Attention stays stable, marking a parametric-memory failure that indicates uncertainty.
Context-rich HaluEval shows larger early-layer instability, whereas knowledge-intensive HotpotQA shows larger late-layer FFN shifts.
On LLaMA3.1-8B, individual layers discriminate correct from incorrect outputs, with best FFN layer 24 (AUROC 0.767) and best Attention layer 20 (0.745).
On SQuAD (layer 24), error rate rises from 16.8% in the robust quadrant (both modules within bounds) to 72.0% in the dual-deviant quadrant.
Logit confidence fails to track mechanistic risk: stubborn errors stay confident in stable states while correct answers in deviant states have low confidence.

The DUD-Probe achieves state-of-the-art AUROC over three LLMs and four datasets, e.g. +17.4% over Semantic Entropy on LLaMA-3.1 HaluEval and +5.0% over the aggregated ICR Probe on Qwen2.5, with AUROC 0.949 on LLaMA-3.1 HaluEval.
DUD-Probe degrades under 5% out-of-distribution versus 15-20% for baselines, e.g. TriviaQA->SQuAD 0.868 vs ICR 0.613 and TriviaQA->HaluEval 0.930.
On Llama-3.1-8B, Attn Only and FFN Only probes beat random, but the full dual-stream probe is best on all datasets (e.g. HaluEval 0.9487 vs 0.9144 and 0.8968).
Removing early, middle or deep layer groups each lowers AUROC (w/o early layers drops HaluEval 0.95 -> 0.85), so uncertainty signals are distributed across depth.
DUD gives a low score (0.08) to a confident wrong answer (logit confidence 0.96) and a high score (0.72) to a hesitant correct one (logit confidence 0.35).
LLMs strongly prefer generating certain numerical tokens, which biases verbalized confidence estimates.

Vanilla verbalization yields very few unique confidence values; Qwen3-32B predicts only eight on SST-2 with over half equal to 95%, and 45-93% of confidences fall in the five most common values across four datasets.
Sparse confidences leave little choice of decision threshold: reaching at least 98% accuracy on SST-2 requires rejecting 39.7% of predictions versus 23.6% for 97.9% accuracy.
With sparse confidences the correct way to compute AUARC is stepwise interpolation; linear (trapezoidal) interpolation wrongly assumes gradual change between thresholds and inflates scores.
Verbalization and sampling approaches score 0.7-4.5 AUARC points lower under stepwise than linear interpolation, while continuous token logprobs are unaffected.
Consistency sampling ranks first under linear interpolation but last under stepwise interpolation, a 12.5-point absolute decrease.
Verbalization logprobs computes confidence as the expected value over verbalized digits weighted by their token probabilities, turning sparse verbalized values into continuous estimates.
Verbalization logprobs uses at least 630 unique values (up to 2,227 on ESCI), an 80x-200x resolution increase, and cuts top-5 concentration from 92% to 1%.
With verbalization logprobs, 98% accuracy requires rejecting only 28.1% of examples instead of 39.7%, salvaging 11.6% of data.
Verbalization logprobs improves on vanilla verbalization by +2.3 AUARC and +0.9 AUROC and on token logprobs by +1.3 AUARC and +4.7 AUROC at no added computational cost.
Verbalization logprobs matches verbalization sampling, the strongest baseline, in AUARC (0.736 vs 0.734) at 1.7x cost instead of 6.8x because it needs one inference call instead of four.
Long retrieved contexts increase latency and cost linearly with document count and include irrelevant content that distracts LLMs and triggers positional biases like lost-in-the-middle.
Query-focused compression matching one query to individual documents or sentences cannot capture inter-document dependencies and implicit intermediate clues in multi-hop QA, causing information loss.
On MuSiQue sub-QA data, LLMs can judge whether evidence suffices; F1 is 70.51 (Llama-3.1-8B), 84.27 (Mistral-7B), 73.12 (GPT-3.5-Turbo) and 83.57 (GPT-4o).
In the Full-evidence setting answerability accuracy declines as hops increase (Mistral-7B 92% at 2-hop to 78.5% at 4-hop), while under Partial evidence it improves with hop length.
LLMs generate related follow-up questions for missing information (GPT-4o relatedness 90.6%, BLEU 0.50), but quality declines with hop count.

Because misjudging unanswerable as answerable stops early and the reverse causes noisy extra iterations, with Full-setting accuracy degrading, IterCOMP uses answerability as a stopping signal with a bounded iteration cap (max 5).

IterCOMP splits documents into sentence-level evidence segments, filters relevant ones, has an LLM judge answerability, and if insufficient generates a targeted follow-up question to pull in new evidence, accumulating a compact reasoning-oriented prompt.

Relevance combines bge-m3 semantic similarity and lexical weighted-overlap similarity (lambda=0.6), and segments above the k-th score percentile are kept (k=90 for MuSiQue/HotpotQA, 85 for 2Wiki), applied at every reasoning step.

Training-free IterCOMP achieves the best EM and F1 on MuSiQue, 2Wiki and HotpotQA with a LLaMA-3-8B reader, e.g. MuSiQue F1 19.92 -> 27.36 (7x shorter input) and HotpotQA 43.63 -> 51.78 over raw documents.
On MuSiQue the average iterations rise to 3.08 for 4-hop questions and compressed prompt length grows from 228 to 403 tokens from 2-hop to 4-hop, so depth and evidence size adapt to complexity.

In ablations removing Iterative Refinement causes the largest drop, removing Answerability Judgment cuts F1 to 23.63 and gives less compact prompts, and combining semantic and lexical similarity beats either alone.
On MuSiQue F1 rises with k to a peak of 27.36 at k=90 then drops at k=95 because too strict a cutoff discards needed evidence; at k>=90 prompts are shorter than Oracle's.
On 500 MuSiQue instances, compression cuts reader-LLM cost by 75.5%-79.4% and speeds up inference across API models.
Fairness failures in generative models persist not primarily because of missing mitigations but because current evaluation practices prevent cumulative, decision-relevant evidence.

Modern generative systems still reproduce representational and stereotyping harms despite widespread mitigations (data filtering/balancing, regularization, prompting, RLHF, post-processing), and fairness methods are fragile, non-generalizable and often traded off against performance.

Fairness results depend on prompt families, paraphrases, decoding, seeds and post-processing; e.g. small prompt variations ('a person' vs 'one person') shift demographic distributions in SDXL and DALL-E 3, so two papers can both be correct yet incomparable.

Safety layers (refusals, deflections, moderation) shape who obtains information or content, and refusal rates and styles differ across gender, nationality, religion and sexual orientation, so disparities arise even when the base model is unchanged.
Many audits evaluate generated content only and silently discard refusals, hiding unequal access and yielding overly optimistic fairness assessments or harm shifting.

Generative models infer protected attributes via proxies (names, hobbies, visual cues), alter tone under identity swaps and have stochastic variability, so counterfactual symmetry assumptions rarely hold.
Fairness conclusions depend on metric choice and labeling pipelines; common representation and quality metrics are embedding-dependent and can change model rankings with fixed generators.

Because prompt suites, decoding settings, scoring and refusal handling differ or are under-reported, fairness results cannot be reliably compared across papers or over time, and protocol choice allows cherry-picking and harm shifting.

In an audit of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (3,200 generations over 4 intersectional slices, 4 prompt families, 5 paraphrases, 4 occupations, 2 decoding regimes), aggregate disparities are at or below the 5% flag line (max six points on title mention), yet worst-slice stereotype-keyword rate exceeds 5% on every slice under F2 and on none under F4.

Fairness Cards are a minimal reporting artifact disclosing prompt families, counterfactual protocols, metrics and decision rules, and refusal handling, enabling reproducibility, comparability and accountability.

Improved data, training or governance, and alignment/safety work alone cannot substitute for standardized evaluation: alignment optimizes average preference while fairness is distributional, so worst-slice gaps can widen and guardrails can amplify access disparities.

The paper recommends mandating Fairness Cards, treating refusals and deflections as first-class fairness outcomes, requiring robustness and uncertainty reporting, standardizing the evaluation surface, and embedding fairness regression tests in governance and post-release monitoring.
The self-attention mechanism is particularly sensitive to quantization errors, and error propagation is highly pronounced in attention layers of quantized models.
Unlike a linear layer whose Jacobian is a fixed weight matrix, the softmax Jacobian J_S(z) is dense and strictly state-dependent, so error amplification varies with the input.

When attention concentrates on a single token the Jacobian norm approaches zero (saturated, safe), while attention spread over two or more tokens lies in sensitive regions where quantization errors are amplified.
The quantization-induced error in attention probabilities can be bounded by constraining the spectral norm of the softmax Jacobian.
Near a local optimum, ||J_S||_2 <= sqrt(Tr(logit Hessian)/lambda_min), so regularizing the trace of the logit Hessian bounds the Jacobian and quantization error.
Minimizing expected loss under zero-mean isotropic Gaussian logit perturbation N(0, sigma^2 I) matches Hessian-trace regularization with strength lambda = sigma^2/2.
For p = softmax(z), ||J_S||_F^2 = ||p||_2^2 - 2||p||_3^3 + ||p||_2^4, computable with element-wise operations and negligible forward overhead.

Jacobian-guided noise injection sets row-wise noise std sigma_i = alpha * sqrt(E[||J_S||_F^2]), concentrating regularization on sensitive positions, updated every T steps, clamped, and disabled at inference.
Jacobian-guided noise injection improves quantized performance consistently for Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B under AWQ, GPTQ and SpinQuant, without significantly degrading full-precision accuracy.
On SigLIP at W4A4, noise injection recovers up to +9% accuracy with ERQ and up to +37% with RepQViT, with gains growing as bit-width decreases.
Noise injection improves over the QAT baseline for SigLIP, so it is usable with existing QAT pipelines.
In SigLIP W4A4 QAT, alpha in [0.5, 1.0] works best (alpha = 0.5 gives 31.37% vs 30.31% baseline) and performance drops to 27.69% at alpha = 50.
Graph federated learning faces pronounced structural heterogeneity because clients hold structurally diverse graphs, and federated learning may even underperform local training.

Existing personalized federated graph learning methods are confined to Euclidean space, assume uniform flat geometry, and need parameter disentanglement, client similarity estimation or auxiliary modules with significant computational overhead.

Client graphs predominantly have negative Forman-Ricci curvature (hyperbolic structure), and curvature values vary substantially across clients, indicating geometric heterogeneity beyond statistical differences.

Theorem 4.1: if client graphs have different average Ricci curvatures, the maximum minimal embedding distortion is at least (c_d/2) max|R_i - R_j|, so no single Lorentz scale K gives low distortion for all clients.

Theorem 4.3: the space-like direction is independent of client identity, I(u;C)=0, while the time-like coordinate x_t has positive mutual information with client identity if its distributions differ across K.

The Lorentz model's time-space decomposition supports parameter decoupling, its linear-algebraic isometries keep aggregated parameters on the manifold, and its exponential map gives closed-form curvature-aware gradients.

FlatLand assigns each client a learnable Lorentz scale K_c (sigmoid reparameterized), initialized from its average Forman-Ricci curvature, and embeds the client's data in that space via the exponential map.

Each Lorentz linear layer's matrix is split into a time-like column m (personalized, kept local with K_c) and a space-like block M (shared); only M is uploaded and averaged by the server as in FedAvg.
Proposition 6.1: applying the aggregated shared matrix still maps any vector in L^n_K to L^m_K with the same Lorentz scale, so representations remain valid hyperbolic points after aggregation.
Under standard FedAvg, FlatLand keeps the O(1/T) convergence rate and adds only minimal overhead such as an O(1) exponential map and curvature estimation.

FlatLand achieves the best or competitive accuracy in most settings, with clear gains on CiteSeer, ogbn-arxiv and Minesweeper (e.g. CiteSeer 10 clients 73.90 vs 72.35 for FED-PUB; Cora 20 clients 82.49).
Reducing embedding dimension from 64 to 4 hurts hyperbolic methods much less than Euclidean ones, and FlatLand's advantage over baselines grows as dimensionality shrinks.
On Cora with 50 clients and only 10% participation, FlatLand achieves 81.82% accuracy while FedAvg reaches only 18.14%.
Fixing K=1 for all clients (w/o TS) performs worse than learning client-specific Lorentz scale parameters, which lets full FlatLand surpass the Local (L) baseline.
Applying the decoupling in Euclidean space (FlatLand (E)) is clearly worse than in Lorentz space, e.g. Cora 20 clients 76.23 vs 82.49 and CiteSeer 20 clients 66.29 vs 72.24.
Diffusion language models offer faster parallel decoding than autoregressive LLMs but have lower generation quality, e.g. 10-32% worse perplexity than AR baselines.

LLM teachers give peaked distributions (near 100% top-1 probability) while DLMs give flatter ones (about 60% at 50% masking), and top-1 token overlap is only about 60%, so logit-level KD from an LLM is ineffective.
DLM teachers' generation quality is far below AR models, so logit-level KD gives marginal gains at higher training cost and sequence-level KD is of limited effectiveness.
Conventional logit- and sequence-level KD, from LLM or DLM teachers, give only marginal gains or degrade over the DLM SFT baseline (e.g. Dolly 15.11 with LLM logit KD vs 18.77 SFT at 8 steps).
SelFusion runs two forward passes in one model: a hard mode with the original random masking and an easy mode with a lower masking ratio that exposes more context.
The easy mode assigns higher probability to ground-truth tokens than the hard mode, with the gap growing from about 6% to about 10% over training, and keeps a distribution close to the student's.
Despite more context the easy mode is not always more accurate and can be overconfident on incorrect tokens; hard-to-easy distillation beats easy-to-hard on several benchmarks.

Per token, the distillation direction follows correctness and confidence: if both correct the higher-probability mode teaches, if both wrong the one with higher ground-truth probability teaches, otherwise the correct mode teaches.
RMSNorm calibration cuts overconfidence mostly on wrong predictions (about 40% to 10% top-1 probability when both modes are wrong, versus 90% to 60% when both are right).
Removing either unidirectional direction or RMSNorm consistently degrades performance, and neither unidirectional variant matches bidirectional KD.
SelFusion beats the strongest baseline (LLM-to-DLM sequence-level KD) by 2-4 points (about 16% relative) and DLM SFT by 1.5-3 points across five benchmarks.
SelFusion exceeds the LLM teacher on multiple benchmarks, e.g. 12.87 vs 11.04 on Self-inst, 17.08 vs 14.95 on Vicuna, 23.21->27.07 on Sinst.

SelFusion needs about 2x per-iteration compute of SFT but removes teacher training, cutting total training cost roughly 2x versus KD with a separately trained teacher, with only 1,280 extra parameters.
