Standard RL such as PPO and GRPO receives only terminal success/failure feedback per episode, about O(1) bits regardless of trajectory length, causing high-variance gradients and sample-inefficient learning on long-horizon tasks.
Appending reflections within an ongoing trajectory induces semantic drift as context accumulates, and reflections conditioned on frozen parameters or injected prompts can disrupt native thinking.
SRPO has the model analyze a completed trajectory with its outcome and synthesize errors into a compact reflection patch.
SRPO prepends the compact reflection patch to the original prompt and regenerates from a clean initial state, preserving task specification fidelity while injecting guidance.
The teacher is the same model as the student operating with hindsight reflection, so no larger teacher, critic or separate reward model is needed.
SRPO teacher-forces the reflection-augmented teacher on the student's own rollouts and minimizes per-token reverse KL, yielding O(T) bits of token-level supervision while staying strictly on-policy.
At inference the learned policy must reach comparable quality without any reflection, because the reflection guidance has been internalized through distillation.
With Qwen3-8B, SRPO reaches 73.3% on AIME'24 with 8% of the training FLOPs of scaled SFT, 3.3 points above standard on-policy distillation and 5.3 above GRPO.
SRPO reaches 64.7% on WebShop (+7.9% over SFT), 76.8% on ALFWorld (+5.6% over Reflexion) and 31.2% on SWE-Bench-Lite (+4.4% over Reflexion).
SRPO outperforms the reflection-trained baselines SCoRe, R3L and RISE.
Counting Stage 1 and 2, SRPO uses 5.4e18 FLOPs versus 20.8e18 for GRPO, about 3.8x fewer.
SRPO's self-distillation outperforms distillation from Qwen3-72B by 0.8 points while using 9x fewer teacher FLOPs.
In a GPT-4 rating of 500 reflections, 67% score 4 or higher for helpfulness and only 8% score 2 or lower.
Reflection helpfulness correlates with rethinking-rollout success improvement at r = 0.72; score-5 reflections give a 34% average improvement versus 5% for score 1-2.
Replacing reflection with a direct retry drops AIME'24 accuracy by 7.5 points.
Appending reflections iteratively without state reset performs 7.0 points worse on AIME'24.
Switching from reverse KL to forward KL drops AIME'24 accuracy by 3.9 points.

Prior work shows mixed evidence: debate, critique loops and mixture-of-agents report gains, while other work finds multi-agent systems add cost or that independent sampling already captures the benefit.
Different model families (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) each achieve the best score on at least one of 11 verifier-scored optimization tasks, so they find structurally different solutions.
Every same-model team scores Q=0 on at least one task, whereas a diverse team (Claude+GPT-4o+Gemini) never scores zero on any task, with aggregate Q comparable to the best same-model team.
In a 2x2 factorial (N=120, three tasks), the model-diversity coefficient is +0.188 (CI [+0.073, +0.299], p<0.001) while the synthesis coefficient is near zero.
When agents read each other's complete outputs, their proposals converge within one round: mean pairwise distance between solution representations falls from 0.315 to 0.229.
Chain, MAgICoRe and Debate have positive same-model MIG (+0.051, +0.044, +0.012) but negative diverse-model MIG (-0.024, -0.035, -0.078), with bootstrap P(same>div) of at least 88%.
No configuration achieves positive aggregate MEG over single-agent baselines; MoA is the only one whose 95% CI includes zero.
MoA, whose proposers never read each other's outputs, keeps positive MIG for same-model and diverse teams (+0.012 to +0.016).

On five of seven tasks, synthesis copies the best proposer's output at least 80% of the time instead of combining parts, and on Erdos GPT-4o outputs the identical constant on 100% of seeds (Q=0.710), so interaction converges to that point.

Critique with diverse models helps when the violated rule is easy to find and fix (Knapsack-50 Debate 2/10 to 10/10 feasibility) but hurts when it is hard to locate (3AP-Free-100: MAgICoRe 6/10 to 3/10, Debate 6/10 to 0/10).

Multi-agent performance depends less on the number of agents than on what information they exchange and when; lower-bandwidth signals such as scores, method descriptions or failure causes may preserve independent exploration.

Pruned LLMs show more repetition-loop degeneration than unpruned ones even when perplexity and task accuracy are largely unchanged; with top-p sampling the repetition rate is 5.9% unpruned, 12.4% width pruned and 15.4% depth pruned after Alpaca fine-tuning.
Replacing only the first two onset tokens with a top-2 alternative reduces CREP of the unpruned model from 5.9% to 0.7% under sampling and from 26.6% to 10.8% under greedy decoding.
P(Coverage >= tau) <= R_T * rho_bar^l_tau: loop entry risk R_T enters linearly while persistence rho_bar is exponentiated by the required in-loop run length.
Under nucleus sampling, persistence rho(c) = a(c)/(a(c)+e(c)), so reducing persistence requires increasing escape mass e(c) inside the nucleus, not entropy over the full vocabulary.
Under capacity constraints from pruning, minimizing forward KL gives a single broadened student approximation that moves probability into intermediate and low-density regions of a multimodal teacher.
Forward KL gives little pressure against student mass on teacher-suppressed tokens; leakage tokens admitted into the nucleus become sampleable and increase entry risk R_T.
Pruning distorts near-tied teacher alternatives at loop-sensitive contexts into one dominant continuation, reducing escape mass and raising rho and its supremum.
Training should suppress leakage toward teacher-suppressed tokens to reduce entry risk and preserve or promote plausible escape alternatives within the nucleus to reduce persistence.

FOCUS reweights each token's distillation term by w = (q/beta + 1 - q)^gamma-style confidence weights emphasizing high-confidence teacher regions, equivalent to standard KD with a reweighted teacher distribution (gradient Z(p - q_tilde)).

RePAIR builds negative samples from repetitive pruned-model outputs and positive samples regenerated from the unpruned model at the first repetition onset, trained with a token-level margin ranking loss; total loss is L_CE + 0.05 L_FOCUS + 1 L_RePAIR.
On WikiText-103 with Llama-3.1-8B, RePAIR alone reaches MAUVE 0.68 and CREP 2.23 (KD: 0.61 and 7.3), and FOCUS+RePAIR gives MAUVE 0.73 and CREP 0.57, with only a small perplexity increase.
On Self-Instruct with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, RePAIR lowers CREP to 0.63 and raises EAD1 to 0.32 versus KD (1.97, 0.28); FOCUS combined with RePAIR gives the best results on most metrics.
Adding FOCUS to UL, SG, DITTO and RePAIR improves generation quality (higher MAUVE, lower CREP) with only slightly higher perplexity.
FOCUS keeps tail agreement stable while substantially raising tail correlation and head agreement, and expands the number of viable head candidates from 148.6 to 202.1.

Most competitive-programming benchmarks use a full-information (batch-style) protocol, so it is unclear how well model-generated programs solve interactive problems where key information is revealed only through queries.

In interactive problems key information is held by an interactor and revealed only in response to the solver's queries under a strict protocol and problem-specific query budget, so success requires an online querying strategy as well as a correct final answer.

Existing benchmarks rarely cover interactive problems, some depend on remote submissions to external online judges blocking offline evaluation, and many report only an overall success metric with little diagnosis of failures.

InteractBench comprises 322 interactive problems curated from Codeforces, AtCoder, IOI and ICPC, each with multi-round interaction, protocol constraints and a query budget, annotated with categories and difficulty tiers.
Offline evaluators (test generators and local interactors) are built by a propose-validate-adjudicate loop capped at three iterations, after which 31 tasks required human expert intervention.

Each task has a verification pool of 15 accepted and 30 rejected submissions (15 human, 15 mutation-derived), and an evaluator is accepted only if the offline harness matches official outcomes on all human submissions and rejects all mutation probes.

The harness runs the solver and a local interactor as two sandboxed processes over standard streams, enforces protocol and budget via counters, and logs transcripts and termination reasons, enabling fully offline evaluation and a failure taxonomy.
A one-time audit submits 5 sampled model solutions per task to official interfaces where permitted and checks that Accepted/Rejected outcomes agree with the offline harness.
Even the most advanced reasoning models achieve limited success on interactive problems, a significant interaction gap versus standard full-information coding benchmarks.

Performance degrades steeply with difficulty: Gemini-3-Pro-Preview reaches 0.961 pass@5 on Easy but the best model reaches only 0.597 on Hard pass@5, and only two configurations (Gemini-3-Pro-Preview, GPT-5.2) exceed 0.400 on Hard pass@5.
Reasoning variants improve pass rates (DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 0.513 overall pass@5 vs 0.262 for DeepSeek-V3.2) but small models stay bottlenecked on Hard (Qwen3-14B 0.000 Hard pass@5).
Graph is the hardest category, with even the best model below 0.500 pass@1, while the Bit category is comparatively easier (Gemini-3-Pro-Preview 0.613 pass@1).

Wrong answers from algorithmic logic errors are the most common failure for many configurations, while protocol violations and query-budget overruns remain frequent and runtime/resource failures (TLE, MLE, RE) are secondary.

As context grows, LLM inference needs to store and retrieve all KV caches, so latency and memory rise; for Llama-3-8B-Instruct-262k with FlashAttention, going from 1K to 1M tokens raises latency by over 3000x.
KV eviction methods discard KV pairs by predefined policies, usually causing significant accuracy loss because essential information is removed.
KV retrieval methods keep all KV pairs and retrieve relevant tokens at decoding, preserving accuracy but not mitigating memory usage, which limits batch size and throughput.

Some attention heads concentrate on a few critical tokens consistently across pre-filling and decoding (consistent heads), while others vary significantly across decoding steps with broad attention (adaptive heads); this occurs across different LLMs and layers.
For consistent heads, critical tokens can be identified from the pre-filling stage using the attention of the last Lobs query tokens (observation window) and used to guide decoding.
CateKV classifies heads into consistent and adaptive types using a coefficient-of-variation-based score over a reference dataset, and classification results are highly similar across samples.
CateKV retains only a small budget of critical KV pairs in consistent heads (chunk-level top-k) and most KV pairs (retention ratio eta) in adaptive heads, chosen by pre-filling attention weights.
A Rademacher-complexity bound on the CV-based classifier's generalization (Lemma 1) bounds the head-classification accuracy P_head that drives CateKV's eviction performance.

On RULER at 128K with r=0.4, eta=1.0 and a consistent-head budget of 2048, CateKV keeps about 41% of the KV cache, outperforms StreamingLLM, SnapKV, PyramidKV and DuoAttention, and is comparable to full attention.
On LongBench, CateKV reduces KV cache to 42% across five LLMs with an average accuracy decline of at most 0.3%; combined with Quest or ShadowKV the decrease is at most 0.2%.

DuoAttention's accuracy declines notably when retrieval heads fall below 0.3 of heads, while CateKV stays near full attention even at an adaptive-head ratio of 0.1, because consistent heads capture cross-query similarity whereas streaming heads cover initial and recent tokens.

In single-sample inference, generic settings (r=0.4, eta=1.0) give Phi-3 2.11x memory and 1.79x latency reductions, and a tuned setting gives Llama-3 up to 2.72x memory and 2.18x decoding latency reductions with under 0.25% accuracy decline.
In batch inference at 40K tokens, generic settings give up to 2.38x batch size and 2.25x throughput, and further compression on Llama-3 gives 4.33x batch size and 3.96x throughput.
In the autoregressive decode phase each token generation reloads the entire KV cache from HBM, so IO rather than FLOPs is the primary bottleneck, creating a memory wall for long contexts.
In the standard decoupled Selector-Computer paradigm, the computer cannot reuse the selector's intermediate computations, creating efficiency bottlenecks.
Importance metrics that rely on extra metadata (partial dimensions, centroids, geometric bounds) either incur additional memory overhead or suffer information distortion.

Top-k selection is cheap but cannot adapt to varying attention entropy, while top-p adapts to the distribution but needs a global softmax and sorting, which adds overhead and breaks the streaming pipeline.

FFD splits the K cache into a 2-bit quantized thumbnail for scanning and an 8-bit residual for refinement (symmetric zero-free mid-rise quantization), replacing metadata-based indexing and avoiding metadata memory overhead.
Top-delta keeps tokens with score s_ij at least m_i minus delta, i.e. attention at least e^-delta of the peak; delta=5 discards only tokens below about 0.67% of peak attention mass.

Estimating the maximum score from only sink and local tokens (pseudo-max), justified by attention being dominated by sink and local tokens, lets the threshold be computed locally so KV blocks are processed independently without global synchronization.
The gap between true max and pseudo-max is below 0.01 in 86.1% of cases, so the approximation is a robust safe relaxation.

FFD runs pseudo-max estimation, 2-bit top-delta selection and 8-bit refinement as fused Triton kernels reusing the scan, and uses full-chain block-wise JIT CUDA graphs that run 99% of decode steps within a graph.
At a matched keep ratio of about 27.3%, top-delta selection is 2x faster than top-k and 25x faster than top-p.

On an RTX 4090 FFD kernel latency scales linearly with a much lower slope than FlashAttention-2, with average speedups of 7.33x (delta=5) and 6.18x (delta=7) and a peak of 11.63x; at 256K it is 0.17 ms versus 1.12 ms.
FFD reaches up to 2.37x throughput over FlashAttention-2 at 16K on RTX 4090 (51.8 vs Quest 47.8 tokens/s) and 1.96x on H100 (87.0 vs 44.5 tokens/s).
KIVI is slower than dense attention in the low-batch regime (22.4 vs 44.5 tokens/s on H100 at 16K) because of dequantization cost.
On RULER at 32K with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, FFD matches the dense baseline on NIAH single-key tasks (100.0) and has minimal degradation on Variable Tracking (98.4 vs 99.6).
Fixed-budget Quest drops sharply on MK-3 (6.0) whereas FFD with top-delta reaches 95.0, and FFD consistently outperforms Twilight on both benchmarks.
On LongBench (21 datasets, 6 categories) FFD with delta=7 achieves the highest overall average of 26.35 among compared methods.

FFD achieves higher recall and lower LSE error than Quest at the same retrieval budget, and maintains higher Spearman correlation across layers, because 2-bit quantization preserves key directionality better than min/max bounds.
The fused 2-bit top-delta configuration achieves 53.96 tok/s, RULER AVG 90.40 and LongBench AVG 25.90, a 2.2x throughput gain over its split-execution counterpart.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with delta=7, FFD gets RULER AVG 85.90 and LongBench AVG 30.11, outperforming KIVI, Quest and StreamingLLM.
Most LLM-based entity matching judges each (anchor, candidate) pair in isolation, ignoring interactions among candidates and the clean-clean constraint that at most one candidate matches.

Manually designed composite pipelines such as COMEM apply the same operator sequence to every anchor regardless of difficulty, so inference cost is a fixed byproduct of the architecture, and cost matters at industrial scale.
Multi-candidate EM with blocking is cast as an episodic MDP per anchor, where actions invoke operators that update candidate scores and accumulate abstract cost until DECIDE or Tmax.

The controller chooses among MATCH (pairwise, lightweight Flan-T5-xl), COMPARE (champion vs challenger preference), SELECT (listwise choice over top-k shortlist) and terminal DECIDE(i)/DECIDE(None), each with a model capacity.
Operators carry a low/high cost label (high = rho x low, rho=2.5 by default), a relative control signal that decouples the policy from any specific pricing or model.

The state concatenates scores, candidate masks, COMPARE frequency, global context (cost, time, max score) and action history; rewards combine terminal correctness, a cost penalty and potential-based shaping on the score margin Phi.
The policy is a 3-layer MLP (768-384-192) trained with PPO and a learned value baseline, trained once on the AB dataset.
Because the controller sees only abstract operators and cost labels, stronger LLMs can be plugged in at inference without retraining as long as operator interfaces and relative cost levels hold.
Zero-shot on other datasets CaRL-EM averages F1macro 76.09 versus 85.64 for in-domain DITTO (about 89%) at 5.9% of DITTO's cost.

CaRL-EM beats the strongest hand-crafted baseline COMEM on average F1macro with about 4.5x cost reduction, and with the same GPT-4o mini backend uses only 22% of COMEM's total cost, forming a new Pareto frontier.
CaRL-EM stops with a no-match decision more readily when evidence is weak, giving higher F1none than the fixed pipeline (e.g. 68.20 vs 60.78), which avoids false positives.

DITTO trained on AB drops from 85.64 to 59.75 F1macro on other datasets, while CaRL-EM stays high; swapping backends without retraining usually raises F1macro and cost, with the controller adjusting MATCH/COMPARE usage.
CaRL-EM uses fewer MATCH/COMPARE calls than COMEM, varies steps with dataset difficulty (more on AG, WA), and is more stable across gold-candidate positions than baselines.
Removing the cost term leaves F1macro unchanged (76.07) but raises cost by about 15%.
Removing MATCH drops F1macro to 65.87 (F1none 49.86), removing COMPARE to 73.69, removing SELECT to 73.26 (cheapest but lower F1id).
Removing the potential-based term Phi lowers F1id and F1macro (75.93) and makes performance less stable (Std 14.56 vs 12.24).
Existing benchmarks evaluate chart and document understanding separately, overlooking the interplay where surrounding narrative provides definitions and constraints needed to interpret charts.

DocHop is a benchmark where the document narrative specifies multi-step compositional constraints while charts supply the numerical values, requiring multi-hop reasoning rather than single-hop lookup.
Questions are grounded on a semantic reference label assigned in the narrative rather than explicit entity names, so models must resolve target entities from the text before aggregating chart values.

Each instance starts from a sampled reasoning trace (a chain of conditional checks across charts); an LLM then generates the numerical data and document text to satisfy the trace, allowing control of reasoning depth D in {2,3,4,5} and chart count k in {2,3,4,6}.
DocHop has 2,074 examples across 6 task categories, 41 question templates, 480 topics and 7 chart types.
Quality is ensured by programmatically executing each trace against data tables to verify answers, human verification of the narrative, and manual inspection of rendered images.
Human annotators exceed 90% accuracy while the best model, GPT-5.2 Reasoning, reaches only 62.83% overall (Table 1).
Reasoning-enhanced variants outperform base counterparts, e.g. GPT-5.2 improves from 40.36% to 62.83% and Gemini-2.5-Flash from 24.88% to 32.02% (Table 1).
Accuracy of GPT-5.2 Reasoning and Gemini-2.5-Pro Reasoning decreases steadily as reasoning depth and number of charts increase, highest at k=2 and D=2 (Fig 5).
Human annotators need roughly five minutes per question, indicating DocHop requires careful multi-step reasoning rather than quick lookup.
Failure examples include attributing chart values to the wrong entity, taking the global maximum instead of the labeled entity set, and OCR errors in value extraction (Fig 4).
The absence of human labels does not imply the absence of human supervision, since data curation, preprocessing and learning-objective choices embed substantial human priors.
ImageNet organizes classes around WordNet synsets, and vision-language datasets depend strongly on metadata design and curation choices.
Even without manual curation, common web queries yield regularized patterns such as canonical object poses, centered compositions and consistent orientations, which models inherit.

Contrastive learning assumes augmented views of one sample depict the same entity and different samples distinct entities; this holds in curated object-centric datasets but not universally, e.g. in multi-entity scenes, textures, microscopy or medical imagery.
When training data scale is increased by adding generic non-object-centric images, DINO performance degrades, showing a mismatch between data priors and the learning objective.

Before large-scale pre-training unsupervised learning was predominantly in-domain with explicit, localized assumptions; modern pre-training is adopted across domains so embedded priors become generic and invisible.

Across CVPR/ICCV/ECCV titles 2013-2025, 'unsupervised' and 'self-supervised' peak around 2021 and then decline despite growing publication counts; at CVPR the 'unsupervised' fraction falls from nearly 4% in 2021 to close to 1% by 2025.
In 17,435 CVPR papers (2015-2025), the share explicitly relying on a named pre-trained model rises from 10.13% in 2015 to 22.17% in 2021 and falls to 15.52% in 2024 and 12.85% in 2025.
Among 287 CVPR 2020-2025 papers titled 'unsupervised', reliance on external pre-training rises steadily and is concentrated in a few backbone families (DINO, CLIP, MoCo, diffusion models, SwAV).

Three hypotheses may explain the decline: comparison pressure favoring scaled pre-trained models, unsupervised learning becoming an implicit component rather than a stated contribution, and user-side indifference to the training paradigm.

Properties attributed to an 'unsupervised' method, such as semantic discovery, objectness or robustness, may be inherited from pre-trained representations, so shared upstream priors can be misread as novel emergent principles.

Ambiguity distorts incentives toward adapting to pre-trained models, marginalizes approaches that avoid pre-training or certain priors, and makes same-scale comparison harder for compute-limited researchers.
Grouping methods with different assumptions under one 'unsupervised' label obscures how a method learns and what it assumes, hindering fair comparison.

Authors should disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives and specify which pipeline components depend on which assumptions, via a checklist covering pre-training dependence, frozen vs adaptive reliance, pre-training data scope, data distribution priors, learning invariances and leakage risks.
Methods using pre-trained features should be tested across pre-training regimes, and relaxing assumptions should be valued as a contribution, not only peak benchmark performance.

In real deployments collaborative agents come from different manufacturers and platforms, with differing sensor types, voxel sizes and network architectures, which makes intermediate features hard to fuse.
One-stage methods learn a dedicated mapping for each pair of heterogeneous modalities, so training cost grows rapidly with the number of modalities.
Two-stage methods map each modality into a shared protocol space with a per-modality converter and reconstructor, improving scalability.

Training converters independently per modality makes each learn a locally self-consistent mapping, producing inconsistent pseudo-protocol distributions, semantic and statistical discrepancies across modalities, and error accumulation, especially when the modality gap is large.

Existing methods model the protocol space only as a distribution-alignment intermediary and do not characterize which semantic factors are shared and which modality-specific statistical confounders should be suppressed.

A structural causal model treats the true semantic factor S as the causal factor and the protocol and heterogeneous-modality statistical noises Np and Nm as confounders that create spurious correlation paths and modality-specific semantic clusters.

Counterfactual intervention via causal metric learning, implemented by the Mask-Guided Intervention via SPD Feature Geometry module, drives each modality's protocol representation toward the weakly observed protocol modality, suppressing pseudo-protocol shifts.

A unified converter combining a semantic context extractor and a context-guided dynamic refiner is trained on multi-modality mixed batches, using global semantics as an anchor to constrain local refinement and reduce background-induced misalignment.
With the Stage-1 converter frozen, a ConvNeXt-based local semantic reconstructor is trained for each modality to restore protocol features to that modality's local space.

For a new modality the converter backbone is frozen and only low-rank bottleneck adapters (initialized with scaling coefficient 0) are trained to align it to the protocol space, plus a local reconstructor.
On OPV2V with Lpp4 ego and three heterogeneous neighbors added progressively, CauseCollab achieves the best AP@0.3 and AP@0.5 against MPDA, HEAL, PnPDA and STAMP.
With a larger modality gap, CauseCollab improves AP by 4.2% at IoU 0.3 and 3.6% at IoU 0.5 for ego CEff and neighbor CRes, and by 0.5%/0.4% for ego Lpp4 and neighbor CEff.
On DAIR-V2X, with Lpp4 and CEff as ego, CauseCollab outperforms all previous methods overall.
Adapting to novel modalities Lsd2 and CEffB1 gives higher average precision with fewer trainable parameters, indicating semantic consistency and parameter reuse.
Removing the causal intervention module significantly lowers AP at IoU 0.3 and 0.5, and removing the intervention mask also degrades performance.

Removing semantic context guidance causes a substantial drop, replacing CGDR or SCE+CGDR with a single-tower ConvNeXt degrades further, and removing the new-modality adapter also degrades performance.

Visualization shows a semantic gap between LiDAR and camera intermediate features; STAMP's protocol features from camera contain semantically irrelevant background noise while CauseCollab's are cleaner and more cross-modally consistent.
Long CoT reasoning makes the KV cache grow linearly with sequence length; e.g. Qwen3-4B generating 32K tokens at batch size 16 needs over 77GB of KV cache, near the limit of an 80GB GPU.
Existing KV compression methods (e.g. RPC, R-KV) score KV importance with attention from recent queries, assuming they are reliable proxies for future attention.

In LRM decoding, global queries attend to distant keys (e.g. early task-solving plans and problem constraints) rather than nearby ones; the corresponding tokens are called Thought Revisiting Tokens (TRT), and their attention distances are clearly separated from those of local queries.
Global queries appear with varying frequency across many layers and heads and occur sporadically and unpredictably in the reasoning trace.

Because TRT are sporadic, recent-query-based methods cannot anticipate which distant KV pairs future TRT will revisit, causing premature eviction of essential KV pairs and degraded reasoning under tight budgets.
Global queries have low similarity to neighbouring local queries but high mutual similarity, and cluster into a small number of similarity groups in the query embedding space (PCA, Fig 4).
A compact set of beacon queries, one representative per global query cluster, can anticipate which KV pairs future global queries will revisit without storing the entire query history.

BeaconKV, a training-free method, scores KV pairs using observation queries made of recent queries plus beacon queries selected by Continual Farthest Point Sampling (FPS), a bounded-buffer online algorithm.
BeaconKV aggregates attention over observation queries by max-pooling rather than mean-pooling, since TRT signals are high-magnitude but rare and mean-pooling would dilute them.

On R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B across AIME24, MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and GPQA-Diamond, BeaconKV generally outperforms RPC and R-KV, with gains up to 31.7 points (Qwen3-14B, AIME24, budget 1024).
On Qwen3-4B with 32K generation on an A100 80GB, BeaconKV with a 2K budget cuts peak memory from 77.0GB to 13.3GB (5.8x) and raises throughput from 82.3 to 356.4 tokens/s (over 4.3x).
At matched 2K and 1K budgets BeaconKV matches RPC's throughput and memory while improving LiveCodeBench accuracy by +6.3 and +12.3 points.
A balanced (16 recent, 16 beacon) observation set gives 64.6% accuracy at 4355.7s latency, while over-allocating to beacons (1,31) gives 63.5% at 10871.3s.
Max aggregation generally outperforms mean aggregation, e.g. 23.3 vs 18.8 at a 256-token budget (Table 2).
BeaconKV consistently outperforms an Initial+Recent baseline, indicating gains come from Continual FPS dynamically capturing evolving global query patterns, not merely preserving early context.

As LLMs scaled to billions of parameters and trillions of tokens, dropout has largely disappeared from pretraining recipes, since single-epoch training on massive data leaves little room for classical overfitting and activation dropout is reported to degrade performance there.

Skipping entire transformer blocks (layer dropout / stochastic depth) yields structured sparsity that reduces active training FLOPs almost linearly with the dropout rate and encourages robustness to reduced-depth execution at inference.

Reported accuracy degradation from layer dropout in decoder-only LLMs may come from suboptimal schedules or hyperparameters rather than fundamental limits, because no controlled large-scale study had varied these systematically.
Layer dropout that drops whole transformer blocks per sample yields higher accuracy than sub-layer dropout that drops attention and FFN sub-blocks separately (Finding 1, Table 1).
For any given layer dropout rate, dropping per sequence yields lower loss than dropping per batch (Finding 2).

For the same training FLOPs, a non-uniform dropout distribution across layers beats uniform; the Increasing Layer Distribution (ILD, rate rising linearly from 0 at the first layer) is recommended as the model scales (Finding 3).
For a fixed training FLOPs budget, a schedule decaying from a maximum rate to zero (DTS) achieves the highest accuracy, outperforming constant and increasing schedules at all scales (Finding 4).
The recommended layer dropout practice is increasing dropout across layers and decreasing dropout across time, which gives the best accuracy for a given training FLOPs budget (Key takeaway 1).

With optimal layer distribution, time schedule and optimizer hyperparameters, layer dropout gives lower loss at the same training FLOPs, or similar validation loss while saving up to 25% of training FLOPs.

Pretraining with layer dropout saves training FLOPs and always leads to better early-exit loss at inference; the decreasing schedule gives the lowest validation loss with competitive early-exit loss (Key takeaway 2, Finding 5).

The average training dropout rate predicts zero-shot robustness to early exit and layer skipping without retraining, so a larger model degrades gracefully toward smaller-model performance when layers are skipped (Finding 6, Key takeaway 3).

At 1.8B-8.2B scale, aggressive layer dropout (p_max=0.99) saves up to 25% of cumulative training FLOPs while largely preserving baseline generalization, enabling zero-shot inference speedups up to 1.55x (Key takeaway 4).
Layer-dropout-trained models enable post-training optimizations such as self-speculative decoding, yielding up to 1.5x inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
MLLMs' vision-language reasoning performance degrades as generations grow longer.
Most MLLMs rely on a single growing context: the image is encoded once as a prefix and later states are carried only through generated text.
Attention to image tokens steadily decays as generation proceeds; under a growing context the total attention mass on the fixed image-token set shrinks as n_t grows.
Prompting-based guidance and training-based alignment for revisiting information remain bound to the same growing-context mechanism and do not fundamentally prevent long-horizon forgetting.

DLMR maintains two learnable input-agnostic latent memories, a visual memory Z(v) compressing image evidence and a reasoning memory Z(r) tracking intermediate conclusions and constraints, on a frozen backbone.
A lightweight memory injector (LoRA on a replica of the frozen MLLM) contextualizes the selected latents into k memory tokens appended to the context.
A discrete LoRA-head router selects at each delimiter-eligible step a memory type s in {v,r} and a token budget k in {4,8,16} (or no injection), with a per-sample cap on injections.
DLMR is trained in three stages with the backbone frozen: latent memory pre-warm via two-teacher alignment, injector training (SFT or GRPO), and router learning with GRPO under a cost-aware reward.
Compared to vanilla Qwen2.5-VL-7B on MathVision, DLMR preserves substantially more visual attention in later decoding and often needs fewer reasoning tokens.

DLMR consistently outperforms CoT, CCoT, SFT, GRPO, Visual-RFT and RCTS-RAG baselines on 3 general and 4 reasoning benchmarks with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL-3-8B; e.g. DLMR RL raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B MathVision from 22.37 to 39.34.
DLMR (SFT) performs best on general benchmarks while DLMR (RL) achieves the strongest reasoning results.
Collapsing the dual memories into a single shared memory lowers the six-benchmark average from 59.73 to 52.05 and MathVision from 35.32 to 22.37.
Freezing the injector lowers the Qwen2.5-VL-7B reasoning average from 72.10 to 69.96 (MMMU 61.00 to 58.14), showing a trainable injector is necessary.
Full adaptive DLMR reaches 53.84 average reasoning accuracy with 677 average tokens, above fixed k=4/8/16 (51.55, 52.71, 52.04) whose average length rises 664 to 732 to 765.
DLMR improves LLaVA-OV-1.5-4B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B and InternVL-3-2B, with reasoning-average gains of +7.2, +7.9 and +6.9 and general-average gains of +6.8, +6.2 and +5.1.
Applied to text-only benchmarks, DLMR improves GSM8K from 68.08 to 83.47 and ARC-Challenge from 44.11 to 55.19 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
DLMR reduces average generated tokens by 9.7% versus Visual-RFT and by 4.2% versus SFT on four reasoning benchmarks, counting memory-generation tokens.

Real-world MCTS applications involve continuous actions and stochastic dynamics, where value estimates are non-stationary and actions cannot be enumerated, complicating both convergence theory and practice.

HOOT couples MCTS with the HOO hierarchical bandit but uses logarithmic exploration bonuses, which fail to guarantee convergence when value estimates are non-stationary because non-stationary rewards lack concentration.
POLY-HOOT adds a polynomial bonus and has non-asymptotic convergence guarantees in deterministic continuous MDPs, but no analogous guarantee exists for stochastic environments.
Stochastic-Power-HOOT is an MCTS algorithm for continuous-action stochastic MDPs that uses a power mean as value backup operator and a polynomial exploration bonus C n^(b/beta)/T_a(n)^(alpha/beta).

The power mean f_n(p) interpolates between the arithmetic mean (p=1, conservative) and the maximum (p to infinity, optimistic), enabling tuning of exploration-exploitation across levels of stochasticity.

For non-stationary continuous-armed bandits satisfying the fixed-arm and optimal-arm convergence properties, an enhanced HOO agent with polynomial bonus achieves ||f_n - f||_inf at most C/n^zeta for some 0<zeta<1/2 (Theorem 1, Mao et al.).
Power mean aggregation of estimators that concentrate polynomially preserves polynomial concentration at a transformed rate (Theorem 2).

Each internal MCTS node is modeled as a non-stationary bandit whose arms are child nodes; concentration rates are propagated inductively from rollout leaves at depth D upward using Q-value concentration (Lemma 1) and Theorem 2.

Stochastic-Power-HOOT converges at rate O(n^-zeta), zeta in (0,1/2), where n is the number of visited trajectories, matching POLY-HOOT's rate while extending the guarantee to stochastic MDPs (Theorem 4).

On stochastic classic control, all methods solve basic CartPole but only Stochastic-Power-HOOT handles CartPole with increased gravity optimally, with particular strength on sparse-reward MountainCar and high-gravity Acrobot (Table 2).
On stochastic MuJoCo tasks it keeps strong performance in 17-dimensional Humanoid, achieving 3.1x the UCT baseline (Table 3).
The optimal p varies by environment: Humanoid benefits from p=2 while the more stochastic Hopper needs p=8 (Table 3).
On CartPole-IG, p=2 and p=4 perform best: too low a p fails to focus search and too high may over-commit to early estimates (Table 4).

REPA aligns diffusion hidden states with pretrained encoders such as DINOv2 to speed convergence, but depends on foundation-model representations that are often unavailable for modalities like point clouds or graphs.
Diffusion models and self-supervised spectral representation learning can both be formulated under a shared stochastic-process parameterization based on perturbation kernels (Sec 3.1-3.2).

Spectral representations built from the diffusion perturbation kernel give time-dependent multi-scale embeddings whose distances reflect local connectivity: small t separates data, large t collapses distances; the diffusion distance expands in the eigenspace of the kernel operator (Prop 4.2).

Diffusion training adds a spectral self-supervised loss L = L_diff + lambda L_s, aligning hidden states with eigenfunctions of a time-varying kernel operator, reusing the same perturbed input plus one additional perturbed view (Sec 4.2, Eq 22).

Minimizing the spectral self-supervised objective is gradient-equivalent to minimizing a KL divergence, i.e. diffusion score distillation, inducing mode-seeking dynamics in representation space (Prop 4.3, Sec 4.3).
On synthetic 2D distributions (2spirals, rings) the method produces cleaner, more compact samples with fewer outliers than the baseline (Fig 2).
Spectral regularization reduces FID by 1.5 on ImageNet-64 (DiT-L/4), 0.2 on ImageNet-256 (DiT-XL/2), 2.8 on CIFAR-10, 3.1 on CelebA and 0.7 on FFHQ, i.e. 15%, 8%, 25%, 11% and 5% relative (Table 1).
The method outperforms the baseline in later stages of training as shown by FID against iterations (Fig 3).
On ShapeNet Chair, Airplane and Car with DiT-3D S/4, where pretrained encoders are unavailable, the method gives strong performance over the baseline (Table 2).
For latent-space ImageNet-256, REPA achieves the best overall performance, while the proposed method improves over its baseline without an external pretrained encoder.
Training time increases by about 10% for ImageNet-64 pixel diffusion, 70% for ImageNet-256 latent diffusion and 20% for Airplane point-cloud diffusion.

Conditional computation is modeled as the coexistence of a full and a partial computation: in the static setting the partial computation is used for every input (magnitude pruning), and in the adaptive setting it forms a confidence score and the full computation is invoked only when needed (early exit).

In high dimensions, for IID Gamma-type weights, the cosine similarity between a weight vector and its one-shot magnitude-pruned (and renormalized) version concentrates to a pruning-rate-dependent deterministic constant tau_q, with explicit rates including an O(n^-1/2) Berry-Esseen term and an exp(-C n eps^2) term (Theorem 2.1).

For w uniform on the sphere, the inner product of w with its renormalized pruned version converges to sqrt(tau_q), a nonlinear function of q that stays close to one under aggressive pruning (Corollary 2.2).
Keeping 60% of the coordinates (q=0.4) gives w^T w_p of about 0.982, an angle of about 10.8 degrees.

In an infinite-width Gaussian limit, empirical kernels and cross-kernels of pruned and unpruned networks converge to deterministic limits, with the only change in the cross-kernel recursion being a factor sqrt(tau_q) on cross terms, so pruning misalignment propagates through depth by a recursion that depends on the activation (Theorem 4.1).
Simulated distributions of the normalized inner product at q=0.9 and d in {10,100,1000,10000} concentrate around the theoretical limit as d increases.
The conditional perceptron is an analytically tractable student-teacher model of early exit where a partial computation forms a confidence score and the full computation runs only when needed.

For the conditional perceptron, given computation constraint mu_c <= 1-eps, generalization error eps_c <= eps_uc + (2 eps/q) A is achievable, with A = 0.5/(1-rho^2) and rho = cos(arccos tau_q + pi eps_uc), so excess error decays polynomially, O(eps^A), as normalized FLOPs approach 1 (Theorem 3.1).
The power-law exponent grows to infinity as the alignment between partial and full computations tends to one.

For frozen backbones with distilled intermediate exits under a Gaussian coupling of exit and final scores, excess error obeys a power of the compute gap with exponent A' = 0.5/(1-rho_l^2), set by the exit-to-final correlation rho_l (Theorem 5.2).

On a frozen 6-block DistilBERT fine-tuned on SST-2 with linear distilled exit heads, excess error versus compute gap is approximately linear on log-log axes over a visible range, and exit-to-final correlation rises with depth: (0.446, 0.553, 0.669, 0.736, 0.977) for exits 1-5.

On ViT-Base (12 layers) fine-tuned on CIFAR-100 with exits at layers 3,6,9,11, excess error scales approximately as a power of the compute gap and deeper exits show sharper decay; measured correlations (0.246, 0.412, 0.589, 0.773) give analytical exponents (0.53, 0.60, 0.77, 1.24).

For ViT-Base, local log-log slopes near the smallest gaps (about 1.56, 3.16, 8.78 for layers 3, 6, 9) are larger than the analytical exponents, suggesting a multiclass correction is needed since the exit rule uses max softmax over 100 classes.

Existing embedding-based and MLLM-based evaluators assess alignment with each modal condition in isolation, which contradicts the simultaneous condition alignment objective of multi-modal image generation and yields poor consistency with human judgments.

Subject-driven customization requires regenerating the subject free-form (pose and position may vary) while following textual edits to some attributes, so judging visual and textual alignment at once is difficult.

Isolated evaluation compares only subject appearance to the reference and ignores intended textual modifications, so it rates images that ignore the text highly (false positives) and penalizes correct edits that reduce visual similarity (false negatives).

UFO uses a vision-language model on the reference image and text to decompose omni-condition alignment into a sequential chain of fine-grained, disentangled Atomic Evaluation Units at local component and global attribute levels.
Each AEU is assigned a relevance class of image-only, text-only or text-and-image, so each attribute is evaluated against the correct condition type.

Each AEU is converted to a VQA query answered Yes/No (score 1/0), and dedicated function calls such as ArcFace (score = 1 minus normalized ArcFace distance) are used for attributes like facial identity.
Each AEU gets an integer weight from 1 to 5 from VLM reasoning about attribute importance, and the final score is the weighted average of AEU scores.
On UFO-Bench, CLIP-T has a negative total Spearman correlation with human ranking (-0.1996), and CLIP-I and DINO reach only about 0.3 to 0.4.

VIEScore and DreamBench++ reach total correlation above 0.55 but only around 0.58 or lower on local editing, because they lack a mechanism to decouple the editing region from the preserved background.
UFO achieves a total Spearman correlation of 0.6889 with human rankings, the highest among compared metrics, with an average improvement of 15.25%.
Removing AEU decomposition (feeding the image to the VLM for a single holistic score) drops correlation with human preference from 0.6889 to 0.5752.
Replacing adaptive weights with uniform weights of 1 drops correlation from 0.6889 to 0.6253.
Existing customization benchmarks mostly cover simple background shifts or single attribute changes and lack diverse, conflicting interactions between textual and visual conditions.
UFO-Bench has 86 reference images across 7 categories with 3 tiers of editing difficulty and 81.97% conflicting condition pairs, spanning Non-Editing, Local, Global and Complex editing paradigms.
Closed-source Doubao (2025-12) achieves the highest total UFO score of 0.7439, measured with four samples per reference-prompt pair (2,640 instances per model).
Open-source Qwen-Image (2025-12) scores 0.7252 total, surpassing closed-source Nano-Banana and outperforming other community models.

Qwen-Image excels at non-editing (0.7635) and global editing (0.7836) but drops to 0.6532 on local editing, suggesting precise text-guided editing remains a challenge for open-source diffusion models.
Real-world LLM workloads have highly skewed, heavy-tailed output length distributions, producing heterogeneous decoding demand and uneven KV cache consumption.
Identically provisioned decoders gradually diverge in KV cache utilization, with some persistently saturated while others stay underutilized.

Round-robin routing fails to balance decoders and can worsen queue buildup and preemption; least-request treats request count as load proxy and saturates under long generations, so vLLM and SGLang keep RR.

PO-IT and Ranking only enable SJF within a single decode instance without cross-instance placement, prediction can add critical-path latency, and Llumnix migrates after imbalance occurs at significant overhead for large KV caches.

A LoRA-fine-tuned lightweight LLM on the request-origin device predicts output length in parallel with cloud-side prefill, hiding prediction latency; its training target is the maximum output length across LLaMA and Qwen models under multiple temperatures.
Underestimating output length triggers queue buildup, preemption and multi-fold latency inflation, whereas moderate overestimation only causes conservative allocation mitigated by PagedAttention.

UAC computes one-sided nonconformity scores over a sliding window of recent requests and sets the upper bound L_up = L_pred + q_alpha, guaranteeing P(L_out <= L_up) >= 1 - alpha under exchangeability.

The global scheduler estimates KV demand B = ceil((L_prompt + L_up)/S), keeps only decoders whose effective free blocks fit it, routes to the feasible decoder with the shortest waiting queue, and reserves blocks atomically; it falls back to RR on timeout and to maximum capacity if none is feasible.

Because per-token latency is stable, decoding time is roughly proportional to output length, so each decoder reorders its queue by L_up (SJF) with a maximum waiting time to avoid starvation, mitigating head-of-line blocking.
On Alpaca, SP-7B reduces MAE by 11.1% over PO-IT and 21.1% over S3, with higher Acc-50 and Acc-100.
UAC substantially lowers underestimation probability and caps residual error versus raw SP or a fixed 10% offset heuristic.
Across ShareGPT and BurstGPT workloads and LLaMA3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-3B, MAPS cuts mean E2E latency by 42.6% and P99 E2E latency by up to 84.8% versus vLLM, SGLang and Llumnix.
At high load MAPS keeps the decoders' queue-length ratio at 0.96 versus 1.36x under vLLM, with queues reduced on both decoders.

MAPS-160M still beats all baselines (E2E P99 improved 21.5%/21.0%/56.8% over SGLang/vLLM/Llumnix) and MAPS stays within 19.8% of the oracle's P99, so limited headroom remains for predictor improvement.
Removing UAC raises P99 and mean E2E latency by 14.3% and 18.4% because underestimation causes preemption and cascading queue delays.

Replacing minimum-queue routing with maximum-capacity routing degrades latency (Qwen2.5-3B P99 and mean up to 1.11x and 1.36x), showing routing should target queue buildup rather than residual memory.
Replacing local SJF with FCFS consistently increases mean and tail latency, more at P99 under higher rates.

Structured deliberation helps citizens develop more informed positions, greater tolerance for opposing views and willingness to accept outcomes they did not initially prefer, and deliberative forums yield knowledge gains, reduced affective polarization and broader legitimacy.

Deliberative polling and citizens' assemblies are limited by facilitators, sampling and venues to a few hundred participants (assemblies typically 50 to 200), leaving a tradeoff between meaningful deliberation for the few and superficial participation for the many.

Engagement-optimized platforms favor emotionally provocative content, create rich-get-richer dynamics dominated by a few accounts, spread falsehoods faster than corrections and reward outrage over understanding.
Online deliberation is limited by cognitive, social, platform-design and market-incentive frictions.
Cognitive overload, motivated reasoning, confirmation bias and correlation neglect limit deliberative capacity and can disadvantage people with less education, time or cognitive resources.
Affective polarization, overestimation of opponents' extremity, peer pressure and the subversion dilemma fragment deliberation, but correcting misperceptions increases support for democratic norms.

Unlimited commenting, reply functions and rich-get-richer loops let a few voices dominate, and advertising-based business models reward short-term engagement and divisive content over deliberative quality.

The four frictions interact and compound, so cognitive overload invites partisan heuristics, mistrust blocks interpretation, design amplifies unproductive voices and market incentives exploit all three.

LLMs can summarize thousands of contributions, translate in real time, adjust language complexity, identify agreement and help participants articulate positions, at marginal cost that is computational rather than human.

Deliberation at scale rests on LLM-mediated reflection, synthesis (clustering and summarizing opinions) and moderation (civility checks, comment recommendation, equitable participation), none of which requires AI to render judgments for participants.
Pro-democratic AI should preserve agency and autonomy, encourage mutual respect, promote equality and inclusiveness, and augment rather than substitute active citizenship.

The four principles are necessary and sufficient for pro-democratic AI; transparency, accountability, safety and efficiency serve them but cannot replace them, and the principles cut across every AI capability rather than mapping to specific frictions.

LLM-suggested rephrasings improved democratic reciprocity without shifting policy attitudes (Argyle et al. 2023), and a Comment Recommendation Module increased participation without reducing perceived autonomy.

Accurate visualizations of opinion distributions significantly increased cross-partisan consensus and willingness to act, and AI-Socratic dialogue reduced extreme positioning through perspective-taking while perceived agency stayed equivalent.
AI that discovers consensus among human-generated positions augments deliberation, whereas AI that generates consensus statements risks substituting for it.

Pol.is, deliberation.io and synchronous platforms limit contributions per user, disable direct replies and use automated turn-taking, creating conditions for broader participation that AI can further enhance.
Deliberation.io, Decidim and Pol.is release open-source components so communities can audit and govern the systems mediating collective reasoning.

LLMs tend toward sycophancy, and sycophantic chatbots increase attitude extremity and certainty, so facilitation must sometimes challenge rather than validate and be evaluated on deliberative quality rather than satisfaction.
LLM training biases (ideological, Western/WEIRD, gender and racial, English-centric) risk misrepresenting underrepresented participants, requiring diverse benchmarks and representative annotation.
Cognitive offloading to LLMs can erode independent reasoning, and LLM messages shift policy attitudes as effectively as human-authored messages, creating temptations to persuade rather than augment.
Deliberative alignment needs resistance to manipulation, faithful representation of minority views and procedural values, and LLM summaries have been shown to underrepresent minority perspectives.
The ML community should build deliberation-focused AI systems evaluated on facilitating informed, inclusive, consensus-building discourse rather than engagement metrics.
Falling rule lists are ordered if-then rules whose risks P(y=1|x) decrease along the sequence, so high-risk cases are decided within the first few rules.

Existing FRL optimizers cannot guarantee full optimality, rely on pre-generated rules (e.g. FPGrowth) too numerous for provably optimal methods, and suffer the interaction bottleneck by outputting one model per iteration.
Falling trees are decision trees constrained so that leaf probabilities adjacent to any root-to-leaf path decrease monotonically with depth, generalizing the falling constraint from lists to trees.

A tree satisfies the falling constraint iff at every internal node with one leaf child and one internal child, the leaf's empirical positive proportion is at least the maximum leaf proportion in the internal child's subtree (Theorem 4.1).
The branching cost H(T) counts internal nodes whose two children are both internal; H(T)=0 means a rule list, and the maximum 2^(d-1) corresponds to a complete tree.
GRAVITree minimizes misclassification rate plus a branching penalty mu*H(T), subject to a depth budget d, minimum leaf support alpha, and the falling constraint.
The Rashomon set R(D,d,mu,eps) contains all falling trees satisfying the support constraint with loss within (1+eps) of the optimal loss.

Child subproblems are coupled because the branching penalty depends on whether both children are internal and the falling constraint ties each child's leaf bounds to its sibling, so GRAVITree recurses first on the higher-probability child and also tracks the best non-leaf solution.

If a candidate split yields a child whose positive proportion exceeds the most recent preceding leaf probability p+_recent, any tree grown from it violates falling and the feature is pruned (Theorem 4.2).
Rashomon sets are stored as loss-sorted heaps so the merge step can terminate early (log-linear instead of quadratic), and subproblems are cached keyed by data subset, depth and quantized p+_recent.
As the branching cost mu increases, the normalized Colless index of the Rashomon set approaches 1 (all rule lists), while Rashomon set size and runtime tend to decrease.

GRAVITree with mu=0.01 generally achieves lower test loss and lower false negative rate than mu=1 (falling rule lists), while rule lists give substantially lower decision sparsity on positive examples.

TreeFARMS generally has lower overall loss than GRAVITree because of its unconstrained model class, but GRAVITree is competitive on false negative rate and generally sparser on positive examples (mu=0.01, alpha=0.05, d=5, eps=0.01).
KV cache memory grows linearly with context length, rapidly surpassing the model's own memory footprint and degrading decoding latency, which hinders long-context inference.
Quantization, pruning/eviction and offloading each retain a limitation: a still-growing cache, risk of discarding important information, or inter-hierarchy transfer latency.
Eviction-based policies implicitly use a one-hot write weight, discarding all but one write candidate and assuming certainty about future access; they cannot adapt to task-specific importance.

ARM organizes the KV cache as a fixed multi-level tree of routers whose leaf buckets each hold a fixed number of KV slots; each token is deterministically routed root-to-leaf by the largest routing logit, with routers trained by a self-supervised objective.

ARM selects bucket slots via Gumbel-Softmax and updates them with sigmoid-gated combinations of new and stored content, so new information is softly integrated without hard eviction and the cache size stays constant.
A policy trained as an MDP learns per-input and per-layer how many memory buckets (Top-M) to retrieve, enabling sparse access for simple inputs and expanded retrieval for harder ones.

Under i.i.d. Gaussian write candidates, optimal gated weights w*=pi make a shared slot retain information in proportion to anticipated usage, with I(a_r; A | r) >= -(d/2) log(1-||pi||_2^2), so sharing capacity beats one-hot eviction.

ARM is built on Llama3-8B, pre-trained on a 10B-token FineWeb-Edu subset, with 256 memory slots (4-level tree, 4 children per node) compared against full attention, sliding window, StreamingLLM, KIVI quantization and CPU offloading.
On language modeling and zero-shot commonsense tasks (Table 1), adapting the pre-trained model to ARM causes minimal change in average performance and perplexity, as with standard caching.
ARM outperforms standard eviction baselines on LongBench (Table 3) and RULER up to 128K context (Table 4), e.g. TREC 62.5 vs 38.0 for full attention in Table 3.

ARM gives significant generation speedup over full-cache methods (full attention, quantization), is on par with sliding window and sink caches, and offloading has the same memory use but significant latency problems (Fig 2).
A single universal text embedding cannot satisfy fine-grained needs, so conditional text embeddings that focus on a specified aspect are crucial.
Existing conditional-embedding methods (InstructOR, C-STS, InBedder, HyperCL) require large data and high fine-tuning cost and sacrifice the LLM's general capabilities.
Training-free prompt methods (PromptEOL, PonTE) compress the text (and condition) into the hidden state of the last token via 'in one word' prompts and use it directly as the embedding.

Prompt-conditioned embeddings still encode condition-irrelevant general information, e.g. average cosine similarity between general and conditional embeddings is 0.763 on TweetEmotion, which degrades distance measurements.

Self-Contrastive Steering (SCS) is a training-free plug-and-play method that derives an unconditional embedding and a conditional embedding from the same prompt-wrapped text and contrasts them to steer the embedding toward condition-related information.

The unconditional text embedding is obtained at a chosen layer by modifying the attention mask and positional encoding to mask the condition, costing only one additional multi-head self-attention computation.

Direct elimination (DE) subtracts the unconditional value vector from the conditional one, while projection-based elimination (PE) removes only the component of the conditional vector along the unconditional vector; a scaling factor alpha controls the post-intervention norm.

With LLaMA3-8B-Instruct, SCS is best in 6 of 7 cases across clustering, STS and triplet alignment datasets and best on average, with gains on all seven datasets, e.g. 6% and 8.2% on the two I.STSB metrics.
The simpler SCS-DE achieves better average performance than PE, indicating projection may be unnecessary.
SCS achieves performance comparable to supervised contrastive learning approaches, showing the potential of directly extracting conditional embeddings from LLMs.
SCS adds only a small runtime overhead per sample (e.g. about 70ms to 80ms in Table 2).
SCS gives consistent gains across LLaMA3-8B, LLaMA3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and their instruct versions, with larger gains on non-instruction-tuned models due to their weaker instruction following.
SCS improves results across six prompts, reduces variance across prompts, and improves across six conditions.
Most multimodal federated learning methods assume all clients deploy an identical architecture, but real clients are heterogeneous in hardware resources and multimodal data distributions.
Heterogeneous encoders map multimodal data into disparate embedding spaces, so prototypes of the same class from different clients reside in incompatible feature spaces.
Direct server aggregation of misaligned prototypes pulls the global prototype toward class decision boundaries and can make performance fall below purely local training.
Logits reside in a shared semantic space across heterogeneous models because each dimension corresponds to a specific class, so logit prototypes need no extra alignment.
MFedPBA aggregates logit prototypes with weights proportional to inverse entropy (plus epsilon), giving lower-uncertainty clients higher weight to form a more reliable global logit prototype.

The server uses modality-specific encoders and a shared decoder to project feature prototypes of different modalities and dimensionalities into a unified space, trained with reconstruction, inter-modal contrastive and Gromov-Wasserstein alignment losses.
The Gromov-Wasserstein distance compares intra-space pairwise distance structures, so it needs no direct correspondence between feature dimensions and suits heterogeneous settings.

The intra-modal alignment loss computes entropy-regularized GW distance (Sinkhorn) between each modality's class-relation cost matrix and that of the global logit prototype, preserving topological consistency.

Clients distill the global feature prototypes (MSE alignment) and global logit prototypes (KL divergence) into local training together with cross-entropy, with total loss L_ce + lambda1 L_fea + lambda2 L_logit.
Under stated assumptions, each client's local model converges at a non-convex rate O(1/T).

MFedPBA achieves the best test accuracy on Caltech101, Reuters, NUS-WIDE and Youtube under M2, M1+ and M1 partitions, e.g. 49.04 vs 45.29 for the best baseline on Caltech101 M2 and 47.92 vs 45.53 on Youtube M2.
MFedPBA maintains superior performance with larger client numbers (e.g. Reuters K100: 57.83 vs 56.64 for the best baseline).
In several settings FedProto underperforms Local training, confirming that naive aggregation of misaligned prototypes causes knowledge contamination.
Removing any server-side module significantly lowers accuracy on Caltech101 M2, and removing the reconstruction loss causes the most severe drop through representation collapse in the latent space.
MFedPBA's bidirectional cost is K^2 C (M_k d_D + d_C), only a negligible increase over FedProto since the number of classes is far smaller than model parameter counts.

Artificial and biological networks are typically non-identifiable: structurally distinct parametrisations implement the same input-output mapping, e.g. through neuron permutation and ReLU scale symmetries in overparametrised networks.

Under a convex differentiable loss and a non-bottlenecked network, all local minima of a deep linear network are global and equivalent to single-layer linear regression, and the global solutions form a high-dimensional manifold.
The paper derives exact parametric equations (general linear solutions, GLS) for the full solution manifold of a two-layer linear network, without assuming data structure or a learning algorithm.

The manifold is partitioned into GLS, least-squares-norm-of-function solutions (LSS), minimal representation norm solutions (MRNS) and minimal weight norm solutions (MWNS), each progressively constraining the weights (MWNS most restrictive).
Hidden-layer representations can vary continuously along the solution manifold while the network output is unchanged, e.g. a GLS can be chosen so representations form the shape of an elephant.
GLS and LSS permit RSMs that depend on the specific choice of input weights (including irrelevant input directions), so they are task-agnostic, non-identifiable and non-comparable representations.
The RSM of MRNS is uniquely RSM=ONO^T and that of MWNS is uniquely X^T V S V^T X, both determined by training data and independent of input-weight choice; these are task-specific representations.

Linear predictivity (R2) between networks is governed predominantly by solution type rather than functional alignment, since task-agnostic higher-rank representations cannot be linearly predicted from lower-rank task-specific ones.

RSA correlations fluctuate unpredictably when task-agnostic solutions are involved, and RSA reliably reflects functional similarity only when constraints enforce unique RSMs; MWNS and MRNS differ from each other even within the same function.

Because representations can change without changing function, an optimal linear decoder trained on an initial representation degrades rapidly along a random walk on the manifold, so drift may be reparametrisation within a functionally equivalent subspace.

Since many synapse and representation configurations implement the same function regardless of solution type, the stability-plasticity dilemma need not hold at the network level and isolated synaptic or representational changes do not suffice to infer function.

Expected loss under i.i.d. input noise is exclusively minimised by LSS, which include MWNS as a subspace, so input-noise robustness does not constrain representations to be task-specific (Corollary 5.3).
The secondary (unseen-data) error is minimised by LSS plus a perturbation in unobserved null directions, so minimising secondary error permits task-agnostic solutions (Theorem 5.1).
Robustness to additive parameter noise selects solutions with task-specific representations, ensuring representational alignment (Theorem 5.4, Corollary 5.5).

In two-layer ReLU networks on MNIST, function-preserving transformations (permutation, scaling, nuisance, duplicate, input-null) expand minimal networks into non-minimal ones with task-agnostic RSMs; non-minimal ones degrade faster under parameter noise, input-null changes have no effect, and test error is not inflated at near-zero noise.
Logits-based UQ suffers from lexical sensitivity and overhead, sampling-based UQ is slow and costly, and numeric verbal confidence is unnatural compared with qualitative markers like 'likely'.

The UM-Lookup maps 115 distinct verbal uncertainty markers to numeric values, built from psychology and decision-science literature, debiased, and aggregated over judgments from more than 300 human annotators.
When a response contains several uncertainty markers, they are averaged into one score (humans average multiple verbal probability terms), giving q = mean(1 - UM-Lookup(u_i)).
The human-sourced lookup quantifier Q_VU-H achieves AUROC significantly above 0.5 in 7 of 8 model-dataset configurations; with GPT-4o on SciQ it beats PE and SE by 4.7% and 5.6% AUROC.

Q_VU-H is frequently outperformed by PE and can fail, e.g. AUROC falls below chance for GPT-4o on GSM8K (about 0.41), because a human score for a marker does not always match the LLM's internal uncertainty.
GPT-4o assigns 0.677 confidence to 'almost certain' (humans 0.92) and 0.355 to 'very likely' (humans 0.853), so human-derived tables do not transfer directly to LLMs.

VOCAL learns a numerical score per uncertainty marker by minimizing a binary cross-entropy loss between the aggregated marker uncertainty of a generation and its correctness, a convex problem under logistic loss.
Because rare markers have unstable learned values, VOCAL applies graph Laplacian regularization over a marker similarity graph so semantically similar markers get similar scores.
VOCAL consistently improves AUROC over Q_VU-H across models and datasets, e.g. raising GPT-4o on GSM8K from 0.41 to around 0.6.
VOCAL achieves the highest AUROC in 5 of 6 settings against single-sample baselines G-NLL and PPL; on GSM-Hard with DeepSeek-V3.1 it reaches 0.715 versus 0.520 (G-NLL) and 0.567 (PPL).
Using one response, VOCAL is competitive with multi-sample UQ baselines (best on SciQ with Qwen2.5-72B, AUROC 0.717), though multi-sample metrics sometimes surpass it on TriviaQA.
VOCAL has average vanilla ECE 0.1314, near the best baseline; with isotonic regression it reaches the best average ECE of 0.0281.
Increasing VOCAL training samples from 100 to 500 raises AUROC from about 0.52 to 0.60.
Training and testing VOCAL on different LLMs' SciQ responses yields AUROC of 0.60-0.72, indicating shared structure but model-specific differences.

Optimistic Optimization algorithms (HOO, SOO, SequOOL) assume only local smoothness around the maximizer but require a hierarchical partitioning of the search space, and their performance depends heavily on that partitioning.

The default axis-aligned rectangle partitioning has a number of cells growing as k^(dn), limiting it to low-dimensional spaces, and may fail to exploit low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional spaces.
The paper studies multi-index functions f(x)=g(Ax) with A an m x d matrix with orthonormal rows and m<d, whose variation lies in an m-dimensional subspace.
For a multi-index function on [-1,1]^d, some z* in R^m with ||z*||_inf at most alpha satisfies f(A^T z*)=f(x*), where alpha is chosen from the cube corners (Proposition 2.5).

An adaptive partitioning scheme partitions the m-dimensional projection of the domain using learned directions A-hat, and a direction selection strategy can choose which direction to split at each depth.

Algorithm 1 learns A-hat by fitting a single hidden-layer neural network to function evaluations at random locations and taking an SVD, with m chosen to explain a desired share (e.g. 95%) of variation.
Adaptive partitions can have better parameters than the default: for f=1-|x1+x2| with A=[1,1], rho_A=1/3 versus rho=1/sqrt(3) for the default scheme (Example 2.9).
A direction selection strategy that splits x1 twice as often as x2 yields a lower near-optimality dimension than the default equal-proportion splitting (Example 2.11).
The paper proposes a two-stage algorithm (learn the partition, then run SequOOL on it) and an interleaved algorithm (Algorithm 2) where learning and optimization alternate.
For multi-index functions, SequOOL on the learned partition with alpha-hat=sqrt(dm)/sqrt(1-dist^2(A,A-hat)) has lower regret than on the default partition, with regret ~O(n^(-beta/d)) (Theorem 4.8).

On Rastrigin, Sphere and Styblinski-Tang, the approach reaches zero regret with fewer samples than other methods, e.g. Rastrigin regret 4.22e-5 for SequOOL vs zero for the method, and zero regret on Styblinski-Tang with about 900 evaluations versus 2000 for RESOO.
Quantization scales alpha across all M layers of an LLM are jointly optimized to minimize perplexity as one 3M-dimensional black-box problem, instead of AWQ's 3M separate 1-D grid searches.

On OPT-1.3B, SequOOL with Algorithm 2 over 72 dimensions reaches WikiText-2 perplexity 16.68 versus 16.92 for AWQ grid search, narrowing the gap to the unquantized 14.47 from 2.45 to 2.21 (about 10% relative).
A widely held but unexamined intuition treats repeated contextual assertions as accumulating evidence, so that sufficient repetition of a candidate answer should always alter a model's prediction.

Under a controlled single-round setting where only repetition varies, LLM predictions behave heterogeneously: some flip immediately, some change only after substantial repetition, some saturate early, and some stay stable under unbounded repetition.

The analysis uses inputs of the form y||x||...||x||z, with a query prefix y, a loop template x repeated N times, and a suffix z, at a fixed suffix target position, isolating repetition from added evidence or multi-turn interaction.
With RoPE, attention logits are finite trigonometric polynomials in relative distance, hence uniformly bounded (Proposition 3.2).

For a decoder-only Transformer under the stated architecture assumptions, the final-layer target representation at every layer converges to a finite limit as N goes to infinity (Theorem 3.6), proved by layerwise induction.

Because representations converge to stable query-dependent limits, repeated assertions do not act as accumulating evidence and may fail to alter a prediction even under unbounded repetition, while in other cases a flip is inevitable.

The answer-shift g(ea,eb) projects the final representation onto the answer-embedding difference direction; its infinite-repetition limit is estimated from a single forward pass at large N via Monte Carlo estimates of the loop attention terms.

At N=1000 on OpenBookQA, MINTAKA and SimpleQA, a large fraction of layers (typically over 90% at tolerance 0.1) show negligible residual variation in attention and FFN answer-shift contributions across six LLMs.
KL divergence between next-token distributions at different repetition lengths plateaus as repetition grows, showing answer-level distribution stabilization.
The representation-level estimate of the limiting answer shift closely tracks the forward-computed output answer shift on OpenBookQA at N=1000 across models, with points concentrated on the diagonal.

The sign of the estimated shift predicts repetition-induced preference changes across Transfer, Correct and Mislead regimes at N=500/750/1000, with mean accuracy around 80-86% (mean F1 up to about 92% for Transfer).
The stability measure shows trends broadly consistent with prior evaluations on SYCON, Farm, BeHonest and SycoEval, apart from a few exceptions.
In vanilla LoRA, parameter updates are constrained to a fixed-rank low-dimensional subspace shared across all input contexts, causing interference among updates for different semantic contexts.
The same token (e.g. 'book') can take different semantic roles across tasks, yet vanilla LoRA reuses highly similar low-rank update directions because of its shared bases.

Input-aware LoRA variants (LoRA-MoE, HydraLoRA, TopLoRA) select low-rank directions per token independently, producing dispersed, uncoordinated updates within the same sentence or task and weak task-level consistency.

U-LoRA replaces LoRA's constant down-projection A with A(x)=G(x)⊙A, where an input-conditioned gate modulates the shared low-rank bases element-wise per token; G(x)≡1 recovers vanilla LoRA and the update stays within the rank-r subspace.

U-LoRA aggregates token features into a softmax-weighted sequence-level directional summary (causally masked in decoder-only models) and adds it to the token-level signal, coordinating utilization within a sentence.
U-LoRA calibrates the gate with a bias-corrected exponential moving average of batch-mean sequence summaries, reducing batch-to-batch gate noise; it is training-time only and frozen at inference.
On Gemma-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-14B, U-LoRA achieves the best average accuracy on the math reasoning benchmark, e.g. 76.02% (r=8) on LLaMA-3-8B vs 71.67% for LoRA r=32.
On GLUE, U-LoRA gets the best average: 84.88%/85.00% (r=8/16) on RoBERTa-Base and 88.13%/88.29% on RoBERTa-Large, above TopLoRA r=16 (84.48%) and LoRA r=32 (83.60%) on Base.

Increasing LoRA rank from 16 to 32 gives only marginal gains (82.82 to 83.60 on RoBERTa-Base), while U-LoRA at r=8 matches higher-rank LoRA, so improvements stem from better use of a fixed rank budget.
Ablation on Qwen3-8B shows removing TOK, SEQ or EMA lowers average accuracy from 83.97 to 78.95, 79.16 and 79.66 respectively, and removing all three gives 78.52, equal to LoRA.
U-LoRA outperforms LoRA at every tested rank in {2,4,8,16,32} and across target-module sets from Q to QKVOGUD on Qwen3-8B.
PCA of RoBERTa-Large updates shows U-LoRA forms the most compact, well-structured task clusters in deeper layers, while TopLoRA updates are scattered without clear clustering.

Most token-pruning strategies (vision-centric and text-guided) raise average ASR over the unpruned LLaVA-1.5-7B (54.01%), e.g. TRIM 62.33%, FitPrune 63.14%, SparseVLM 62.73%, with text-guided pruning the worst.

As pruning ratio rises from 0% to 80%, ASR rises substantially while utility stays stable, and random pruning keeps ASR stable (52.73%), so safety loss stems from biased token selection rather than token reduction.
Query-based compression (LLaVA-Mini, LLaVA-MQT) reduces ASR (LLaVA-Mini 31.98% vs 54.01% baseline) even at 99.3-99.8% compression, so safety need not trade off against acceleration.

Pruning removes background tokens that act as a benign semantic buffer, forcing attention to collapse onto a few retained foreground tokens carrying malicious semantics, which then dominate generation under jailbreak prompts.
TRIM concentrates attention on a few foreground tokens whereas LLaVA-Mini keeps attention balanced across the whole image.

Sharpening TRIM's image-token attention by lowering temperature from 1.9 to 1.0 reduces attention entropy from 2.8 to 2.3 and raises ASR from 58% to 65% while SQA accuracy stays stable, linking attention collapse to vulnerability.

With malicious energy S and safety buffer energy N, density rho = S/(S+N); pruning drives N toward 0 so rho approaches 1 even if S is unchanged, while random pruning keeps E[rho] approximately unchanged.
Safety-Aware Pruning is training-free and inference-time with three steps: Malicious Anchor Identification, Benign Token Restoration and Attention Reallocation.
Malicious anchors are the top-m retained visual tokens ranked by MSA score, the product of text-to-visual attention and cosine deviation from a precomputed safety-aligned semantic vector.
BTR uniformly samples k pruned background tokens and swaps them for the k lowest-importance retained tokens, keeping sequence length unchanged.
AR scales malicious-anchor attention by (1 - lambda) and redistributes the removed mass uniformly to the restored benign tokens, requiring no softmax recomputation.
Across five pruning methods SAP reduces average ASR by 18.8-27.6% (relative), e.g. PruMerge 61.88 to 44.78, with utility changes within about 2%.
On TRIM, BTR alone gives modest ASR gains (MM-Safety 65.87 to 63.89), AR alone lowers it to 53.57 but cuts MMBench from 66.92 to 63.23, and combining both gives 52.78 with MMBench 67.27.
SAP adds negligible cost over TRIM: latency 57.19 ms vs 55.90 ms, memory 14.53 GB, identical 2.22T FLOPs, versus 94.29 ms for the original model.
With TRIM+SAP, attention entropy is restored toward the original model's pattern, mitigating attention collapse.
Applying MAI, BTR and AR to textual tokens (SAP-dagger) reduces FasterVLM MM-Safety ASR by 62% (72.02 to 10.32), showing the principle is modality-agnostic.
Prior work analysing MoE models has struggled to recover clear, interpretable patterns of expert specialisation, e.g. Mixtral shows no obvious topic-based expert assignment.

Real-world data contains far more fine-grained categories (micro-domains) than an MoE layer has experts (typically 8 to 128), so by the Pigeonhole Principle multiple micro-domains must be routed to the same expert.

The Domain Specialisation Hypothesis predicts an expert covers semantically similar micro-domains explainable by a single concept, while the Superposed Specialisation Hypothesis predicts experts cover semantically disjoint micro-domains that can only be explained by multiple concepts.

Following superposition theory, rarely co-activated, dissimilar domains interfere little when sharing an expert, so the router is incentivised to co-locate dissimilar domains, letting an expert perform computation in superposition.
