With a load-balancing loss and small batches containing few macro-domains, the router is pushed to spread tokens of one macro-domain across experts, encouraging routing of dissimilar inputs to the same expert, contrary to the DSH.

SAE latents predict expert selection far more accurately than token co-occurrence statistics or sparse linear probes, reaching macro-F1 0.73 for routing prediction on gpt-oss-20b, and serve as feature-level proxies for micro-domains.

Clustering the explanations of each expert's top-20 predictive SAE latents gives mean 10.8 clusters on OLMoE-1B-7B (layer 15) and 11.3 on gpt-oss-20b (layer 20), far above the DSH prediction of 1 but below random assignment (about 16.6).

Because expert-predictive latents fall in many distinct clusters, routing is explained only by multiple semantically disjoint micro-domains, supporting the SSH over the DSH, though experts retain some thematic coherence.

RouterInterp selects the top-45 SAE features per expert by approximated ablation effect, collects contexts where each feature and the expert are active (routed vs non-routed), and prompts an LLM explainer to synthesise a single prose explanation merging overlapping patterns.

Explanations are scored by an LLM scorer predicting whether held-out windows (15 positive, 85 negative per expert) contain tokens routed to the expert, reported as F1, with human-LLM agreement comparable to human-human agreement.

RouterInterp reaches mean F1 0.492 on gpt-oss-20b and 0.602 on OLMoE-1B-7B versus 0.383 and 0.305 for Expert Impact AutoInterp and 0.299 and 0.342 for Unigram Lookup, winning at every layer (about 65% over Unigram Lookup on gpt-oss-20b).

Verbalising token statistics only modestly helps (0.35 to 0.42) and full activating windows give 0.417; bigram explanations are narrow (P 0.39/R 0.59) and window explanations broad (P 0.30/R 0.81), while grouping evidence by SAE feature improves both (P 0.47/R 0.64).
Layer 16 of gpt-oss-20b has the worst SAE reconstruction (FVU 0.19-0.23) and weakest routing prediction, and RouterInterp performance correlates with SAE reconstruction quality across layers.
Existing Image-to-CAD and Point Cloud-to-CAD pipelines use renderings, photos or 3D scans as input, which presuppose the target CAD model already exists in the physical or virtual domain.
In early conceptual design CAD models do not exist and design intent is unstructured and incomplete, a generative demand that reconstruction pipelines do not address.

Mapping hand-drawn sketches and text to CAD code faces asymmetric alignment between sketches and text, logical consistency (minor deviations cause compile failures or geometric distortion), and sparse feedback where cross-entropy fails to capture geometric fidelity.
No publicly available dataset jointly contains CadQuery code, hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions.

HiCAD restructures DeepCAD, using CAD-Recode CadQuery code, synthetic hand-drawn style sketches, partial and complete text generated with Qwen3-VL-32B from code, render and geometric parameters, and removes duplicates with DINOv3 sketch similarity above 0.99.
Four tasks cover unimodal to multimodal intent and low to high information density: sketch-to-CAD, complete-text-to-CAD, sketch plus partial text, and sketch plus complete text.

Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment fine-tunes a pre-trained VLM (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct) with cross-entropy on interleaved data from the four tasks, mitigating single-task overfitting and promoting cross-modal alignment and positive transfer.
Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning initializes from the CMTA model and optimizes a spatial-aware reward jointly for geometric and topological consistency with GSPO, across multiple tasks.

HiCAD outperforms general-purpose VLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5, Claude-3.7, Qwen-VL-Max) and CAD-specific models (CAD-Coder, Cadrille) across all four tasks, with performance improving as inputs go from single to multiple modalities.
Replacing independent single-task SFT with CMTA improves all tasks, e.g. IoU on sketch plus partial text rises from 66.61% to 72.39%.
Adding SARL reduces invalid rate (IR) to about 0.2%-0.4% across tasks while IoU continues to increase (e.g. sketch-only IoU 66.87% to 69.09%).
Applying SARL jointly across tasks substantially outperforms single-task SARL on all metrics.
On 100 real human-drawn sketches, general-purpose VLMs achieve IoU below 10%, showing poor ability to handle real sketches, which motivates the robustness comparison.
Hu et al. (2025) show that when at least one agent produces a correct seed, debate acts as Bayesian posterior updating that amplifies correctness and can outperform majority vote.
Choi et al. (2025) show that under symmetric information flow, Dirichlet belief updates form a martingale with zero expected improvement, so majority voting can dominate.

The two theories are compatible: debate is corrective when asymmetric signals such as a correct seed exist and neutral when agents are symmetric with unconstrained information flow, so the question is when and how to invoke debate.
Existing frameworks apply debate uniformly across instances, conflating corrective and neutral regimes and incurring computational overhead where expected contribution is minimal.
LASE uses a designated leader that synthesizes auxiliary critiques from supporters through a directed 1:1 star topology, forcing the system into the corrective regime with positive expected drift.
LASE invokes interaction only when the leader's initial response is uncertain (U=1), judged from min logprob and max entropy signals, stopping early when U=0.
On MATH-500 (2,000 samples), accuracy is 85.5% for high-confidence generations (min logprob at least 0.99) versus 50.9% below 0.50, and falls to 30.4% when entropy exceeds 1.0.
Under the seed-conditional assumptions, LASE accuracy is at least leader-only accuracy plus P(U=1)*rho*delta (Theorem 3.7).
LASE expected cost equals leader cost plus P(U=1) times one peer interaction, which is strictly below static debate cost whenever P(U=1)<1.
A leader-centric 1:1 scheme grows as O(T) cross-agent context inclusions versus Theta(T n^2) for all-to-all debate, an Omega(n^2) reduction.
LASE strictly improves expected cost over static debate while keeping positive expected accuracy gain over leader-only inference (Corollary 3.9).
On Gemini-2.0-Flash and GPT-4.1-mini, LASE outperforms majority voting and multi-agent debate, e.g. 65.2% on GPQA-Diamond versus MV 62.7% and MAD 62.1%, and 87.2% on MATH-500.
LASE cuts average token usage by over 10x versus MAD, e.g. 0.4k versus 5.6k on GSM-Symbolic (14x) and 1.1k versus MAD 11.8k and MV 5.2k on MATH-500.
Running LASE five times in parallel with majority voting adds +0.8% over single-path LASE, uses tokens comparable to MV with N=7, and significantly outperforms MV.
Large reasoning models apply long explicit <think> reasoning uniformly regardless of query complexity, wasting compute and latency on trivial questions.

Prior approaches to learning when to reason suffer from training inefficiency (long-trajectory GRPO has prohibitive VRAM and time cost), data curation difficulty, and an initialization gap from training from scratch.
A model-specific difficulty proxy is obtained by contrasting mode-conditioned accuracy (e.g. Pass@k) of SHORT (<think>\n\n</think>) versus LONG reasoning mode on the same query.
LONG-mode generation length is heavy-tailed, with a small fraction of queries triggering disproportionately long traces, so routing directly translates into cost control.
Larger tau routes more queries to LONG, and intermediate thresholds preserve overall accuracy while reducing LONG usage (Table 1, Fig 3).
Offline synthesis produces paired reasoning and non-reasoning responses via forced chat templates, and SFT on self-generated correct samples teaches mode-following at the template level.

RPO restricts gradient updates to the single initial branching token (T=1) with group-normalized per-mode advantages and KL regularization to the post-SFT reference, treating the rest of the rollout as environment output.
Since backprop activation memory scales with the number of updated tokens, setting T=1 removes the linear dependence on CoT length, cutting peak VRAM for long-context GRPO (Table 2).
With matched accounting on an 8B model, RPO reduces total training compute to about 0.02x that of AdaptThink (Table 5).

On larger and mid-scale backbones RPO reduces Think% with modest accuracy change, e.g. Qwen3-8B Avg Think% 57.3% to 44.8% with Pass@1 63.8% to 62.0% (RAR 0.90 to 0.72), and Exaone4-1.2B Think% 43.4% to 23.6% (RAR 0.85 to 0.49).
SFT alone strongly reduces Think% and tokens, and RPO then refines the root decision to match query difficulty, with direction configuration-dependent.

On R1-1.5B RPO routes 20.5% to LONG with average accuracy 51.3 (RAR 0.96); AdaptThink reaches Avg P@1 56.5 (RAR 0.74) at a far larger training budget, so the two are points on a budget-accuracy frontier.
Intermediate RPO checkpoints give multiple feasible Think%/Pass@1 operating points, so a checkpoint can be chosen to satisfy a compute budget, but the frontier depends on the RL prompt set.

Operator learning seeks the unknown ground-truth operator G between separable Banach function spaces A and U from N input-output function pairs, e.g. mapping a PDE initial condition to its solution at a later time.
A neural operator is a composition of a lifting operator P, T operator layers L_t (each involving a linear operator K_t, bias b_t and a pointwise activation), and a projection operator Q.

Each operator layer can be defined as the minimizer of a Bregman-regularized optimization problem over function spaces, so the activation operator is implicitly defined as a Bregman proximity operator.

When the Bregman distance is Euclidean and Psi_t is built from a strongly convex Legendre function psi, the layer reduces to the gradient of the conjugate, nabla Psi*_t(M_t v + K_t v + b_t), recovering a broad class of classical neural operator layers (Proposition 3.4).

For a general p-uniformly convex Legendre psi (not the squared norm) and g_t=0, the layer takes a Bregman form that includes the inverse activation operator, defining a new family of Bregman neural operators (Proposition 3.5).

Specializing to Fourier layers with convolutional kernels on the torus gives the Bregman Fourier neural operator, whose update has the form v_{t+1}=sigma(sigma^{-1}(v_t)+K_t v_t) with the linear operator outside the activation.

For sigmoidal-type homeomorphic activations, Bregman neural operators are universal approximators of continuous operators on compact sets: for any epsilon there is N_theta with sup error at most epsilon (Theorem 4.1).
On 2D Navier-Stokes (nu=1e-4), BFNO achieves lower error for every depth T; FNO degrades from T=8 and ResFNO from T=16, while F-FNO improves until T=16 and BFNO until T=64.

With cross-validated depth T in {4,8,16,32}, BFNO is consistently superior or comparable to FNO, ResFNO and F-FNO, with notable gains on 1D Burgers and 2D Navier-Stokes (nu=1e-4); 2D Darcy is the exception.

Under z_t=sigma^{-1}(v_t), BFNO is a discretization of dz/dt=K(t)sigma(z), whereas residual architectures discretize dv/dt=sigma(K(t)v); placing the linear operator outside the activation mitigates vanishing gradients differently.

BFNO's learned weights are sharply peaked at 0 (Laplace-like) while FNO, ResFNO and F-FNO are Gaussian-like, suggesting implicit regularization toward identity and mitigation of vanishing/exploding gradients.
